reads.title: Weekend Update #203: A Week Which Demonstrated Why Trump Is So Helpful To Russia
reads.subtitle: Operation Vivaldi; Russia Batters Ukraine At Range; Trump, Diesel And Ukrainian Energy Strikes.
reads.body:
Hi All,
This was a week which crystallized a number of things. When you add them all together, however, the key thing is that it demonstrated just how important the USA has become, through the Trump administration, in aiding the Russian war effort. This might have been hidden in all the distracting stardust being thrown in the air about the Graham Tariff Bill, or the recently announced (extremely weird) possible sale of some motley air defense capabilities to Ukraine (arrival uncertain and unknown). However, behind the stardust which the press seems too out of its depth to properly interrogate the reality is that the war has entered into a fascinating contrast.
Phillips’s Newsletter is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

On the land, where the Ukrainians were less reliant on the USA, it is the Ukrainians who are showing the initiative and dealing some substantial blows to Russian military strength. If what we are hearing about Operation Vivaldi is only partially true, the Ukrainians are continuing to advance in the combined operations of infantry and UAVs.

-
- Are Ukrainian Initiatives Paying Real Dividends Now?
In the ranged war, relying on Ukrainian sources, the Ukrainians are also showing some important strengths—when they concentrate on the right targets. However it is in their ranged campaign against the Ukrainians, aided enormously by the USA starving Ukraine of air defense (a great example of why relying on the weapons of another power is always so dangerous) that the Russians are being their most effective—and almost certainly will continue to be so for the upcoming winter.
Add it up, and what we see is that Russia’s area of initiative in the war has been enormously abetted by the USA and Donald Trump.
Share

Operation Vivaldi: Ukrainian Initiative On The Front Line
For weeks now there have been unconfirmed reports of an ongoing Ukrainian operation to push Russian forces back from outside of Lyman and, possibly, back into Luhansk. I’ve referred to this a few times, including in last weekend’s update. However, without formal Ukrainian confirmation, I did not want to say too much about it. At that point, we had some more general statements from Zelensky about Ukraine taking the initiative in the land war, but nothing specific.
This week, something changed and the Ukrainians started speaking specifically about their operation and even gave it a code name—Operation Vivaldi.
Vivaldi is being conducted, it seems, primarily by the 3rd Army Corps commanded by  Gen Andrii Biletskyi. Biletskyi confirmed this publicly on Sept. 15, saying the corps had launched Vivaldi under conditions of "maximum information silence." The name refers somewhat cheekily to Antonio Vivaldi’s The Four Seasons (shout out to Baroque music). That is because the Ukrainians are saying the operation has four stages—or “seasons” and we are only now in the first stage. Biletskyi also asked the public not to "give away the spoilers" because the operation still requires silence.
There was this excellent story in The Kyiv Independent, which quoted Biletskyi and which provides a good overview of what we know and, crucially, what we do not know about Vivaldi.
Since then there has been more information coming out from Ukrainian sources. Yesterday (September 19) there were some official statements released by the Chief of Staff and Deputy Commander of the Third Army Corps, Petro Horbatenko. You can read much of what he said in this report.
Horbatenko also described an ongoing operation making substantial progress.
“We will continue to make progress in a week. Accordingly, in the near future we will inform you about new details regarding the operation and new results regarding its success….We continue to move. What was announced is one figure, it will increase over time. New data on successes and liberated settlements will come, we just can't reveal and talk about everything yet. The enemy on this section is broken, disorganized. He is trying to transfer special forces units there to close the breakthrough, simply grinding them into "meat", without achieving any success,”
Horbatenko also confirmed that the Ukrainians are still in stage 1 of the four stages of Vivaldi. He, and others, have also spoken about 75 sq kms being liberated.
These latest reports also provided some detailed news about the military units involved, which are units of the 60th separate mechanized brigade, the 125th separate heavy mechanized brigade, the battalion tactical group of the 3rd assault brigade, the 3rd separate reconnaissance and 25th separate anti-tank battalions of the corps, the 66th separate mechanized brigade, the 85th tactical group of the 8th SSO regiment, the Artan special unit of the GUR, and the 10th border detachment "Dozor".
That is important as it shows the preparation the Ukrainians have put into this. This is a range of specialized units, all of which have seemingly been specially prepared for the operation.
And, not to reinforce this point every week, but it shows how the Ukrainians have been adapting their forces for the land war for a long time. In the Kyiv Independent story there was this description of how the Ukrainians are advancing in the modern battlespace and not suffering massive casualties.
Instead, territory is taken by small groups of infantry and assault teams that focus on concealment, while being supported constantly by drones that scan the battlespace, strike enemy targets and shelters, and drop supplies and ammunition to the teams on the ground.
This kind of extremely close and precise action, only possible if highly trained and motivated troops and drone forces can operate extremely well together. This minimizes the amount of time the attacking forces need to spend in the open, allowing them to move swiftly from point to point, take cover, and still be supplied.
It’s exactly what General Havrylov laid out as the intention 9 months ago—when the western media, led by its deeply flawed analytical community, was still saying Ukraine needed to draft more of its young population and send them to the front.
Now, with the Ukrainians keeping a lid on the specifics of the advance. Information about how much territory they have retaken is coming more from Russian sources than Ukrainian. And we need to be very careful with this. Rybar, a Russian source, has the Ukrainians crossing over into Luhansk Oblast.

-
- Ukrainian data also supports the idea that something significant is going on. There has been a notable comments on Russian tactics and casualties as part of the Vivaldi discussion. Deputy Commander of the 3rd Corps, Maksym Zhorin, talked about the lack of adaptation in the Russian military:
“In addition to the advance itself, we can say that during this operation a fairly large number of enemy officers were also destroyed and a fairly significant number of enemy personnel were taken prisoner. Perhaps, in recent years, this is the largest replenishment of the exchange fund that came from the Ukrainian side,”
Horbatenko was even more pithy on Russian losses, saying: “Russian tactics generally do not change. These are just meaty assaults.”
And Ukrainian claims of Russian casualties over the past week (this is for all fronts, not just Vivaldi) have spiked. The Ukrainian General Staff claimed 11,090 Russian personnel losses in the seven daily reports from 14 to 20 September 2026, an average of about 1,584 a day. Here is a breakdown.

-
- This is a crushing casualty rate, btw. If it were maintained for a month (30 days) it would be equal to 47,529. For 31 days we are talking over 49,000.
We must obviously be careful about not over-reacting to this. I dislike it intensely when people talk about a Russian “collapse” which makes it seem like the Ukrainians can start making swift advances. That still seems very unlikely in this battle space. Even large gaps in the line can be closed with drone forces and humans cannot survive for very long out in the open. So please rein such talk in.
However, the reality of this summer’s fighting seems to be this. Ukraine is demonstrating the capacity to take the initiative with new and better ways of fighting, which keep Ukrainian casualties down and ratchet Russian ones up. And the best thing about it is that the USA cannot help the Russians that much at this point—which is a major contrast to the next story.
Share

Russia Batters Ukraine At Range
The last week was actually a lighter week than the one before when it came to Russian ranged attacks on Ukraine. They launched attacks every night, but with a smaller number of systems than the seven days previously. Here is a table of the number of units attacking—mostly drones (which means Geran/Shaheds) from Sept 14-19. We do not have last night’s figures yet.

-
- This contrasts with the week before, when in one night alone there was a Russian attack with 453 drones.
The reality of the ranged war, even with these reduced attacks, remains the same however. Ukraine can do little to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. The attack on 17 September, for instance, the only example of the Russians making a large ballistic missile assault last week, saw the Ukrainians claiming that they could not intercept one of them. The Ukrainian Air Force listed only Shahed/Gerans and Banderols as being neutralized that night.
Note: Banderols are cruise missiles, not ballistic missiles.
And even with the reduced weight of attack, the Ukrainians were hit hard this week. The night of the ballistic missile attack saw Kyiv targeted, and possibly water infrastructure hit.
Indeed, this slower week could be a sign of the Russians stocking up for larger attacks in the fall and winter. They have a track record of doing that.
This is the reality. Ukraine, because of the US depriving it of Patriots. Even in the announcement yesterday that the US might be selling some air defense capability to Europe to pass on to Ukraine, there was no mention of Patriots. What was announced was some “possible” sale of deficient systems. Indeed, the press did not even know how to report what happened—as in this CBS report.
In a congressional notification, the State Department said that it made “a determination approving a possible Foreign Military Sale to the Government of Ukraine” for buying air defense development upgrades and related equipment and services.
According to the statement, the Ukrainian government requested to buy S-300 Clone missiles, GAM-67 missiles, Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, as well as various launchers, counter-drone radars, trailers and spare parts.
My guess is that this is a political stunt by the Trump administration to look like it is doing something, when it is not. It will make no difference this winter.
And there we have it. Confirmation that, even on a relatively less damaging week, the big advantage that the Russians have is the one provided by the USA—which is doing nothing to help Ukraine in this vital area, and indeed is stringing the Ukrainians along and leaving them exposed.
Without this help, Putin and the Russians would be deprived of the strongest military card that they can play.
Share

## Trump, Diesel And Ukrainian Energy Strikes
Another area where the Ukrainians confirmed that they can be effective when not impeded in the USA, is their ongoing campaign against Russian fuel production. We have confirmation of that this week because Donald Trump came out and pleaded with the Ukrainians to do Putin a favor and stop attacking Russian refineries.
Things were so bad, that Trump begged once and lied twice—before the Ukrainians made it clear exactly what their position is. It was a fascinating “exchange” that started last Sunday (13 September). Then Trump said this to the press:
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia…We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting, that’s hurting the world.”
Even Trump has to know that it is his war with Iran that has so distorted the world oil market and done most of the work causing the steep rise in world diesel prices (which are pretty remarkable). One study is that the Iran War has caused three times the reduction in world diesel supplies as that caused by the Ukrainian campaign against Russian oil.
However, Trump decided to blame the Ukrainians and help Putin when discussing the issue publicly. And this was not all. On September 14, Trump doubled-down on his claim that the rise in diesel prices was Ukraine’s fault but, miraculously, claimed that he had gotten the Ukrainians and the Russians to agree to stop all energy attacks. He tweeted:
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!…The World's Diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia/Ukraine War, not Iran.”
It is still shocking how the President of the USA can just make up nonsense, spew it out, and some people will believe him.
We could see that this latest announcement was complete and total nonsense because on the subsequent days, both the Ukrainians and Russians went out and openly attacked energy targets. Overnight on 14–15 September, the Ukrainians hit the Syzran refinery and on Thursday 17 September a Ukrainian drone attack damaged an oil refinery at Yaroslavl (both refineries are still reportedly out of action).

-
- The Yaroslavl Refinery (Northeast Of Moscow) Is HitZelensky even openly contradicted Trump, in denying any deal had been reached. He said Ukraine might consider a deal, but as of now “Russia hasn’t stopped striking our energy sector… And our responses to them for this are tangible.”
It was a revealing exchange. As always for Trump, Ukraine is the baddies and Russia is to be protected. That will never change.
The more interesting thing is the confirmation of the seriousness of the Ukrainian campaign on Russian oil production. It is why this must be the key target of the Ukrainian ranged campaign. If the Ukrainians have no ability to defend themselves against Russian ballistic missiles because of the USA, the least they can do is not listen to the USA when the American president pleads with them to stop their most effective strategic campaign.
For now, they seem to have received the message.
Have a good rest of the weekend everyone.
Thanks for reading Phillips’s Newsletter! This post is public so feel free to share it.
Share

reads.title: Oil: The Middle East Oil Tap Is Closing for Good, and Markets Have Not Priced It. It CANNOT Be Defended.
reads.subtitle: Every defence I built assumed you could route around a failure. Against a 20,000 dollar drone that returns tomorrow, there is nothing left to route to. The only defence left is removing the intent.
reads.body:
I have spent the last 20+ years making things survivable. Security, resiliency and crisis management, supply chain security, primary and secondary risk. I find the single point of failure in a system, then I build the infrastructure from ground up and find the workaround and the redundancy that gets most of what sits in your home to you on time from your electricity, to your tooth paste to your cigarettes and your botox.
I have built and run those frameworks for some of the largest companies on the NYSE, for London Stock Exchange and the Toronto Stock Exchange, and the discipline has one article of faith at its core: whatever breaks, you can route around it. That has been my experience through war, conflict, coup d’eta or natural disasters.
Subscribe now
Share
This Existential War in the Middle East has forced me to a conclusion I NEVER EVER expected to say out loud, and never thought I would put in writing. The redundancy that holds up global critical national infrastructure, and the oil and gas grid at the centre of it, is now exposed to a long-term collapse that has no military answer. Nothing in the standard toolkit of deterring, deny, detect, delay, defend, demarcate, destroy, routes a country out of this against an enemy that is state-level, competent, determined, qualified, and can deliver a warhead or a drone for cheap.
The reason is simple, and it sits underneath every plan I have ever drawn. Redundancy ONLY protects you when the enemy cannot reach the fallback. You harden the primary node, and when it goes you drop to the secondary, and the system keeps breathing.
The moment an adversary can strike the primary, the secondary and the tertiary, cheaply, and repeat it tomorrow and the day after, the workaround is dead. There is nothing left to route to. The whole architecture of modern infrastructure defence assumes failures are isolated and fallbacks are safe, and a cheap drone breaks both assumptions at once.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
The threat, measured the way I was trained to measure it
A real threat needs three things present together: capability, intent, and opportunity. Take any one away and the threat is theoretical. What has changed in this war is that all three now sit in the same hands at the same time. Iran, the Ansarallah Houthis, and the Unity of Arenas structure behind them are capable, they are motivated, and the opportunity is the entire map. Thousands of aim points. Pumping stations, pipelines, compressor stations, terminals, most of them standing on open desert or buried ten to twenty metres under sand, none of them movable, all of them mapped.

-
- For twenty years, defending critical national infrastructure and multibillion dollar factories, or power-plants against terrorism was a solvable problem because the attacker was rarely capable, rarely persistent, and rarely cheap. Remove those limits and the problem inverts.
I cannot write a plan that protects an entire regional oil network, pump by pump, across thousands of kilometres, against a patient and qualified enemy who comes back the next morning at scale, every morning.... The honest answer is that no such plan exists, and I say that as someone whose profession is to produce workarounds provide soautlions and exactly that plan a client, a company, a CEO or the board expects from me.
The math that breaks the defence
Even if we remove the politics from the current situation the problem is still an arithmetic problem, and the arithmetic does not favour the defender. To hold the line of defence or your forward line of defence, the defender (You and me) has to succeed everywhere, every time, along the full length of the system.
The attacker (or the capable, determined and the on budget enemy) has to succeed JUST ONCE, with a drone that costs ten or twenty thousand dollars, and then do it again next week. No air-defence screen, no radar picket, no budget closes a gap shaped like that across a whole country. A single interceptor can cost more than the drone it kills by 100x or even 1000x more, and there are more targets than interceptors will ever exist to cover. The cost-exchange ratio runs the wrong way, permanently, and cost-exchange is what decides a war of attrition against infrastructure.
That forces a question larger than any one pipeline or field. Set aside this station or that terminal and ask the general version. Which piece of critical national infrastructure anywhere is safe against a cheap kamikaze drone in this world of cheap drones? On the current balance, the answer is ZERO, and that answer is not specific to the Gulf. It is the new baseline condition of the industrial world that everyone is keeping hush because we do not yet have any solutions.
The order of effects
The first-order effect is a forced, repeatable stoppage with no reliable fallback, which turns what used to be a temporary outage into a standing liability forever. A node is not down until it is repaired. It is down until the war that can reach it is over.
The second-order effect is financial, and it is the one the market has not priced. Once infrastructure cannot be defended by hardware, the risk premium on it stops being cyclical and becomes structural. Insurers, lenders and shippers reprice the whole asset class, capital backs away from exposed nodes, and the century-old logic of building redundancy as protection inverts, because a second and third node are now additional targets rather than additional safety. You cannot buy your way to resilience in a domain where every new asset is one more thing the enemy can hit for twenty thousand dollars.

reads.title: USA & Iran: Iran Now Fights on Martyrdom. America Fights on Ambition. Nobody Left to Say Wait.
reads.subtitle: The seasoned war planners on both sides are home, off the field. The men who replaced them read fear on one side and ambition on the other, and neither is inclined to say the word wait.
reads.body:
Every analysis of this war counts hardware. Missiles, interceptors, carrier groups, pipeline stations, tanker traffic. The count that decides how this ends is a different one that I keep track of: the number of experienced people still sitting in the two rooms where the decisions get made.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Over the past twelve months, both the IRGC and the Pentagon have emptied those Strategic and Operations rooms of the men who built the current doctrines, and the chairs have been refilled by people with the opposite instincts of the ones who left.
The decision to fire a weapon sits with a person, and that person either carries the memory of a war gone wrong or he does not. “Institutional memory” is the quiet stabilizer of every standoff. It is the reason the Cold War produced a hundred near-misses incidents for war but ZERO exchanges.

-
- Signal, Not Noise by AJ is now a Substack BESTSELLER in the category of #5 Rising in World PoliticsThe people in the room had internalized the cost, knew where the off-ramps were, and knew the difference between a Signal and an attack. If we have these institutional memories of both out of both rooms in the same year and you have not changed a single weapon on either side. You have changed the only thing that governs whether the weapons are used.
That is the variable the pace of this war has buried but I want you to keep note of it anyways. Everyone is tracking the arenas week to week, so no one is tracking the slower and more decisive shift underneath: the seasoned diplomats and old war planners on both sides are home now, seeing it play out on television, and the men who replaced them carry fear on one side and ambition on the other, with thin experience common to both.
Subscribe now
Share
What experience actually buys in a standoff
Under my thinking and my form of strategic realism, I treat “military deterrence” as a a language or as a “communication system” before it is a “firepower system”. Two adversaries avoid the WORST outcome by reading each other correctly, holding the line without stepping over it, and leaving each other a way down or an off-ramp that does not look like surrender.
Every part of that is a judgment call, and judgment is the product of qualified experience. The veteran commander knows that a “probing strike” is a message and not the opening of a general or a broader war. He knows which threats are theatre and which are real. He knows that pressure is meant to be survived, not necessarily answered in kind at every rung. He is, above all, the man in the room most willing to say the single most stabilizing word in any crisis, which is “wait”.
Remove him and you do not just lose the “institutional memory”, but you lose the interpreter of that Signal, to read what was meant by every action and counter action. The new man reads the same “probing strike” as the first blow of the war he was told his whole career was coming, and he answers it as such.
The escalation that follows is NOT caused by any new weapon or any new intent. It is caused by a misreading the experienced man would not have made. This is how most wars that nobody wanted begin, through the compounding of small misreadings by people who lack the memory to place them correctly.
Iran: a chair filled by martyrdom, and why that breaks the math
Iran’s loss is very specific. The assassination campaign of the past year has killed a disproportionate share of its military architects, the “cool-headed” planners who designed the layered doctrine Iran now fights with that I have written about and explained here over the past few months. The men who build a system understand its limits and its purpose. The men who inherit it after their mentors are killed tend to understand only that they are owed vengeance.
So the IRGC chair is now filled by commanders operating on something of anger, and martyrdom or perhaps even fear after a year of losses and public assassinations. They have said openly that they “seek victory, and that even in death, they remain victorious”.

To me, that single sentence is one of the most blinding sentences to have ever been translated in this war and it belongs in the “strategic column”, because it rewrites the entire payoff matrix that American power is built to exploit.
Every single coercion model the United States military and the “American Institutions” use assumes that their adversaries prefers living to dying.
Deterrence only works by raising the cost of an action until the price of pursuing it exceeds the value of the prize, and the ultimate price on the table is DEATH.
Against an actor or an adversary who scores HIS OWN DEATH as a “win”, that lever is completely disconnected from the machine.
You cannot threaten to impose a “cost your opponent has already priced” as a benefit. Truly, America has NEVER EVER fought an organized military that is truly a determined force that literally sought death on this scale, not in Iraq (the Iraqi forces surrendered in mass), not in Afghanistan at the command level (they were irregular militias and armies), and not in Vietnam.
The “seeking of martyrdom as a posture” removes the top step of the American escalation ladder, which means the usual method of buying restraint by threatening annihilation buys nothing at all here.
America: a chair filled by ambition, and a principal who is replaceable
The American loss runs in the opposite direction and produces the mirror-image danger. The seasoned combat Generals were pushed toward the exit out of the Pentagon forever, and the department is now led, at the political level, by a media personality elevated to the newly returned “Secretary of War” during the prelude to a possible regional or even a Global war.
Below him, the uniformed chairs are increasingly held by officers who are newer, hungry, and aware that this is the “first war” of real consequence in their command, the first with the size, the scale, and the potential to widen into a regional or even global war, and the one their entire lineage of mentors since 1979 has waited their whole careers to fight.
Ambition is a different failure mode than fear, and in some ways a worse one for stability. Fear makes a commander jumpy and prone to preemption, which is dangerous enough. Ambition gives him a “positive incentive” to act, to be THE man who broke Iran, to leave a legacy in the sand rather than a stalemate.
The restraining instinct that comes from having already earned your reputation is missing in someone still trying to make it. When the frightened and the ambitious face each other across a line, the frightened side over-reads threats and the ambitious side under-weights costs, and both are pushing the same direction.
Layered on top is a second-order instability that has no equivalent on the Iranian side: the American principal is himself replaceable in the middle of the crisis. A Secretary of War who can be fired or forced to resign, in an administration that runs on the logic of “the fall guy”, means the chain of command can turn over at the worst possible moment.
“Command continuity” is one of the few things a country in a standoff cannot afford to lose, and here it is NOT guaranteed. A crisis that arrives during a leadership turnover at the top of the war department is a crisis being managed by people still learning where the light switches are.
Subscribe now
Share

> SIGNAL, not noise is a reader supported platform, please consider becoming a paid subscriber if you find my work insightful or if it resonates with you.
Kindly share, like, and restack to help amplify my SIGNAL.
The order of effects

- The first-order effect is a higher baseline rate of miscalculation. Two rooms full of inexperienced readers of each other’s signals will misread more often, and each misread carries a live chance of a response the situation did not require. The probability of an accidental escalation is a function of WHO is interpreting the incidents, and both interpreters just got worse in the same year.

- The second-order effect is the loss of the brake. In a mature standoff, a tactical incident is contained because someone senior on each side has both the standing and the memory to absorb it and step back.

With the veterans gone, an incident that would once have been walked back instead runs up the ladder, because the men holding the rungs are motivated to climb rather than to stop. The system loses its shock absorber at the exact moment it needs it most.

reads.title: Support Gaza Journalist Huda Skaik's Journey to University of London
reads.subtitle: We have until Wednesday to help a Drop Site contributor raise $50,000
reads.body:
About a year and a half ago, we launched a fundraising campaign to help a Pakistani student, Areeba Fatima, cover expenses for the journalism program she’d been accepted into at Columbia University. This summer, she walked across the stage a graduate, and along the way, produced some terrific reporting for Drop Site, including this investigation into state violence in Kashmir or her recent story on fellow Columbia student Mahmoud Khalil’s new lawsuit against Columbia itself.
All of that was thanks to the generosity of Drop Site readers. Areeba’s success, and your generosity, emboldened us to try it again.
We now have a new opportunity we wanted to get in front of you. Huda Skaik is a young Palestinian journalist from Gaza and a Drop Site contributor. She has been accepted to the University of London, where she wants to sharpen her already formidable journalistic skills. Everything is approved, but for the final visa she needs to raise money to cover her funding gap—unfortunately by this coming Wednesday.
Drop Site is launching a campaign to raise the remaining $50,000 she needs by September 23 to support Huda’s journey from Gaza to the University of London.
Donate to support Huda
Full funding for Huda’s remaining two years of study and living costs has to be secured to meet the financial requirements of the UK visa process. And she’s on a hard deadline. Between the costs the scholarship doesn’t cover, accommodation and living expenses, her visa, and her evacuation and travel out of Gaza, the total comes to about $116,000. We’ve raised part of it, but we still need to raise the remaining $50,000 by Wednesday, September 23.
I think we can do it. If 2,000 people reading this email give $25 each, we’ll hit the target by the end of the afternoon. (Double-check my math, but I think that’s right.) 100% of the contributions will go toward her scholarship and we will of course cover the processing fees and all that on our end.)
If you’d like to make a larger gift to help close the gap, please reach out to majorgiving@dropsitenews.com or ryan@dropsitenews.com and we can let you know how to earmark it directly to Huda.

-
- Huda Skaik, 21, reporting from Gaza Alongside video reports and documentaries, Huda has published more than 70 articles at outlets around the world, including The Nation, Al Jazeera, and Middle East Eye.
Huda earned an “unconditional scholarship” offer to study journalism at the London university, entering directly into her second year. Her passport is ready. The university recognized both her academic record and the exceptional circumstances she’s working under.
That’s where you come in.
Currently displaced and living under extraordinarily difficult conditions, Huda remains committed to her work, sharing her vital perspective on the genocide in Gaza with the world.  We’re asking you to chip in whatever you can. $5, $20, $100—it all adds up. If enough of us pitch in, we can make this happen for Huda.
Donate to support Huda
“I am not asking for help simply to attend university. I am asking for the chance to continue telling stories, studying journalism, and using my work to make sure the experiences of people in Gaza are heard.” - Huda Skaik
Every dollar you give goes directly toward Huda’s evacuation, education, and living costs. If you can’t support directly, please consider sharing Huda’s fundraising page with others in your network.
Let’s do this together,
Ryan and the Drop Site team

reads.title: Saudi Aramco cuts oil shipments to Europe; Midterm voting begins; 16 killed in Pakistan mosque bombing
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: September 18, 2026
reads.body:
- Satellite image shows a large smoke plume rising from Aramco’s Jizan Bulk Plant storage tanks in Jazan City, Saudi Arabia, on September 8, 2026, after Ansarallah strikes. Photo by Gallo Images/Orbital Horizon/Copernicus Sentinel Data 2026.Friday, September 18, 2026 – Ansarallah leader claims U.S. is directly supporting Saudi Arabia, rejects accusations of striking Mecca. Fighting continues in Taiz as government forces claim 30 Ansarallah fighters killed. One killed, two wounded after Saudi intercepts drone over Taif. Over 112,000 displaced in Yemen. Saudi Aramco tells European customers they will receive no crude next month after pipeline attack. U.S. clears possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia. Italy prepares naval mission, calls for more ships in Red Sea. Iran strikes tanker in Hormuz. Massive government rally in Tehran. U.S. approves visas for Iranian president, foreign minister to attend UN General Assembly. South Korea rules out involvement in Hormuz “conflict,” says “minimum level” of action needed to protect shipping. FT: Iran shifts trade overland as U.S. blockade disrupts Gulf routes. Iran-U.S. war and Hormuz disruption cost Arab economies nearly $150 billion in the first month, UN agency says. Amnesty: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in 2022 protest crackdown. Two women shot by Israeli forces in central Gaza. Five children rescued from damaged home as Gaza government announces emergency plan for buildings at risk of collapse. Israeli settler attacks injure at least six Palestinians across the occupied West Bank. Israel adds 2,167 units to E1 settlement plan, bringing total to 3,401. “The whole case is related to her journalistic work”: Palestinian-American journalist detained by Israel at Hasharon. Qatar pledges 1.3 million liters of fuel for Gaza, enough for just 16 days of health sector needs. Two wounded as Israeli ceasefire violations continue in southern Lebanon. Early voting begins in midterm elections. Forty-six Senate Democrats demand Pentagon accounting of Iran war costs. White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE. Trump administration weighs at least 12 data center projects on federal public lands. Microsoft executive calls AI “largest theft of labor in human history.” Man who sprayed Rep. Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison. Pentagon reinstates mandatory testosterone screening for male service members over 30. Pakistan mosque bombing kills at least 16. Spanish police clear migrants from Ceuta. Russians vote in first parliamentary election since Ukraine invasion. Belarus continues military drills near NATO border. Chinese coast guard ship collides with Philippines government vessel near Palawan. Philippines school shooting leaves three dead in third deadly attack since June.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Ansarallah leader claims U.S. is directly supporting Saudi Arabia, rejects accusations of striking Mecca: Ansarallah leader Abdul-Malik al-Houthi claimed the U.S. is directly supporting Saudi military operations against Yemen, saying Washington has deployed “a joint force of 200 military experts” who are “managing the operations” from Saudi Arabia. He said Saudi forces are fighting “with aircraft obtained from America” and “bombs purchased from America,” and claimed Riyadh is seeking greater direct U.S. involvement in the war.

- On Sunday, Ansarallah told U.S. officials it would limit Red Sea attacks to Saudi ships and continue to uphold the U.S.-Ansarallah ceasefire during Oman-facilitated talks in Muscat, Reuters reported.

- Al-Houthi said that an end to the conflict requires Saudi Arabia to halt its attacks on Yemen and lift its blockade. “This is what we want, this is our issue: for Saudi Arabia to stop its aggression against us,” he said, adding that Riyadh must “end its blockade of our people” and stop depriving Yemenis of the country’s oil and gas resources.

- Al-Houthi also rejected Saudi allegations that Ansarallah had targeted Mecca, calling the accusation “a great lie” and accusing Riyadh of using it to encourage other countries to join the conflict. “Our lives, our souls, our wealth, and everything we possess are a sacrifice for Mecca and the Islamic holy sites,” he said.

- Fighting continues in Taiz as government forces claim 30 Ansarallah fighters killed: Yemeni forces, backed by Saudi airstrikes, are attempting to regain a foothold in the contested mountainous district of Al-Waziyah in western Taiz governorate, along the approaches to Yemen’s Red Sea coast and the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Saudi-backed forces claimed 30 Ansarallah fighters were killed and 60 wounded, figures that could not be independently verified. They also reported airstrikes on positions around Al-Dhikra Junction, Al-Damna and Al-Rahida.

- In nearby Mocha, a strategic Red Sea port captured by Ansarallah last week, Saudi-backed forces said airstrikes targeted Ansarallah movements, reinforcements, and supply routes as they seek to regain territory along the coast.

- One killed, two wounded after Saudi intercepts drone over Taif: one person was killed and two others wounded, one critically, by falling debris after an Ansarallah drone was intercepted and destroyed over Taif, Saudi Civil Defense said on Thursday. Several buildings and vehicles were also damaged.

- Over 112,000 displaced in Yemen: More than 112,000 people have been displaced in Yemen in the last two weeks amid renewed fighting between Ansarallah and Saudi-backed government forces, according to the UN migration agency. Nearly 3,000 others have fled by sea to Djibouti, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.

- “Our resources are very, very, very limited and our stocks will be depleted very soon,” Abdusattor Esoev, IOM’s Chief of Mission in Yemen, said in a statement.

- Saudi Aramco tells European customers they will receive no crude next month after pipeline attack: Saudi Aramco told at least two European refiners they will receive no Saudi crude under their regular contracts next month, with the decision applying to all European buyers, Bloomberg reported on Friday.

- The move follows last week’s drone attack that forced Saudi Arabia to shut its key East-West pipeline to the Red Sea. The pipeline is expected to partially restart within days but could take up to six weeks to return to full operation.

- U.S. clears possible $24.3 billion sale of 48 F-35s to Saudi Arabia: The State Department approved a possible Foreign Military Sale of 48 F-35 Lightning II fighter jets and related equipment to Saudi Arabia and notified Congress of the proposed deal.

- The Saudi Embassy in Washington welcomed the proposed sale, saying, in a post on X, it reflects the “strength and enduring nature of the Saudi-U.S. strategic partnership” and the continued advancement of defense cooperation between the two countries.

- Italy prepares naval mission, calls for more ships in Red Sea: Italy is preparing to deploy additional naval assets to the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab amid concerns over merchant shipping, Al-Monitor reported.

- Italy, which participates in Aspides, the European Union’s naval mission to protect commercial shipping in the Red Sea, said Thursday it was preparing its own naval mission rather than waiting for a broader EU response. “After what I said, something moved within Aspides, but we need more ships,” Defense Minister Guido Crosetto told Reuters, adding that “the only nations really supporting [security efforts] are Italy and Greece.”

- Rome has not specified how many ships it could send or detailed the measures under consideration.

## Iran

- Iran strikes tanker in Hormuz: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said it struck a Togo-flagged oil tanker in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, according to the state broadcaster. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations separately said a tanker had been hit by an unknown projectile in the strait, though it was unclear if it was referring to the same incident.

- Massive government rally in Tehran: Hundreds of thousands of Iranians rallied in Tehran on Friday in the biggest government-organized demonstration since the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. The state broadcaster estimated over 300,000 people in the demonstration, which featured drones and weaponry on parade.

- Tens of thousands of Iranians who have registered with volunteer units, or who wish to sign up, joined the rally. Tehran’s Republican Guard chief, Gen. Hassan Hassanzadeh, told the state broadcaster that over 600,000 had registered to participate in the training.

- U.S. approves visas for Iranian president, foreign minister to attend UN General Assembly: The Trump administration approved visas for Iran’s “core delegation,” including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to attend next week’s UN General Assembly meetings in New York.

- The decision comes more than six months into the U.S.-Iran war, with negotiations over reopening the Strait of Hormuz and returning to nuclear talks remaining stalled.

- On Wednesday, the Trump administration denied visas to a high-level Palestinian delegation, including Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas, for the same UN General Assembly gathering, marking the second consecutive year Palestinian officials have been denied entry. The State Department cited, among other reasons, the Palestinian Authority’s pursuit of legal action against Israel at the International Court of Justice and International Criminal Court.

- The U.S. is barring Iranian officials attending the UN General Assembly from purchasing luxury goods or obtaining wholesale club memberships. “On one side stands a brutal economic war, deliberately designed to inflict maximum pain and suffering on every Iranian citizen,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei wrote on X, criticizing the measure. “On the other stands the theatrical announcement of measures to stop Iranian officials from supposedly shopping at an American wholesale club.”

- South Korea rules out involvement in Hormuz “conflict,” says “minimum level” of action needed to protect shipping: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said Friday that Seoul will not deploy troops in a way that could involve the country in an overseas conflict, Yonhap reported.

- Lee said South Korea nevertheless needs to undertake a “minimum level of activities” to protect its citizens, vessels, and crude oil transportation routes. Seoul is reviewing ways to strengthen those measures, while its Cheonghae naval unit has expanded the scope of its activities in the region.

- Last week, a South Korean assessment team returned from the United Arab Emirates after reviewing security conditions in the region. U.S. President Donald Trump is pressing allies to contribute to securing freedom of navigation through the Strait.

- FT: Iran shifts trade overland as U.S. blockade disrupts Gulf routes: Iran is increasingly routing trade through its land borders, particularly Turkey, after the U.S. naval blockade and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz curtailed maritime trade, the Financial Times reports.

- Before the war, more than 80% of Iran’s roughly 180 million tons of annual trade moved by sea from its Gulf coast. Iran’s non-oil exports fell 28% and imports 26% in the five months ending August 22 compared with last year.

- Trade with Turkey rose 19% to $3.2 billion in the first half of the year, while imports through the Gürbulak-Bazargan land crossing surged 250% in the five months to August 12.

- But long border delays and limited infrastructure mean even doubling overland and Caspian trade cannot replace lost maritime trade, experts told the FT. Moving Iran-China trade overland rather than by sea could also add an estimated $18 billion a year in costs.

- Iran-U.S. war and Hormuz disruption cost Arab economies nearly $150 billion in the first month, UN agency says: The ongoing conflict and disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz caused losses equivalent to roughly 4% of Arab states’ combined GDP during the first month alone, according to the UN Economic and Social Commission for Western Asia (ESCWA).

- ESCWA Executive Secretary told a UN Security Council meeting on maritime security that the disruption is affecting far more than oil and gas, driving up freight and insurance costs, threatening food security, and weighing on investment across the region.

- Around 25% of global seaborne oil trade and 19% of LNG shipments have historically passed through Hormuz.

- U.S. sanctions on Iranian airlines threaten supply chain for essential medicines, researchers warn: The Trump administration’s latest sanctions on Iran’s aviation sector threaten the supply chain for essential medicines and medical supplies in Iran, Bourse & Bazaar Foundation researchers wrote.

- Over 60% of Iran’s medical imports arrive by air, making them roughly seven times more dependent on aviation than Iranian imports generally.

- Over 30% of medical imports through Tehran’s main airport are hormone-based medications, including insulin and cancer treatments, the report noted. Another 10% are vaccines and 6% blood products.

- U.S. offers up to $15 million for information on IRGC financial networks: The State Department’s Rewards for Justice program issued a new appeal for information about Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) alleged use of digital asset exchanges and other financial mechanisms to evade sanctions and access international financial systems. The reward offers up to $15 million for information leading to the disruption of the IRGC’s financial mechanisms.

- Amnesty: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in 2022 protest crackdown: A new report by Amnesty International has found that Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity during their suppression of the nationwide “Woman Life Freedom” uprising in 2022. The report, more than 1,000 pages long, details the use of “murder, torture, enforced disappearance, imprisonment, rape and persecution on political, gender, ethnic and religious grounds.” It also identifies 87 officials it says should be criminally investigated for crimes against humanity.

- “[Iranian authorities] waged a widespread and systematic attack against a civilian population demanding dignity, human rights and fundamental political change, pursuant to a state policy of using lethal force to obliterate dissent,” Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International’s Secretary General, said in a statement. “This report is being published at a time when people in Iran are also facing the devastating consequences of unlawful attacks by the USA and Israel. Amnesty International unequivocally opposes violations of international law by all parties and rejects any attempt to instrumentalize the suffering of victims of human rights violations in Iran to justify unlawful attacks that inflict further civilian harm.”

## Palestine

- Two women shot by Israeli forces in central Gaza:

- Two Palestinian women were wounded by Israeli gunfire toward residential homes and tents sheltering displaced Palestinians in the Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camps in Central Gaza on Friday, according to WAFA.

- Five children rescued from damaged home as Gaza government announces emergency plan for buildings at risk of collapse:

- Civil Defense crews rescued five children who became trapped on the second floor of their home after its staircase collapsed in the Sabra neighborhood, south of Gaza City. The families were evacuated and warned not to return to the house, which had been damaged by Israeli attacks and remains at risk of collapse.

- Two days ago, the collapse of another residential building in Gaza City killed 21 Palestinians, including 12 children and five women.

- The IDF responded to Drop Site on the collapse, saying “the IDF did not strike the building in question during the war.” The building, however, showed visible cracks and signs of damage from Israel’s assault on Gaza, which damaged 80% of structures across the Strip, including two-thirds that were destroyed, according to the UN.

- More than 2,000 damaged buildings across Gaza are at risk of collapse, according to Civil Defense. Gaza authorities and representatives from international, UN, and Arab organizations agreed Friday on an emergency plan to address hundreds of war-damaged buildings at risk of collapse across the Strip, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. The meeting called for the immediate entry of heavy machinery, specialized equipment, fuel, and oil, as well as the allocation of land for shelters for residents living in unsafe buildings.

- Israeli settler attacks injure at least six Palestinians across the occupied West Bank:

- Hebron: Armed Israeli settlers, protected by Israeli forces, attacked Palestinian farmers trying to reach their land in Wadi Al-Shannar, east of Halhul, on Friday. The settlers assaulted and detained several farmers, according to WAFA.

- Ramallah: Five Palestinians were injured after Israeli settlers threw stones at their vehicle near the entrance to Yabroud, east of Ramallah, causing the vehicle to overturn.

- Jericho: A Palestinian was injured when Israeli settlers attacked families in Khirbet Allan, north of Jericho in the Jordan Valley. The settlers attempted to steal sheep, attacked residents with stones, and damaged a Palestinian-owned vehicle.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli forces beat a Palestinian man outside Lions’ Gate, one of the entrances to Al-Aqsa Mosque.

- Israel adds 2,167 units to E1 settlement plan, bringing total to 3,401: Israel added a tender for 2,167 housing units to its E1 settlement expansion plan in the occupied West Bank, Reuters reported, on top of 1,234 units announced in August.

- The E1 project would cut the occupied West Bank off from East Jerusalem and disrupt territorial contiguity between its northern and southern areas. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich has said the plan would “bury” the idea of a Palestinian state.

- Bidding is scheduled to open October 25, two days before Israel’s parliamentary election.

- “The whole case is related to her journalistic work”: Palestinian-American journalist detained by Israel at Hasharon: Palestinian-American journalist and Drop Site contributor Naqaa Hamed is being held in Hasharon, a temporary detention facility in central Israel, and is expected to be transferred to Damon Prison, where most Palestinian female prisoners are held.

- Hamed’s lawyer told Drop Site she was accused of incitement against Israeli settlers and the army, communicating with the enemy, and cooperating with the enemy during a military court session on Thursday.

- Her lawyer argued that Hamed was a professional journalist and her arrest came solely because of a campaign targeting her by Israeli settlers. He told Drop Site “the whole case is related to her journalistic work.” The military court ruled to extend her detention by six days to complete their “investigation.” Mahajneh submitted an appeal.

- The Committee to Protect Journalists condemned Hamed’s detention, saying “Unsubstantiated espionage allegations must not be used to criminalize journalism, and the systemic harassment and intimidation targeting her work in the occupied West Bank must end.”

- Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen called for her immediate release, saying in a post on X, “Another American citizen wrongfully detained by the Israeli govt.”

- Report: Israel kills one, wounds 15 on Thursday, total ceasefire violations reach 4,931: Israel committed 19 ceasefire violations in Gaza on Thursday, killing one Palestinian and wounding 15 others, bringing the total documented violations since the ceasefire took effect to 4,931, according to a document shared by the Palestinian side with mediators and obtained by Drop Site News.

- Since the ceasefire took effect, 1,387 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks—including 297 children, 140 women, and 42 elderly people—and 4,784 wounded, nearly half of them children, women, or elderly.

- Only 35% of the agreed humanitarian and commercial aid has entered Gaza since the ceasefire began, according to the document, while overall movement of people through the crossing has reached just 39.1% of the agreed level.

- Qatar pledges 1.3 million liters of fuel for Gaza, enough for just 16 days of health sector needs: Qatar signed an agreement with the United Nations to provide Gaza with approximately 1.3 million liters of fuel, its Foreign Ministry announced on Thursday. The grant is intended to keep hospitals, medical centers, and other essential humanitarian infrastructure operating, amid severe shortages resulting from Israel’s restrictions despite the nominal ceasefire.

- The World Health Organization estimates that Gaza’s health sector needs about 80,000 liters daily. At that rate, Qatar’s 1.3 million-liter grant would cover only about 16 days of healthcare operations. If shared with water, sanitation and other humanitarian services—as Qatar says it will be—it will last considerably less.

- The announcement provides no delivery schedule.

- Trump’s “Board of Peace” to brief countries at UN on stalled Gaza reconstruction and governance plans: The U.S.-controlled Board of Peace will brief representatives from dozens of countries, the EU, and UN agencies on September 23, during the UN General Assembly, on its stalled plans to rebuild and govern Gaza, The Times of Israel reported.

- The meeting will cover negotiations over Hamas’s weapons and hear from the Palestinian technocratic committee (NCAG) about 71 projects for its first six months.

- None of the projects has a start date as the initiative remains frozen because Israel rejects the Board’s plan to decommission the weapons of all armed factions, despite Hamas accepting its terms on July 30.

## Lebanon

- Two wounded as Israeli ceasefire violations continue in southern Lebanon:

- Bint Jbeil: Two people were wounded in Israeli shelling in the Chaqra area on Friday, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported. Israeli artillery also targeted Wadi Nahle on the outskirts of Chaqra.

- Marjayoun: Israeli forces raided Deir Mimas and searched several homes. Israeli troops also threw six stun grenades around the position they had taken near the town’s inner entrance, as the Lebanese army deployed reinforcements nearby.

- Tyre (Sour): Israeli artillery shelling targeted the towns of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun on Friday morning, following intense shelling before and after midnight.

## U.S. News

- Early voting begins in midterm elections: In-person voting early voting for the midterm election began on Friday in a handful of states. More expansive early voting is scheduled to begin in the coming weeks.

- Earlier this week, the Supreme Court rejected President Donald Trump’s bid to restrict mail ballots.

- One tenth of all Americans this year is a resident of a different congressional district than in 2024, according to a report by Project Democracy, following an unprecedented flurry of redistricting in the House that has redrawn the congressional map.

- 46 Senate Democrats demand Pentagon accounting of Iran war costs: Forty-six members of the Senate Democratic caucus, led by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, sent a letter demanding Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth provide a full breakdown by Sept. 30 of costs incurred in the Iran war and details on the administration’s $67 billion supplemental funding request.

- The lawmakers accused the Pentagon of failing to provide “basic information,” despite its requests for tens of billions in additional funding.

- The letter, signed by every Democratic caucus member except Sen. John Fetterman, comes a day after the Congressional Budget Office put the war’s cost at $38 billion through its first five months and projected ongoing costs of $2 to 3 billion monthly.

- White House withdraws Lance Schroyer’s nomination to lead ICE: The White House withdrew its nomination of Lance Schroyer, a former Oklahoma Highway Patrol major and ally of DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Thursday, less than three months after President Donald Trump nominated him.

- The nomination’s rescission surprised officials in the Department, according to several DHS insiders cited by the Washington Post.

- Schroyer faced mounting resistance in the Senate, where Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul had not scheduled a confirmation hearing, and border czar Tom Homan had suggested the role should go to someone “who knows the job.” ICE has not had a Senate-confirmed director in over a decade.

- Trump administration weighs at least 12 data center projects on federal public lands: The Bureau of Land Management is reviewing proposals covering more than 17,600 acres across Arizona, Idaho, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, and Wyoming for data centers and related infrastructure, an unprecedented use of public land that local officials in several states told The Washington Sun they were unaware was under consideration.

- The largest proposal, a 10,200-acre project from nuclear startup Valar Atomics near Green River, Utah, would co-locate a data center with small nuclear reactors.

- Another case involves the Idaho-based firm Rhea Data, which has proposed a 4,000,000-square-foot data center near Boise powered partly by a new natural gas facility. Only one such project, on federal land in Nevada, has been approved so far. It remains on hold amid a legal challenge.

- Microsoft executive calls AI “largest theft of labor in human history”: Microsoft’s director of applied science called the training of large language models the “largest theft of labor in human history” and “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” the Washington Post reported, according to a document unsealed Thursday as part of a lawsuit filed by the New York Times against Microsoft and OpenAI. The unsealed legal brief quotes internal documents obtained via legal discovery.

-  Separately, Anthropic said yesterday in a blog post that its Claude chatbot “‘leads’ 26% of Anthropic’s AI R&D work,” and that “AI systems are increasingly being used to build the next version of themselves,” The Post reported.

- Man who sprayed Rep. Ilhan Omar with vinegar sentenced to 14 months in prison: Anthony Kazmierczak, 56, was sentenced Thursday to 14 months in prison and three years of supervised release, during which he cannot make contact with Rep. Ilhan Omar, who he assaulted with a water-and-apple-cider-vinegar spray during a Minneapolis town hall in January.

- U.S. District Judge Joan Ericksen noted that the attack “wasn’t a spur-of-the-moment act,” given that Kazmierczak had secured tickets weeks in advance. He also texted acquaintances before the attack indicating he planned to “do something” involving Omar.

- Kazmierczak, who has Parkinson’s disease and whose attorney argued that he had not taken his mental health medications prior to the attack, apologized to Omar in court on Thursday.

- Pentagon reinstates mandatory testosterone screening for male service members over 30: The Pentagon issued updated guidance Thursday requiring mandatory testosterone deficiency screening for male active-duty and reserve service members over 30, after temporarily rescinding earlier guidance this month. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in July the screening and testosterone replacement therapy initiative was an effort to keep troops “on the leading edge of lethality.”

- The screening will reportedly assess military personnel for symptoms including erectile dysfunction, reduced sexual desire, and diminished physical performance, and will also document risk factors like obesity and diabetes.

- A corresponding clinical guideline for female service members remains under review, the director of t

reads.title: THE ENERGY WINTER: IRAN, REFINING, AND THE COMMISSION'S OWN GOAL
reads.subtitle: Record-low gas, diesel shortages, shrinking refining: Europe's winter of crisis. Marco | Independent Analyst 18 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
Europe enters the winter of 2026 with gas storage at 15-year lows, diesel supplies approaching five-year lows, and a refining industry in structural decline. Three forces are converging: the war in Iran, the collapse of European refining capacity, and the political choices of the European Commission. This article examines all three.

## I. The Iran War: The Trigger
The war in Iran, which began in late February 2026, has disrupted the Strait of Hormuz—through which approximately one-fifth of the world’s oil and LNG flows.
The impact on Europe has been immediate:

- EU oil and gas import bill: +€6 billion since the war began

- European gas prices (TTF): +70% since the war started

- Brent crude: +50% since the war started

- Diesel prices at the pump (EU): Record €2.11 per litre in April 2026
Europe was particularly exposed because it had become dependent on Gulf refined products after cutting off Russian supplies. In 2025, the EU imported approximately 35% of its jet fuel and 20% of its diesel. The Gulf was the primary supplier, providing 56% of jet fuel imports and 34% of diesel imports.
When Hormuz was disrupted, those supply chains broke. European refineries pushed jet fuel production to maximum capacity, at the expense of diesel. But it wasn’t enough. By late August, jet fuel stocks were 6% below the five-year minimum.
The Iran war exposed a vulnerability that had been building for years. But it did not create it. It merely accelerated a crisis that was already underway.

## II. The Refining Crisis: The Structural Problem
Europe has enough crude. What it lacks is the industrial capacity to turn that crude into the fuels that heat homes, power trucks, and keep planes in the air.
Europe’s refining capacity has been declining since 2009:

- -20% capacity lost since 2009

- ~30 refineries closed across Europe, including 5 in Italy alone

- 9 million barrels/day projected capacity by 2035, down from 14 million at the start of the century
Europe’s Refining CapacityCurrent capacity~11 million b/dProjected 2035 capacity~9 million b/dDecline since 2009-20%Refineries closed~30 (5 in Italy)Diesel import dependence~20%Jet fuel import dependence~35%
Gianni Murano, president of Italy’s Unem, described the paradox: “While Europe reduces production capacity, other regions of the world are building new, ever-larger and more efficient refineries. Refining is not just about the future of fossil fuels, but above all about Europe’s ability to preserve a strategic industrial base during the energy transition.”
The consequence: Europe imports crude, ships it to refineries in the Middle East and Asia, and buys back the refined products at a premium. The refining margin—the “crack spread”—has become the most profitable part of the oil business, and Europe has largely given it away.
Murano added: “There was a conviction that from tomorrow it would be possible to move everyone by electric vehicle and that refineries could be done without. It didn’t work out that way.”

## III. The Commission’s Policy: The Political Choice
Here is the fact that official communications rarely mention: the decision to stop buying Russian gas was made in Brussels, not in Moscow.
On 26 January 2026, the 27 EU member states formally adopted the regulation on the gradual phase-out of Russian pipeline gas and LNG imports. The regulation was published in the Official Journal and entered into force the following day. The ban on LNG imports takes effect from the beginning of 2027; the ban on pipeline gas from autumn 2027.
This is not a Russian embargo. It is European legislation. The text was negotiated by the Council and the European Parliament, with an agreement reached on 3 December 2025. The von der Leyen Commission guided the entire process, presenting the roadmap on 6 May 2025 and pushing for rapid adoption.
The REPowerEU Regulation — Key FactsAdopted by the Council26 January 2026Entered into force27 January 2026LNG import banFrom beginning of 2027Pipeline gas banFrom autumn 2027Sanctions for non-complianceUp to €40 million or 3.5% of global turnover
Yet the Commission’s public narrative tells a different story.
On 1 July 2026, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stated that Russia “used energy as a weapon and cut off gas supplies to Europe”. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova responded: “Ursula is an excellent liar. Russia has never cut off gas for Europe. Any EU citizen can sue her for this lie and win.”
On 11 March 2026, von der Leyen declared that returning to Russian fossil fuels would be a “strategic mistake” that would make Europe “more dependent, more vulnerable and weaker.”
On 20 March 2026, she categorically ruled out buying Russian gas “even in the event of power outages in the EU.”
These statements confirm that the Commission made a political choice not to buy Russian gas, regardless of the consequences for prices and energy security. It was not Russia that closed the taps. It was Brussels that decided to stop buying.
The costs of this choice are now visible. On 27 August 2026, von der Leyen herself admitted that “energy prices in Europe are still 2-3 times higher than in the United States and China” and that “energy is now the main factor limiting our competitiveness and our independence.” She also revealed that dependence on imported fossil fuels has already cost over €50 billion more since the beginning of the Middle East crisis.

## IV. The Court of Auditors: “The Strategy Is Stalled”
On 9 September 2026, the European Court of Auditors published a special report that effectively demolished the Commission’s energy strategy. The auditors concluded that:

- The REPowerEU plan “still lacks effective governance tools to guide its implementation”

- EU funding has played “only a secondary role” in ending dependence on Russian oil and gas

- “Not enough investment has been induced” to accelerate the clean energy transition and strengthen cross-border connections

- Four years after its launch, “REPowerEU is stalled, despite several hundred billion euros made available”

- “Russian fossil fuels are still imported indirectly into the EU through third countries (e.g., Turkey, China or India)”
Mihails Kozlovs, the Court member responsible for the report, stated that the Commission’s claims about the plan’s effectiveness “contradict the statements of the Commission President, who instead boasted of its effectiveness by telling only part of the truth.”
In simple terms: the EU’s energy strategy has been a documented failure, according to the EU’s own audit institution. Not only has it cost hundreds of billions, it has not even achieved its stated goal of eliminating energy dependence on Russia.

## V. Gas Storage: 15-Year Lows
As of 9 September 2026, EU gas storage was 67.33% full—12.3 percentage points below the 79.63% recorded at the same date in 2025. The level is well below the five-year average of 84%.
EU Gas Storage — September 2026Storage level (9 Sept)67.33%Year-on-year change-12.3 percentage pointsFive-year average84%Germany54.98% (from 74.22%)Italy84.06% (from 89.68%)France74.69% (from 89.21%)
The reasons for the low storage levels are counterintuitive. During the summer, spot prices were higher than forward prices for winter. This eliminated the economic incentive for operators to inject gas into storage. Why buy gas at €60/MWh in July to sell it at €55/MWh in January?
Now, Europe faces the winter with thin inventories and rising prices:

- TTF gas price: ~€80/MWh, +150% year-on-year, the highest since January 2023

- EU winter gas bill: Projected at €117 billion, or 0.6% of GDP

- Inflation impact: Could push eurozone inflation toward 4%

- ECB response: Two additional rate hikes expected

## VI. What This Means for Citizens

## Italy: The Hardest Hit

- Household electricity price: €0.345/kWh (vs. G20 average of €0.163)

- September 2026 electricity bill estimate: €0.3193/kWh, up from €0.2875 a year earlier

- Gas price: €1.37 per cubic metre, up from €1.05 a year earlier

- Annual household cost increase: ~€877 for a typical family
Italy — Household Energy Costs (2026)Electricity (Sept 2025)€0.2875/kWhElectricity (Sept 2026)€0.3193/kWhGas (Sept 2025)€1.05/m³Gas (Sept 2026)€1.37/m³Annual increase (energy)€515Annual increase (fuel)€362Total annual increase€877

## Germany and the UK
German household electricity prices are €0.356/kWh, more than double the G20 average. UK prices are €0.324/kWh.

## VII. The Ukraine War: A Marginal Factor
The war in Ukraine has added a third layer of stress. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries have intensified, hitting targets as far as Omsk, 2,675 kilometres from the border.
Since March 2026, Russian refining capacity has fallen by approximately 1.3 million barrels per day—a quarter of the total. In August, capacity dropped to 4 million b/d against the usual 5.5 million.
Russia has responded by banning gasoline exports in April and diesel exports in July. For Europe, which historically imported 23% of its diesel from the former Soviet Union, the loss of approximately 850,000 barrels per day of Russian exports has been significant.
But here is the key point: the Ukraine war is marginal compared to the structural refining crisis and the Iran war. The real problem is not Russian refineries being hit. The real problem is that Europe no longer has its own refineries to compensate.

## VIII. Conclusion
Europe’s energy crisis is not a story about scarcity. It is a story about the destruction of industrial capacity—and the political decisions that made it worse.
Three factors are converging:

- The Iran war disrupted Gulf refined product supplies that Europe had become dependent on.

- The refining crisis has left Europe unable to process its own crude into the fuels it needs.

- The Commission’s political choices—the REPowerEU regulation adopted on 26 January 2026—severed energy ties with Russia without building adequate alternatives.
The wars in Iran and Ukraine have exposed this vulnerability, but they did not create it. They merely accelerated a decline that has been underway for two decades.
And the decision to sever energy ties with Russia was not a Russian action. It was a European one. The Commission’s claims that Russia “cut off” the gas are contradicted by the legislative record and by the statements of the Commission’s own auditors.
The cost is being borne by European households, who face record bills for electricity, gas, and fuel. A typical Italian family will pay approximately €877 more in 2026. German and British families face similar increases. And the worst may be yet to come.
Until Europe rebuilds its refining capacity and acknowledges the true cost of its political choices, it will continue to pay the price of its own deindustrialisation.
