reads.title: THE LOCOMOTIVE WAR
reads.subtitle: How Russia Is Strangling Ukraine's Railways Marco | Independent Analyst 17 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
On the morning of 13 September 2026, a Russian drone struck a train at Yahodyn station, less than two kilometres from the Polish border. The locomotive was hit directly. There were no casualties — passengers had been evacuated fifteen minutes earlier. The train’s engine was destroyed.
Minutes before, a diplomatic train carrying Boris Johnson, former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt, and several European security advisers had passed through the same station. It had left ahead of schedule. Ukrzaliznytsia, Ukraine’s state railway operator, later stated it was “quite likely” the drone had been aimed at the diplomatic train.
This was not an isolated incident. It was the latest operation in a systematic Russian campaign against Ukraine’s railways — a campaign that has destroyed over 500 locomotives since February 2022, more than half of them in 2026 alone.
This article examines the strategy behind the campaign, the technical trap that makes it so effective, and what it means for Ukraine’s ability to sustain its economy and war effort.

## I. The Yahodyn Strike: What Happened
The facts are well-documented across multiple international outlets:
ElementDetailDate13 September 2026LocationYahodyn station, Volyn oblast, ~2 km from Polish borderTargetLocomotive of a Kyiv–Warsaw passenger trainCasualtiesNone (passengers evacuated 15 minutes before impact)Diplomatic trainBoris Johnson, Carl Bildt, Jonathan Powell, David Petraeus — on separate train, already in PolandUkrainian assessmentUkrzaliznytsia: “quite likely” the diplomatic train was the intended target
Boris Johnson’s reaction on X:

> “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day — even on civilian railways.”
Carl Bildt shared a video of the attack on X, writing: “Gli attacchi contro di noi si stanno intensificando.”
David Petraeus, former CIA director, was on another train at Yahodyn station when the drone struck. He described the attack as “terrifying” and accused Putin of “trying to terrorise Ukrainian civilians.”

## II. The Numbers: 500+ Locomotives Lost
The scale of the campaign is staggering. According to Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, speaking on 15 September 2026:

> “Since the start of the full-scale invasion, over 500 locomotives have been damaged or completely destroyed by Russian attacks — more than half of them this year alone.”
MetricValueSourceLocomotives damaged/destroyed since 2022500+Sybiha, Interfax-UkraineLocomotives lost in 2026 alone192 (first six months)Ukrzaliznytsia, Rail JournalLocomotives lost 2022-2025217Ukrzaliznytsia, Rail JournalPassenger carriages lost249Ukrzaliznytsia, RailMarketRailway infrastructure attacks in 20261,535+Ministry for Communities and Territories DevelopmentUkrzaliznytsia employees killed52UkrzaliznytsiaUkrzaliznytsia employees injured317Ukrzaliznytsia
The acceleration is stark: in the first six months of 2026, Russia destroyed 192 locomotives — nearly as many as in the previous four years combined (217).
Before the war, in April 2021, Ukrzaliznytsia operated 1,532 locomotives (749 electric, 783 diesel). The loss of 500+ units represents roughly one-third of the pre-war fleet.

## III. Why Locomotives? The Strategic Logic
Russia is not targeting passenger carriages. It is targeting the traction — the locomotives that make the trains move.
Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, head of Ukrzaliznytsia, explained the tactic:

> “There are Shaheds guided apparently by a camera. In other words, the pilot on the other side can see clearly what he is hitting. The goal was not simply to destroy the locomotive; the strike hit the cabin directly.”
Andrii Kharuk, military expert, added:

> “Installing a camera on a Shahed is not technically difficult. Such modifications effectively transform the Shaheds into large FPV drones, allowing operators to guide them toward moving targets like trains.”
The logic is simple:
TargetLocomotiveCarriageCostHundreds of thousands of eurosTens of thousandsProductionComplex, long lead timesSimple, rapid productionReplaceabilityDifficult (limited stock)Easy (continuous production)Strategic impactParalyses entire lineLimited damageDefenceIsolated, identifiable targetDiffuse target
As one analyst put it: “They hit traction, i.e. locomotives, because they understand that without traction there is no movement.”

## IV. The Gauge Trap: 1,520mm vs 1,435mm
This is where the strategy becomes devastatingly effective.
Ukraine’s railway network uses 1,520mm broad gauge — a legacy of the Soviet Union. The European Union uses 1,435mm standard gauge.
SystemGaugeCountriesUkraine (ex-USSR)1,520 mmUkraine, Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Finland, BalticsEU1,435 mmAll EU member states
The consequence: European locomotives cannot run on Ukrainian tracks without modification. They must either:

- Change bogies (slow, costly, impractical for locomotives)

- Use variable-gauge carriages (rare, expensive)

- Transload cargo at border crossings

## V. The Bogie Problem: Why Carriages Can Be Swapped, Locomotives Can’t
This is the technical heart of the trap — and it is crucial to understanding why Russia’s strategy works.
Carriages (and freight wagons): Their function is to carry. The bogies are relatively simple components that can be swapped in blocks. In an operation called “bogie exchange,” the carriage body is lifted and placed on a new set of bogies with the correct gauge. This is a standard operation at border crossings.
Locomotives: Their function is to generate traction. The engine, transmission, and onboard systems are integrated into the bogie itself. This makes bogie replacement an operation that is extremely more complex, lengthy, and costly — often considered impractical. As one technical analysis concluded, while bogie exchange is “possible” for locomotives, “it is often more practical to use two different locomotives.”
In short: for a carriage, the bogie is an “accessory.” For a locomotive, it is part of the “heart.”
Spain is developing variable-gauge bogies for freight wagons, with a €5.48 million grant from Madrid to Kyiv. But this technology is for freight wagons only — not locomotives.

## VI. Ukraine’s Urgent Appeal
On 15 September 2026, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha issued an urgent appeal to Ukraine’s partners:

> “To keep this lifeline running, Ukraine urgently needs replacements. We call on all our partners to urgently assist us in finding locomotives compatible with the 1520 mm gauge as well as in financing to accelerate the procurement of new ones.”
The problem: Only a handful of countries have compatible rolling stock:
CountryGaugeCompatibilityFinland1,524 mmCompatibleEstonia, Latvia, Lithuania1,520 mmCompatibleKazakhstan1,520 mmCompatibleMoldova1,520 mmOffered 20 locomotives (August 2026)
Sybiha acknowledged the difficulty:

> “The search for such locomotives is complicated by the different track widths. In most European countries, the standard gauge of 1,435 mm is used, while in Ukraine it is 1,520 mm. For this reason, potential suppliers of such machines are few. These are mainly the Baltic states and Finland. Another option is the conversion of existing locomotives to the Ukrainian standard.”

## VII. The Diplomatic Train: A Target?
The Yahodyn strike raises a disturbing question: was the diplomatic train the intended target?
Ukrzaliznytsia’s statement:

> “The diplomatic train had left the station earlier than expected because of the timetable change... due to constant threats of Russian strikes” — and therefore it was “quite possible that it could also have been the intended target.”
Carl Bildt confirmed:

> “It was not our train, but the one that left a few minutes after us toward the Polish border. It was evacuated as the Russian drone approached and no one was injured. Our train only received an evacuation warning.”
Dr. Katarzyna Pisarska, president of the Warsaw Security Forum, who was in the same carriage as Johnson, told the BBC that the attack occurred about 30 minutes after their train had crossed into Poland.
The Russian Defence Ministry claimed the attack was aimed at “railway infrastructure facilities in western Ukraine that are used to transport military cargoes from European countries.”
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk held an emergency meeting and warned:

> “The escalation of the actions from the Russian side is becoming a reality, and they are getting closer and closer to our border.”

## VIII. The Broader Campaign: 1,500+ Attacks
The Yahodyn strike is part of a much larger campaign. According to Ukraine’s Ministry for Communities and Territories Development:
MetricValueAttacks on railway facilities (2025–early 2026)1,535+Infrastructure assets damaged17,000+Attacks on railway infrastructure in 2026 alone1,534 (as of August 2026)
Ukrzaliznytsia’s assessment:

> “These figures demonstrate the systematic and targeted nature of hostile actions aimed at disabling the locomotive fleet in order to reduce the ability of rail transport to ensure uninterrupted freight and passenger services.”
The private sector has also been hit: ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih lost 15 locomotives used to maintain continuous production cycles at its iron and coke facilities.

## IX. What This Means for the War
Ukraine’s railways are not just transportation. They are the lifeline of the country:
➡️ Evacuation of civilians from frontline areas
➡️ Transport of essential cargo and military supplies
➡️ Export of grain and other vital goods
➡️ 90% of export cargo moves by rail
Ukrzaliznytsia has lost 40% of its rolling stock, according to Ukrainian political analyst Pavlo Hai-Nyzhnyk. The company has also reported shortages of locomotives and carriages due to the cessation of spare parts supplies from Russia and Belarus.
The strategic goal is clear: Russia is not trying to massacre civilians. It is trying to paralyse Ukraine’s logistics — to destroy and disrupt things faster than Ukraine can repair and rebuild them.

## X. Conclusions: The Slow Strangulation
The locomotive war is a textbook example of asymmetric warfare applied to logistics. Russia is not destroying the entire railway network. It is striking its weakest, most irreplaceable link: the traction.
What the evidence shows:

- 500+ locomotives destroyed since 2022, more than half in 2026 alone

- A 1,520mm gauge trap that prevents EU locomotives from running on Ukrainian tracks

- A bogie problem that makes locomotive replacement far harder than carriage replacement

- 1,500+ attacks on railway infrastructure in 2026

- An urgent Ukrainian appeal to partners for compatible locomotives
What remains unclear:

- Whether the Yahodyn strike was specifically targeting the diplomatic train

- Whether Western partners can supply enough compatible locomotives to replace losses

- Whether Spain’s variable-gauge bogie technology can be adapted for locomotives
The bottom line: Ukraine’s railways are being strangled — not by a single decisive blow, but by a thousand cuts. Each destroyed locomotive is a train that will never run, a cargo that will never move, an evacuation that will never happen.
And Europe, for all its pledges of support, cannot simply send its own locomotives. The gauge is different. The bogies don’t fit. The trap is technical, and it is working.

## Sources and Dossiers

reads.title: THE MENDEL PARADOX: ZELENSKY'S WAR ON HIS CRITICS AND THE YERMAK CORRUPTION CASE
reads.subtitle: Ukraine's former press secretary was sanctioned and blocked from the European Parliament, while the president's former chief of staff faces money laundering charges. Marco | Independent Analyst 18 S
reads.body:
## Introduction
On 13 September 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signed Decree No. 901/2026, imposing ten-year sanctions on Ioulia Mendel, his former press secretary. Three days later, Mendel was denied entry to the European Parliament in Brussels, where she had been invited to speak at an event on peace in Ukraine. She delivered her speech via video link.
The official reason for the sanctions: “disinformation and Russian propaganda.” The unofficial reason, according to Mendel and her supporters: retaliation for her repeated accusations of corruption against Zelensky and his inner circle.
At the centre of those accusations is Andriy Yermak, Zelensky’s former chief of staff, who was arrested in May 2026 on money laundering charges. He was released after posting €2.7 million bail. The case, known as “Midas,” involves the alleged embezzlement of $100 million from Energoatom, Ukraine’s state nuclear company.
The paradox is stark: a journalist who accused the president of corruption is sanctioned, while the president’s former right-hand man, accused of laundering millions, is free on bail. This article examines the facts, the timeline, and the implications.

## I. The Sanctions Against Ioulia Mendel
Ioulia Mendel served as press secretary to Volodymyr Zelensky from 2019 to 2021. After leaving the administration, she became one of the most vocal critics of the president, accusing him of corruption and authoritarian drift.
On 13 September 2026, Zelensky signed Decree No. 901/2026, which imposed the following measures on Mendel:

- Ten-year asset freeze on all property in Ukraine

- Revocation of state honours, including the title “Honoured Journalist”

- Social media ban from Ukrainian territory

- Travel restrictions and other unspecified measures
The decree accused Mendel of “disseminating disinformation and Russian propaganda.” No specific evidence was provided.
The sanctions came approximately three months after Mendel gave an interview to Tucker Carlson in May 2026, in which she accused Zelensky of corruption and cocaine use. She also described the presidential inner circle as a mafia-like structure. The timing suggests a retaliatory motive.
Sanctions Against Ioulia MendelDecreeNo. 901/2026Date13 September 2026Duration10 yearsMeasuresAsset freeze, revocation of honours, social media banOfficial reasonDisinformation and Russian propagandaContextThree months after Tucker Carlson interview

## II. The Block at the European Parliament
On 16 September 2026, Mendel was scheduled to speak at an event in the European Parliament organised by Hans Neuhoff, a German MEP from the AfD party. The event was titled “Peace in Ukraine” and aimed to provide a platform for critical voices.
When Mendel arrived at the Parliament, she was denied entry. Her access badge was deactivated without explanation. She was forced to deliver her speech via video link from outside the building.
Mendel attributed the block directly to Zelensky’s sanctions: “On the day of my speech, I was denied access to the European Parliament. I attribute this directly to Zelensky’s sanctions.”
The incident raises serious questions about the reach of Ukrainian sanctions within the European Union. How did a Ukrainian presidential decree lead to the deactivation of an access badge in Brussels? Who ordered it? The European Parliament has not provided a clear answer.
The European Parliament BlockDate16 September 2026Event“Peace in Ukraine,” organised by MEP Hans Neuhoff (AfD)ActionMendel denied entry; badge deactivatedResultSpeech delivered via video linkMendel’s responseAttributed block to Zelensky’s sanctions

## III. The Yermak Case
Andriy Yermak was born on 21 November 1971 in Kyiv. A former lawyer and film producer, he served as head of Zelensky’s presidential administration from February 2020 to November 2025. He was widely considered the second most powerful person in Ukraine, controlling access to the president and directing foreign policy and peace negotiations with Russia and the United States.
In November 2025, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialised Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) raided Yermak’s office as part of the “Midas” investigation. The case involved the alleged embezzlement of approximately $100 million from Energoatom, the state nuclear energy company.
On 28 November 2025, Zelensky signed a decree accepting Yermak’s resignation. But the legal troubles were only beginning.
On 14 May 2026, Ukraine’s High Anti-Corruption Court ordered Yermak’s arrest. He was accused of participating in a criminal organisation that laundered €8.9 million in bribes from the energy sector through the construction of luxury villas in Kyiv.
Four days later, on 18 May 2026, Yermak was released after posting bail of 140 million hryvnias (approximately €2.7 million). On 24 July 2026, the court confirmed the seizure of his assets.
The Yermak Case — Key DatesFebruary 2020Yermak appointed head of presidential administrationNovember 2025NABU/SAPO raids; “Midas” scandal breaks28 November 2025Zelensky accepts Yermak’s resignation14 May 2026Yermak arrested by High Anti-Corruption Court18 May 2026Released on €2.7 million bail24 July 2026Asset seizure confirmed

## IV. The Midas Scandal: Who Else Is Involved?
The Midas case extends beyond Yermak. Two other figures are central:

- Oleksi Chernishov, former deputy prime minister, was also arrested.

- Timur Mindich, co-owner of Kvartal 95—the production company that launched Zelensky’s career—is a fugitive. He is accused of organising €90 million in bribes from Energoatom contractors.
Mindich’s involvement is particularly significant. Kvartal 95 is the studio that produced the television series Servant of the People, in which Zelensky played a fictional president. The company became a symbol of Zelensky’s rise to power. Now, its co-owner is accused of orchestrating a massive corruption scheme.
The fact that Yermak, Chernishov, and Mindich are all linked to Zelensky’s inner circle raises uncomfortable questions about the president’s own knowledge and involvement. No evidence has emerged directly implicating Zelensky, but the pattern is troubling.
Key Figures in the Midas CaseNameRoleStatusAndriy YermakFormer head of presidential administrationReleased on bailOleksi ChernishovFormer deputy prime ministerArrestedTimur MindichCo-owner of Kvartal 95Fugitive

## V. The Paradox
The central paradox of this affair is simple: Ioulia Mendel, a journalist who accused the president of corruption, has been sanctioned and blocked from the European Parliament. Andriy Yermak, the president’s former chief of staff, accused of laundering millions, has been released on bail and remains free.
Mendel vs. YermakNameAccusationConsequenceIoulia MendelDisinformation and Russian propaganda10-year sanctions, EU Parliament blockAndriy YermakMoney laundering (€8.9 million)Released on €2.7 million bail
If Mendel’s accusations were false, why not sue her for defamation? If they were true, why is she being punished while the accused walks free? The official justification—”disinformation and Russian propaganda”—does not explain the disparity.

## VI. The FBI Connection (Unverified)
On 17 September 2026, Ukrainian activist Marta Havryshko posted on X: “Yuliia Mendel should testify to the FBI about everything she knows regarding the alleged corruption in Zelensky’s inner circle. And I suspect she knows a lot. If the sanctions against her and the subsequent wave of attacks by pro-government bloggers and self-proclaimed ‘opinion leaders’ were retaliation for speaking out, that also deserves serious examination.”
This claim is unverified. There is no official confirmation that Mendel has been contacted by the FBI or that an investigation is underway. It should be treated as speculation until corroborated.
However, the mere mention of FBI involvement is significant. It suggests that the corruption allegations against Zelensky’s inner circle are being taken seriously by US law enforcement, at least according to some sources. We will continue to monitor this angle.

## VII. The Streisand Effect
The sanctions and the Parliament block have had the opposite of their intended effect. Instead of silencing Mendel, they have amplified her voice.
Her case is now international news. The Le Parisien headline read: “Guerre en Ukraine : l’ancienne porte-parole de Zelensky dit avoir été privée de discours au Parlement européen.” The story has been picked up by media across Europe and beyond.
The Streisand effect is in full swing: the attempt to censor Mendel has drawn more attention to her accusations than any interview or article could have. Zelensky’s inner circle may have won a temporary victory by silencing a critic, but they have lost the broader battle for public opinion.

## VIII. Strategic Implications
For Ukraine: The case undermines Ukraine’s moral authority. The country presents itself as a democracy fighting for European values. Censoring critics and blocking them from EU institutions contradicts that narrative. It also fuels Russian propaganda, which portrays Ukraine as a corrupt, authoritarian state.
For the European Union: The block at the European Parliament raises questions about the EU’s independence. If a Ukrainian presidential decree can prevent a journalist from entering the Parliament, what does that say about EU sovereignty? The incident has embarrassed the Parliament and raised concerns about undue foreign influence.
For the United States: The Yermak case and the alleged FBI interest suggest that corruption in Ukraine is not just a domestic issue. It affects US aid and investment. If American taxpayer money is being diverted into private villas and offshore accounts, the American public has a right to know.
For Russia: The Kremlin will exploit this case to argue that Ukraine is a failed, corrupt state. It will use Mendel’s sanctions as evidence that Kyiv is no different from Moscow. This is a propaganda gift that Russia did not have to work for.

## IX. Conclusion
The Mendel paradox is not just about one journalist. It is about the nature of power in wartime Ukraine. It is about the limits of censorship and the cost of silence. It is about a president who came to power promising to fight corruption, and who now finds himself surrounded by corruption allegations.
The facts speak for themselves:

- Mendel was sanctioned for 10 years.

- Yermak was arrested for money laundering and released on bail.

- The European Parliament blocked Mendel from entering.

- The official reason for the sanctions was “disinformation.”

- The real reason, many suspect, was retaliation.
If Ukraine wants to be part of Europe, it must respect European values. If it wants to defeat Russia, it must be better than Russia. Silencing critics is not the way. It is the path to authoritarianism.

reads.title: THE MENDEL PARADOX
reads.subtitle: How Zelensky Sanctioned His Own Spokeswoman — And Barred Her from the European Parliamen Marco | Independent Analyst 17 September 2026
reads.body:
## Introduction
On 13 September 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky signed decree No. 901/2026, imposing ten-year sanctions on his former press secretary, Iuliia Mendel. The sanctions include asset freezes, a ban on commercial operations, a block on her social media presence from Ukraine, and the revocation of state awards.
Three days later, on 16 September, Mendel was denied entry to the European Parliament in Strasbourg, where she had been invited to speak at a side event organised by the AfD on the theme “Ukraine: Dare Peace. Diplomacy, Not Escalation.”
She gave her speech anyway — via video link. The room was full. The hope for peace, she said, was “almost palpable.”
This article examines the facts, the paradox, and what it reveals about the state of Ukrainian democracy and European censorship.

## I. Who Is Iuliia Mendel?
ElementDetailRolePress secretary to President Zelensky (2019–2021)BackgroundJournalist, former presenter on Ukrainian TVCurrent statusSanctioned by presidential decree (13 Sept 2026)Reason given“Dissemination of disinformation and Russian propaganda”Media appearancesTucker Carlson (May 2026), JDD (Aug 2026), European Parliament (virtual, Sept 2026)
Mendel worked alongside Zelensky for two years. In her own words, she was “among his most faithful propagandists.” She now accuses him of authoritarian drift and of making the war the foundation of his political survival.

## II. The Sanctions: What Do They Entail?
The decree imposes:

- Asset freeze on all property in Ukraine

- Ban on commercial operations and participation in privatisation

- Block on social media from Ukrainian territory

- Revocation of state awards and honorary titles

- Ten-year duration
The sanctions were announced three days before Mendel was due to speak at the European Parliament. The timing is not coincidental.

## III. The European Parliament Block
Mendel was invited by the AfD to a side event at the European Parliament. Such events are routinely organised by political groups. The Parliament itself stated it “does not approve the content of such events” but manages organisational matters.
Yet Mendel was denied access to the building.
She attributed the block directly to Zelensky’s sanctions. The European Parliament has not provided a legal explanation.
Fabio De Masi, German MEP (Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance), raised the case in plenary:

> “Ukraine is sinking further into chaos. A prosecutor general accused of corruption has fled abroad. There have been shootouts between law enforcement. And now the former spokesman of Mr Zelensky has been sanctioned by Zelensky himself for speaking out against Ukraine’s NATO membership, for his commitment to peace, and for opposing the forced conscription of young people. Yet he has always condemned Russia’s attacks too.”
De Masi added:

> “If such conditions prevail in Ukraine, if the country is increasingly transforming into a mafia state, then this European Parliament should not just nod through further billions... but must finally put the question at the centre of debate.”

## IV. The Yermak Paradox
Mendel’s most pointed question is this:

> “Why am I, Iuliia Mendel — former press secretary of Zelensky — under sanctions, and not Andriy Yermak?”
Andriy Yermak was the head of Zelensky’s Presidential Office from 2020 to 2025. He was the most powerful unelected figure in Ukraine — the “true power behind the throne.”
AccusationStatusSourceLaundered $10.5 million through luxury properties in the Dynasty complex near KyivVerifiedNABU, SAPOInvolved in the Energoatom scandal ($100 million kickback scheme)VerifiedNABUConvinced Zelensky that a full-scale invasion would not happenVerifiedThe GuardianConsulted an astrologer for top appointmentsVerifiedSAPO, NYTArrested in May 2026VerifiedCaliber.AzReleased on €3.2 million bailVerifiedCaliber.Az
Yermak was arrested by NABU — an independent anti-corruption body. He was released on bail. He has not been sanctioned by Zelensky.
Mendel, by contrast, has been sanctioned for speaking.

## V. The Streisand Effect
The sanctions and the Parliament block have had an unintended consequence: they have amplified Mendel’s voice.

- Her interview with Tucker Carlson has millions of views.

- She has been interviewed by JDD, cited in European Parliament, and covered by international media.

- The block made her a symbol of censorship.
As the Russian commentator @ZePrisoner noted: “The situation with Mendel is a magnificent own goal for the globalists who finance the war and for the usurper Zelensky.”
The comment is propagandistic, but the analysis is correct: censorship backfired.

## VI. What This Means
The Mendel case raises three fundamental questions:

- For Ukraine: If the government sanctions its own former spokeswoman for criticising the war, what does that say about democracy?

- For Europe: If the European Parliament bars entry to a speaker invited by a political group, on what legal basis?

- For the West: If the fight against “Russian disinformation” becomes a tool to silence dissent, who is the real target?
The paradox is clear:
➡️ Yermak — accused of corruption, money laundering, and consulting an astrologer — is free.
➡️ Mendel — accused of “disinformation” for criticising the war — is sanctioned.
The question is not whether Mendel is right. The question is why the system treats her as a threat.

## VII. Conclusions
The Mendel case is not an isolated incident. It is part of a broader pattern:

- The criminalisation of dissent in Ukraine

- The use of sanctions as a political weapon

- The complicity of European institutions in silencing critics
As Fabio De Masi said in the European Parliament: “If the country is transforming into a mafia state, then we must finally put the question at the centre of debate.”
The European Parliament did not.
Instead, it barred Mendel from entering.
The paradox is not just Ukrainian. It is European.

reads.title: THE WHITE GOLD WAR: RUSSIA'S SEIZURE OF EUROPE'S LARGEST LITHIUM DEPOSIT AND THE COLLAPSE OF THE US MINERALS DEAL
reads.subtitle: When Russian forces captured the village of Shevchenko in June 2025, they didn't just take a settlement. They took the crown jewel of Ukraine's mineral wealth—and exposed the fragility of Washington's
reads.body:
## Introduction
The war in Ukraine is not only a territorial conflict. It is a resource war. And in June 2025, Russia won a decisive battle in that war without firing a single shot at the prize itself.
The village of Shevchenko, in the Donetsk region, is unremarkable by any conventional measure. It sits roughly ten kilometres from Velyka Novosilka, a town that fell to Russian forces in January 2025. Its pre-war population was measured in hundreds. But directly adjacent to its ruins lies something that has made it one of the most strategically significant pieces of real estate in Europe: one of the continent’s largest lithium deposits, with estimated reserves of 13.8 million tonnes of ore and an average lithium oxide content of 1.5 percent.
When Russian forces seized the village, they seized the future of Europe’s battery supply chain. They also seized the centrepiece of the minerals agreement that Kyiv and Washington had signed just weeks earlier. The Shevchenko deposit is now under Russian control. The US-Ukraine minerals deal has lost its most valuable asset before it ever extracted a single tonne.

## I. The Deposit: Why Shevchenko Mattered
The Shevchenko lithium deposit was discovered in 1982 by Soviet geologists. For four decades, it remained undeveloped—first because the Soviet Union had other priorities, then because independent Ukraine lacked the capital and technology to exploit it.
What makes Shevchenko exceptional is not just its size. It is its geology.
According to Ukraine’s National Geological Survey, the deposit contains more than 90 percent spodumene—a lithium-aluminium silicate that is significantly easier and cheaper to process than petalite, the mineral found in most other Ukrainian lithium deposits. Spodumene is the preferred feedstock for battery-grade lithium carbonate and hydroxide. Petalite requires more complex, more capital-intensive processing.
In practical terms: Shevchenko was the cheapest, most efficient lithium project in Ukraine. It was also the one most attractive to Western investors.
Beyond lithium, the deposit contains tantalum, niobium, beryllium, caesium, rubidium, and tin—all critical minerals with defence, aerospace, and electronics applications.
Shevchenko Deposit — Key DataDiscovery1982Ore reserves13.8 million tonnesLithium oxide content1.24–1.5%Primary mineralSpodumene (>90%)Additional mineralsTantalum, niobium, beryllium, caesium, rubidium, tinLocationDonetsk Oblast, near Velyka NovosilkaStatus (June 2025)Under Russian control

## II. The US-Ukraine Minerals Deal: A Race Against Time
On 30 April 2025, the United States and Ukraine signed the United States–Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund agreement. The Ukrainian parliament ratified it on 8 May, and President Zelensky signed it into law on 12 May.
The deal was framed as a landmark. It established a joint fund giving the US priority rights to invest in Ukrainian mineral extraction projects. The agreement covered 57 critical minerals, including lithium, uranium, cobalt, and rare earth elements. Ukraine committed to contributing 50 percent of all revenues from new rents and new licenses for mineral production to the bilateral fund.
From Washington’s perspective, the logic was straightforward: secure access to the critical minerals that China dominates, reduce supply chain dependence, and channel American capital into Ukraine’s reconstruction.
From Kyiv’s perspective, the logic was equally clear: bind the United States to Ukraine’s economic future, ensuring continued political and military support.
There was just one problem. Russia was already moving.

## III. The Fall of Shevchenko: Timeline of a Strategic Loss
The Russian capture of Shevchenko was not a sudden event. It was the culmination of a methodical advance in western Donetsk.
DateEventJanuary 2025Velyka Novosilka falls to Russian forces30 April 2025US-Ukraine minerals agreement signed8 May 2025Ukrainian parliament ratifies the deal12 May 2025Zelensky signs ratification into law26 June 2025Russian MoD announces capture of ShevchenkoSeptember 2025US delegation scouts titanium, zirconium, hafnium depositsJanuary 2026Ukraine awards Dobra lithium deposit to investors linked to Trump alliesMay 2026Zelensky announces Russia plans to exploit 18 deposits in occupied territories
The timing was brutal. The Shevchenko deposit fell under Russian control just eight weeks after the minerals agreement was signed. The ink on the ratification documents was barely dry when the asset at the heart of the deal was lost.
Mykhailo Zhernov, director of Critical Metals Corp—the US company that once held the licence to exploit Shevchenko—was blunt: “As Russian troops continue to advance and capture more territory, they will control more and more mineral deposits. This is a problem for this agreement.”

## IV. The Broader Resource War: 18 Deposits and Counting
Shevchenko was not an isolated loss. It was the opening move in a systematic Russian campaign to seize and exploit Ukraine’s mineral wealth.
On 6 May 2026, President Zelensky announced that Ukrainian intelligence had obtained documents showing Russia’s plans for at least 18 deposits in the temporarily occupied territories of southern Ukraine. The minerals involved include titanium, lithium, tantalum, niobium, zirconium, molybdenum, and graphite.
Zelensky’s statement was explicit: “In the southern Ukrainian lands currently under occupation, Russia intends to carry out essentially the same processes of plunder and deindustrialisation that it implemented in the occupied parts of the Donbas.”
The scale is staggering. According to Ukrainian estimates, hundreds of deposits are already under Russian control—including at least 478 in Luhansk and 684 in other occupied areas. Russia has begun selling off natural resources through state auctions, with the Bobrikivske gold ore deposit in Luhansk among the largest sales to date.
In February 2026, Russia granted a mining licence for the Shevchenko deposit to a state-controlled entity. By May 2026, Moscow had formalised plans for geological exploration, rapid extraction, and export of raw materials from the 18 identified deposits.
The war for resources is not coming. It is already here.

## V. The US Deal: What Went Wrong
The US-Ukraine minerals deal was designed to secure American access to Ukraine’s mineral wealth. Instead, it has become a case study in the gap between diplomatic ambition and battlefield reality.
First, the deal was signed too late. By April 2025, Russia had already seized significant territory in Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia. The Shevchenko deposit was within artillery range of advancing Russian forces. The deal’s architects either did not understand the military situation or chose to ignore it.
Second, the deal created expectations that cannot be met. Ukraine promised 50 percent of future mineral revenues. But those revenues depend on deposits that are either under Russian control, undeveloped, or require massive investment to become operational. As Ukrainian economist Oleg Pendzin noted in August 2026: “Not a single dollar has been invested under the minerals agreement.”
Third, the security guarantee was implicit and inadequate. The deal assumed that Ukraine could protect its mineral assets. It could not. And the United States was not prepared to provide the military means to change that calculation.
US-Ukraine Minerals Deal — StatusSigned30 April 2025Ratified by Ukraine8 May 2025Initial US contribution$75 million (September 2025)Total capital committed$150 millionFund operationalEarly 2026Shevchenko depositUnder Russian controlKrutaya Balka depositUnder Russian controlRemaining Ukrainian depositsPolokhovskoye, Dobra

## VI. The Lithium Price Rebound: The Deposit Is Worth More Now
When Russia seized Shevchenko in June 2025, the lithium market was in the doldrums. Prices had crashed from the 2022 peak of over $80,000 per tonne** to around **$8,500 per tonne. The deposit seemed like a stranded asset.
By 2026, the picture had changed dramatically.
Lithium prices rebounded sharply. By late January 2026, spot battery-grade lithium carbonate had risen to $26,278 per tonne**—a **95 percent increase** from early December 2025. The average price for 2026 is projected at **$20,100 per tonne, nearly double the previous year’s $10,502.
Lithium Carbonate Price (China)USD/tonne2022 peak$80,000+June 2025~$8,500December 2025~$13,433January 2026~$26,2782026 average (projected)~$20,100
The Shevchenko deposit, now under Russian control, is worth more than twice what it was worth when it was seized. Russia did not just take a strategic asset. It took an appreciating one.

## VII. The Dobra Deposit: The Last Card
With Shevchenko and Krutaya Balka under Russian control, Ukraine’s remaining major lithium asset is the Dobra deposit in the Kirovohrad region.
In January 2026, Ukraine awarded development rights for Dobra to Dobra Lithium Holdings, a company whose shareholders include Ronald S. Lauder, a billionaire friend of Donald Trump. The deposit consists of two sites—Stankuvatskaya and Nadya—with total reserves of approximately 1.2 million tonnes of lithium ore.
The Dobra tender was seen as a test of the US-Ukraine minerals deal. It was also a signal that Kyiv is willing to offer its remaining assets to politically connected American investors in exchange for continued support.
But Dobra is not Shevchenko. Its reserves are smaller, its geology less favourable, and its development timeline longer. The loss of Shevchenko is not offset by the award of Dobra. It is merely partially compensated.

## VIII. The Strategic Implications
The Russian seizure of Shevchenko has implications that extend far beyond Ukraine.
For Europe: The EU imports nearly 100 percent of its lithium, primarily from China. Ukraine was supposed to be a domestic source—a way to reduce dependence on Chinese supply chains. That hope is now significantly diminished. The Shevchenko deposit, the largest in Eastern Europe, is under Russian control. Europe’s green transition just became more dependent on China, not less.
For the United States: The minerals deal was a central pillar of Washington’s strategy to secure critical mineral supply chains. The loss of Shevchenko undermines that strategy. It also raises questions about the viability of investing in Ukrainian mineral assets when the security situation remains unresolved.
For Ukraine: The loss is both economic and psychological. Ukraine holds 22 of the 50 US-designated strategic materials and 25 of 34 EU critical raw materials, including graphite, lithium, titanium, beryllium, and uranium. But those reserves are only valuable if they can be extracted, processed, and exported. With two of four major lithium deposits under Russian control, Ukraine’s mineral leverage has been substantially reduced.
For Russia: The seizure of Shevchenko is a victory in the resource war. It gives Moscow control over a deposit that could supply Europe’s battery industry for decades. It also provides a bargaining chip in any future negotiations—a tangible asset that can be traded, developed, or simply held as leverage.

## IX. The Unanswered Question
The fundamental question raised by the Shevchenko seizure is this: can a minerals deal work in a war zone?
The answer, based on the evidence, is no. The US-Ukraine minerals agreement was built on the assumption that Ukraine could protect its mineral assets. That assumption was false. Russia has demonstrated that it can seize territory—and with it, the resources beneath it—faster than any investment agreement can respond.
The deal’s architects in Washington and Kyiv failed to account for the most basic reality of war: the battlefield determines what is mine and what is yours. No contract, no fund, no legal framework can override that.
If the United States wants access to Ukraine’s critical minerals, it must first ensure that Ukraine can defend them. That requires military support, not just investment agreements. It requires a strategy for victory, not just a framework for extraction.

## X. Conclusion
The village of Shevchenko is a ruin. Its pre-war population has fled. Its buildings are rubble. But beneath the rubble lies one of Europe’s most valuable mineral deposits—and it is now under Russian control.
The US-Ukraine minerals deal was signed in April 2025. By June 2025, its centrepiece was lost. The deal continues to exist on paper. But paper does not mine lithium. Paper does not build batteries. Paper does not power electric vehicles.
The white gold of Shevchenko now belongs to Moscow. And Europe’s green transition—the transition that was supposed to reduce dependence on authoritarian regimes—has just become more dependent on them than ever.

Hey all!
Nicholas from the Unusual Whales team, here! This week is a bit of an extension of last week’s issue on advanced options strategies. This time, we’re covering some VERY high risk strategies (risk of ruin), and should not be attempted by inexperienced traders. I want to preface as well that the strikes utilized in this write-up were chosen for simplicity for explanation; NOT to represent a suggestion for a trade anyone should take.
With that said, let’s dive on in.

## The Short Straddle
A trader who wants to speculate on a decrease in volatility and relatively little movement in AAPL can sell a Short Straddle. The trader receives a credit, or premium, for selling both a Put and a Call at the same strike price and expiration. The short Put carries the obligation to buy 100 shares at the strike price if assigned, while the short Call carries the obligation to sell 100 shares at the strike price if assigned.
You sell an AAPL $335 Short Straddle expiring September 28, 2026, selling the $335 Call for approximately a $5.80 credit and selling the $335 Put for approximately a $4.62 credit, receiving a total net credit of approximately $10.42 per share, or $1,042.40, to express this view. Your two breakeven prices at expiry are approximately $324.58 on the downside ($335 - $10.42) and $345.42 on the upside ($335 + $10.42).

-
- The maximum profit at expiry is approximately $1,042.40, which occurs if AAPL finishes exactly at the $335 strike price, allowing both options to expire worthless. Since the time component of your trade plan may not extend all the way to expiration, you should be prepared to buy to close at a variety of AAPL prices as the market value of your $335 Short Straddle changes.
Because AAPL can theoretically rise without limit, the short Call creates unlimited upside loss potential. The downside risk is also substantial, though technically limited because AAPL cannot fall below $0. Selling a Straddle therefore carries a high risk of ruin, as a large adverse move in either direction, such as an unexpected earnings result, major news event, or acquisition announcement, can result in very large losses.

## The Short Strangle
A trader who wants to speculate on a decrease in volatility and a relatively neutral AAPL price can sell a Short Strangle. The trader receives a credit, or premium, for selling both the Put and the Call. The short Put carries the obligation to buy 100 shares at the Put strike price if assigned, while the short Call carries the obligation to sell 100 shares at the Call strike price if assigned.
You sell an AAPL $327.50 / $342.50 Short Strangle expiring September 28, 2026, selling the $327.50 Put for approximately a $2.05 credit and selling the $342.50 Call for approximately a $2.55 credit, receiving a total net credit of approximately $4.60 per share, or $460.40, to express this view. Your breakeven prices at expiry are approximately $322.90 on the downside ($327.50 - $4.60) and $347.10 on the upside ($342.50 + $4.60).

-
- The maximum profit at expiry is $460.40, which occurs if AAPL finishes between $327.50 and $342.50, allowing both options to expire worthless. Since the time component of your trade plan may not extend all the way to expiration, however, you should be prepared to buy to close at a variety of AAPL prices as the market value of your $327.50 / $342.50 Short Strangle changes.
Because AAPL can theoretically rise without limit, the short Call creates unlimited upside loss potential. The downside risk is also substantial, though technically limited because AAPL cannot fall below $0. A sharp adverse move, such as an unexpected earnings result, major news event, or acquisition announcement, can therefore result in very large losses. The fixed-risk version of a Short Strangle is a Short Iron Condor.

## The Synthetic Short
A trader who wants to speculate on decreasing price and increasing volatility can open a Synthetic Short. The trader may pay a small debit, receive a small credit, or open the trade for exactly $0.
Suppose stock XYZ is trading at $25.50. You forecast a decrease in price and an increase in volatility.
You open a $25 Synthetic Short at exactly $0.00, no cost, to express this view. How is this possible? The $25 Call bid price is $3.00 and the $25 Put ask price is also $3.00, so when you sell the $25 Call you receive exactly $3.00 and you use that credit to pay for the $25 Put.

-
- The breakeven price for this trade is the exact price of the underlying when you entered since this structure behaves almost exactly like shorting 100 shares of XYZ: theta, vega, and gamma are all roughly zero and delta is roughly -100.
The max loss on this position at expiry is theoretically unlimited, since XYZ price can increase indefinitely. The max gain of a Synthetic Short is large but theoretically capped, since XYZ price can only decrease to $0. Since the loss on a Synthetic Short is theoretically unlimited, this structure carries a high “risk of ruin”. The unlimited loss can be mitigated by buying a further OTM Call, which caps upside losses but makes the position more expensive to open (i.e. the debit becomes larger) and removes some of the similarities to shorting 100 shares: theta becomes negative, vega and gamma become positive, and delta drops below -100.

## The Synthetic Long
A trader who wants to speculate on increasing price and increasing volatility can open a Synthetic Long. The trader may pay a small debit, receive a small credit, or open the trade for exactly $0.
Suppose stock XYZ is trading at $27. You forecast an increase in price and an increase in volatility.
You open a $27 Synthetic Long at exactly $0.00, no cost, to express this view. How is this possible? The $27 Put bid price is $3.25 and the $27 Call ask price is also $3.25, so when you sell the $27 Put you receive exactly $3.25 and you use that credit to pay for the $27 Call.

-
- The breakeven price for this trade is the exact price of the underlying when you entered since this structure behaves almost exactly like owning 100 shares of XYZ: theta, vega, and gamma are all roughly zero and delta is roughly +100.
The max loss on this position at expiry is theoretically very high but capped, since XYZ price can only decrease to zero. The max gain of a Synthetic Long is theoretically unlimited, since XYZ price can increase indefinitely. Since the loss on a Synthetic Long is theoretically very high (but not technically unlimited), this structure carries a high “risk of ruin”. The unlimited loss can be mitigated by buying a further OTM Put, which caps downside losses but makes the position more expensive to open (i.e. the debit becomes larger) and removes some of the similarities to owning 100 shares: theta becomes negative, vega and gamma become positive, and delta drops below +100.
Hopefully these strategy breakdowns are helpful! Again, the above strategies have significantly higher risk than some of those we’ve looked at in the past, and definitely aren’t for use by beginners!
Thank you as always for reading! Happy trading, and stay safe out there during all this headline risk!
NOTE: This post is not financial advice. The stock market is risky, and any trade or investment is expected to have some, or total, loss. Please do research before any trade. Do not use this information for investment decisions. Check terms on site for full terms. Agree to terms before considering this information.

reads.title: The PSYOP: The Untranslated Name Is a Weapon. How Western Media Runs Information Warfare on You, One Word at a Time.
reads.subtitle: Every one of these names is a thesis its owner wrote about itself. Western media leaves them untranslated on purpose, so you never read it. Not a style choice, but a psyop, and you are the target.
reads.body:
The West calls them the “Houthis.” They call themselves “Ansar Allah”, which means “Supporters of God.” That gap between the two names is NOT a translation choice, and it is not an accident. It is a weapon, and it is pointed at you.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Years ago I sat on a closed panel with a senior American diplomat in the Middle East who had run the Iran file for years, a person who advised policymakers at the highest level. This person rattled off a string of Iranian and regional groups by their Arabic and Persian names.
I made an offhand comment that they “seemed to be doing exactly what their names say”. This person went blank and did not know what a single one of those names actually meant. Here was someone literally shaping American foreign policy towards Iran and these other organizations whose own words s/he had never once translated, and it struck me that this was not one person’s blind spot. It was the whole system working the way it was built to.
Western media almost never translates these names. It “anglicizes” them and leaves them as “foreign noise”, so you NEVER stop to ask what these groups call themselves, or why. That is not laziness. It is one of the oldest and quietest techniques in information warfare, and it is being run on YOU every time you read the news.
I am not doing this article because I am “for” or “against” any of these groups. I try hard to be unbiased and view things from a strategic realism lens. Many are designated terrorist organizations that have killed enormous numbers of civilians. I am doing it to expose THE mechanism your own governments use, because a public that cannot read the words being used to manage it is a public being managed through psychological operation and control through language.
Subscribe now
Share
Get 7 day free trial
The tell: the Houthi rename

- As I said above, the group the West calls the “Houthis” calls itself Ansar Allah, “Supporters of God.” Watch what the media does in the gap between those two names, because that gap is the operation laid bare.

The group chose a movement name, a broad, faith-framed claim to legitimacy rooted in a confederation of tribes. Western media discards that and renames them after the surname of ONE family, Hussein al-Houthi, the founder.

The effect shows up in how YOU react. “The Houthis” sounds like ONE clan, a single bloodline, a private family feud, small and dismissible.

Ansar Allah sounds like a mass movement with a cause. The media picked the version that shrinks them, and it picked it consistently, across every outlet, for years.

This is the core psychological operation and a move against your understanding and worldview, and it does three things at once.

- It demeans, by reducing a movement to a household.

- It diminishes, by making a broad force sound like a faction.

- It divides, by planting the idea that this is one family’s war rather than a rooted, popular movement.
You were handed all three conclusions before you formed a single thought of your own. That is not reporting. It is perception management and a PSYOP, and the rename is the delivery mechanism.
The point is not that “Supporters of God” is the truer or more sympathetic label. It is a self-chosen name, a claim, exactly as any group’s name is a claim about itself. The operation is not that the media hides a flattering truth. It is that the media swaps in a version built to shape your reaction, then removes the group’s own words so you never notice the swap happened.
The same operation, run across the whole region
Once you know the technique, you see it everywhere, because it is applied to nearly EVERY group in the theater. Each of these names is a compressed statement of identity and intention, and each is kept untranslated so the statement never reaches you.

- “Hezbollah” means “Party of God.”

- Hassan “Nasrallah”, the Hezbollah leader assassinated by Israel, bore a name meaning “Victory of God.”

- Ayatollah, the clerical rank, means “Sign of God.”

- Hamas is an acronym of Harakat al-Muqawama al-Islamiyya, “Islamic Resistance Movement,” and the word hamas on its own means “zeal.”

- Jabhat al-Nusra, the group once led by the man now installed as Syria’s president, means “the Support Front.”

- Hayat Tahrir al-Sham, his rebrand, means “the Organization for the Liberation of the Levant,” a name that declares an ambition well beyond one country’s borders.
Share
Leave a comment
In Iraq the pattern holds.

- Kataib Hezbollah means “the Battalions of the Party of God.”

- Asaib Ahl al-Haq means “the League of the Righteous.”

- Ansar al-Islam means “Partisans of Islam.”

- The umbrella term “the Islamic Resistance” states its purpose in the open.

- Al-Qaeda means “the Base,” or “the Foundation.”

- The Taliban in Afghanistan means “the Students,” seekers of religious knowledge.

- Al-Shabab in Kenya means “the Youth,” its fuller name “Movement of the Mujahideen Youth,” and mujahideen means “those who wage jihad,” the strivers.
Wider still, the technique adapts.

- Boko Haram in Nigeria is not Arabic at all. It is a Hausa phrase meaning, roughly, “Western education is forbidden,” while its formal Arabic name, Jama’at Ahl al-Sunna li-Da’wa wal-Jihad, means “Group of the People of the Sunnah for Preaching and Jihad.”

- In Iran, the Janfada mobilization draws on the Persian jān-fadā, “self-sacrifice,” one who gives their life or soul.  The state’s own instruments carry it too.

- The IRGC is Sepah-e Pasdaran-e Enqelab-e Eslami, “the Army of the Guardians of the Islamic Revolution,” and its air-defense and engineering arm, Khatam al-Anbiya, means “Seal of the Prophets,” a title of the Prophet Muhammad himself.
Every one of these is a thesis, a self-written sentence about what the group is and what it means to do. And every one is kept untranslated, so the thesis is quarantined from the public that is funding the war against it.

-
-
> SIGNAL, not noise is a reader supported platform, please consider becoming a paid subscriber if you find my work insightful or if it resonates with you.
Kindly share, like, and restack to help amplify my SIGNAL.
Subscribe now
Why this is warfare, not translation policy
Call this what it is. In information warfare, you do not always need to lie. Often it works better to CONTROL what the target can and cannot understand, because a population that cannot read the words in front of it will accept the meaning you assign to them.
The untranslated name is a textbook case. The group’s own self-definition is removed, and into that vacuum the media installs its own frame, dismissive and flattening, and the public absorbs the frame believing it reached the conclusion itself.
The Effect
A public that knew these names meant “Supporters of God,” “Party of God,” or “the League of the Righteous” would ask sharper questions about the war fought in its name with their sons and daughters (i.e. why are we fighting the Supporters of God, why are we fighting the Party of God, why are we fighting the Leave of the Righteous and so on), because it would understand it is facing movements with coherent identities and mass followings, not disposable foreign syllables.
A public that hears ONLY untranslatable noise stays incurious, and an incurious public is the entire objective so you can volunteer and allow your sons and daughters to go to the next war without questioning any of it. Curiosity is what the operation is built to prevent, because curiosity leads to questions, and questions lead to answers, and if you answered those questions yourself, you would become a public that is harder to march into a war.
There is a darker layer under that, the oldest one in this kind of warfare. Strip a people of their meaning and you have begun dehumanizing them. A named, understood adversary is a human actor with reasons. An untranslated string of syllables is an abstraction, and abstractions are far easier to bomb, to kill, to blockade, and to starve, because the public feels nothing for a word it was never allowed to understand. The refusal to translate does the preparatory work of every war. It turns people into noise before the ordnance ever falls.
Again, this is not about getting your sympathy, on the contrary, this is to inform you of the operations being run on domestic audiences globally and everyone all at the same time especially in Western media and societies and more specifically across Europe and the Americas. The rest of the world calls them out by their actual meanings of their word, especially in the Arabic, Persian or other regional languages.
That is my from of strategic realism telling you how I see the world, and it cuts every way at once. Understanding what an adversary calls itself does NOT make the adversary “right”. Al-Qaeda calling itself “the Base” does not soften what it did. But refusing to know what it calls itself makes you a worse strategist, a worse citizen, and a more manipulable one. The translation is not sympathy. It is intelligence, in both senses of the word.
What to do with this information…
I am not asking you to admire any of these groups.  Never.
Understanding an adversary’s name is not endorsing its cause. Never.
I am asking you to see the military and Psychological Operation running on you, because that is the thing that actually threatens your ability to think clearly. Every name in this article is a sentence its owner wrote, and you were handed each one with the meaning cut out, then handed a replacement meaning by the same institutions selling you the war.
Share
That is information warfare in its purest and most deniable form.
No lie is told.
A word is simply left untranslated, and your understanding is shaped in the gap.
The counter is not to trust the groups. It is to translate everything, question every frame you did not build yourself, and treat every untranslated name as a place where someone decided what you were allowed to know. Once you start reading the words they left blank, you see the whole apparatus. And an operation you can see is one that no longer works on you.
I look beyond the headlines to find the SIGNAL, not the noise. If this gave you SIGNAL worth keeping, please follow, subscribe, and restack.
My subscribers, Signal Seekers and I are now Rising in World Politics right here on @Substack.
Signal, Not Noise!

reads.title: U.S. Makes, Israel Takes: The Real Story of U.S.-Israeli Military Cooperation
reads.subtitle: The Iron Beam laser and Arrow anti-ballistic missile systems are touted as examples of Israeli military ingenuity. But they were largely developed and financed by the U.S.
reads.body:
- Iron Beam high energy laser weapon systems are displayed during the Security Equipment International at London Excel on September 10, 2025 in London, England. Photo by John Keeble/Getty Images.Subscribe now
When Israel deployed its Iron Beam laser weapon for the first time last December, the announcement by leading Israeli defense firms Rafael and Elbit Systems was met with fawning coverage worldwide. The futuristic laser system, designed to shoot drones and rockets out of the sky, was celebrated as a demonstration of the Israeli weapons industry’s technological sophistication.
The Israeli Ministry of Defense described Iron Beam as “Israel’s first domestically developed laser interception system,” while touting the country as a pioneer in missile defense. The Arrow anti-ballistic missile system, another key example of Israel’s purportedly homegrown ingenuity, was heavily employed to defend from Iranian missile attacks during two recent wars.
That alleged ingenuity is at the center of a debate roiling Washington this month as Congress returns to debates about whether to create a new office in the Pentagon to coordinate U.S. and Israeli military research, testing, and industrial production, giving institutional architecture to a relationship that is already deeply intertwined on a de facto basis. The legislation, known as Section 219, was included in the House-passed National Defense Authorization Act, but remains contested in the Senate. Backers of the bill argue that tighter coordination with Israel should not be seen as a giveaway or cost to the United States, but rather is a boon to U.S. military capacity because the U.S. benefits more from the partnership than Israel. Arrow and Iron Beam are routinely held up as case studies of such innovation.
But the real story of how these weapons were developed is quite different. In fact, both weapons systems were developed and financed by the United States before being handed off to Israel by acts of Congress, according to government documents and interviews with key personnel involved in their development—despite warnings from U.S. intelligence agencies that transferring the tech to Israel effectively hands it over to U.S. adversaries such as China and Russia.
The pattern has long been cause for concern inside the intelligence community and among some in the Pentagon, but the mandates have come directly from Congress.
David Pyne, who worked as a civilian in the Pentagon office that oversaw development of the Arrow 2 program in the early 2000s, said it still bothered him that the American military put in so much work, and American taxpayers footed the bill, yet the U.S. couldn’t even fully benefit from the system. “They didn’t contribute a dime into the program, but the thing that pissed me off at the time, and obviously since, is that they would not share the final product,” said Pyne in relation to Israeli participation in the program.
Israel did spend money on the program, which is typically described as being split roughly down the middle by the U.S. and Israel. The U.S. directly contributed more than $4 billion, while Israel’s portion was paid for largely with U.S.-supplied foreign military financing.
That left Pyne frustrated at the amount of control Israel retained over the technology. “They wouldn’t allow us to use the technology we co-developed with them at 100% U.S. taxpayer expense,” Pyne said.
Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) became the primary contractor producing Arrow 2, though the U.S. maintained a veto over who it could be sold to, which it exercised at one point in the case of India. In 2002, Boeing cut a deal with IAI to make component parts for it, and the U.S. has ultimately been able to exploit some of the technology.
A veteran and former top national security aide to Sen. Mike Lee of Utah, Pyne currently serves as deputy executive director of the U.S. Task Force on National and Homeland Security. While working as a civilian for the Defense Department, Pyne traveled to Tel Aviv to try to work out an agreement in which the U.S. could benefit from the research it was carrying out and financing, but was repeatedly rebuffed, he said, eventually signing a lopsided agreement in June 2001. “I’d love to say that this was unusual, but I believe that was standard operating procedure for all missile defense systems we co-developed with Israel,” he said. “That was just what we were willing to agree to.” While public statements from the U.S. and Israel emphasized the joint nature of the program, he said, in reality the U.S. put in the work and the money, while Israel and Israeli companies got the benefit.
A former Pentagon contractor who worked on the Iron Beam project—speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitivity of the program—told Drop Site that even in the early 2000s, the program was controversial inside the Joint Technology Office. Congress had mandated the program’s details be shared with the Israelis, but the intelligence community refused to sign off on such knowledge transfers, they said, warning that Israel would immediately resell the technology to the Chinese.
A Defense Intelligence Agency report from 1999 backs up the contractor’s claim. The report was covered by the Washington Times in an article headlined “Israel Suspected of Transferring U.S. Laser Weapon Data to China.” The DIA found that Rafael had obtained restricted American technology from TRW Inc., the U.S. defense contractor running the THEL project, in 1996, which led TRW to halt further transfers. Israel responded with a tenacious pressure campaign on the State Department and the company’s subcontractors, trying to restart the technology transfers. The DIA also found evidence that Israel was routinely transferring the technology to China and covering up the arrangement from the U.S. TRW was bought by Northurp Grumman in 2002.
Intelligence analysts would even bring Israeli defense industry marketing brochures to meetings, the contractor said, to demonstrate how flagrantly Israel was advertising its willingness to sell secret American technology to China. “We had tons of intelligence to justify not sharing the information with Israel but we were under pressure from Congress to figure it out and transfer the IP to Israel,” said the contractor. “No matter how much evidence the intelligence community produced, the response we received from DOD leadership was that it’s congressionally mandated, therefore we have to execute on the program.”

-
- Iron Beam laser weapon. Photo: Israeli Ministry of Defense/Wikimedia Commons.

## To THEL and Back
In February 1996, at the White Sands Missile Range in New Mexico, the U.S. military for the first time successfully destroyed a mid-flight warhead with a laser. The program, called Nautilus, was officially a joint U.S.-Israeli collaboration, but as a later Government Accountability Office report confirmed, the U.S. military “provided primary management functions for the program” while the “Israel Ministry of Defense provided support.”
Two months later, President Bill Clinton met with Prime Minister Shimon Peres and agreed to enter into a deeper collaboration to produce a Tactical High-Energy Laser (THEL), backed by U.S. money and research, with the aim of producing a defensive weapon that could shoot down Hezbollah rockets at the Lebanese border.
At that point the program was operating under a memorandum of agreement, signed in 1996, that set out the terms of the deal. Lobbyists working on behalf of Israel kicked into gear. Between 1997 and 2001, the Israeli weapons maker Rafael and the Israeli Ministry of Defense spent more than $4.4 million lobbying Congress and the White House on weapons programs, according to foreign agent registration disclosures.
In 1999, using the NDAA—the same must-pass legislation lawmakers are currently using to further fuse the two militaries—Congress mandated the Secretary of Defense to develop a high-energy laser master plan and lay out funding needs. The next year’s NDAA ordered the implementation of that program—aligning it with the agreement tying the program to Israel—and designated a senior civilian official to oversee it. By the late 1990s, the U.S. had spent more than $100 million on the program. In 2004 and 2005, Congress set aside $17 million and then $8 million for the program.
A 2024 bill provided $1.2 billion to Israel to boost its laser program, with President Joe Biden visiting to celebrate the partnership. “We have reaffirmed the unshakeable commitment to the United States to Israel’s security, including partnering with Israel on the most cutting edge defense systems in the world, including the U.S. support for the Iron Dome and Israel’s new laser-enabled system called the Iron Beam,” he said. Under President Obama, the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding that pledged $38 billion over ten years to support Israel’s military.
The laser eventually shot down more than two dozen Katyusha rockets in tests, but the cost was soaring—more than $300 million at the time—and the chemicals used to produce the laser were deeply toxic and corrosive. The Joint Technology Office had also been researching steady-state lasers, less toxic and less corrosive to the equipment, but not enough advances had come along. So in 2005, THEL was canceled.
In 2007, Ehud Barak, who had returned to office as Israeli minister of defense, pushed to bring back the laser program, which Northrop Grumman was pursuing as “Skyguard,” but most of the investment and resources on missile defense were still directed to kinetic interceptors like the Iron Dome.
In the meantime, research continued on the solid-state laser program that would become Iron Beam, almost exclusively funded by the U.S. In 2019, Democratic Rep. Ted Lieu introduced H.R. 1795, the United States-Israel Directed Energy Cooperation Act. It was enacted the next year as part of the NDAA, instructing the Department of Defense to conduct laser research with Israel, citing THEL as the historical precedent. “THEL became Iron Beam,” the contractor said.
In a November 2023 Senate floor speech following the October 7 attacks, Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) urged her colleagues on the Senate Appropriations Committee to fund Israel’s missile defenses, calling for replenishing Iron Dome and David’s Sling and “investing in the development of the Iron Beam system,” as part of a push to win $1.2 billion in funding for the system. Congress ultimately approved the funding as part of an April 2024 national security supplemental, which appropriated $5.2 billion in total for Israeli missile defense, including the $1.2 billion requested specifically for Iron Beam.
What kind of lobbying effort was underway is less clear from federal records than it should be. After 2001, Rafael stopped filing as a foreign agent, and began filing under the Lobbying Disclosure Database, which is created for American companies or foreign companies acting independently of a foreign government, like British Petroleum. But Rafael is a 100% Israeli-state-owned company. By not filing as a foreign agent, the bulk of the company’s work remains obscured.
Rafael has received most of the public credit for the laser innovation, and controls the intellectual property, even as much of it was developed and funded by American taxpayers. Rafael did not respond to requests for comment for this story.
A review of public records also points to possible support from researchers at a variety of American universities, including Cornell University, for the project. Cornell, for instance, received a $100,000 grant from the Israeli Ministry of Defense (MOD)—money that likely originated with the U.S. Department of Defense—at the same time to provide research support to help improve fiber laser technology. This was one of several major financial contributions that the MOD made to Cornell researchers. The grants were noted in a 2020 announcement by the ministry’s research arm, the Directorate of Defense Research and Development (DDRD), which credited a decade of work by DDRD, Rafael, Elbit Systems, and unnamed academic institutions who contributed to the project.
By following a series of papers published by researchers at American universities, volunteer researchers with The Anti-War Initiative have been able to trace the incremental breakthroughs that culminated with Iron Beam.
Take Rafael Systems researcher Anatoly Parahovnik. Parahovnik became a research assistant at the University of Central Florida in the fall of 2017 specifically to help Rafael overcome engineering gaps, according to his LinkedIn and academic citations. Parahovnik was working on a central problem related to the laser technology: how to handle the extreme heat it created. According to his LinkedIn résumé, “After successfully introducing new technologies from academia at Rafael Advanced Defense Systems, [Parahovnik was] selected to pursue Ph.D. as means to close a gap the firm was experiencing in liquid cooling methods for cooling electronics.”
The position at the university was paid for by the MOD, according to an email provided to Drop Site from summer 2017. “I’m hiring a guy from RAFAEL and I want to make sure he will be supported for at least several semesters,” wrote his mentor Yoav Peles to the MOD, a request that was quickly approved. The email was obtained as part of an investigation by anti-war researcher Mila Halgren for Responsible Statecraft.

-
- A 2017 email from Tal Yehoshua of the Israeli Ministry of Defense to Yoav Peles at the University of Central Florida approving a request for research support.Parahovnik’s 2022 dissertation makes clear the work he was doing was directly useful to Rafael:

> The adiabatic thermalization mode at the micro scale under terrestrial conditions can be used to manage high frequency thermal loads, like radar, laser systems and a range of high-frequency applications. The nature of heat transfer pertinent to the piston effect in forced convection flows is poorly understood, but if properly revealed, it holds great potential to revolutionize copious critical technologies that depend on effective thermal transport.
A key 2020 research paper, co-authored by Parahovnik and his UCF mentor Peles, notes that the work was “funded mainly by the Office of Naval Research” as well as the Israel Ministry of Defense. “The authors would like to acknowledge the Cornell NanoScale Science & Technology Facility (CNF) for staﬀ support, help, and use of facilities in the fabrication of the microdevices,” it goes on. The paper was published in Physical Review Applied and titled, “Subcooled Flow Boiling of Carbon Dioxide Near the Critical Point Inside a Microchannel.” Another paper, presented that year at the 2020 Intersociety Conference on Thermal and Thermomechanical Phenomena in Electronic Systems, includes a similar acknowledgment. A 2021 paper in the International Journal of Heat and Mass Transfer included the same funding disclosure.
Another Rafael researcher identified by The Anti-War Initiative, Tomer Rokita, came to the University of Michigan for a year of research on hypersonics. The involvement of U.S. universities in the program reflects a broader phenomenon of Israel drawing on the support of elite U.S. researchers to help advance its defense programs. American institutions and companies are producing the breakthroughs, paid for by U.S. taxpayers—sometimes routed through the Israeli MOD—yet it is Israeli companies who claim the IP and profit from sales of the new technology.

-
- U.S. National Security Adviser Susan Rice gives a speech to the press in front of the Israeli missile system "Arrow II" at the Palmachim Airbase on May 9, 2014 in Rishon LeZion, Israel. Photo by Ilia Yefimovich/Getty Images.

## Broken Arrows
The Arrow program began in the late 1980s under the Reagan administration’s Strategic Defense Initiative, with the United States committing to fund the development of an Israeli interceptor capable of destroying ballistic missiles. By 1993, the U.S. government had already committed roughly $390 million to Arrow and its follow-on experiments, according to the Government Accountability Office, which warned at the time that Washington risked being drawn into financing much of the complete system—including its missiles, launchers and radar—without independently assessing its overall costs or alternatives.
That support continued as Arrow evolved from an experimental interceptor into a multilayered operational system that boasted new and more advanced capabilities. The Arrow 2 is designed to intercept ballistic missiles in or near the atmosphere, while Arrow 3 targets them at greater ranges and altitudes, outside the atmosphere.
Congressional appropriations records indicate that the United States had provided just over $4 billion for the Arrow program by fiscal year 2021. Subsequent appropriations for Arrow 2 and Arrow 3 bring the cumulative public total to approximately $5 billion.
U.S. financing remains embedded in Arrow’s current procurement. The Missile Defense Agency’s fiscal year 2026 procurement justification records $609 million in prior-year procurement funding for Arrow 3 components, followed by $80 million in fiscal year 2024, $50 million in 2025 and a requested $100 million in 2026.
The Iron Beam technology meanwhile has been hailed as a solution to the problems created by modern missile defense systems, where expensive and slow-to-manufacture interceptor munitions are required to shoot down cheaper missiles and drones that can be fired in abundance. Israel has touted its deployment of Iron Beam during the recent war in Lebanon, portraying it as an example of the country’s military ingenuity despite its origins in decades of U.S. military assistance.
But even then this system, created with tremendous U.S. financial assistance and other forms of handholding, is not a panacea to the problems faced by Israel in its wars.
The directed laser does not work effectively in all weather conditions and requires the operator to maintain a consistent lock on a moving target for an extended period of time. Consequently, the system is less likely to solve the challenging mathematics of missile interception than to place an additional band-aid on diminishing U.S. and Israeli interceptor stockpiles.
Regardless of the shortcomings of the system, more such joint projects are likely to be developed with the support of U.S. taxpayers as Congress searches for ways to defend against ever-cheaper drones and missiles, while also responding to a push from Israel lobby organizations in Washington to merge the country’s defense sectors in a way that future administrations will find difficult to unwind—whether the American public likes it or not.
