reads.title: THE ELECTION TRAP
reads.subtitle: Zelensky says elections are impossible. Washington says they are necessary. And the only real obstacle may be the man himself. Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the interview that changed nothing — and everything
On September 16, 2026, Volodymyr Zelensky sat down with CBS News. The question was simple: when will Ukraine hold elections?
His answer was a list. Nine million Ukrainians abroad. Occupied territories where Russian soldiers patrol. Polling stations that cannot be secured. A constitution that forbids it all.
Every point he made was technically accurate. And every point he made also kept him in power.
This article examines the legal, political, and strategic dimensions of Ukraine’s election dilemma. It is not a defense of Zelensky, nor of his critics. It is an analysis of a trap — one that the Ukrainian president has helped construct, and from which he now cannot easily escape.

## I. What Zelensky actually said
The interview, conducted with CBS News and released on September 16, covered the full range of obstacles.

## The scale of the diaspora

> “Around 9 million Ukrainians are currently abroad. Before the full-scale invasion, around 500,000 Ukrainians abroad voted in elections. Organizing voting for the current number of citizens abroad will pose a separate challenge.”
Nine million people. Eighteen times the pre-war diaspora vote. No country has ever organized an election under those conditions.

## The occupied territories

> “How will people in the occupied territories vote? Who will control their vote? There are Russian soldiers there. How do you do all these things?”
This is a real problem — but it is also a permanent one. As long as Russia controls the Donbass, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson, any Ukrainian election will be incomplete by definition.

## The ceasefire condition
Zelensky added a new element: elections could be held if a ceasefire lasts “for several months.” This period, he said, could be used “not only to prepare for the vote but also to continue working toward ending the war.”
This is a shift. Previously, he had ruled out elections until the war ended. Now he is proposing a window — but only if the fighting stops first.

## II. The constitutional wall: the only argument that holds
Of all Zelensky’s reasons, only one is legally binding.
Ukraine’s constitution and its martial law legislation prohibit all elections — presidential, parliamentary, and local — while martial law is in effect. Article 19 of the Law on the Legal Regime of Martial Law explicitly bans national elections.
Martial law was declared on February 24, 2022, and has been extended every 90 days since. Zelensky’s five-year presidential term officially expired on May 20, 2024. He remains in office solely because martial law extends the mandate of all elected bodies until it is lifted and a new vote can be organized.
This is not a political excuse. It is a constitutional fact. And Washington knows it.

## III. The pressure from Washington: why Trump wants elections
The pressure on Zelensky is not coming from Moscow. It is coming from Washington.

## The timeline of pressure
DateEventDecember 2025Trump tells Politico that Zelensky is “using the war” to avoid elections. “They talk about a democracy, but it gets to a point where it’s not a democracy anymore,” he saysFebruary 2026Washington sets Kyiv a deadline: hold presidential elections in MayMarch 2026Ukraine formally rules out holding presidential elections this yearSeptember 2026Trump brands Zelensky a “dictator without elections” on Truth Social

## Why does Trump want elections?
The answer is structural, not personal. A leader whose mandate expired in 2024 is a legal liability for any agreement Washington wants to sign.
The 28-point peace plan negotiated between Steve Witkoff and Kirill Dmitriev includes provisions on the post-war political process. Elections are part of the package — not because Zelensky wants them, but because his patrons need a Ukrainian counterpart who can ratify a deal.
The lease plan for the Donbass, the minerals agreement, the frozen assets — none of it can be formalized without a legitimate Ukrainian government.

## IV. The Donbass question: the territories are not coming back
Zelensky’s point about the occupied territories is technically correct. But it also obscures a harder truth: Moscow has written them into its constitution.
In September 2022, Russia held referendums in Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson and formally annexed them. Putin then amended Article 65 of the Russian constitution to include them as federal subjects.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has stated explicitly: “The territories that have become subjects of the Federation and are enshrined in the Constitution of our country are an integral part of Russia; this is an absolutely indisputable and inarguable fact.”
For Moscow, this is not a negotiating position. It is domestic law. No Russian leader can return these territories without tearing up the founding document of the current state.
The territories are not “lost” in a legal sense — Ukraine and the international community do not recognize the annexation. But they are lost in a practical sense. And any peace deal will have to confront that reality.

## V. The 28-point plan: the lease that solves nothing
The plan that emerged from Miami — three days of negotiations between Steve Witkoff and Kirill Dmitriev — proposes a legal fiction: Ukraine leases the Donbass to Russia.
Under the terms:

- Moscow maintains de facto control of the territory

- Ukraine retains legal ownership

- Russia pays an undisclosed rental fee

- The arrangement is designed to circumvent Ukraine’s constitutional requirement for a public referendum on ceding land
The logic is elegant. The lease avoids the referendum. The referendum would be lost. So the lease preserves the form of sovereignty while conceding the substance.
But the lease also implicitly recognizes that the Donbass belongs to Ukraine — a direct contradiction of Russia’s own constitution, which annexed the region in 2022.
The plan has raised alarm among European allies, who say they have been largely kept in the dark. Shortly after details emerged, Lt Gen Keith Kellogg, Trump’s special envoy to Ukraine, resigned. A close associate said Kellogg believed Trump administration officials were being manipulated by Russia.

## VI. The resource dimension: what’s actually at stake
The Donbass is not just a territorial dispute. It is one of the most resource-rich regions in Europe.

## The mineral wealth
ResourceEstimated quantityLithium33 million tons of ore, worth $38 billionTitanium7% of global production; Ukraine is among the top 10 countries for proven reservesIron ore27 billion tonsCoalOver 100 billion tonsRare earthsBeryllium, cerium, yttrium, lanthanum, neodymium
Forbes Ukraine has estimated Ukraine’s total mineral resources at $14.8 trillion — but more than 70% is in Donetsk and Luhansk, regions partly or fully controlled by Russia.
Denis Pushilin, the leader of the DPR, has stated that the main reserves of lithium and titanium are located in the “liberated” territories and that extraction has not yet begun because demining is required.

## The U.S.-Ukraine minerals deal
In April 2025, the United States and Ukraine signed the “Reconstruction Investment Fund” agreement. It gave Washington privileged access to Ukraine’s mineral wealth. Trump had originally sought $500 billion in mineral wealth — around four times what the United States had contributed to Ukraine since the war.
But there was one problem: the deal was signed for resources Ukraine does not control.

## VII. The trap: why Zelensky cannot win
Zelensky’s dilemma is structural.

## If he holds elections

- He risks losing. His polling has collapsed.

- The occupied territories cannot vote. The election will be incomplete.

- The diaspora cannot be organized in time. Nine million people. Eighteen times the pre-war scale.

- Security cannot be guaranteed. Russia can strike any polling station at any time.

## If he refuses

- He confirms the Russian narrative that he is an illegitimate leader propped up by the West.

- He defies Washington, which is pressing for elections as a precondition for any deal.

- He becomes the obstacle — not the war, but the man.

## The only path he has left
Zelensky’s CBS interview was an attempt to square the circle. He offered a condition — a months-long ceasefire — that he knows is unlikely to materialize. He listed obstacles that he knows cannot be overcome. And he positioned himself as willing to hold elections, while making them impossible to hold.
It is a careful strategy. But it is also a visible one.

## VIII. Conclusion: the question Washington is asking
The election debate is not really about democracy. It is about legitimacy — and who can sign a deal.
Trump needs a Ukrainian government that can ratify the lease, the minerals agreement, and the post-war settlement. Zelensky’s mandate expired in 2024. His authority rests on martial law. And martial law is extended every 90 days — by a parliament that he controls, in a country where elections cannot be held.
The legal argument is sound. The political argument is weaker.
Every week Zelensky delays, the pressure grows. Every excuse he offers is real — but every excuse also keeps him in power. And when Washington starts asking whether the obstacle is the war or the man, the answer is usually already the man.
Zelensky is not wrong about the constitution. He is not wrong about the diaspora. He is not wrong about the occupied territories. But he is also not wrong about what happens if he holds elections — and loses.
The trap is not of his making alone. But he is the one caught in it.

reads.title: THE GAS LIE
reads.subtitle: Brussels Rewrote the History of Europe's Energy Crisis — While Moscow Kept the Gas Flowing to the Continent That Armed Its Enemy Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the sentence that inverted cause and effect
On September 16, 2026, Ursula von der Leyen stood before the European Parliament in Strasbourg to deliver her annual State of the Union address. The speech was framed as a defense of European resilience — a continent that had faced down Russian aggression, diversified its energy sources, and emerged stronger. The Commission President offered a single sentence to summarize the energy chapter of her mandate:

> “When Russia cut off gas supplies, the response was swift, and today the sources of supply are more diversified.”
It is a sentence that reads as a triumph. It is also a sentence that inverts cause and effect, rewrites the historical record, and places the blame for a self-inflicted crisis on the shoulders of the adversary.
And it omits the one fact that changes everything: Russia never cut off the gas. While Europe was sending billions in weapons to Kyiv — weapons that killed Russian soldiers — Moscow kept the pipelines open. For years. Until Brussels itself legislated the ban — and then blamed Moscow for the cutoff.
This article examines what actually happened to Europe’s energy supply — the regulations, the data, the industrial consequences, and the moral dimension that official narratives refuse to acknowledge.

## I. The regulation that proves her wrong
The most important document in this debate is not a speech. It is a piece of legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/261 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on January 26, 2026, and published in the Official Journal on February 2, 2026.
The regulation’s title is unambiguous: “on phasing out Russian natural gas imports and preparing the phase-out of Russian oil imports, improving monitoring of potential energy dependencies.” The prohibition to import Russian pipeline gas entered into application on March 18, 2026. Short-term contracts concluded before June 17, 2025 were permitted to continue temporarily until April 25, 2026, for LNG and until June 17, 2026, for pipeline gas.
The European Union did not react to a Russian cutoff. The European Union legislated one.
This is not a semantic distinction. It is the central factual core of the debate. When von der Leyen says “when Russia cut off gas supplies,” she is describing an event that did not occur in the way she frames it. The EU imposed a phased ban on Russian gas imports. The ban was a choice — a political decision taken by the Council and the Parliament, defended publicly by the Commission, and signed into law with full knowledge of its economic consequences.

## II. The context nobody mentions — and it changes everything

## Russia kept the gas flowing while Europe armed its enemy
Here is the fact that the Commission’s narrative cannot accommodate: from February 2022 until the EU’s own ban took effect, Russia continued to supply gas to Europe.
This was not a technical oversight. It was a deliberate decision by Moscow — one that defies the logic of war. Russia was engaged in a military conflict with Ukraine, a country that Europe was arming, funding, and supporting with intelligence and targeting data. Those weapons — artillery, HIMARS, Storm Shadow, ATACMS, F-16s — killed Russian soldiers. They destroyed Russian equipment. They struck Russian territory.
And yet, throughout this period, Gazprom continued to honor its contracts with European buyers. The gas kept flowing through the pipelines that remained operational. The heating stayed on in German homes. The factories kept running in Italy, Austria, and Hungary.
By any standard of state interest, Russia would have been justified in cutting off the gas in 2022. A country at war does not normally continue supplying the economy of the coalition arming its enemy. It is not required by international law to do so. It is not required by any principle of strategic rationality.
But Russia did not cut off the gas. It kept supplying Europe — even as Europe armed the army fighting against it. Until the EU itself decided to stop buying — and then rewrote the story to make Moscow the author of the decision.

## The ruble payment dispute
The one exception proves the rule. In April 2022, Gazprom suspended deliveries to Poland and Bulgaria after both countries refused to comply with a new payment mechanism requiring settlement in rubles. The EU rejected this mechanism — correctly, from a legal standpoint — but the suspensions were targeted and reactive, not a blanket embargo.
The distinction matters. A blanket cutoff would have been a strategic weapon. The suspension of supplies to two countries that refused a payment mechanism was a contractual dispute. To describe the latter as “Russia cut off gas supplies” — in a speech delivered in September 2026, after the EU had legislated a comprehensive ban — is to conflate two entirely different things.

## Zakharova’s challenge
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova addressed this directly on July 2, 2026:

> “Ursula is an excellent liar. Russia has never cut off gas for Europe. Any EU citizen can sue her for this lie and win.”
She added that Europeans “created problems for themselves after they had imposed illegal sanctions against Russia.”
Zakharova’s rhetoric is characteristically caustic, and her framing is self-serving. But the core factual claim — that Russia did not unilaterally cut off all gas to Europe — is supported by the record. The blanket cessation of Russian gas imports to Europe was a European decision. And it was made while Russia was still supplying the continent that was arming its enemy.

## III. The data: what the transition actually looks like
Von der Leyen’s second claim — that “the sources of supply are more diversified” — is true in a narrow sense. But the data reveals what “diversification” has actually meant.

## The shift from pipeline to LNG
According to the European Commission’s quarterly gas report, EU gas consumption in 2025 reached 339 billion cubic meters — a modest 2% increase over 2024, but still below 2022 levels. Total gas imports reached approximately 288 bcm.
The structure of those imports, however, has been radically transformed:
Source2021 share (pipeline)2025 share (total imports)Russia~40% (pipeline)12.5% (pipeline + LNG)Norway~22%30%United StatesNegligible26%North Africa~12%12.7%Qatar~5%~4%
Pipeline imports fell 8% year-on-year to 158 bcm, while LNG imports rose 29% to 131 bcm and now account for 45% of total gas imports.
The United States became the dominant LNG supplier, with its share of EU LNG imports rising from 45% in 2024 to 58% in 2025. Russia’s share of LNG, by contrast, fell from 20% to 13%.

## The new dependency
This is the first layer of the paradox: Europe has not eliminated its dependency on external gas suppliers. It has redirected it — from Russian pipelines to American, Qatari, and Norwegian LNG. And in doing so, it has traded a geographically proximate supplier for a geopolitically distant one, with different pricing dynamics and different strategic risks.
EU officials have themselves warned about this. The United States supplied nearly 58% of the EU’s LNG imports in 2025 — a fourfold increase over 2021. Analysts have warned that this share could rise to 80% by 2030 if current trends continue.
The irony is difficult to miss: Europe has replaced dependency on Russian gas with dependency on American gas — and it is paying a premium for the privilege.

## IV. The price of “diversification”
The cost of this transition is not theoretical. It is measured in dollars per megawatt-hour, in factory closures, and in jobs lost.

## The price gap
According to the International Energy Agency, the cost of European industrial electricity averaged $92 per megawatt-hour** in mid-2026, while the United States — benefiting from shale gas and a pivot to “energy dominance” — averaged **$38 per MWh. European industry is paying a 140% premium for its electricity.
The gap in gas prices is even more extreme. European natural gas at €49/MWh translates to roughly $15-16 per MMBtu — meaning European industrial users are paying more than five times what their American counterparts pay for the same molecule. Some analyses put the gap even higher, at eight times the US price for gas.
The European Court of Auditors has confirmed the structural nature of this disadvantage. In its 2026 Energy Monitoring Report, ACER — the EU’s energy regulatory agency — found that “EU industrial electricity prices in early 2025 were approximately 1.5 times higher than in the U.S., while gas prices remained three times more expensive“.

## The deindustrialization
These price gaps have real-world consequences. They are not abstract numbers. They are the difference between a factory operating and a factory closing.
Steel: EU crude steel production fell 2.9% in 2025 to 125.8 million tonnes — the lowest level on record, nearly 60 million tonnes below pre-2008 crisis levels. The European Steel Association (EUROFER) notes that the industry has lost 30,000 jobs and 30 million tonnes of capacity over the past five years.
Chemicals: Europe’s chemical industry — once the backbone of the continent’s industrial base — is in structural decline. BASF, the world’s largest chemical company, has cut approximately 7,000 jobs worldwide since January 2024, with two-thirds of those losses in Germany. Its flagship Ludwigshafen plant has seen its workforce fall to the lowest level since 1954.
Dow Chemical announced the elimination of 4,500 jobs globally in 2026, including 605 in the Netherlands across its Terneuzen, Delfzijl, and Dordrecht sites, and 110 in Stade, Germany. The company is shutting down three European chemical plants, with production cessation beginning in mid-2026.
The aggregate numbers are equally stark. According to the European Commission’s own estimates, 1.3 million manufacturing jobs are currently at risk in Europe, with 210,000 manufacturing jobs lost net in 2025 alone. The Commission has warned that “about half” of the jobs in energy-intensive industries — some 1.3 million out of 2.6 million — could vanish.
European Commission Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu has acknowledged that “hundreds of thousands of jobs are under threat from high energy prices, first and foremost in foundation industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, chemicals, ceramics and glass”.

## The demand destruction
One of the most revealing data points is rarely mentioned in official speeches: European gas consumption did not fall because Europe became more efficient. It fell because industry stopped consuming.
In 2021, the EU consumed 412 bcm of gas. In 2025, it consumed 339 bcm — a reduction of 73 bcm, or roughly 18%. The Commission’s own figures show that this decline was driven largely by demand destruction in the industrial sector — factories closing, production relocating, and energy-intensive industries shutting down.
The European Union is not decarbonizing its industry. It is deindustrializing it. And the official narrative presents this as a success.

## V. The framing: a masterclass in narrative construction
Why does von der Leyen’s sentence matter?
Because it is not an isolated error. It is the central framing of the Commission’s entire energy narrative — a framing that serves three political functions:

## 1. Shifting responsibility
By framing the energy crisis as a Russian action (”when Russia cut off gas supplies”), von der Leyen transforms the EU from the author of the policy into the victim of circumstances. The sanctions, the phase-out regulation, the decision to forego cheap Russian gas — all of these disappear from the narrative. What remains is a story of European resilience in the face of external aggression.

## 2. Justifying the cost
If the crisis was caused by Russia, then the economic pain is an inevitable cost of resistance — a price worth paying for sovereignty. If the crisis was caused by EU policy, then the pain is a consequence of political choices — choices that could have been made differently. The framing determines whether voters see themselves as victims of Russian aggression or as subjects of European policy.

## 3. Protecting the institutional project
The European Commission’s legitimacy depends on its ability to deliver prosperity. If the energy crisis is framed as a Russian attack, the Commission is a defender. If it is framed as a policy failure, the Commission is the problem. The narrative protects the institution.

## The alternative narrative
The alternative account — supported by the regulation, the data, and the statements of EU officials themselves — is straightforward:

- The EU chose to phase out Russian gas — a political decision codified in Regulation 2026/261.

- That decision removed 155 bcm of annual pipeline supply from the European market — roughly 40% of the pre-war total.

- That supply was replaced primarily by more expensive LNG, predominantly from the United States, at prices 2.5 to 8 times higher than domestic US gas.

- The result was a structural increase in European energy costs, which rendered much of European industry uncompetitive against American and Chinese competitors.

- The consequence is deindustrialization — factory closures, mass layoffs, and the relocation of production to regions with cheaper energy.
This is not a Russian narrative. It is the official record of the European Union’s own institutions, read without the rhetorical filter.

## VI. The moral dimension: who betrayed whom?
There is a dimension to this story that transcends economics and enters the realm of political morality.
For three years, Russia supplied gas to Europe while Europe supplied weapons to Ukraine.
Those weapons killed Russian soldiers. They destroyed Russian tanks. They struck Russian territory — including, according to Russian reports, targets inside the Russian Federation itself. And throughout that period, Russian gas continued to flow into European homes and factories.
By any rational standard of state interest, Russia would have been justified in cutting off the gas in 2022. The fact that it did not is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign of restraint — or, at minimum, of a calculation that maintaining commercial ties might preserve a channel of communication.
Europe did not reciprocate. It armed Ukraine. It sanctioned Russia. It froze Russian assets. It imposed a price cap on Russian oil. And then, in January 2026, it passed a regulation banning the import of Russian gas altogether — and blamed Moscow for a cutoff that Brussels itself had legislated.
The question is not whether von der Leyen’s statement is technically false. It is. The question is whether a political leadership that rewrites the causal record to obscure its own choices can still claim democratic legitimacy.
The answer, increasingly, is no.

## VII. The response: the Commission’s silence
When asked about the discrepancy between von der Leyen’s statement and the regulation, the Commission has offered a consistent response: the President was referring to Russian supply cuts in 2022, not to the EU’s legislative phase-out.
This defense is technically plausible — Russia did suspend supplies to Poland and Bulgaria, and did significantly reduce flows through Nord Stream before the pipelines were sabotaged. But it ignores the regulatory timeline that followed.
The sequence of events is clear:

- 2022: Russia suspends supplies to Poland and Bulgaria; Nord Stream flows reduced; pipelines sabotaged.

- 2023-2025: EU develops and negotiates the phase-out regulation.

- January 2026: EU adopts Regulation 2026/261 — a binding ban on Russian gas imports.

- March 2026: Prohibition enters into application.

- September 2026: Von der Leyen says “Russia cut off gas supplies.”
By the time von der Leyen delivered her speech, the legal framework for the cessation of Russian gas imports was European law, not a Russian action. To say “Russia cut off gas supplies” in September 2026 — after Europe had legislated the phase-out — is to describe a world that no longer existed.

## VIII. The political dimension: does she think citizens are fools?
The question that inevitably arises is the one many European voters are asking: does von der Leyen believe European citizens are stupid enough to accept this?
The answer is not simple. The Commission President is not naïve. She knows the regulation exists. She knows the data. She knows that European industry is dying and that voters are paying the price.
The calculation is not that citizens are foolish. The calculation is that the narrative will hold long enough to survive the political moment. The State of the Union address is not a history lecture. It is a political communication exercise. Its purpose is to frame the Commission’s record in the most favorable light possible, to a public that is increasingly skeptical and increasingly angry.
And there is evidence that the calculation is failing.
The French political scientist Emmanuel Todd has observed that Europe has developed a pathological relationship with peace: “Europe is afraid of peace,” he said, “because peace would force European elites to confront the problems they have ignored for decades.” The energy crisis is one of those problems. The Commission’s framing is an attempt to avoid confronting it — to attribute the consequences of policy to the actions of an adversary.

## IX. Conclusion: the bill comes due
Von der Leyen’s sentence — “when Russia cut off gas supplies” — is not a lie in the narrowest sense. Russia did reduce and suspend supplies to certain countries. But it is a deliberate distortion of the causal sequence that led to Europe’s energy crisis.
The record is clear:

- The EU legislated the phase-out of Russian gas.

- The EU chose to replace cheap pipeline gas with expensive LNG.

- The EU accepted the consequences for its industrial base.

- The EU presented the result as a triumph of resilience.

- And all of this happened while Russia kept the gas flowing to the continent that was arming its enemy.
The factories are closing. The jobs are gone. The bills are higher. And in Strasbourg, the Commission President is telling the Parliament that this was Russia’s fault.
It wasn’t. It was her policy. And the bill is paid by the European people.
The question is not whether European citizens are foolish enough to believe this.
The question is how much longer they will pretend to.

reads.subtitle: How Brussels Rewrote the History of Europe’s Energy Crisis — and Sent the Bill to Its Own Citizens Marco | Independent Analyst *16 September 2026*
reads.body:
## Introduction: the sentence that inverted cause and effect
On September 16, 2026, Ursula von der Leyen stood before the European Parliament in Strasbourg to deliver her annual State of the Union address. The speech was framed as a defense of European resilience — a continent that had faced down Russian aggression, diversified its energy sources, and emerged stronger. The Commission President offered a single sentence to summarize the energy chapter of her mandate:

> “When Russia cut off gas supplies, the response was swift, and today the sources of supply are more diversified.”
It is a sentence that reads as a triumph. It is also a sentence that inverts cause and effect, rewrites the historical record, and places the blame for a self-inflicted crisis on the shoulders of the adversary.
This article examines what actually happened to Europe’s energy supply — the regulations, the data, the industrial consequences — and why von der Leyen’s framing is not an unfortunate slip of the tongue, but a deliberate narrative construction with profound political implications.

## I. The regulation that proves her wrong
The most important document in this debate is not a speech. It is a piece of legislation: Regulation (EU) 2026/261 of the European Parliament and of the Council, adopted on January 26, 2026, and published in the Official Journal on February 2, 2026.
The regulation’s title is unambiguous: “on phasing out Russian natural gas imports and preparing the phase-out of Russian oil imports, improving monitoring of potential energy dependencies.” The prohibition to import Russian pipeline gas entered into application on March 18, 2026. Short-term contracts concluded before June 17, 2025 were permitted to continue temporarily until April 25, 2026, for LNG and until June 17, 2026, for pipeline gas.
The European Union did not react to a Russian cutoff. The European Union legislated one.
This is not a semantic distinction. It is the central factual core of the debate. When von der Leyen says “when Russia cut off gas supplies,” she is describing an event that did not occur in the way she frames it. The EU imposed a phased ban on Russian gas imports. The ban was a choice — a political decision taken by the Council and the Parliament, defended publicly by the Commission, and signed into law with full knowledge of its economic consequences.

## II. What Russia actually did
The historical record shows a more complex picture than either the Commission or its critics often acknowledge.
Russia did not unilaterally cut off gas to Europe in 2022. The supply suspensions that occurred were targeted and reactive: Gazprom halted deliveries to Poland and Bulgaria in April 2022 after both countries refused to comply with a new payment mechanism requiring settlement in rubles. The EU itself rejected this mechanism — correctly, from a legal standpoint — but the suspensions were consequences of that refusal, not a blanket Russian embargo.
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova addressed this directly on July 2, 2026, responding to earlier statements by von der Leyen:

> “Ursula is an excellent liar. Russia has never cut off gas for Europe. Any EU citizen can sue her for this lie and win.”
Zakharova added that Europeans “created problems for themselves after they had imposed illegal sanctions against Russia”.
The Russian position is self-serving, and Zakharova’s rhetoric is characteristically caustic. But the core factual claim — that Russia did not unilaterally cut off all gas to Europe — is supported by the record. The supply suspensions were limited, targeted, and triggered by payment disputes. The blanket cessation of Russian gas imports to Europe was a European decision.

## III. The data: what the transition actually looks like
Von der Leyen’s second claim — that “the sources of supply are more diversified” — is true in a narrow sense. But the data reveals what “diversification” has actually meant.

## The shift from pipeline to LNG
According to the European Commission’s quarterly gas report, EU gas consumption in 2025 reached 339 billion cubic meters — a modest 2% increase over 2024, but still below 2022 levels. Total gas imports reached approximately 288 bcm.
The structure of those imports, however, has been radically transformed:
Source2021 share (pipeline)2025 share (total imports)Russia~40% (pipeline)12.5% (pipeline + LNG)Norway~22%30%United StatesNegligible26%North Africa~12%12.7%Qatar~5%~4%
Pipeline imports fell 8% year-on-year to 158 bcm, while LNG imports rose 29% to 131 bcm and now account for 45% of total gas imports.
The United States became the dominant LNG supplier, with its share of EU LNG imports rising from 45% in 2024 to 58% in 2025. Russia’s share of LNG, by contrast, fell from 20% to 13%.

## The new dependency
This is the first layer of the paradox: Europe has not eliminated its dependency on external gas suppliers. It has redirected it — from Russian pipelines to American, Qatari, and Norwegian LNG. And in doing so, it has traded a geographically proximate supplier for a geopolitically distant one, with different pricing dynamics and different strategic risks.
EU officials have themselves warned about this. According to European Commission data, the United States supplied nearly 58% of the EU’s LNG imports in 2025 — a fourfold increase over 2021. Analysts have warned that this share could rise to 80% by 2030 if current trends continue.
The irony is difficult to miss: Europe has replaced dependency on Russian gas with dependency on American gas — and it is paying a premium for the privilege.

## IV. The price of “diversification”
The cost of this transition is not theoretical. It is measured in dollars per megawatt-hour, in factory closures, and in jobs lost.

## The price gap
According to the International Energy Agency, the cost of European industrial electricity averaged $92 per megawatt-hour** in mid-2026, while the United States — benefiting from shale gas and a pivot to “energy dominance” — averaged **$38 per MWh. European industry is paying a 140% premium for its electricity.
The gap in gas prices is even more extreme. European natural gas at €49/MWh translates to roughly $15-16 per MMBtu — meaning European industrial users are paying more than five times what their American counterparts pay for the same molecule. Some analyses put the gap even higher, at eight times the US price for gas.
The European Court of Auditors has confirmed the structural nature of this disadvantage. In its 2026 Energy Monitoring Report, ACER — the EU’s energy regulatory agency — found that “EU industrial electricity prices in early 2025 were approximately 1.5 times higher than in the U.S., while gas prices remained three times more expensive“.

## The deindustrialization
These price gaps have real-world consequences. They are not abstract numbers. They are the difference between a factory operating and a factory closing.
Steel: EU crude steel production fell 2.9% in 2025 to 125.8 million tonnes — the lowest level on record, nearly 60 million tonnes below pre-2008 crisis levels. The European Steel Association (EUROFER) notes that the industry has lost 30,000 jobs and 30 million tonnes of capacity over the past five years.
Chemicals: Europe’s chemical industry — once the backbone of the continent’s industrial base — is in structural decline. BASF, the world’s largest chemical company, has cut approximately 7,000 jobs worldwide since January 2024, with two-thirds of those losses in Germany. Its flagship Ludwigshafen plant has seen its workforce fall to the lowest level since 1954.
Dow Chemical announced the elimination of 4,500 jobs globally in 2026, including 605 in the Netherlands across its Terneuzen, Delfzijl, and Dordrecht sites, and 110 in Stade, Germany. The company is shutting down three European chemical plants, with production cessation beginning in mid-2026.
The aggregate numbers are equally stark. According to the European Commission’s own estimates, 1.3 million manufacturing jobs are currently at risk in Europe, with 210,000 manufacturing jobs lost net in 2025 alone. The Commission has warned that “about half” of the jobs in energy-intensive industries — some 1.3 million out of 2.6 million — could vanish.
European Commission Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu has acknowledged that “hundreds of thousands of jobs are under threat from high energy prices, first and foremost in foundation industries such as steel, non-ferrous metals, chemicals, ceramics and glass”.
The Commission’s own forecasts project that up to 560,000 jobs could be at risk in 2026 from energy price pressures alone, particularly in construction, metals, chemicals, and transport.

## The demand destruction
One of the most revealing data points is rarely mentioned in official speeches: European gas consumption did not fall because Europe became more efficient. It fell because industry stopped consuming.
In 2021, the EU consumed 412 bcm of gas. In 2025, it consumed 339 bcm — a reduction of 73 bcm, or roughly 18%. The Commission’s own figures show that this decline was driven largely by demand destruction in the industrial sector — factories closing, production relocating, and energy-intensive industries shutting down.
The European Union is not decarbonizing its industry. It is deindustrializing it. And the official narrative presents this as a success.

## V. The framing: a masterclass in narrative construction
Why does von der Leyen’s sentence matter?
Because it is not an isolated error. It is the central framing of the Commission’s entire energy narrative — a framing that serves three political functions:

## 1. Shifting responsibility
By framing the energy crisis as a Russian action (”when Russia cut off gas supplies”), von der Leyen transforms the EU from the author of the policy into the victim of circumstances. The sanctions, the phase-out regulation, the decision to forego cheap Russian gas — all of these disappear from the narrative. What remains is a story of European resilience in the face of external aggression.

## 2. Justifying the cost
If the crisis was caused by Russia, then the economic pain is an inevitable cost of resistance — a price worth paying for sovereignty. If the crisis was caused by EU policy, then the pain is a consequence of political choices — choices that could have been made differently. The framing determines whether voters see themselves as victims of Russian aggression or as subjects of European policy.

## 3. Protecting the institutional project
The European Commission’s legitimacy depends on its ability to deliver prosperity. If the energy crisis is framed as a Russian attack, the Commission is a defender. If it is framed as a policy failure, the Commission is the problem. The narrative protects the institution.

## The alternative narrative
The alternative account — supported by the regulation, the data, and the statements of EU officials themselves — is straightforward:

- The EU chose to phase out Russian gas — a political decision codified in Regulation 2026/261.

- That decision removed 155 bcm of annual pipeline supply from the European market — roughly 40% of the pre-war total.

- That supply was replaced primarily by more expensive LNG, predominantly from the United States, at prices 2.5 to 8 times higher than domestic US gas.

- The result was a structural increase in European energy costs, which rendered much of European industry uncompetitive against American and Chinese competitors.

- The consequence is deindustrialization — factory closures, mass layoffs, and the relocation of production to regions with cheaper energy.
This is not a Russian narrative. It is the official record of the European Union’s own institutions, read without the rhetorical filter.

## VI. The response: the Commission’s silence
When asked about the discrepancy between von der Leyen’s statement and the regulation, the Commission has offered a consistent response: the President was referring to Russian supply cuts in 2022, not to the EU’s legislative phase-out.
This defense is technically plausible — Russia did suspend supplies to Poland and Bulgaria, and did significantly reduce flows through Nord Stream before the pipelines were sabotaged. But it ignores the regulatory timeline that followed.
The sequence of events is clear:

- 2022: Russia suspends supplies to Poland and Bulgaria; Nord Stream flows reduced; pipelines sabotaged.

- 2023-2025: EU develops and negotiates the phase-out regulation.

- January 2026: EU adopts Regulation 2026/261 — a binding ban on Russian gas imports.

- March 2026: Prohibition enters into application.
By the time von der Leyen delivered her speech in September 2026, the legal framework for the cessation of Russian gas imports was European law, not a Russian action. To say “Russia cut off gas supplies” in September 2026 — after Europe had legislated the phase-out — is to describe a world that no longer existed.

## VII. The political dimension: does she think citizens are fools?
The question that inevitably arises is the one the user posed: does von der Leyen believe European citizens are stupid enough to accept this?
The answer is not simple. The Commission President is not naïve. She knows the regulation exists. She knows the data. She knows that European industry is dying and that voters are paying the price.
The calculation is not that citizens are foolish. The calculation is that the narrative will hold long enough to survive the political moment. The State of the Union address is not a history lecture. It is a political communication exercise. Its purpose is to frame the Commission’s record in the most favorable light possible, to a public that is increasingly skeptical and increasingly angry.
And there is evidence that the calculation is failing.
The French political scientist Emmanuel Todd has observed that Europe has developed a pathological relationship with peace: “Europe is afraid of peace,” he said, “because peace would force European elites to confront the problems they have ignored for decades.” The energy crisis is one of those problems. The Commission’s framing is an attempt to avoid confronting it — to attribute the consequences of policy to the actions of an adversary.

## VIII. Conclusion: the bill comes due
Von der Leyen’s sentence — “when Russia cut off gas supplies” — is not a lie in the narrowest sense. Russia did reduce and suspend supplies to certain countries. But it is a deliberate distortion of the causal sequence that led to Europe’s energy crisis.
The record is clear:

- The EU legislated the phase-out of Russian gas.

- The EU chose to replace cheap pipeline gas with expensive LNG.

- The EU accepted the consequences for its industrial base.

- The EU presented the result as a triumph of resilience.
The factories are closing. The jobs are gone. The bills are higher. And in Strasbourg, the Commission President is telling the Parliament that this was Russia’s fault.
The tiger is not paper. The tiger is out of breath. And the Commission President is standing in the Parliament, insisting that the breathlessness is the price of freedom — while the industries that once made Europe rich close their gates one by one.
The question is not whether European citizens are foolish enough to believe this.
The question is how much longer they will pretend to.

reads.title: THE MAN WHO CALLED KALLAS THE REAL HYBRID THREAT
reads.subtitle: Inside the European Parliament clash that exposed the EU's double standard on disinformation, the Leipzig drone dispute, and the growing revolt against the war consensus Marco | Independent Analyst *1
reads.body:
## Introduction: a voice that refuses to be silenced
On September 15, 2026, in the plenary chamber of the European Parliament in Strasbourg, something happened that is increasingly rare in European politics. A sitting Member of the European Parliament told the EU’s foreign policy chief, to her face, that she — not Vladimir Putin — was the greatest hybrid threat to Europe.
The MEP was Ľuboš Blaha, a Slovak representative from the Smer-SD party. The target was Kaja Kallas, the EU’s High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.
The exchange was not a diplomatic disagreement. It was a rupture — a moment when the carefully managed consensus of the European institutions cracked open, and the raw divisions beneath became visible.
This article examines what Blaha said, the context in which he said it, the disputed Leipzig drone incident that formed the backdrop to his remarks, and what the episode reveals about the state of European democracy in 2026.

## I. The resolution: designating Russia as the “main threat”
On the same day Blaha spoke, the European Parliament adopted a resolution titled the “European Democracy Shield” — a report on foreign interference and threats to European democracy.
The resolution was adopted by 420 votes in favor, 220 against, and 26 abstentions. It designated Russia as “the main external threat to the security and democratic integrity of the European Union”. The report also named Iran, Belarus, China, and North Korea as sources of hostile activity, including cyberattacks, sabotage, espionage, and signal jamming. It called for expanded sanctions on individuals and entities involved in disinformation campaigns, and for the creation of an EU Centre for Democratic Resilience to coordinate national efforts against foreign information manipulation.
The report’s rapporteur, Swedish MEP Tomas Tobé, framed the resolution in stark terms: “This report is not about regulating political opinions. It is about protecting our democracy from foreign influence operations. Russian bots are not free speech. Foreign interference is not free speech. And manipulating our elections is certainly not free speech.”
The resolution passed comfortably. But the 220 votes against it — nearly a third of the chamber — revealed something the headline numbers obscured: a significant bloc of MEPs refuses to accept the framing.

## II. Blaha’s intervention: “You are the warmonger”
Blaha rose to speak during the debate on the resolution. What followed was not a policy critique. It was a direct, personal indictment.

> “The biggest hybrid threat to Europe is not Russia, ladies and gentlemen: it is Mrs. Kallas sitting here, who wants to drag us into a nuclear war.”
He then turned to the Leipzig drone incident — a case that had dominated German headlines for weeks — and used it to accuse the German establishment of orchestrating a false flag operation:

> “Do you know what despair looks like? When the German establishment, just to defeat the AfD in elections, organizes an intelligence operation in Leipzig and blames Russia. They destroyed their relations with Russia and still lost the election. Not even Mr. Bean would have done it better. You are not only losers, you are also inept.”
Blaha then broadened his attack to the entire trajectory of EU policy toward Russia:

> “Mrs. Kallas, you ramble on about hybrid threats, when in reality the opposite is happening. It is you who have been waging a bloody war against Russia for years. Your anti-Russian rhetoric is comparable to the Nazis’; the harsh truth is that Russia has not invaded any EU country. It is you who attacked Russia.”
And he closed with a phrase that has since circulated widely on social media:

> “You are an extreme warmonger, Mrs. Kallas. Get lost already.”
All MEPs from Smer-SD voted against the resolution.

## III. Kallas’s position: “Europe must impose a greater cost”
Kallas did not respond directly to Blaha during the session. But her speech earlier in the debate laid out the case he was attacking.
She pointed to four incidents in the previous 48 hours as evidence of a coordinated Russian campaign:

- A Russian warship firing flares at a Danish helicopter

- NATO jets shooting down a drone over Lithuania

- Russia striking a passenger train near Ukraine’s border

- Poland recovering a drone from its waters
“These are not accidents,” she said. “Putin will not stop unless he is stopped. So as Russia is willing to take greater risks, Europe must impose a greater cost.”
She called for:

- Tighter restrictions on Russian diplomats traveling within the Schengen area

- A ban on visas for Russian former combatants

- A review of tourist visas for Russian citizens

- Expanded sanctions on Russia’s “shadow fleet”
Kallas also rejected arguments that Ukraine should surrender territory for peace. “Nobody wants peace more than Ukrainians,” she said. “If aggression pays off, then we will see more of it.”

## IV. The Leipzig dispute: a case that refuses to close
The Leipzig drone incident is at the center of the dispute — and it remains unresolved in the public record.

## What happened
In early August 2026, German authorities discovered a drone loaded with explosives near the Leipzig/Halle airport, close to Ukrainian cargo aircraft. The drone was defused. German investigators identified suspects with connections to Russia.
On September 9, Chancellor Friedrich Merz used the incident in a Bundestag debate to attack the AfD, accusing the party of being “on the side of Russia” and criticizing AfD deputies who, according to Merz, laughed when he mentioned the attack.
German authorities formally attributed the operation to individuals acting on behalf of Russian state structures.

## The Russian denial
On September 15 — the same day as the European Parliament debate — Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR) issued a statement claiming that NATO intelligence agencies had privately found no evidence of Russian involvement.
According to the SVR, NATO member states’ intelligence services “informed their national authorities that there was not even the slightest evidence of Russian involvement. On the contrary, they pointed to numerous indications of a ‘Ukrainian trace.’”
The SVR added that “many in the West are merely pretending to believe the German leadership, which has baselessly blamed Russia.”
The German government has not publicly responded to the SVR’s claim. The case remains disputed — with Germany maintaining its attribution to Russia, and Russia claiming that NATO’s own intelligence contradicts Berlin’s position.

## V. The double standard: who defines “disinformation”?
The European Parliament’s resolution is titled the “European Democracy Shield.” Its stated purpose is to protect European democracy from foreign interference and disinformation.
But the debate exposed a fundamental question: who defines what counts as disinformation — and who decides which speech is protected?
The resolution calls for expanded sanctions on “enablers of disinformation” — a category that includes cryptocurrency exchanges, advertising networks, hosting providers, and third-country entities that help Russia circumvent sanctions. It also calls for stronger enforcement of digital rules and for online platforms to do more against “bot-driven election interference.”
Tobé’s framing — “Russian bots are not free speech” — is a direct rejection of the classical liberal position that speech should be regulated only in narrowly defined circumstances. It establishes a category of speech — foreign-origin, state-linked, or algorithmically amplified — that is deemed outside the protection of free expression.
Blaha’s intervention was, in essence, a challenge to that framing. His argument was not that Russian disinformation is legitimate. It was that the EU’s definition of disinformation is being used to silence dissent — that the “hybrid threat” framework has become a tool for delegitimizing any voice that opposes the war consensus.
This is not a fringe concern. In Germany, Chancellor Merz has said: “Bitte komme mir keiner mit Free Speech.” He has proposed a Klarnamenpflicht (real-name requirement) for social media, arguing that a liberal society must protect citizens from “false information.” Critics, including the legal blog Lawblog and journalist Julian Reichelt, have argued that this position is “bordering on a constitutional suspicion case” — a direct challenge to Article 5 of the German Basic Law, which establishes freedom of expression as a defensive right against the state, not a government mandate to control truth.
The European Parliament resolution and the German domestic debate are part of the same trajectory: the redefinition of free speech as a privilege granted by the state, rather than a right protected from it.

## VI. The Göring mechanism, revisited
The Dossier #118 describes the mechanism of manufactured consent, as articulated by Hermann Göring in his 1946 Nuremberg interview:

- External threat — Tell the people they are under attack.

- Denounce dissent — Label pacifists as traitors.

- Enforce conformity — Obtain compliance through fear.
The European Parliament debate was a live demonstration of this mechanism in operation.

- The external threat is Russia — designated as the “main threat” by a resolution adopted by 420 votes.

- The dissent is represented by figures like Blaha, who are accused of being “on the side of Russia” for questioning the consensus.

- The conformity is enforced through resolutions, sanctions, and the moral framing of the debate itself.
But the mechanism is now producing resistance. The 220 votes against the resolution — nearly a third of the Parliament — are a measure of that resistance. And Blaha’s intervention, however impolite, is a signal that the consensus is not as solid as its architects believe.

## VII. The Slovak exception: why Blaha matters
Blaha is not an isolated figure. He represents a broader current in European politics — one that is skeptical of the war consensus, critical of EU institutions, and increasingly vocal.
The Smer-SD party of Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has consistently opposed military aid to Ukraine and criticized EU sanctions on Russia. Slovakia, along with Hungary, has been a persistent dissenting voice in EU foreign policy debates.
Blaha’s intervention was more aggressive than most, but it reflected a sentiment that is growing across the continent: the perception that the EU’s “hybrid threat” framework is being used not to protect democracy, but to silence opposition to a war that a significant portion of Europeans do not support.
This sentiment is not confined to Slovakia. It is present in:

- Hungary, where Viktor Orbán has consistently opposed sanctions and military aid

- Germany, where the AfD has surged to 30% in national polls

- France, where Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National leads in presidential polling

- Italy, where the coalition government has balanced Atlanticism with skepticism
The European Parliament resolution was an attempt to formalize the consensus. But the 220 votes against it — and the visibility of Blaha’s intervention — suggest that the consensus is weakening, not strengthening.

## VIII. Conclusion: the crack in the shield
The “European Democracy Shield” was designed to protect the EU from foreign interference. But its adoption revealed that the greatest threat to the EU’s democratic legitimacy may not be external at all.
It may be internal: the growing perception among European voters that their governments are using the language of democracy to justify policies that undermine it — censorship, escalation, and the suppression of dissent.
Blaha’s words were impolite. They were aggressive. They were, by the standards of parliamentary decorum, unacceptable.
But they were also a question: if the EU’s definition of “disinformation” includes speech that challenges the war consensus, what is left of free speech?
The 220 votes against the resolution suggest that a significant portion of the European Parliament is asking the same question.
And the answer will determine whether the “European Democracy Shield” protects democracy — or buries it.

reads.title: THE MORAL PRESSURE
reads.subtitle: Merkel, Gates, and the Architecture of Private Power Over Public Health Marco | Independent Analyst 16 September 2026
reads.body:
On 9 September 2026, Angela Merkel sat down for a podcast interview with Handelsblatt’s Meckel & Matthes. The episode was framed around Sachsen-Anhalt and artificial intelligence. What it actually produced was one of the most candid admissions by a former head of government about how private wealth operates inside democratic systems.
Merkel described, in her own words, how Bill Gates used money as an instrument of political pressure on sovereign governments. She named the mechanism. She named the target. She named herself as the object of the pressure.
The German mainstream press did not report it. This article examines what she said, what it means, and why the silence matters.

## I. The Admission
Merkel’s account centres on the financing of Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance — the public-private partnership co-founded by the Gates Foundation in 2000 to fund immunisation in low-income countries.
Her description of how Gates operated:

> «Er hat dann auch sozusagen die Kraft gehabt, qua Geld moralischen Druck auszuüben.»
(”He had the power, so to speak, to exercise moral pressure through money.”)
She then explained the concrete mechanism:

> «Wenn wir nicht genug gegeben haben, stand man gleich schlecht da. Und dann hat er jedem afrikanischen Regierungschef gesagt: ‘Da, die Merkel, die war dieses Jahr geizig.’»
(”If we didn’t give enough, you immediately looked bad. And then he told every African head of government: ‘Look, Merkel was stingy this year.’”)
And finally, the sentence that should have been a headline across Europe:

> «Er wurde plötzlich mindestens so freundlich von irgendeinem Regierungschef auf der Welt empfangen wie ich.»
(”He was suddenly received by some head of government in the world at least as courteously as I was.”)
A democratically elected Chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany, in office for sixteen years, stating on the record that a private billionaire was accorded the diplomatic treatment of a head of state. Not as a complaint. As an observation. As a description of how things worked.

## II. What Merkel Actually Said — and What She Did Not
Precision matters here, because the version circulating on social media is not a verbatim transcript.
The viral paraphrase — “Bill Gates hat mich beim Thema Impfen erpresst” (”Bill Gates blackmailed me on vaccination”) — is the wording of Stefan Homburg, former professor of public finance at Leibniz University Hannover, published on X on 15 September 2026.
Merkel did not use the word erpresst (blackmailed). She used moralischer Druck (moral pressure). The distinction is not semantic pedantry — it separates a documented admission from a paraphrase that can be dismissed as exaggeration.
ElementMerkel’s actual wordsHomburg’s paraphraseNature of pressure”moralischer Druck” (moral pressure)”erpresst” (blackmailed)MechanismGates told African leaders Merkel was “geizig” (stingy)SameDiplomatic statusGates received “at least as courteously as I was”SameContextPodcast Handelsblatt, 9 Sept 2026X post, 15 Sept 2026
The substance is Merkel’s. The word “blackmail” is Homburg’s. Both point to the same architecture.

## III. The Silence
Between 9 and 16 September 2026, the following German outlets published no article on Merkel’s Gates admission:
OutletCoverageDer SpiegelNoneFAZNoneSüddeutsche ZeitungNoneTagesschau / ARDNone — despite Merkel explicitly referencing the tagesthemen broadcast that gave Gates nine minutes of airtime in 2020Die ZeitNonetazNoneWeltNone
Those that did cover it: Nius (libertarian-leaning), RT Deutsch, and individual accounts on X.
This is not a case of a story being buried after publication. It is a case of a story never being picked up. The original source — Handelsblatt’s own podcast — exists. The quotes are on the record. The speaker is the most consequential German politician of the past two decades.
The absence of coverage is itself a data point. It belongs in the same analytical category as the mechanism Merkel described: the operation of influence that does not need to be hidden because it is not reported.

## IV. The Architecture of Influence
Merkel’s testimony is not an isolated anecdote. It describes the visible surface of a documented apparatus.
Academic research presented at the ECPR (European Consortium for Political Research) conference in September 2026 examined the Gates Foundation’s political footprint in Europe. Its findings:
IndicatorFigureMeetings with UK ministers~10 per yearMeetings with European Commission~100 total”Policy and advocacy grants” 2007-2024Over $400 millionFrench presidents metEvery one in office over the past 25 yearsPermanent officesLondon, BerlinFunction of those officesRelationship-building with governments — described in the paper as functioning like embassies
The study’s conclusion, in the authors’ own words, raises “important questions about the political influence of a private foreign foundation — controlled by one of the richest men in the world — on European democratic processes.”
This is not conspiracy. It is grant-making, convening power, and access. It is legal. It is also, by any honest definition, a form of governance exercised without a mandate.

## V. The Money Question
The claim that Gates “made money from vaccines” requires precision, because the crude version is false and the precise version is more troubling than the crude one.
What is documented:

- Gates has publicly stated that his vaccine investments returned 20 to 1 — $10 billion invested producing an estimated **$200 billion in economic benefits**.

- The Gates Foundation invested $750 million in AstraZeneca**, funded the Serum Institute of India, and held a **$40 million stake in CureVac.

- The Global Health Investment Fund, associated with the foundation’s ecosystem, targeted 5-7% returns on drugs and vaccines, with a 60% capital guarantee.
What requires clarification:
The “$200 billion” is a macroeconomic estimate — years of life saved, productivity recovered, healthcare costs avoided. It is not cash in Gates’s account. This distinction is real and should not be elided.
What remains structural:
The foundation invests in pharmaceutical companies, then advocates for governments to purchase the vaccines those companies produce. This is a conflict of interest by any standard applied to public officials. It has never been treated as one because the actor is private and the framing is philanthropic.

## VI. The Deaths: India, 2009
In 2009, PATH — a Seattle-based NGO heavily funded by the Gates Foundation — conducted HPV vaccine trials on 14,000 tribal girls in Khammam district (Telangana) and Vadodara district (Gujarat).
Seven girls died.
An Indian parliamentary inquiry documented severe ethical violations:
FindingDetailConsentForms signed by hostel wardens, not parentsDisclosureTrials presented as public health initiative, not experimentalPopulationTribal girls — among India’s most vulnerable communitiesDeaths7, officially attributed to drowning, snakebite, pesticides, malariaCausal link to vaccineNot established by the inquiry
The deaths were not causally linked to the vaccine. That is the official finding and it should be stated.
The ethical violations were established. That is also the official finding, and it is rarely stated.
The distinction between “the vaccine did not kill them” and “they were enrolled in a trial without informed consent and then died” is the distinction between a legal defence and a moral question. Only one of those gets reported.

## VII. The Deaths: Chad, 2012
In December 2012, in the village of Gouro, Chad, 50 children were reported paralysed following a MenAfriVac vaccination campaign against meningitis A.
MenAfriVac was developed by the Meningitis Vaccine Project, a partnership between the WHO and PATH, funded by the Gates Foundation.
The programme’s overall record is one of genuine success: between 2010 and 2015, 255 million people across Africa received the vaccine, and confirmed meningitis A cases collapsed from over 250,000 during the 1996 epidemic to 80 in 2015.
The Gouro incident was never fully explained. Allegations of a cover-up by Chadian authorities were never resolved. Fact-checking organisations subsequently found that the “50 paralysed children” narrative was decontextualised and instrumentalised by anti-vaccine networks — but they did not establish that the event itself was fabricated.
The pattern repeats: a real event, a contested causal chain, a narrative that serves one side or the other, and a full explanation that never arrives.

## VIII. The Systemic Deaths: USAID and PEPFAR
The largest mortality figures associated with this system are not adverse events. They are consequences of withdrawal.
Following the 2025 suspension and restructuring of USAID and PEPFAR — the US global health programmes that the Gates Foundation had both complemented and, in practice, depended upon — independent modelling produced the following projections:
MetricFigureAdditional HIV/AIDS deaths per year630,000Children under 5 dead in 20254.8 millionIncrease vs. 2024+200,000 — first rise this centuryProjected additional child deaths by 2045 (if 30% cuts permanent)16 million
These deaths are not caused by Gates. They are caused by the withdrawal of public funding.
But they are caused by a system in which public health in low-income countries was allowed to become dependent on a combination of US congressional appropriations and private philanthropic capital — neither of which is accountable to the populations it serves.
When the public funding stopped, the private funding did not fill the gap. It was never designed to. Philanthropy complements; it does not replace. The architecture was always fragile. The fragility was always known. It was not addressed.

## IX. The Mechanism: Lie as Governance
This is Dossier #121 — The Lie as Governance — applied to a new domain.
The mechanism has three components:

- Remove responsibility. The deaths are attributed to unrelated causes, to local authorities, to withdrawal of funds by others. The structure that created the vulnerability is never named.

- Justify the cost. The benefits are real and are emphasised. Lives were saved. The trade-offs are described as unavoidable. The question of who authorised the trade-off is not asked.

- Protect the institution. The philanthropic framing shields the operation from the scrutiny applied to states and corporations. Criticism is coded as anti-science, anti-vaccine, or conspiracy.
Merkel’s testimony breaks the third component, and only the third. She did not accuse Gates of anything. She described, accurately, how he operated. In doing so, she confirmed that the access and pressure were real — and that the Chancellor of Germany was on the receiving end.
The other two components remain intact. The deaths in India and Chad remain attributed elsewhere. The structural dependency that produced the USAID mortality figures remains unexamined in mainstream discourse.

## X. Conclusions

- Merkel’s admission is real and on the record. She described money as an instrument of moral pressure on sovereign governments, and herself as its object.

- The word “blackmail” is not hers. It is Stefan Homburg’s paraphrase. The substance is hers; the escalation is his.

- The German mainstream press did not report it. Spiegel, FAZ, Süddeutsche, and Tagesschau published nothing. Nius and RT Deutsch did.

- The influence apparatus is documented. Over $400 million in advocacy grants, permanent offices in London and Berlin, access at head-of-state level.

- The financial structure creates conflicts of interest. Foundation investments in vaccine manufacturers combined with advocacy for government purchases.

- Deaths exist in three distinct categories. Ethical violations in trials (India 2009), unresolved adverse events (Chad 2012), and systemic mortality from funding withdrawal (USAID/PEPFAR 2025-2026). They should not be conflated.

- The mechanism of governance-by-narrative is intact. Responsibility is displaced, costs are justified, the institution is protected.

- The question is not whether Gates saved lives. He did. The question is who authorised him to decide which lives, with what priorities, and under what accountability.
Merkel said it herself: “He was received at least as courteously as I was.”
That sentence is the whole dossier.

## Sources and Dossiers
Primary sources:

- Angela Merkel, podcast Meckel & Matthes, Handelsblatt, 9 September 2026

- Stefan Homburg, X post, 15 September 2026

- Indian parliamentary inquiry report on HPV trials, 2010

- ECPR conference paper on Gates Foundation political influence, September 2026

- Gates Foundation public statements on investment returns

- PEPFAR/USAID impact modelling, 2025-2026
Dossiers:

- #118 — Il Meccanismo del Consenso

- #119 — Il Meccanismo del Consenso: Quattro Fattori

- #121 — La Menzogna come Governance
Independent analysis. No ideology. Just facts.
Marco | Independent Analyst ⚖️

reads.title: The Saudis Fired a Chinese Missile. A Day Later Washington Blinked.
reads.subtitle: For two years Trump left the Riyadh ambassador chair empty. Within a day of the Saudi missile message, he rushed a nominee to the Senate. You read a signal by the move it forces, and this forced one.
reads.body:
Two days ago a video surfaced of a Chinese-made ballistic missile, allegedly fired by Saudi Arabia at the Houthis in Yemen. The missile either “crash-landed intact” or failed on impact, and that detail was the thing worth reading.
A missile that does not explode can be recovered, photographed, and passed around the world’s media. I wrote that this was NOT a “battlefield failure” but rather a “battlefield choice”. It was the choice to send a SIGNAL.
Riyadh, fed up with American inaction against the Ansarallah Houthis in Yemen, was telling Washington the loudest way it could that it has OTHER suppliers, OTHER options, OTHER patrons, if the United States will not act.
Signal, Not Noise! By AJ Signal is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
An unexploded Chinese missile in a Saudi salvo is a sentence, and the sentence was: we do not have to wait for you.
How you confirm a SIGNAL, without the noise
You cannot confirm what a signal meant by asking. You confirm it by watching what the other side does next. A message that changes nothing was noise. A message that forces the other side to MOVE was received, understood, and taken seriously.
Leave a comment
Share
So the real test of the Saudi missile was never in the wreckage. It was in Washington’s response.

- If the United States shrugged, the missile was a coincidence and my read was wrong.

- If Washington moved, and moved fast, then the message had landed. Today Washington moved rapidly.
Subscribe now
Get 7 day free trial
Two years of an empty chair, filled in a day
The United States has NOT had a full-time, Senate-confirmed ambassador in Riyadh since the end of the Biden administration. For nearly two years, through the entire second Trump term and through this regional war, the most important American relationship in the Gulf has been run by “temporary American caretakers”. The chair at the top table in Riyadh sat empty, and Washington did not appear to mind.
Then, within a day of the Saudi missile message going viral and getting assessed by Washington, Trump moved to fill it. He nominated a new ambassador to the Kingdom and sent the nomination to the Senate. After twenty-plus months of leaving the post vacant, Washington suddenly needed its own voice in Riyadh, immediately.

-
- The speed is the answer to the question. Governments do NOT scramble a two-year-vacant nomination into a capital overnight for no reason. Something changed, and the thing that drove that change was likely the Chinese-made missile that landed in Yemen.
The selectivity is the harder tell…
Let me show you why I am confident in my reading, and I will do this by widening the lens and zooming out, because that is where my SIGNAL sharpens. Saudi Arabia was NOT the only Gulf capital Washington left without a confirmed ambassador.
The United States ran much of its Middle Eastern regional diplomatic bench empty through this war, posts sitting vacant or under caretakers across the Gulf. Of all of them, the one Washington rushed to fill first was the one that had just fired a Chinese-made missile to make a point.
Subscribe now
Give a gift subscription
Share
If Trump had filled every empty Gulf post at once, you could call it housekeeping and move on. He did not. He moved on the single capital that had just signaled it COULD look elsewhere. You do not rush a diplomat back into a relationship you ignored for two years unless that relationship just did something that alarmed you. The choice of which chair to fill first, and how fast, is the confession.
The exchange, move by move
Let me lay the sequence in order and the whole bargain is visible.

- First, Saudi frustration with American inaction against the Houthis. A client concluding its patron was not delivering.

- Second, the Chinese-made missile, fired and “conspicuously left intact”, a costly, deniable, unmistakable demonstration that Riyadh has another supplier and is willing to show it.

- Third, within 24 hours, Washington moving to put its own man back in the room after ignoring the relationship for the entire term.
The missile said, we can drift toward Beijing. The rushed nomination is Washington answering, please do not. Between a great power and its most important regional client, that is a complete exchange.
One side raised the cost of being taken for granted. The other paid, fast, to bring the temperature down.
Why this is the story under the headlines
The relationship this exposes is not the automatic partnership it is sold as. It is being renegotiated in real time, through signals and slights, and Riyadh just showed it holds more leverage than Washington likes to admit.
For decades the assumption was simple: Saudi Arabia needed American protection more than America needed Saudi cooperation. That assumption is what let Washington leave the ambassador’s chair empty for two years without cost.
The missile tested it and the rushed nomination answered it.
Riyadh now has a second patron it can gesture toward, a Chinese arsenal it can fire in public, and the demonstrated ability to make Washington jump. The dependence runs both ways now, and the Kingdom knows it.
That is what the episode reveals when you read the response instead of the rhetoric. When a client fires a rival power’s weapon to get your attention, and you answer by rushing back a diplomat you could not be bothered to send for two years, the client is not the one who blinked.
