reads.title: How Ansarallah Swept Past Saudi-Backed Forces to Control Yemen’s Red Sea Coast
reads.subtitle: A lack of cohesion among Saudi-backed forces helped pave the way for Ansarallah to seize the entirety of Yemen’s Red Sea Coast and control the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- Forces loyal Yemen’s Saudi-backed government stand near a pick-up truck in the Hays district, south of Hodeidah on September 5, 2026. Photo by Khaled ZIAD / AFP via Getty Images.Yemen’s Ansarallah completed their control of the Bab al-Mandab on Friday following sweeping gains yesterday in the most significant shift in territorial control in five years of the country’s long-running civil war.
Following days of escalating fighting in the western mountains of Taiz governorate, Saudi-backed forces of the Internationally Recognized Government (IRG) of Yemen appeared to collapse on Thursday, allowing Ansarallah, also known as the Houthis, to seize the strategically important port-city of Mocha. On Friday, Ansarallah forces took Mayum island, also known as Perim, which lies on the Yemeni side of the Bab al-Mandab Strait two miles off Yemen’s west coast. The small volcanic island acts as a natural choke point in the strait, narrowing the Red Sea channel to nine miles from the coast of Djibouti.
Ansarallah fighters posted videos online of military vehicles driving down the runway—built in 2022 by the United Arab Emirates—at Mocha’s newly developed airport. Footage also showed detainees being released from the city’s central prison as Ansarallah took control.
The advance puts the Houthis in direct control of one of the world’s busiest shipping lanes. Around one-third of international cargo shipping passes through the strait, a route that has become increasingly important for oil exports in the wake of the U.S. war on Iran, which has shut off access through the Strait of Hormuz on the opposite side of the Arabian Peninsula.
Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, hailed what he called a “resounding victory” for Ansarallah. “Iran’s might in the Strait of Hormuz and the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the U.S. and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse,” he wrote in a social media post.
Saudi airstrikes were reported late on Thursday night and into Friday around Dhubab and Mocha, hitting the port and airport.
Yemen’s civil war, which had been largely dormant since a Houthi-Saudi ceasefire was brokered in 2022, reignited in July when Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Sana’a airport to prevent an inbound Iranian passenger plane from landing in the Houthi-controlled capital. The plane later touched down safely in Hodeidah. The Mahan Air flight was the first passenger jet to land in Houthi territory since Israel destroyed five commercial planes belonging to Yemen’s state airline Yemenia in May last year.
In response, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade on all Saudi-linked vessels, disrupting the Kingdom’s export of oil to Asia from its Yanbu terminal on the west coast that was exporting an average of 4 million barrels of oil per day to bypass the closed Strait of Hormuz. Houthi attacks on Saudi vessels followed, forcing the rerouting of Asian-bound oil tankers north through the Suez Canal and the much longer route east via the Cape of Good Hope.
The incident relaunched fighting on the ground between Iranian-allied Ansarallah and the Saudi-backed IRG. The latter has been consolidating its power under Saudi direction since the sudden withdrawal by the UAE of its forces and support for Yemen’s anti-Houthi Southern Transitional Council (STC) in January during a spectacular falling out between the Kingdom and the Emirates.
Since the violent UAE-Saudi split at the beginning of the year, Saudi Arabia has sought to consolidate its hold over the Yemeni government and armed forces. A Yemeni Supreme Military Committee, created in January with the task of unifying the multiple fighting units including those previously under UAE command, is headed by Saudi commander Lieutenant General Mutlaq bin Salem Al-Azima. But any attempts at cohesion appear to have failed.
Witnesses described to Drop Site armed men looting weapons, and combat vehicles from retreating IRG forces heading into the suburb of Buraiqa, five miles west of the Aden, highlighting the fractured nature of the anti-Houthi side. Other fighters were filmed selling their weapons as they fled on the road east of Bab al-Mandab.
“They continue to grossly underestimate the capabilities of the Houthis,” Farea al-Muslimi, a research fellow at the London-based Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa program, told Drop Site. “At the same time, there is a fundamental problem of military coordination for the IRG forces.”
Saudi-backed National Resistance Forces led by Tareq Saleh, nephew of Yemen’s long-standing president Ali Abduallah Saleh, who was killed by the Houthis in 2017, were heading the fight against Ansarallah on the Red Sea coast until their withdrawal on Thursday. Saleh and his fighters have subsequently been accused of betrayal and cowardice by Yemeni media channels and in social media posts by other fighters in the Saudi-backed side.
Tareq Saleh’s media office did not respond to Drop Site’s request for comment on Thursday’s retreat.
A day earlier, the IRG Minister of Defense came under attack from southern fighters while visiting the frontline against the Houthis in Al-Dhale, the home territory of UAE-backed STC leader Aidrous al-Zubeidi, who fled into exile in January during the Saudi push back against the STC that ended the UAE’s decade-long military presence in Yemen.
In the midst of Ansarallah’s advances on Thursday, Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salaman reportedly called President Trump twice to appeal for U.S. strikes against the Houthis. Provisional numbers from airstrikes monitor Yemen Data Project recorded 77 Saudi air raids between September 4 and 10, marking the heaviest period of Saudi bombing on Yemen since early 2022.
The Houthis also stepped up attacks inside the Kingdom this week, launching a wave of ballistic missiles and drones on Tuesday that hit state oil facilities in Abha, Najran and Aramco’s facility in Jizan resulting in 73 wounded civilians, according to Saudi officials.
Residents in Aden, which remains under IRG control, told Drop Site News that hundreds of displaced families were arriving in the city from the Red Sea coastal towns and villages. At least 46,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated last week, according to new figures released on Friday by the International Organization for Migration (IOM), up from 18,500 reported by IOM on Tuesday.
The price of crude oil, already rising to over $100 a barrel this week due to the U.S.-Iran conflict over the Strait of Hormuz, jumped a further 6.5% on Thursday following Ansarallah’s territorial gains.
Rising oil prices are expected to have a further knock-on effect on borrowing costs set by central banks. The European Central Bank put up its interest rate by a quarter point on Thursday. Bank President Christine Lagarde cited the region’s instability in the decision, saying in a press conference that “the conflict in the Middle East continues to generate inflation pressures, and inflation is set to remain well above target for an extended period.” The U.S. Federal Reserve is due to announce its decision on rates next week.
Ansarallah officials sought to downplay any threat to shipping in the Bab al-Mandab. Their Supreme Political Council released a statement after the gains on Thursday saying that “navigation in the Red Sea remains safe” although Saudi vessels remain a target.
The Saudis are now forced into a whole new war with the Houthis, says Al-Muslimi. “This is unprecedented and they can’t let the Houthis get away with attacks like this inside Saudi Arabia. The economic impact would be too huge and it would set a precedent for anyone else who wants to attack them.” As for the international community and their response to the Houthi capture of the Bab al-Mandab, Al-Muslimi added: “They are out of tools, time and imagination.”
Leave a comment
Share

reads.title: Ansarallah completes takeover of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, strikes Saudi pipeline; Oil tops $108
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: September 11, 2026
reads.body:
- Diesel price displayed at a gas station in New York, the United States, on Sept. 4, 2026. Photo by Zhang Fengguo/Xinhua via Getty Images.Friday, September 11, 2026 – Ansarallah seizes Yemen’s Red Sea coast to Bab al-Mandab. Saudi forces launch two airstrikes on Yemen’s Mocha airport. Pumping station on Saudi’s critical East-West oil pipeline reportedly struck. Axios: U.S. President Donald Trump declined Saudi requests to strike Ansarallah as they advanced. Six districts captured in operation against Saudi-backed forces in western Yemen, Ansarallah says. International Organization for Migration: At least 46,000 displaced in Yemen as fighting escalates. Iranian officials praise Ansarallah advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it destroyed U.S. unmanned vessel at entrance to Strait of Hormuz. Oil climbs above $108 as U.S. diesel prices hit record high. South Korea, Iran discuss Strait of Hormuz. Satellite images indicate likely oil slicks near Strait of Hormuz after U.S. attack on tankers. Vance secretly called military commanders directly for unfiltered Iran war assessments. Israeli drone strike kills Palestinian, wounds nine in southern Gaza. Nine Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza on Thursday. Israel kills Hamas’s Qassam Brigades Khan Younis commander. Israeli forces, settlers carry out attacks and arrests across occupied West Bank. Somaliland offers to deploy 2,000 troops for Gaza stabilization force. Israeli soldiers detail “calculated mass killing” of Palestinians in new documentary. Israel detonates 1,100 tons of explosives at Ali Al-Taher ridge, blast registers like 4.2-magnitude earthquake. Israel continues attacks across other districts in southern Lebanon. Republicans blindsided by Trump’s $5,000 check pledge, sources say. GOP election officials from seven states urge Supreme Court to block Trump’s mail voting rule. Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for November. Appeals court deals ICE ninth straight loss on mass detention policy. Former Environmental Protection Agency officials warn data center boom poses growing public health threat. Russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese leader Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian arrive in New Delhi for BRICS summit. Peru joins U.S. Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition. Fire kills at least 29 people, mostly students, in DRC’s rebel-held Bukavu. Ukrainian drone attacks kill two, wound seven in Russia’s Belgorod region. International Energy Agency cuts forecast on Russian oil production after Ukraine attacks.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Yemen

- Ansarallah seizes Yemen’s Red Sea coast to Bab al-Mandab: Ansarallah (also known as Houthi) forces swept through the remaining stretch of Yemen’s Red Sea coast in an 18-hour offensive, securing the coastline from Mocha south to the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to Al Jazeera.

- Saudi-backed Yemeni forces completely withdrew from the area following the battle of Al-Waziyah, west of Taiz, and the Ansarallah capture of the Khalid ibn al-Walid military base. With government forces abandoning Mocha, Ansarallah fighters encountered little resistance as they advanced south, taking Dhubab and then Murad, the last coastal town held by government forces.

- Ansarallah naval forces subsequently moved offshore, seizing Mayyun Island (also known as Perim) in the Bab al-Mandab Strait two miles off Yemen’s west coast and advancing into Zuqar Island, where fighting is ongoing.

- Saudi forces launch two airstrikes on Yemen’s Mocha airport: Saudi military forces carried out two airstrikes on Mocha airport in western Yemen, the Ansarallah-affiliated Al-Masirah reported, following the Ansarallah takeover of Mocha. Six missiles also targeted the port in Mocha, according to AFP.

- Pumping station on Saudi’s critical East-West oil pipeline reportedly struck: Satellite imagery showed plumes of smoke near Saudi Arabia’s critical East-West oil pipeline early Friday, while NASA’s fire-monitoring system detected fires in the area, amid reports that Yemen’s Ansarallah targeted a pumping station along the pipeline. Saudi authorities have not yet announced an incident at the site.

- The East-West Pipeline has become increasingly important since the outbreak of the U.S.-Iran war, allowing Saudi Aramco to move crude from the kingdom’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea and bypass the Strait of Hormuz.

- Axios: Trump declined Saudi requests to strike Ansarallah as they advanced: Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called U.S. President Donald Trump twice on Thursday, urging him to launch strikes against Yemen’s Ansarallah as they advanced along the Red Sea coast toward Bab al-Mandab, two U.S. officials told Axios. Trump declined, with Washington saying it has no plans to intervene directly for now.

- A senior Trump administration official said Washington was focused on ensuring “freedom of navigation in the Red Sea” while “empowering our regional partners to take the lead.”

- More than 100 U.S. military advisers are providing intelligence and targeting support to Saudi Arabia’s military campaign against Ansarallah through a newly established joint forces command, according to a new report from CNN, with one official putting the total closer to 200 troops.

- Six districts captured in operation against Saudi-backed forces in western Yemen, Ansarallah says: Ansarallah said Friday that the group had taken control of six districts across Taiz and Hodeidah governorates, covering some 5,400 square kilometers, during a large-scale military operation launched on September 3 to expel Saudi-backed forces from parts of Yemen’s western coast.

- Military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the operation came amid a 12-year Saudi assault and blockade on Yemen, aimed at pressuring the country over its demands and its support for the Palestinian people, with attacks intensifying in recent months.

- “The armed forces affirm that maritime navigation is safe for all companies, with the exception of Saudi ships,” Saree said, adding that operations would continue under an equation of “siege for siege” and “escalation for escalation” until “the aggression is stopped and the blockade on our people is lifted.”

- IOM: At least 46,000 displaced in Yemen as fighting escalates: At least 46,000 people have been displaced across Yemen’s West Coast and Taiz governorate since fighting escalated last week, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Friday, warning that the number is “alarmingly rising by the hour.” On Tuesday, the UN agency had put the number at around 18,500.

- Entire villages have reportedly emptied in Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, and al-Ma’afer as fighting moved closer to populated areas, while large numbers fled Mocha overnight. Displaced people are arriving in Lahj and Aden, with others moving north toward Ibb. The key Mocha–Taiz road has also reportedly been cut.

- IOM said it temporarily suspended all operational movements on Friday because of the deteriorating security situation, while emergency stocks have already been depleted following the recent flood response.

- For Drop Site, Carolina Pedrazzi and a reporter in Yemen spoke to families in the Jabal Zaid displaced persons camp—some of whom were facing their second or third displacement. Read the piece here.

- Iranian officials praise Ansarallah advances along Yemen’s Red Sea coast: Senior Iranian officials praised Ansarallah’s rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coastline.

- Iranian Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref hailed the “victories of the heroic nation of Yemen.” Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, congratulated Ansarallah on what he called a “resounding victory.” “Iran’s might in the Strait of Hormuz and the homegrown resolve of the resistance have driven the US and its allies into a tactical and strategic impasse,” Mokhber said.

- Iran’s Foreign Ministry called for an end to Saudi Arabia’s blockade of Yemen and an immediate return to negotiations between Saudi Arabia and Ansarallah.

## Iran

- IRGC says it destroyed U.S. unmanned vessel at entrance to Strait of Hormuz: Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said Thursday that it struck and destroyed a U.S. unmanned surface vessel, a “Saildrone Explorer-type,” at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported.

- In its statement, the IRGC Navy said it targeted the vessel and “foiled its aggressive mission,” claiming the U.S. military had recently deployed unmanned vessels to the Strait to avoid directly confronting Iranian forces.

- Since March 2025, Saildrone and Palantir have partnered on AI-powered autonomous maritime surveillance.

- Oil climbs above $108 as U.S. diesel prices hit record high: Oil prices continued to climb on Friday, with Brent crude futures rising $1.05, or 1%, to $108.68 a barrel, after surging more than 6% on Thursday.

- In the U.S., the average price of diesel reached a record $6.06 a gallon on Friday, surpassing $6 for the first time, according to AAA data cited by AFP. The rise comes in the wake of increasing attacks along key shipping routes in the Middle East.

- South Korea, Iran discuss Strait of Hormuz: South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi discussed developments and navigation through the Strait of Hormuz in a phone call on Friday, according to Seoul’s Foreign Ministry.

- Cho expressed concern over the regional situation and reiterated South Korea’s support for free and safe navigation through the strait. The two agreed to maintain communication.

- The call came after Seoul dispatched an inspection team to assess a potential deployment of South Korean troops to the region at the behest of the U.S.

- Satellite images indicate likely oil slicks near Strait of Hormuz after U.S. attack on tankers: Satellite images from the European Copernicus programme show what experts say are likely oil slicks off Iran’s coast, east of the Strait of Hormuz, following U.S. attacks that sank oil tankers in the area, AFP reported.

- Images taken Wednesday and Thursday show long brownish streaks on the water around 20 kilometers off the Iranian coast, near coral reefs designated as wetlands of international importance.

- Two of the tracks begin at locations where the tankers Kylo and Riesco transmitted their last signals before being sunk on September 5 and 8, respectively. The U.S. military said Tuesday that it had destroyed five tankers in the Gulf of Oman in response to Iranian ballistic missile attacks on a U.S. warship.

- Vance secretly called military commanders directly for unfiltered Iran war assessments: Vice President JD Vance made an unusual effort over the spring and summer to call U.S. military commanders across the Middle East, Europe, and Asia directly, seeking unvarnished assessments of the Iran war, according to a Thursday report from The New York Times.

- Commanders told Vance their stockpiles of Patriot interceptors, Army Tactical Missile Systems, and Precision Strike Missiles were at their lowest levels ever, with one theater down to fewer than 100 Patriots by late spring, prompting Vance to develop deep private concerns about the war’s strategy that contrasted sharply with Trump’s continued public claims that the U.S. had “already won the war” and faces no supply problems.

## Palestine

- Israeli drone strike kills Palestinian, wounds nine in southern Gaza: A Palestinian was killed and nine others, including children, were wounded on Friday when an Israeli drone struck a group of people in the Al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis, southern Gaza, according to WAFA.

- Nine Palestinians killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza on Thursday: An Israeli drone struck a vehicle north of Khan Younis, killing one Palestinian. Another drone strike targeted a group of Palestinians in the Al-Qubba area of Al-Mawasi, killing three and wounding five.

- Another Israeli strike killed a Palestinian family, including two children, as they slept in Beit Lahia in northern Gaza: Momen Ahmad, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their two daughters, sisters Lana, 12, and Bana, 8.

- The family had repaired two rooms in the middle of their partially destroyed home and were living there when it was struck. No one survived.

- Residents spent hours trying to recover the family from beneath the rubble as Israeli forces continued firing toward the area. “We managed to recover three bodies. There is also a little girl—we managed to recover part of her body, but the rest is still under the rubble,” a relative, Zuhair Al-Haisami, told Drop Site’s Mohamed Ahmed.

- Watch the dispatch from Mohamed Ahmed here.

- A ninth Palestinian died from wounds sustained in an Israeli strike on Al-Mawasi, north of Khan Younis, earlier in the day.

- Israel kills Hamas’s Qassam Brigades Khan Younis commander: Hamas’s armed wing, Al-Qassam Brigades, confirmed Friday that Israel killed Mohammed Al-Yazouri, a member of its General Military Council and commander of its Khan Younis brigade, in a strike Thursday, describing it as a “cowardly Israeli assassination operation.”

- The Israeli military claimed the strike killed a company commander and another member of the Khan Younis brigade.

- Israel signed a ceasefire agreement with Hamas on October 9, 2025, and has since killed 1,359 Palestinians and wounded more than 4,570 in Gaza.

- Israeli forces, settlers carry out attacks and arrests across occupied West Bank: Israeli forces detained around 30 Palestinians on Thursday, including two journalists and a former prisoner, during raids in several areas of the occupied West Bank.

- Nablus: Israeli settlers, accompanied by Israeli soldiers, attacked Palestinian homes in the Al-Dhahra and Al-Hara Al-Tahta areas of Beita on Friday morning and stole a number of sheep, according to WAFA.

- Tubas: Settlers attacked a thyme crop belonging to a Palestinian farmer in the northern Yarza community, east of Tubas, on Thursday, removing and stealing a fence and destroying irrigation networks supplying the crop.

- Somaliland offers to deploy 2,000 troops for Gaza stabilization force: Somaliland President Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi said Wednesday the breakaway Somali region—recently recognized by Israel—is willing to deploy 2,000 troops for the planned U.S.-led International Stabilization Force (ISF) in Gaza, but is waiting for a formal request from Washington or Israel, according to The New Arab.

- Speaking at the MEAD conference in Washington, Abdullahi said his forces, which include an army of about 25,000 soldiers and a 1,500-person coast guard, are “ready” to contribute to the unit, which under Trump’s Gaza plan would secure areas following an Israeli withdrawal, train Palestinian police, and support aid delivery.

- Last month, Uganda became the first African state to join the ISF, a move that sparked domestic debate over whether Kampala acted without African Union consultation.

- Israeli soldiers detail “calculated mass killing” of Palestinians in new documentary: A new documentary by Israeli co-directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor which premiered at the Venice Film Festival features interviews with 24 Israeli military intelligence officers and soldiers about “Israel’s calculated mass killing of Palestinian civilians in Gaza,” according to the film’s synopsis. The film is titled “NAZA,” a reference to an Israeli military acronym for civilian casualties, including men, women and children.

- “Interviewees describe hacking little girls’ phones to see when their fathers came home and then bombing their houses, listening while the people on the line screamed and pleaded for help, while mothers cried over their burning daughters,” Vulture reported. Another officer recalls blowing up a building with 500 people in it to go after one target. All of the soldiers spoke on condition of anonymity and their appearance and voices were digitally altered.

- The film builds on previous reporting published by +972 Magazine, Local Call, and The Guardian. At a press conference following the premiere, Szor also reminded everyone that Palestinian journalists have reported on these facts.

## Lebanon

- Israel detonates 1,100 tons of explosives at Ali Al-Taher ridge, blast registers like 4.2-magnitude earthquake: The Israeli military detonated 1,100 tons of explosives beneath the Ali Taher Ridge on the outskirts of Nabatieh Al-Fawqa in Nabatieh, southern Lebanon on Thursday night, claiming to have destroyed an underground complex belonging to Hezbollah, The Times of Israel reported.

- Seismic waves from the explosion recorded at 9:08 p.m. were comparable to a magnitude-4.2 earthquake, Lebanon’s National Center for Geophysics said.

- The Israeli military said it would “reorganize” its deployment but continue to occupy the Ali Al-Taher Ridge through surveillance and firepower. The Israeli Army Radio reported Friday that Israeli forces have withdrawn from the Ridge to rear lines in the Shaqif area.

- The force of the explosion sent rocks and debris onto the Khiam–Marjayoun road, leaving it completely blocked on Friday, according to NNA. Residents of several villages in the Marjayoun district also appealed for water supplies after dust and debris from the blast covered homes, roads, and vehicles.

- Israel continues attacks across other districts in southern Lebanon:

- Tyre (Sour): Israeli forces carried out airstrikes, artillery shelling, and large-scale demolitions in Mansouri, including blowing up most of the town’s public school. Two consecutive airstrikes targeted infrastructure and residential neighborhoods, according to NNA.

- Marjayoun: Israeli forces moved into the Wadi Al-Jamal area on the northern outskirts of Meiss Al-Jabal, accompanied by artillery shelling that targeted a house and machine-gun fire in the area.

## U.S. News

- Republicans blindsided by Trump’s $5,000 check pledge, sources say: Key congressional Republicans, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune, were not briefed before President Donald Trump’s Wednesday pledge to send $5,000 checks to every American adult if Republicans hold Congress, according to more than a dozen lawmakers and aides cited by NOTUS.

- GOP Rep. Chip Roy criticized the plan on social media, saying “dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” and a senior Senate Republican aide told the outlet flatly “it’s not going to happen,” citing inflation concerns and the estimated $1.2 trillion cost, or 3.5% of GDP.

- GOP election officials from seven states urge Supreme Court to block Trump’s mail voting rule: Republican chief election officials from seven states, including Georgia’s Brad Raffensperger and Kansas’s Scott Schwab, filed a brief Wednesday urging the Supreme Court not to let Trump’s mail-in ballot order take effect before the November midterms, saying it’s too late to implement it responsibly.

- The officials, alongside numerous current and former local election authorities, said: “attempting to implement the rule now will almost certainly lead to mistakes, delays and confusion for both voters and election officials.”

- Trump signed the order in March, and it was formalized in an August U.S. Postal Service rule allowing the service to withhold ballot delivery from states that don’t submit voter eligibility lists.

- A preliminary injunction from a Boston federal judge currently blocks the order from taking effect before November. On Thursday, the First Circuit Court of Appeals denied the Trump administration’s request to lift this injunction, ruling in a nine-page opinion that the administration failed to show the rule wouldn’t cause “chaos and widespread voter disenfranchisement.”

- Supreme Court blocks Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for November: The U.S. Supreme Court once again prevented Missouri from using its Republican-redrawn congressional map for the November election, marking the second time this week the justices have weighed in on the state’s chaotic redistricting fight.

- Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins said his office would direct local election authorities to use the 2022 congressional map, which would position Democrats to retain their Kansas City-area seat.

- The reversal followed a whiplash sequence in which Justice Brett Kavanaugh initially deferred to Missouri’s Supreme Court favoring the old map, only for federal Judge Stephen R. Clark to rule hours later that the new GOP-drawn map should be used to avoid “wreaking havoc” on election fairness, prompting state officials to briefly follow Clark’s ruling, before it was appealed back to the Supreme Court.

- It remains unresolved how officials will reconcile using a different map in the general election than the GOP-redrawn map used to nominate candidates in August’s primary.

- Appeals court deals ICE ninth straight loss on mass detention policy: The 4th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled 2-1 Thursday against ICE’s policy of detaining immigrants living inside the U.S. for years without bond, ICE’s ninth straight loss at the federal appellate court level, with Judge Nicole Berner comparing the approach to the “historical stain” of Japanese internment during World War II.

- Nine of the 11 appellate circuits to consider the issue have now found the administration misread a 1996 immigration law that established deportation and detention policies, and which prior administrations interpreted as making detention mandatory only for people who had recently crossed the border.

- ICE abandoned this interpretation in July 2025 in favor of treating even longtime U.S. residents as “seeking admission” and subject to detention without bond.

- Former EPA officials warn data center boom poses growing public health threat: A group representing more than 800 former EPA employees released a report warning that Trump administration policies weakening pollution safeguards and speeding data center approvals threaten to worsen health risks.

- The report, from the Environmental Protection Network, cites academic modeling which projects that data center air pollution could contribute to roughly 600,000 asthma cases, 1,300 premature deaths, and more than $20 billion in annual public health costs by 2028.

- It also lists 30 federal actions it says will increase pollution risks, including easing restrictions on diesel generators and off-grid gas plants and proposing to let developers begin construction before air pollution permits are approved.

- Former EPA enforcement official Larry Starfield noted the agency’s staffing is at a four-decade low, leaving it ill-equipped to monitor or enforce pollution limits at the scale of the data center buildout, and UC Riverside professor Shaolei Ren, who led the report’s underlying analysis, warned “the actual impact could be worse than we modeled” given the administration’s explicit push toward increasing the use of fossil fuels.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Putin, Xi, Pezeshkian arrive in New Delhi for BRICS summit: Russian President Vladimir Putin arrived in New Delhi Friday ahead of an 11-member BRICS summit expected to be dominated by the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, joined by Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian for his first visit to India as president and Chinese President Xi Jinping for his first India visit since 2019.

- The ongoing war in Iran and the Gulf is expected to be the central fault line in the meeting, given the recent addition of several Gulf monarchies to the bloc, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, and the body’s recent failure to agree on a joint statement concerning the war in May.

- India, which maintains ties with both Iran and Israel while balancing relations with Washington, has turned increasingly to Russian oil amid the Iran-driven energy crisis, even as its foreign minister recently visited Kyiv and Zelenskyy thanked India for its “commitment to ending this unjust war.”

- Peru joins U.S. Shield of the Americas anti-cartel coalition: President Keiko Fujimori announced that Peru will join the U.S.-led “Shield of the Americas” coalition against drug cartels during Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s visit on Thursday.

- Fujimori said Peru’s participation would speed intelligence-sharing and joint action against transnational criminal groups, citing her country’s experience fighting the Shining Path insurgency.

- Rubio’s visit, part of a three-country Latin American tour also covering Ecuador and Colombia, built on existing defense ties between the countries, including Peru’s January designation as a major non-NATO ally and a possible $1.5 billion U.S. military sale approved by Rubio, which would upgrade Peru’s Callao Naval Base.

- Peru is also seeking relief from 12.5% U.S. tariffs imposed in July that have hit its blueberry, grape, and avocado exports. China continues to outpace the U.S. in bilateral trade with Peru, with Peru-China trade up 35% in the first half of the year compared to a 20% rise with the U.S. Rubio’s Thursday visit prompted China’s embassy in Lima to preemptively declare that “the Western Hemisphere is not anyone’s ‘backyard.’”

- Fire kills at least 29 people, mostly students, in DRC’s rebel-held Bukavu: A fire that broke out in the Chimpunda neighborhood of Bukavu, capital of the eastern DRC’s South Kivu province, killed at least 29 people, including 19 girls and five boys, after spreading to two local schools and about 300 wooden homes, according to an AFC/M23 rebel spokesperson.

- Another local official said the fire was “followed by a violent stampede that forced students to trample over one another or look for a dangerous way out,” with many fainting or losing consciousness during the chaos.

- Bukavu has been controlled since February 2025 by the Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 movement. Thursday’s fire is one of several that have recently blazed through the city, including one last Sunday that destroyed more than 45 houses.

- Ukrainian drone attacks kill two, wound seven in Russia’s Belgorod region: Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia’s Belgorod border region killed two people and wounded seven Thursday, according to regional authorities.

- One man was killed when a drone detonated at an unnamed facility in Novy Oskol, injuring five others in various locations, while a second man was killed and a woman injured when a drone struck their car in Shebekino, near the Ukrainian border.

- International Energy Agency cuts forecast on Russian oil production after Ukraine attacks: The International Energy Agency has lowered its forecast for Russian oil production as Ukrainian drone strikes continue to damage refineries and other energy infrastructure.

- The agency cut its 2026 forecast by 125,000 barrels per day to 8.7 million bpd and reduced its 2027 projection by 235,000 bpd to 8.6 million bpd.

- The decline comes as Moscow itself has downgraded its 2026 production forecast to a 17-year low and lowered its fuel-export projections for both 2026 and 2027 because of the war which has increasingly seen Ukraine targeting refineries and other energy production facilities inside Russia.

reads.title: Democrats Are Urging Trump to Re-Escalate on North Korea
reads.subtitle: Several Democrats are pressing Trump to reverse his cutback of joint military drills, even as peace groups argue the move could open the door to diplomacy with North Korea.
reads.body:
- Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., walks down the House steps after the last votes of the week in the U.S. Capitol on Friday, May 15, 2026. Photo: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images.This article is being co-published with Capital & Empire.
Earlier this month, a coalition of 50 antiwar and foreign policy groups reached out to the top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee with an unusual plea: Please don’t attack President Trump—at least not for his decision to de-escalate tensions with North Korea as he focuses his attention on the Mideast.
The groups were worried that an almost instinctual Democratic response to Trump’s decision to scale back military exercises with South Korea would be to attack him from a hawkish direction, call him weak on national security, and demand ever more confrontation. Instead, they suggested, take the win, and celebrate the reduction in hostile tension.
The advice was not taken. In a draft letter circulating on Capitol Hill and obtained by Drop Site News, House Foreign Affairs Committee ranking member Gregory Meeks and at least 20 Democrats are calling on Trump to “reverse course,” arguing that he handed North Korean leader Kim Jong Un “unilateral concessions for which you got nothing in return” by scaling back the Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises.
Support Drop Site. Make a tax-deductible gift or subscribe for free:
Several Democrats who signed the Meeks letter have also backed legislation calling for a formal end to the war between North and South Korea, which has been going on for more than 70 years, taking on a devastating toll on civilians and carrying the constant risk of nuclear war. Nine of the current signatories—Reps. Brad Sherman, Mark Pocan, Dave Min, Gabe Amo, Jonathan Jackson, Dina Titus, Ted Lieu, Sarah McBride and Jim Costa—are also cosponsors of the current Peace on the Korean Peninsula Act. Sherman is the bill’s lead sponsor.
In the September 1 letter, organizations including Win Without War, the Quincy Institute, Just Foreign Policy (where this author was once employed), and Women Cross DMZ acknowledged “serious doubts” about Trump’s motivations but argued that scaling back the exercises could nevertheless provide “a rare opening for long-overdue diplomatic progress.” They urged lawmakers to back South Korean President Lee Jae Myung’s efforts to reopen dialogue with Pyongyang and pursue a formal end to the Korean War.
Cathi Choi, executive director of Women Cross DMZ, told Drop Site that despite “serious concerns about Trump’s motivations and methods,” the reduction presents “a crucial window to de-escalate tensions.” Responding to the argument that scaling back the exercises without a reciprocal concession weakens Washington’s negotiating position, Choi said: “Diplomacy is not a gift. It’s an imperative for our collective security.”
Choi also pointed to South Korean President Lee’s push for renewed diplomacy and greater South Korean control over the country’s defense. “If Congress wants to preserve the U.S.-ROK alliance, they should listen to what South Korean leadership is actually asking for,” she said.
The fight echoes an earlier split among Democrats over Trump’s diplomacy with North Korea. During Trump’s first-term negotiations with Kim, Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., was among a small group of Democrats urging the party to support diplomatic openings even while opposing Trump more broadly. In a 2018 letter, Khanna and 14 other House Democrats called for an incremental approach to negotiations that included ending U.S.-South Korea “decapitation” military exercises. Khanna also criticized Democratic leaders for demanding complete denuclearization before offering concessions, arguing that Democrats should not try to “out-hawk Trump on North Korea.”
Trump has framed the exercise reduction as an opening to revive talks with Kim in an August 16 Truth Social post, while also tying the decision to Seoul’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran.
Meeks and the other signatories that Trump instead weakened Washington’s hand by making concessions without securing reciprocal steps from Pyongyang. North Korea has also continued missile testing in recent months.
Trump announced on August 16 that he had ordered the Pentagon to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises with South Korea, just hours before the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises were set to begin. He cited their cost, his relationship with Kim and Seoul’s refusal to join the U.S. war against Iran, while arguing that the drills sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea.
The exercises nevertheless began as scheduled on August 17. Two days later, the United States and South Korea announced that Ulchi Freedom Shield would end after five days instead of the planned 11. Some live-training exercises were also canceled or replaced with simulations, while drills planned for the second week were scrapped.
The Meeks letter repeatedly describes Trump as having “halted” the exercises, though Ulchi Freedom Shield began as scheduled and was subsequently shortened, with some exercises canceled.
The lawmakers also place the exercises within Washington’s broader struggle to maintain its position in the region, pointing to Pyongyang’s ties with China and Russia and arguing that a strong U.S.-South Korea alliance is necessary to counter Chinese influence. They warn that Trump’s actions could jeopardize South Korea’s $350 billion investment commitment in the U.S., including in U.S. shipbuilding, and strengthen calls for Seoul to develop its own nuclear weapons.
The debate over which approach the U.S. should take to North Korea is also tied directly to the war with Iran and the strain it has placed on military resources. The Democrats accuse the administration of draining “essential U.S. munitions” and pulling missile-defense assets away from South Korea to support the war. In an August CNN interview, Meeks himself warned that the United States was “running low on munitions” and described “panic” over ensuring the military had what it needed. Rather than question the sprawling military footprint that produced that strain, Democrats are demanding that Washington preserve it.

reads.title: The 9/11 wars were a bigger crime than you think
reads.subtitle: 9/11 was a terrible crime. What followed was the crime of the century
reads.body:
- It’s exactly a quarter of a century since 2,977 people were killed by al-Qaeda terrorists in New York, Arlington and Pennsylvania.
The US elite – and its allies – responded by launching a series of wars and violent acts.
According to Brown University’s Costs of War project, up to 4.7 million people were killed in the post-9/11 wars, both through direct violence and the consequences of destabilisation, such as disease and hunger.
Between 37 and 59 million people were displaced from their homes.
Millions of children were driven into hunger.
Over 7,000 US soldiers and more than 8,000 US military contractors were killed. Taken together, that is about five times the number of people killed on 9/11 itself.
BattleLines with Owen Jones is a reader-supported publication. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Hundreds of thousands of US and allied personnel were wounded. 1.8 million US veterans now have an officially recognised disability because of the wars.
An astonishing 30,177 US service members and veterans of the post-9/11 wars died of suicide.
The estimated financial cost to the US alone was $8 trillion. The bill doesn’t end there. Caring for post-9/11 veterans is projected to cost up to $2.5 trillion by 2050.
That was money diverted from infrastructure, services and the real economy.
According to Nobel Prize-winning economist Joseph Stiglitz and public policy expert Linda Bilmes, this helped destabilise the US economy in the run-up to the 2008 financial crash. The war was financed through debt rather than taxation, driving up interest costs, while the conflict also contributed to higher oil prices. US consumers, they noted, kept up their levels of consumption by borrowing against surging house prices.
The success of the ‘War on Terror’ can be judged by another key statistic: 3,329 people were killed by terrorism worldwide in 2000. By 2014, that figure had soared to 32,685.
Iraq was plunged into violent chaos, with a sectarian bloodbath detonated by the US-led invasion. All of this helped give rise to ISIS, which seized large swathes of Iraq and Syria, with apocalyptic consequences for its victims.
A two-decade-long occupation of Afghanistan – with hideous war crimes committed by the Western occupiers helping to drive an escalating insurgency – ended with the Taliban back in power, stronger than ever.
Torture became Western state policy. A worldwide network of secret prisons and rendition flights was established, with detainees abducted and transferred beyond ordinary legal protections.
Share
Drone warfare and targeted killing were normalised. This was the dawn, too, of mass surveillance.
Muslims were demonised, setting off a tidal wave of bigotry which helped drive the rise of the far right.
Donald Trump himself was a direct consequence of all this chaos – threatening the very future of an already compromised US democracy.
Indeed, the War on Terror boomeranged home. Trumpism has redirected its rhetoric and institutions against migrants and political dissidents.
Before the attacks, the West seemed to be at the apex of its power. The post-9/11 wars played a pivotal role in the bloody, chaotic death spiral of Western hegemony that came next.
The September 11th attacks were a terrible crime.
What Western elites used those attacks to justify was the crime of the century.
You can order my book The Fall of The West: How They Really Lost It here

reads.title: Many Iranians Forced to Take Out Loans to Pay for Daily Essentials
reads.subtitle: While the Trump administration’s sanctions are driving many Iranians into debt, there is little indication they will trigger an uprising that would deliver victory to the U.S.
reads.body:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. Please consider making a tax-deductible donation to support our work today.
Subscribe now

-
- An Iranian woman looks at fruit while shopping in the traditional Grand Bazaar in southern Tehran, Iran, on September 1, 2026, amid rising tensions between Iran and the United States. Photo by Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images.A video that recently went viral on Iranian social media shows people eating caviar and rare salmon for breakfast in Tehran, a meal costing around 10 million tomans ($50), the monthly wage for many Iranians. Another viral video shows a man wrapping a thick piece of red meat between two layers of bacon, adding additional meat, and then wrapping the concoction in a bun soaked with fat.
Such videos have become increasingly popular in Iran as the country grapples with the rising cost of meat and other food staples.
The head of Iran’s Association of Meat and Protein Products Packing Industry said in late May that in response to the high prices, demand for meat products had fallen 50% compared with the previous year. Last summer, one kilogram of mutton cost around 1 million tomans; this summer, the same portion reached 2 million tomans ($10).
The announcement of a new campaign of sanctions targeted against Iran on August 24—dubbed Operation Economic Outcast by the U.S. Treasury Department—and aimed at further turning the screws on the Iranian economy, has been met with a shrug by many ordinary Iranians already exhausted from trying to survive during a rapid collapse of living standards unseen in the country’s modern history.
The new campaign, which has so far included the sanctioning of several banks and airlines servicing Iran, comes on top of a blockade of the country’s southern ports, which has halted the import of basic resources. As the sanctions campaign continues, the Iranian rial has collapsed, falling Wednesday to a record low of roughly 2.34 million rials to the dollar, making already scarce imports dramatically more expensive.
Iranians have now been forced to navigate a situation in which obtaining the bare necessities of life requires accepting potentially ruinous personal debts, or is simply impossible.
“A packet of tea that used to cost 300,000 to 600,000 tomans [$2-4] now costs one million tomans [$5] after the war. Why should a packet of tea cost one million tomans when a worker’s daily wage is not even one million tomans? If you are a day laborer, you have to give up even buying tea,” said a construction worker in Tehran, who like others who spoke to Drop Site for this article, requested anonymity to avoid retaliation. “Soap, dental floss, tobacco, and goods like these have become unaffordable for us. Our situation has become embarrassing. To buy the personal hygiene products we actually want, we have to take out loans.”

## Food and Medicine
While the Iranian government initially sought to cushion the economic crisis at the start of the year by providing approximately 80 million people with monthly electronic food credits for four months, worth 1 million tomans—about $7 when the program was announced—the payments were rapidly eroded by inflation and the rial’s continuing collapse.
At the start of the calendar year, the country’s minimum wage rose to 10 million tomans per month, equivalent at the time to $100. But with the outbreak of the war and a rise in the dollar exchange rate, the minimum wage by September had once again fallen to the equivalent of $80—even as the price of food rose 3.6% in August alone and stood approximately 128% higher than a year earlier.
According to Consumer Price Index (CPI) reports published by Iran’s Statistical Center, which measure the price of a basket of basic items for each household, prices for basic goods are 2.7 times higher than two years ago, while wages have not moved or have even declined.
“Before, even buying small quantities of fruit was a source of embarrassment, and people would feel ashamed, for example, to buy half a kilo of something. But now, even buying fruit one piece at a time is no longer something to be ashamed of. People simply don’t have the money to spend, and those who have children or a pregnant wife cannot cut fresh fruit and vegetables from their shopping list,” said a 35-year-old resident of Tehran. “I’m not even talking about expenses like entertainment or going to restaurants. Ordinary household shopping alone eats up an average salary. The reason you walk around the city and see everyone angry and arguing with each other is this situation. People see that they are constantly working, but every day they are getting poorer. These things put a lot of pressure on people’s nerves.”
Even though many people have cut parts of their diets, such as protein, dairy products, or fresh vegetables, because of economic pressures, the financial burden of rising medical prices continues to weigh on them.
Sanctions and the naval blockade, which have prevented raw materials needed for the production of medicines from entering Iran—along with the destruction of a large number of pharmaceutical manufacturing plants during the war—have had a significant impact both on the availability of medicines and on their cost.
“The increase in the price of raw materials, the inability to secure foreign currency, and other economic problems have caused medicine prices to rise and production to decline. On the other hand, because pharmacists cannot adjust their selling prices in line with their costs, it costs them more to produce the medicines than they can sell them for, putting them under even greater pressure, which also affects the market,” Dr. Shahram Kalantari, head of the Iranian Pharmacists Association, told the Mehr news agency. “All of this is happening while the government is unable to properly repay its debts to pharmacists and pharmacies, placing them under even greater economic pressure.”
The prices of basic painkillers like ibuprofen and antibiotics like amoxicillin have doubled or tripled over the past year, leaving many Iranians in a constant struggle to track down lifesaving medicines which are normally widely available.
“Poverty in Iran has been increasing,” said Javad Hoseini, the head of Iran’s State Welfare Organization, according to ILNA, the Iranian labor news agency. “And today the population living below the absolute poverty line has risen from 16 million to 34 million people, while people’s economic resilience has declined and Iran is facing the widespread nature of poverty.”
That estimate came just weeks before the second wave of U.S. attacks, and before the new U.S. blockade and economic sanctions campaign that have raised the level of economic warfare against Iranians to an unprecedented level.

## Buy Now, Pay Later
In the absence of a functional economy where individuals can use their wages to purchase the goods they need, Iran has seen an explosion of short-term personal loan programs, referred to as “Buy Now, Pay Later” services, where individuals can use debt to finance the purchase of clothing, food, and small consumer goods.
An online women’s clothing store that operates on Instagram launched its own loan service just two months after the most recent war began, citing what the store itself described as “numerous customer requests.”
Yet even this stopgap measure has done little to keep the gears of the economy turning, as low cash liquidity in an economy increasingly running on debt and deferred payments means retailers lack the money to replenish their inventories. This summer, Iran’s Purchasing Managers Index, known as the Shamkh, showed contracting net figures for new orders, inventories, sales, and exports for the 16th consecutive month.
“The economic situation has become such that people genuinely need installment plans even to buy ordinary clothes for themselves. But the problem with buy-now-pay-later services is that they make it harder for us to buy and replace our raw materials,” said the manager of a clothing store. “On the other hand, if we refuse to offer these services, our sales will decline. Selling the products and hoping that the money comes back is better than keeping the goods in storage and waiting for people’s economic situation to improve.”
While some U.S. officials initially framed the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran as an effort to liberate Iranians from authoritarian rule, the subsequent sanctions campaign and blockade have been bluntly described as a means of destroying Iranian society by deepening economic deprivation and provoking domestic unrest.
“We have the blockade, and we are going to have the toughest sanctions in history,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in August, adding: “We are going to collapse this regime.” Earlier, Bessent told the Senate Banking Committee that Washington had “created a dollar shortage” in Iran, sending its currency into freefall and causing inflation to explode—“and hence we have seen the Iranian people out on the street.”
Iran’s total trade has fallen by an estimated 25–35%, with imports declining faster than exports, while the workforce has dropped by about 450,000 from a year earlier, according to figures provided by the Iranian government. The International Monetary Fund forecasts that the economy will contract by 6.1% in 2026, as inflation drives up business expenses and consumers cut back their own spending, including on food and basic household goods.
While the U.S. sanctions are succeeding in causing the impoverishment of Iranians, there is little indication that they are set to trigger an uprising that would deliver victory in the U.S. campaign.
Many Iranians who spoke to Drop Site said that their concerns had shifted to merely surviving rather than pursuing political change or confronting a government that has intensified its hold on society amid the war.
“I can see with my own eyes that despite having a steady income—or sometimes even earning more money than I did in some previous months—I am getting poorer every day. When I go to a café, I have to go through the entire menu and choose the cheapest thing available. Even that cheapest option gets more expensive every day,” said a 27-year-old student living in the city of Karaj. “Our lives weren’t like this before. We didn’t have to count every penny and calculate every expense. Like many others, I have turned to credit-payment services and installment purchases because I cannot afford the cost of living. A pair of sneakers costs the equivalent of one month’s salary for a person in Tehran, and the ‘buy now, pay later’ services even exist for buying food, which shows just how bad people’s economic situation has become. In such circumstances, it is obvious that everyone’s focus just shifts toward survival.”

## Rising Inequality
At the same time that the Trump administration announced its Economic Outcast program against Iran, Iranian government spokesperson Fatima Mohajerani, responding to a question about poverty rates in Iran in late August, told reporters: “The publication of statistics and figures related to the issue of poverty is subject to security restrictions. Although the government has the figures and statistics on this issue, it cannot make the numbers public.”
The Iranian government’s revenues are also declining day by day under the pressure of sanctions and restrictions on oil exports caused by the blockade.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed that the Iranian government is unable to pay the salaries of its employees and security forces, though no such reports have emerged in Iran, and government employees and soldiers continue reporting for work.
But a recent announcement that the government plans to increase consumer energy and gasoline prices inside Iran—both normally subsidized by government spending—shows clear signs that the country is under financial strain.
A large share of the expenditure items in Iran’s current-year budget have been devoted to the war, even though most of the reconstruction work for war-related damage—estimated at between $20 billion and $40 billion, according to Meysam Zohourian, a conservative member of the Iranian parliament—has not even begun.
Iranian President Massoud Pezeshkian and Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, speaking publicly just days apart late last month, both warned that the costs of running the country must somehow be covered and that the welfare and essential needs of the population cannot be postponed indefinitely.
“No matter how strong we are militarily, if the people are hungry and we do not have financial circulation, economic growth and domestic production, we will not endure,” said Ghalibaf on August 21. Days later, Pezeshkian echoed his sentiments with apparent frustration, stating, “Some say sanctions have no effect at all. I really don’t know what to say to those people.”
Their remarks were directed at domestic hardliners who made demands for major upfront sanctions relief and reparations a condition for negotiations, as well as other segments of the Iranian establishment alleged to be opposed to talks entirely.  But the comments have also fueled speculation about the government’s concerns over how much economic pressure the population can withstand.
At the same time, amid growing deprivation, the display of excesses such as wrapping red meat in bacon, or cafés serving caviar for breakfast has heightened the sense of inequality in Iran. In the comments section of an Instagram post showing the preparation of a meat dish, one user wrote: “Eating something like this even once has become a dream for me,” while another added: “I hold the country’s officials responsible for this situation.”
