reads.title: U.S.-Iran MOU expires without agreement; Israeli strikes kill 11 in Lebanon; DNC votes to abolish ICE
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 17, 2026
reads.body:
- People carry a lifeless body pulled from the rubble after an Israeli airstrike on Deir Al-Zahrani in Lebanon on August 15, 2026. Photo by Houssam Shbaro/Anadolu via Getty Images.Monday, August 17, 2026 – Sixty-day negotiating period for U.S.-Iran Islamabad agreement ends without final deal. U.S. President Donald Trump tells Iran to “put up the white flag of surrender,” threatens to bomb Oman. Iran reaffirms that Oman deal is separate from full Hormuz reopening. Iran says Qatar is holding Iranian pilots as POWs. Drones target Kurdistan Prime Minister’s office, Intelligence Chief’s residence. Ansarallah says it struck Mokha and Marib. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government says it carried out 181 military operations in 24 hours. Israel continues its assault on Gaza. Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank. Jared Kushner meets with Hamas leadership in Cairo. Regional powers condemn Israel for rejecting the Gaza roadmap. Over 70 Palestinian families face eviction in Lydd. Palestinian Red Crescent evacuates 74 people from Gaza. Palestinian paramedic released by Israel after more than two months. At least 10 Palestinian women prisoners contract scabies in Israel’s Damon Prison. Israeli Supreme Court considers case of detained Palestinian journalist. Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill 11 amid supposed ceasefire. Lebanese leaders condemn Saturday attacks; Hezbollah vows response. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun says Israel is pushing to end UNIFIL presence as Israeli military activity surges in southern Lebanon. Democratic National Committee votes to back abolishing ICE. Trump orders reduction of joint military exercises with South Korea. Attorney General Todd Blanche declines to pledge Department of Justice independence from Trump on prosecutions. Supreme Court again rejects Trump’s bid to overturn E. Jean Carroll verdict. UAE trained mercenaries in Sudan. Fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile State displaces thousands as RSF advances. Russia jails opposition party chairman for 11 years over anti-war comments. Taiwan plans record defense spending amid growing Chinese pressure. Somali troops claim to retake Baidoa from opposition forces. India claims to foil Pakistan-backed militant plot. Syrian detainee dies in government custody amid torture allegations. British prime minister exchanged messages with an impersonator posing as Trump aide.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Sixty-day negotiating period for U.S.-Iran Islamabad agreement ends without final deal: The 60-day period set out for negotiations following the U.S.-Iran Islamabad memorandum of understanding ended Monday without a final agreement or a joint announcement of an extension.

- Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Monday there was no 60-day deadline in the Islamabad memorandum, adding that Tehran does not formulate its policies under pressure or ultimatums, the Islamic Republic’s News Agency reported.

- He said the memorandum provided for 60 days of talks on sanctions relief and the nuclear issue, with the possibility of an extension if no agreement was reached.

- However, according to Baghaei, those talks never began because the U.S. breached the memorandum weeks after it was signed. “We did not start any negotiations at all, and the U.S. violated the understanding from the very beginning; as a result, the issue of a 60-day deadline became entirely moot,” Baghaei said.

- A senior Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran has reportedly given Washington “a few weeks” to fully implement the memorandum and “will not wait indefinitely” for the U.S. naval blockade to end, warning that Iran would be prepared to escalate tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider region if diplomacy fails.

- Trump tells Iran to “put up the white flag of surrender,” threatens to bomb Oman: U.S. President Donald Trump called on Iran to “put up the white flag of surrender” and threatened to bomb Oman, which is currently in talks with Tehran regarding the administration of the Strait, if it obstructs U.S. efforts to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the shit out of them,” Trump told Fox News Monday.

- Asked about U.S. weapons stockpiles in the Middle East, he claimed, “What we have used so far is peanuts.”

- Trump said he was under no pressure to end the conflict. “I have no time schedule…I’m not in a hurry,” adding, “The midterms have nothing to do with my thinking.”

- Iran reaffirms that Oman deal is separate from full Hormuz reopening: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Monday that an “understanding” has been reached in negotiations with Oman on a transit route through the Strait of Hormuz.

- Baghaei said the talks have proceeded slowly, “but we had planned, and still plan, to finalize the understanding in the form of a package: the map plus a joint statement.”

- The talks with Oman, Araghchi said, focus narrowly on mapping new navigation lanes for ships, since the previous routes are no longer operational. Whether the Strait actually reopens, he said, “will depend on the fulfillment of other conditions to which the United States must adhere.”

- Iran says Qatar holding Iranian pilots as POWs: Iran formally accused Qatar of holding three Iranian military pilots as prisoners of war for about six months and asked the Red Cross to intervene on Saturday.

- In a letter to ICRC President Mirjana Spoljaric Egger, Brig. Gen. Mohammad Bagherzadeh, who heads Iran’s committee for missing personnel, said the pilots were shot down over Qatar during a March 2 mission against an “enemy military base.”

- Bagherzadeh said Qatar has denied the prisoners contact with their families and urged the ICRC to visit them and help secure their release.

- Qatar denied these accusations, with a Foreign Ministry spokesperson saying that the pilots entered Qatari airspace and ignored radio warnings before being shot down. Qatar claims rescue teams recovered the remains of one pilot, repatriated in July, and Tehran never answered an April invitation to review the Qatari search operation for the other two.

- Drones target Kurdistan Prime Minister’s office, Intelligence Chief’s residence: Two explosive-laden drones targeted the office of Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani and the residence of the head of the region’s intelligence agency on Monday, Asharq Al-Awsat reported. Barzani said the Kurdistan Region’s Counter-Terrorism Directorate determined that the attacks were carried out using “Iranian drones,” calling them “a dangerous escalation and a direct threat to the security and stability of the region.”

## Yemen

- Ansarallah says it struck Mokha and Marib: Yemen’s Ansarallah said on Sunday that it had struck Saudi-backed military forces in the Red Sea port of Mokha and in Marib, the country’s oil-rich province, with ballistic missiles and drones, according to the Ansarallah-affiliated Saba news agency.

- Operations at Mokha were suspended on Sunday, with the port’s director saying that strikes had killed seven people and caused an estimated $16 million in damage.

- Ansarallah’s spokesperson also claimed a missile attack on a “Saudi military vessel and four escort ships” off Mokha in the Red Sea on Monday.

- Yemen’s Saudi-backed government says it carried out 181 military operations in 24 hours: The armed forces of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government said they used drones, artillery, and rocket launchers in 181 operations against Ansarallah from Saturday to Sunday, according to military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nuzaili.

- Al-Nuzaili claimed the strikes killed and wounded dozens of Ansarallah fighters and destroyed equipment and weapons depots along front lines stretching from the Red Sea coast to the Saada and Marib areas.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 48 hours, two Palestinians were killed and 18 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. Three bodies were also recovered from beneath the rubble.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,399 killed, with 174,310 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,265 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,198, while 813 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel continues its assault on Gaza:

- Israeli forces killed a Palestinian man in Deir Al-Balah, striking him as he walked through Nuseirat refugee camp on Saturday evening, and wounded four others in strikes that day.

- Israeli artillery also shelled densely populated areas of Khan Younis on Saturday, causing additional injuries and displacement. Forces opened fire toward Bureij and Jabalia refugee camps, bombarded Gaza City’s Al-Zaytoun neighborhood, and demolished homes and residential buildings in Al-Tuffah neighborhood and Rafah.

- An Israeli airstrike on a Khan Younis tent encampment wounded at least 5 Palestinians on Sunday, while a separate strike on an apartment in Nuseirat wounded several others.

- Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank:

- Hebron: Mohammed Al-Mutawwar, 27, an intensive care nurse at Dura Governmental Hospital, was shot in the back during a Friday evening attack on the town of Sa’ir by Israeli settlers, according to the Palestinian Nursing and Midwifery Association. The bullet severed his spinal cord, causing permanent paralysis, the association said. A young woman was also shot in the back and head during the attack, the Palestinian Red Crescent said.

- Israeli settlers under military protection attacked the Al-Ras area of Hebron city early Sunday, shooting two Palestinians and beating eight others, the Palestinian Red Crescent said. A 60-year-old man was shot in the back and hand; a 46-year-old man was shot and then detained by Israeli forces. A 66-year-old woman was among those beaten.

- In the village of Massafer Yatta, Israeli settlers broke into a Palestinian home, besieged the family, vandalized the yard, and then held a celebration on the family’s balcony, Israeli lawmaker Ofer Casif said on Sunday.

- Jenin: Israeli forces on Monday arrested two Palestinian farmers in Faqqu’a after armed settlers detained them while they were picking prickly pears on their land near a newly established outpost.

- Qalqilya: Residents of Azzun protested the continued closure of the town’s main northern entrance, sealed by Israeli forces since October 7, 2023, restricting movement and hurting local businesses.

- Nablus: Israeli settlers, backed by the army, on Monday continued for a ninth consecutive day to besiege three families’ homes in Qusra amid attempts to seize them. Israeli forces have also blocked access roads, forced residents from two homes and turned 16 others into military posts. In Beit Dajan, Israeli forces on Monday demolished a residential structure and two agricultural structures and filled in a water well.

- Bethlehem: About 10 Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian doctor Majed Dwayat with stones and sticks in Jannatah, east of Bethlehem, breaking his hand and smashing his car’s windows, WAFA reported on Sunday.

- Kushner meets with Hamas leadership in Cairo: President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and “Board of Peace” member Jared Kushner met Hamas leaders in Egypt on Sunday to press the group to disarm and relinquish authority in Gaza, Axios reported.

- The Hamas delegation, led by political leader and chief negotiator Khalil Al-Hayya and including several senior leaders, attended talks with Kushner, Trump’s board envoy Nickolay Mladenov, and Egyptian, Qatari, and Turkish mediators, according to Reuters. Tony Blair was also at the talks, according to Axios.

- A source familiar with the meeting told Axios that the talks sought “concrete, verifiable steps” toward Hamas decommissioning its weapons and military infrastructure, transferring governing authority to a Palestinian technocratic administration, and permitting an international force to deploy—commitments the group has already agreed to and repeatedly reaffirmed.

- At an earlier meeting with Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, Al-Hayya stressed Hamas is ready to implement the agreement “as soon as Israel announces its commitment to it.”

- Kushner and Mladenov met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Monday.

- Regional powers condemn Israel for rejecting Gaza roadmap: Eight Muslim-majority countries issued a joint statement on Sunday condemning Israel for rejecting the roadmap saying, “Israel now bears responsibility for obstructing the efforts to bring peace in Gaza.” The statement signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Egypt, Jordan, Qatar, Indonesia, and Pakistan, called on the Board of Peace and the U.S. to take “immediate and concrete measures” to keep any party from obstructing the plan’s implementation.

- Over 70 Palestinian families face eviction in Lydd: Israel has ordered the eviction of more than 70 Palestinian families in the city of Lydd in Israel, according to Wafa. Israeli authorities issued the orders under the pretext of “seizing state lands.”

- Palestinian Red Crescent evacuates 74 people from Gaza: The Palestine Red Crescent Society, with the help of the World Health Organization, evacuated 74 people from Gaza through the Rafah crossing on Sunday, including 38 patients and 36 companions, WAFA reported.

- When it first reopened Rafah earlier this year, Israel promised it would allow 50 Palestinian patients, with up to two companions each, to leave Gaza daily. Since the ceasefire began, 11,186 people, out of 28,600 scheduled, have passed through the crossing, a compliance rate of 39.1%.

- Nearly 20,000 patients, including thousands of children and cancer patients, require treatment that is unavailable in Gaza.

- Palestinian paramedic released by Israel after more than two months: Palestinian Red Crescent Society paramedic Waseem Al-Mughari, 33, was released Sunday after 68 days of enforced disappearance, Healthcare Workers Watch (HWW) reported.

- HWW said an Israeli-backed armed militia intercepted his marked ambulance on Salah al-Din Road on June 9 while he was on duty. The militia subjected him and six PRCS colleagues to field interrogation before handing Al-Mughari over to Israeli forces.

- At least 10 Palestinian women prisoners contract scabies in Israel’s Damon Prison: These cases come amid severe overcrowding, poor ventilation, and shortages of cleaning supplies and clothing, the Palestinian Prisoners’ Society said Monday. More than 90 Palestinian women are currently held at the prison, including pregnant women, minors and prisoners with chronic health conditions. The group said scabies has continued to spread through Israeli prisons since May 2024, while Israeli prison authorities have failed to adequately address the conditions driving the outbreak or provide effective treatment. The group described the continuing outbreak and denial of medical care as part of a broader system of “torture and systematic medical neglect.”

- Israeli Supreme Court considers case of detained Palestinian journalist: The Israeli Supreme Court held a session Sunday to review the case of Palestinian journalist Mohammad Arab, Haaretz reported.

- Israeli forces detained Arab on March 14, 2024, while he was working as a correspondent for Al-Araby TV inside the Al-Shifa Hospital complex in Gaza City.

- Since March 2024, he has been held under Israel’s “Unlawful Combatants Law,” which permits the state to hold individuals indefinitely without formal charge or trial, and his detention has repeatedly been extended at six-month intervals.

- Reports from his lawyers indicate that Arab’s health has deteriorated drastically over the course of his 29 months in custody, and he previously engaged in a hunger strike to protest the prison’s conditions.

- The court considered an appeal by his lawyers to halt the repeated six-month extensions of his detention. The hearing concluded without a ruling, and Arab remains detained at the Ketziot prison in the Negev desert.

## Lebanon

- Israeli strikes on Lebanon kill 11 amid supposed ceasefire: Israeli strikes on Ansar and Deir Al-Zahrani in southern Lebanon on Saturday killed 11 people and wounded 19, the highest single-day toll since the June ceasefire, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.

- Israeli strikes on Ansar killed seven, including a mother and four children, and killed four in Deir Al-Zahrani, where 17 others were wounded.

- Israel claimed its attacks targeted “Hezbollah infrastructure” in response to activity against Israeli troops in the Ali Al-Taher Heights, which Israel claimed is inside what it calls its “security zone.” A Hezbollah drone struck a combat engineering unit near the Ali Al-Taher Saturday, injuring three Israeli soldiers, the Israeli military later claimed on Sunday.

- Separately on Saturday, Israeli forces razed the last remaining houses in the town of Mais Al-Jabal, began constructing an earthen barrier near Khallet Haris-Haddatha, deployed troops along the road between Mais Al-Jabal and Wadi Slouki, and fired artillery at Taybeh, Kfar Tibnit, Zawtar Al-Sharqiya and Mansouri.

- On Monday, Israeli forces targeted Aitaroun in Bint Jbeil district with artillery and machine-gun fire, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency. Israeli warplanes also carried out two rounds of strikes on Mansouri in Tyre (Sour) district.

- Lebanese leaders condemn Saturday attacks; Hezbollah vows response: Leaders from Lebanon’s government condemned Israel’s escalation in the country’s south on Saturday, while Hezbollah promised an “appropriate” response to the strikes.

- President Joseph Aoun called the attacks “a clear message against the negotiation process and U.S. efforts to implement the agreement.”

- Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned Israel’s killing of civilians, noting that the women and children killed in Ansar were “not ‘military infrastructure.’”

- In a statement Saturday, Hezbollah warned that Israel’s continuing violations and “attempts to impose a fait accompli” would draw an “appropriate response.” The group demanded that Lebanese authorities abandon what it called “humiliating direct negotiations” under U.S. sponsorship, arguing that these negotiations made the government “complicit” in Israeli attacks on the country. Hezbollah has refused to engage in direct talks with Israel and was not a party to the deal.

- Aoun says Israel pushing to end UNIFIL presence as Israeli military activity surges in southern Lebanon: The United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon (UNIFIL), the UN peacekeeping mission deployed in southern Lebanon, said Monday that Israeli military activity in the area had increased significantly over the past two weeks, recording an average of 137 Israeli projectiles per day between August 5 and 16, including 208 on Saturday and 185 on Sunday.

- The figures came as Lebanese President Joseph Aoun renewed calls to extend UNIFIL’s mandate. “Israel rejects UNIFIL’s presence and has been pushing in this direction for nearly a year, while we are demanding that it remain,” Aoun said, adding that Lebanon’s first choice is to extend the force’s mandate, with an alternative international force alongside the Lebanese army as a second option.

## U.S. News

- DNC votes to back abolishing ICE: The Democratic National Committee approved a non-binding resolution Saturday during its summer meeting in Austin urging Congress to abolish ICE and wind down the immigration detention system, alongside a more strongly backed separate proposal calling for reforms to the agency.

- The resolution passed in Austin calls for federal legislation to abolish ICE, for the agency’s operations and its detention infrastructure to conclude and close down, to condition DHS appropriations on reducing ICE’s operations, to terminate private prison contracts and to release immigration detainees except under limited circumstances. It also calls for expanded civil rights oversight in the U.S. immigration system.

- In response to Saturday’s vote, DNC Chair Ken Martin said official party positions are set every four years at the national convention but that Democrats remain united in opposing current enforcement tactics.

- Trump orders reduction of joint military exercises with South Korea: President Donald Trump said Sunday he instructed War Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” U.S. participation in joint military exercises with South Korea, complaining in a social media post that Seoul had not joined U.S. efforts on Iran’s “denuclearization” while praising his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.

- The announcement, which caught the Pentagon off guard according to a senior U.S. military official, comes as the U.S.’s 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises with South Korea began on Monday.

- Blanche declines to pledge DOJ independence from Trump on prosecutions: Attorney General Todd Blanche refused Sunday to pledge that the Justice Department would “always act independently” of the White House, telling NBC’s Meet the Press that “no attorney general should ever pledge that” and that President Donald Trump should “of course” have a voice in individual prosecution decisions, according to Axios.

- Blanche called it an “extraordinarily false narrative” that Trump directs him to prosecute specific people, even as Trump has repeatedly named individuals he wants charged, including former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James, both of whom the DOJ has prosecuted.

- During a separate interview with Fox News, Blanche said that Trump “would expect me to tell him no” in cases of legal disagreement, saying “the president loves disagreement.”

- Supreme Court again rejects Trump’s bid to overturn E. Jean Carroll verdict: The Supreme Court denied a second request from President Donald Trump’s lawyers to reconsider throwing out a jury’s $5 million finding that he sexually abused writer E. Jean Carroll in the 1990s and later defamed her, according to the Associated Press.

- Trump paid the $5 million judgment shortly after the Court refused to take up his appeal in June.

- Trump and the Justice Department are separately asking the high court to toss out a second Carroll verdict totaling $83 million, arguing presidential immunity shields him from being sued over 2019 comments he made about her while in office, a case the court has not yet acted on.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- UAE trained mercenaries in Sudan: Seven Colombian mercenaries told the Financial Times that UAE-based GSSG recruited, trained and deployed about 2,000 fighters to support Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces, according to an investigation from the outlet published on Saturday.

- “It’s the Emirates that put in the most money and resources,” one former commander explained.

- Around 300 specialists trained in drones and anti-aircraft weapons at Emirati bases, including in Abu Dhabi, and traveled through UAE-backed hubs in Somalia and Libya.

- One battalion fought beside the RSF in the siege and capture of El Fasher, where Yale estimates 60,000 civilians were killed in the weeks after its fall. Fighters said GSSG paid bonuses when the city fell.

- Fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile State displaces thousands as RSF advances: Clashes between the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have forced thousands of residents to flee parts of southeastern Blue Nile State, with civil society monitors reporting civilians crossing the river by small boat after the RSF-aligned Tasis Coalition seized the strategic town of Geissan near the Ethiopian border on Tuesday.

- The Blue Nile Civil Society Initiative warned that military operations during a period of extreme weather in the region pose a direct threat to civilians and called for an immediate ceasefire and safe humanitarian corridors to reach stranded populations.

- The RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North, have advanced in both Geissan and the border town of Kurmuk in August.

- Russia jails opposition party chairman for 11 years over anti-war comments: A Russian court sentenced Lev Shlosberg, deputy chairman of the liberal Yabloko party, to 11 years in a penal colony after convicting him of “discrediting” the armed forces and spreading false information about the war in Ukraine following comments criticizing the invasion.

- Shlosberg used his closing statement to demand an immediate ceasefire and denounce the war as a catastrophe for Russia, stating “one day the entire nation will shudder at this list ​of martyrs,” from the conflict.

- The sentence comes a week after Russia’s Supreme Court barred Yabloko—the only registered party calling for an end to the war—from participating in next month’s parliamentary election.

- Taiwan plans record defense spending amid growing Chinese pressure: Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te said Taiwan’s 2027 defense budget will rise to the equivalent of $31.4 billion USD, exceeding 3% of GDP for the first time, as Taipei accelerates military modernization in response to mounting Chinese pressure.

- Lai called the spending “an investment in peace,” while Taiwan continues developing submarines and expanding preparations for scenarios including a Chinese maritime blockade.

- The increase also reflects sustained U.S. pressure on Taipei to shoulder more of its own defense costs.

- Somali troops claim to retake Baidoa from opposition forces: Somali federal forces stated that they had driven opposition fighters out of the city of Baidoa after heavy clashes. Federal authorities said that they had repelled an attack by Laftagareen’s forces using vehicle-borne explosives and that around 30 assailants were killed, while statements on social media by Laftagareen’s office claimed that the city center was still held by his movement.

- Baidoa has been a flashpoint since federal troops seized the city in March after forces loyal to former South West state president Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen broke with Mogadishu over constitutional disputes.

- India claims to foil Pakistan-backed militant plot: Indian security agencies arrested more than 200 alleged members of what Home Minister Amit Shah claimed was a militant network backed by Pakistani intelligence in a coordinated operation across 14 states.

- Shah said the crackdown targeted what he called the “Shahzad Bhatti Network” and prevented planned “subversive attacks,” with authorities claiming to recover pistols, ammunition, and grenades bearing Pakistan Ordnance Factory markings.

- Syrian detainee dies in government custody amid torture allegations: Mohammad Ghamira, a resident of rural Latakia and former member of the Syrian Civil Defense, died in government custody while he was being held over a financial complaint, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, which said that accusations of torture had emerged in connection with his death.

- Ghamira developed severe bleeding in detention over several days, and after release was found to have suffered a brain hemorrhage, falling into a coma and dying in intensive care at a nearby hospital.

- Syria’s Interior Ministry said that it had initiated an investigation into the circumstances of Ghamira’s death.

- British prime minister exchanged messages with an impersonator posing as Trump aide: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham engaged with messages from someone impersonating White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles before growing suspicious the contact was illegitimate, four officials told Politico, prompting the British embassy in Washington to raise concerns with the White House.

- One person briefed on the exchange said a “few messages” were sent after Burnham entered No. 10 but described them as “of no significance.”

- A Whi

reads.title: Hormuz grinds to a halt again; Gaza’s cancer patients dying at 2-3 times prewar rate; DHS surveilled left-wing groups in Minnesota
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 14, 2026
reads.body:
- Ships are anchored in the Strait of Hormuz off the coast of Bandar Abbas, Iran, on August 10, 2026. Photo by Ali Saeedi/Getty Images.Friday, August 14, 2026 – Two ships attacked in Strait of Hormuz, UAE blames Iran. U.S. sends new carrier to Middle East. Traffic through Hormuz seems to grind to a halt. U.S. threatens economic punishment for Iran that has “never been seen” as War Secretary Pete Hegseth vows indefinite blockade. U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, roughly 25% of fleet, in Iran war. Drones intercepted over Iraqi Kurdistan. Iraqi state oil company says UAE firm is buying its crude. Ansarallah says it struck Saudi Aramco facility. Iran rejects U.S. claims that flights to Yemen carry military personnel or equipment. Israel attacks fishermen off Gaza coast. Israel continues its assault on the occupied West Bank. Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz orders transfer of West Bank enforcement powers; Palestinian commission says move advances annexation. Israel blockade on oil and spare parts from entering Gaza endangers thousands, MSF says. Gaza cancer patients dying at 2-3 times prewar rate, Reuters reports. Jared Kushner to visit Israel next week. Israel continues military activity in Lebanon despite “ceasefire.” Israel demolished a 60-apartment complex in Lebanon, official says. Human Rights Watch urges UN to keep international force in southern Lebanon beyond 2026. Flock Safety announces mandatory audit changes amid mounting scrutiny over misuse. DHS documents show broad surveillance of left-leaning groups during Minnesota immigration crackdown. Border czar Tom Homan defends ICE plan to equip officers with electric shock gloves. Trump signs proclamations imposing drone tariffs, allowing limited foreign warship construction. Vice President JD Vance asks Department of Justice to investigate hospitals over transgender care. DOJ finds California prisons systematically fail to protect women from guard sexual abuse. Federal judge dismisses Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard. Progressive Florida slate rally moves to church after venue tried to bar Rep. Rashida Tlaib. CIA behind Ecuadorian fishing attacks, WaPo reports. Russia rejects Black Sea ceasefire proposal. UN warns that 650,000 refugees in South Sudan could lose food aid. Chadian president pardons jailed opposition leaders. Hundreds across Canada target Elbit suppliers in “people’s arms embargo.”
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Two ships attacked in Hormuz, UAE blames Iran: The UAE accused Iran of attacking two vessels affiliated with the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company on Thursday, while the ships were transiting the Strait of Hormuz. No injuries were reported as a result of the attack.

- The UAE Foreign Ministry called the attack a violation of UN Security Council Resolution 2817 and an “act of piracy” by Iran’s Revolutionary Guard Corps. It demanded that Iran halt its attacks and “completely and unconditionally” reopen the Strait.

- U.S. sends new carrier to Middle East: The U.S. aircraft carrier USS George Washington headed to the Middle East on Thursday to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has been deployed in the region for more than 250 days, according to an announcement from the Navy.

- The George Washington strike group departed Vietnam on August 12, the Navy said.

- The Lincoln’s deployment had been expected to end in May but was extended as the U.S. war on Iran continued.

- The news comes after reports this week that multiple sailors had attempted to jump overboard from the USS Abraham Lincoln amid grueling deployment conditions for the ship’s 5,000-person crew.

- Traffic through Hormuz seems to grind to a halt: West-to-east tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has collapsed after a brief burst of outbound flows, according to data published by Kpler on Thursday.

- From August 7 through 13, 19 tankers carried 16.7 million barrels out of the Gulf. Nearly all of that moved during the first four days with 16 tankers carrying 16.3 million barrels.

- From August 11 through 13, just three Iran-linked tankers crossed, carrying only 0.4 million barrels combined.

- U.S. threatens economic punishment for Iran that has “never been seen” as Hegseth vows indefinite blockade: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened to impose measures on Iran that have “never been seen in the history of economic isolation on a country,” during a Thursday interview on Newsmax.

- Bessent described the plan as a “combination of economic isolation” and “the continued blockade in the Strait of Hormuz” of Iranian ports.

- Separately, U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. can maintain its naval blockade of Iranian ports “indefinitely” on Thursday, as the standoff over the Strait of Hormuz drags on.

- Hegseth told reporters in Panama that the U.S. could “rotate ships in and out” to keep up the embargo. “We’ll hold it as long as we need to,” he said.

- U.S. has lost 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones, roughly 25% of fleet, in Iran war: The U.S. military has lost at least 45 MQ-9 Reaper drones during its war with Iran, representing about a quarter of the pre-war fleet and a potential taxpayer cost exceeding $1.3 billion, according to three officials cited by The Washington Post on Friday.

- The losses add to a broader depletion of U.S. munitions, including more than 850 Tomahawk cruise missiles and over 1,000 Patriot and THAAD missiles fired in the campaign’s first month.

- The Trump administration is seeking a $67 billion supplemental budget from the U.S. Senate to restock the arsenal.

- Iranian forces intercepted and destroyed an MQ9-Reaper drone over Hormozgan province on Friday, according to Iranian state TV.

- Drones intercepted over Iraqi Kurdistan: Iraqi air defense systems intercepted drones over the northern Kurdish province of Erbil early Thursday, Iraqi security sources told Al Jazeera.

- Local media footage showed the remnants of the drones falling onto a residential area near Erbil International Airport. No casualties were reported.

- It was not immediately clear where the drones were launched from or what their intended target was. Erbil, the capital of Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdistan region, hosts U.S. forces and has been struck repeatedly by Iran.

- Iraqi state oil company says UAE firm is buying its crude: Iraq’s state oil marketing company SOMO confirmed Wednesday that Abu Dhabi’s ADNOC is among the firms buying its crude and now helping transport Iraqi crude through the Strait of Hormuz, following a Bloomberg report that ADNOC’s trading arm offered Iraq to use its “dark-transit” shuttle system.

- Under the arrangement, tankers make short crossings with their tracking systems switched off, then transfer the crude to other vessels outside the Persian Gulf. The strategy has helped maintain exports through the blockaded Strait.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah says it struck Saudi Aramco facility: Yemen’s Ansarallah movement announced operations against Saudi Arabia and around the Bab Al-Mandab on Thursday as fighting continued in the city of Taiz in southwestern Yemen, with a military source telling the Yemeni outlet Saba that two drones struck an Aramco facility in Jizan. This follows two previous attacks claimed by Ansarallah on the same facility in late July and August.

- The source said the operation answered Saudi violations of Yemeni airspace and sovereignty in Saada and Hajjah and warned of further retaliation.

- Saba separately reported that Ansarallah targeted the Bab Al-Mandab area with two missiles. Details were not immediately available.

- In Taiz, a shell fired by Saudi-backed forces struck the wholesale fish market in Salah district, causing extensive property damage. No casualties were reported.

- Iran rejects U.S. claims that flights to Yemen carry military personnel or equipment: Iran rejected U.S. allegations that Iranian commercial flights to Sana’a are transporting military personnel or equipment in violation of UN Security Council Resolution 2216, calling the claims “completely baseless” and unsupported by evidence, Iran’s Mehr News Agency reported.

- In a letter to UN Secretary-General António Guterres and the Security Council president, the Iranian envoy claimed recent Iranian flights to Yemen were “humanitarian in nature” and accused Washington of trying to “distort the facts” and divert attention from its own military actions and support for the blockade of Yemen.

## Palestine

- Israel attacks fishermen off Gaza coast: Israeli naval boats opened fire on a fishing boat west of Gaza City on Friday, according to WAFA, injuring three fishermen.

- Israel continues its assault on the occupied West Bank:

- Nablus: Israeli forces blocked Israeli and foreign aid groups trying to access three homes in Nablus town of Qusra. The homes have been under siege by settlers for nearly a week, according to WAFA, who are also preventing families from accessing basic necessities during the assault. (Israeli anti-occupation Knesset member Ofer Cassif said he used his parliamentary immunity to cross an Israeli police blockade and deliver some water, food and medicine to the families. Cassif also said he brought equipment to restore their water supply, which had been cut by “settler terrorists.”) Separately, in the city of Nablus, Israeli forces detained four Palestinians during a Friday morning raid, ransacking several homes. Israeli forces also expelled Palestinian families at gunpoint on Thursday and seized three newly built, multi-story homes in Jalud, south of Nablus, converting them into military posts and watchtowers, Haaretz reported.

- Hebron: Israeli forces detained a 14-year-old in the village of Al-Kum, WAFA reported on Friday. On Thursday evening, Israeli settlers attacked Palestinian homes in Al-Buweira with stones and fired live ammunition toward them, and then raided the area, detaining dozens in the process.

- Jenin: Israeli settlers wearing military uniforms assaulted a Palestinian crew from an electrical utility on Friday, briefly detaining two and seizing money from one of them, WAFA reported. Israeli settlers attacked a vehicle between the towns of Arraba and Ya’bad on Thursday evening, using pepper spray and wounding three of the vehicle’s passengers, including a child.

- Ramallah: Israeli settlers damaged Palestinian property between the villages of Al-Mughayyir and Abu Falah on Friday, dismantling water tanks. Israeli settlers also began to establish a new colonial outpost near the Palestinian towns of Silwad and Deir Jarir on Friday, setting up a tent on land owned by the former town.

- Katz orders transfer of West Bank enforcement powers; Palestinian commission says move advances annexation: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz ordered the military to prepare a plan to transfer enforcement powers over Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank to the Israel Police, saying the military should not “chase youth in the hilltops” and citing an “expected welcome increase in the number of settlers” following the government’s approval of new settlements.

- The directive, which has not yet taken effect, represents an advanced step in Israel’s “administrative and legal annexation” of the occupied West Bank by further shifting authority from the military administration to Israeli civilian institutions, treating settlers increasingly as though they were inside Israel while Palestinians remain subject to military rule, the Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said.

- Palestinian Authority Vice President Hussein al-Sheikh condemned the move, saying it “represents a new attempt to impose Israeli law and sovereignty over the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and to entrench the unlawful annexation of Palestinian territory.”

- Israel blockade on oil and spare parts from entering Gaza endangers thousands, MSF says: Israel is placing thousands of Palestinians in Gaza at heightened risk of death and severe illness as hospital generators, ambulances, water pumps, and water trucks begin to fail, the medical charity Doctors Without Borders (MSF) said.

- MSF noted the rising costs of engine oil, which can exceed $1,300 per liter, 20 times its price six months ago.

- It also highlighted the risks electricity rationing posed to hospital operations and water access. A damaged generator, for example, forced MSF to cut daily water production from 600,000 to 350,000 liters, depriving more than 40,000 people of water each day.

- “This is not bureaucracy,” said the group’s Filipe Ribeiro. “It is a deliberate effort to make existence itself impossible.”

- Gaza cancer patients dying at 2-3 times prewar rate, Reuters reports: Gaza cancer patients are dying at two to three times the prewar rate after Israel destroyed the enclave’s only specialized cancer hospital and blocked thousands from leaving for treatment, Reuters reported on Thursday.

- An estimated 17,000 cancer patients now have no access to chemotherapy or advanced care inside Gaza. Another 20,000 patients are registered for treatment abroad, including 5,000 with cancer, but have not been permitted to leave.

- Doctors report three to five cancer deaths daily, up from one to two before the war. Gaza’s remaining hospitals lack up to 70% of essential medical supplies, while specialists warn toxic materials from Israeli explosives may be accelerating cancer rates.

- “Every day my disease progresses,” said a 33-year-old woman with cancer. “I am just waiting to die.”

- Kushner to visit Israel next week: Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and Board of Peace member, plans to visit Israel next week for talks on Gaza, Axios reported.

- The visit is reportedly set to focus on advancing the Board of Peace’s plan. Netanyahu said Israel “rejects” Trump’s 15-point roadmap, which would include Hamas disarmament and a phased Israeli withdrawal.

- A U.S. official told Axios the two sides “see eye-to-eye on the strategic goal, but Israel has expressed some doubts about the plan.”

## Lebanon

- Israel continues military activity in Lebanon despite “ceasefire”:  Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks across southern Lebanon on Thursday and Friday, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

- Israeli forces carried out two explosions in Bint Jbeil and Kounine in Bint Jbeil district and a large explosion in Markaba in Marjayoun district. Forces also bulldozed homes in Bani Hayyan in Marjayoun district, where fires broke out amid continued shelling.

- Israeli warplanes and drones meanwhile repeatedly struck the outskirts of Mansouri and Majdal Zoun in Tyre (Sour) district, alongside demolition operations in the al-Mashaa neighborhood east of Mansouri.

- On Thursday, the Israeli army carried out detonations and demolitions in Taybeh, Aita Al-Jabal, and Bani Hayyan, according to L’orient Today. Israeli Merkava tanks were also seen moving near the eastern outskirts of Kfar Shuba.

- Israel demolished a 60-apartment complex in Lebanon, official says: Ten days ago, Israeli forces demolished a residential complex of around 60 apartments in Kfar Tibnit, in Lebanon’s Nabatieh region, the town’s mukhtar told L’Orient Today.

- The mukhtar said “one of the major demolitions” targeted the Ward complex, made up of 14 buildings. “The complex was completely destroyed,” he said. Several other homes were similarly targeted.

- HRW urges UN to keep international force in southern Lebanon beyond 2026: Human Rights Watch called on the UN Security Council Thursday to delay UNIFIL’s planned withdrawal from southern Lebanon and ensure a robust international force remains to protect civilians. The Security Council voted in August 2025 to extend UNIFIL’s mandate for a final time through 2026, before the latest war erupted in March and Israeli forces displaced hundreds of thousands of people and occupied large areas of southern Lebanon.

- HRW said the security situation has since “dramatically worsened,” with Israeli attacks killing more than 4,333 people and wounding over 12,250 since March 2, according to Lebanon’s Health Ministry.

- “Pulling the plug on UNIFIL without a robust international force in place would effectively abandon millions of Lebanese civilians to an uncertain and potentially disastrous fate,” HRW’s UN director said.

## U.S. News

- Flock Safety announces mandatory audit changes amid mounting scrutiny over misuse: Flock Safety, whose network of automated license plate cameras is used by law enforcement agencies in 49 states, announced Thursday it will require customers to implement an audit tool flagging abnormal searches, shorten its data retention from 30 to seven days, and mandate that officers enter a case number before running searches.

- A Washington Post investigation earlier this month found nearly 50 instances of officers charged or accused of misusing the cameras, often to track romantic partners or family members.

- Six employees of the Savannah, Georgia police department were fired earlier this week for searching for friends and family using Flock technology.

- More than 50 agencies nationwide have canceled or suspended Flock contracts since the start of the year, according to tracking group DeFlock.

- DHS documents show broad surveillance of left-leaning groups during Minnesota immigration crackdown: The Department of Homeland Security opened an investigation into labor unions, climate groups, and progressive organizations during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota earlier this year. Homeland Security launched the investigation days after Border Patrol agents fatally shot nurse Alex Pretti in January, using administrative subpoenas to obtain years of financial records from the groups, according to the New York Times.

- Homeland Security obtained financial records of a number of non profits and prominent unions, including the Sunrise Movement, the Communications Workers of America, and the Service Employees International Union.

- Documents reviewed by the Times also detail an undercover surveillance operation in which agents infiltrated Signal group chats and took names and license plate numbers of people at meetings in churches, libraries, and parks.

- Prosecutors ultimately indicted 15 people connected to the “antifa” in June after presenting grand jurors with a slide claiming 18 groups, including the AFL-CIO, were part of a conspiracy to obstruct immigration agents.

- Homan defends ICE plan to equip officers with electric shock gloves: White House border czar Tom Homan defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s plan to spend up to $20 million on electric shock gloves for officers, telling Fox News a de-escalation tool that could help avoid deadly force.

- The gloves, known as G.L.O.V.E. and manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC, have drawn criticism from civil rights groups and Democrats amid concerns that ICE agents have been too quick to use force, with at least six people shot and killed by immigration agents since last year, including motorists in Maine and Texas last month.

- Homan said deployment of the devices would take “awhile” as the agency works out training protocols.

- Trump signs proclamations imposing drone tariffs, allowing limited foreign warship construction: President Donald Trump signed two proclamations Thursday, one imposing tariffs on drones and drone parts and another directing the Navy to allow limited foreign shipbuilding.

- The drone memorandum sets a 100% tariff on “particularly sensitive” drones and 25% on smaller, less security-sensitive models, alongside a 15% tariff on drones from the European Union, Japan, and several other countries, taking effect 21 days after signing, with tariffs on less sensitive components phased in after 180 days.

- The Navy directive orders War Secretary Pete Hegseth to replace the Advanced Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch Systems with traditional steam and hydraulic systems, establish a fifth naval shipyard, and temporarily permit foreign shipbuilders to construct up to two American warships in their own shipyards as part of efforts to accelerate production.

- Vance asks DOJ to investigate hospitals over transgender care: Vice President JD Vance sent the Justice Department a government report accusing hospitals of using misleading billing codes for transgender health procedures to secure insurance reimbursement, asking Attorney General Todd Blanche to investigate dozens of hospitals nationwide, according to Politico.

- The report from the Department of Health and Human Services, titled “Wolves in White Coats,” found that providers billed nearly $50 million for puberty-blocking drugs for patients ages 9 to 17 using endocrine disorder diagnosis codes rather than gender-related ones. The report was released two days after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services cut off Medicaid funding for gender-affirming care for minors.

- Major medical groups including the American Medical Association and American Academy of Pediatrics support gender-affirming care and have criticized the administration’s actions, with AAP President Susan J. Kressly warning that “allowing the government to determine which patient groups deserve care sets a dangerous precedent.”

- DOJ finds California prisons systematically fail to protect women from guard sexual abuse: The Justice Department found that California’s prison system has systematically failed to protect incarcerated women from sexual abuse and harassment by guards, with staff tasked with investigating misconduct often themselves accused of abuse.

- Federal judge dismisses Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard: Judge Richard G. Stearns of the U.S. District Court in Massachusetts dismissed the Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard University Thursday, ruling that the antisemitic incidents cited in the March lawsuit were “too isolated and episodic” to show the school violated Title VI of the Civil Rights Act.

- The lawsuit had accused Harvard of turning “a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis” following pro-Palestinian campus protests after the Gaza war began in 2023.

- Progressive Florida slate rally moves to church after venue tried to bar Rashida Tlaib: A Friday “Chomp the Oligarchy” rally for a slate of progressive Florida candidates in the Fort Lauderdale area was relocated to a church after its original venue canceled the original booking unless organizers agreed to bar Rep. Rashida Tlaib from speaking, a campaign spokesperson told Drop Site’s Ryan Grim.

- The rally, organized with the Florida Youth Justice Coalition, Gen-Z for Change, and Miami DSA, features Tlaib and Senate candidate Angie Nixon, alongside congressional candidates Elijah Manley (FL-20) and Oliver Larkin (FL-25) and Colorado Democratic congressional nominee Melat Kiros.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- CIA behind Ecuadorian fishing attacks, WaPo reports: The CIA was behind the April attacks on three Ecuadorian fishing boats near the Galápagos Islands, first reported on by Drop Site contributor Camila Lourdes Galarza, according to a new investigation from the Washington Post.

- Last month, Galarza first reported for Drop Site that the Ecuadorian prosecutor assigned to investigate the attacks and 36 survivors’ allegations of kidnapping and torture by U.S. personnel, told a colleague she was facing internal pressure and institutional stonewalling that was preventing her from pursuing potential U.S. involvement. She was assassinated on June 14.

- Russia rejects Black Sea ceasefire proposal: Russia rejected a proposal for a ceasefire on cargo shipping in the Black Sea amid intensifying attacks in recent weeks that have increased global grain prices.

- Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova called it a “deliberate policy aimed at destabilizing ​civilian shipping in the Black Sea,” as a result of Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in the region and rejected the idea of returning to a previous 2022-2023 ceasefire on ships carrying grain.

- The rejection comes after Turkey had floated proposals to both sides for a halt to military operations at sea. Reuters also reported that Ukraine separately transmitted an offer through a third party to stop attacks on civilian targets.

- UN warns that 650,000 refugees in South Sudan could lose food aid: UN agencies warned that more than 650,000 refugees and asylum seekers in South Sudan could lose access to food assistance within weeks because of a severe funding shortfall, with the World Food Programme (WFP) saying no refugees may be receiving food aid by October unless new money is secured.

- The warning comes as South Sudan faces one of the world’s worst hunger crises, with 7.8 million people experiencing acute food insecurity and 2.2 million children acutely malnourished.

- The WFP says it needs $37 million for refugee operations to avoid ceasing aid to 180,000 internally displaced people by October and hundreds of thousands more by this winter.

- Chadian president pardons jailed opposition leaders: Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Deby pardoned former prime minister and main opposition leader Succes Masra, along with eight other opposition figures, ending prison terms that critics had denounced as politically motivated.

- RSF confirms Kurmuk capture as fighting escalates across Sudan: The UAE-backed RSF said it seized Kurmuk, the strategic Blue Nile border town on Thursday, with regional monitors reporting Ethiopian support for the operation. Clashes continued there and in Amburu, North Darfur. In North Kordofan, the army said it repelled an RSF assault involving more than 250 combat vehicles on Jabra al-Sheikh, while two civilians were killed in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers. RSF drone attacks were also reported on Khartoum and Omdurman for a second consecutive day.

- Hundreds across Canada target Elbit suppliers in “people’s arms embargo”: Activists with Arms Embargo Now picketed facilities from British Columbia to Newfoundland on Thursday, targeting more than 40 companies tied to Israeli arms manufacturer Elbit Systems, including Ontario-based TTM Technologies, which has shipped millions of dollars in circuit boards for precision-strike munitions. The campaign has already pushed Montreal-based Apollo Microwaves to end its Elbit contracts and Scotiabank, once Elbit’s largest foreign shareholder, to divest its roughly $500 million stake. Report from Christopher Ketchum is here.

reads.title: U.S. Infrastructure Strikes Have Left Iranians in the South Without Livelihoods
reads.subtitle: U.S. airstrikes last month in southern Iran targeted civilian infrastructure, including fishing ports, bridges, telecommunications networks, power plants, hospitals, and transportation corridors.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- The bridge linking Bandar Abbas and Kehuristan, destroyed in a U.S. strike, is seen in Iran's Hormozgan province on July 19, 2026. Photo by Amir Hossein Khorgooei/Anadolu via Getty Images.AHVAZ, Iran—When U.S. missiles struck the harbor outside in the port city of Badar Abbas last month, Sajjad saw his livelihood literally go up in smoke.
The small wooden fishing boat that had supported the 56-year-old and his family for years was reduced to a charred husk, along with dozens of other boats lining the docks. Sajjad told Drop Site News that nearly every fisherman he knows lost a vessel that night. Replacing a single boat now costs around 2 billion tomans (around $1,050)—far beyond what most families can afford.
“Both my children are in university,” Sajjad said. “Everything depended on that boat. Soon,  I may not even be able to pay their tuition.”
When U.S. strikes resumed in early July following a two-month pause, the attacks focused heavily on southern Iran. Interviews with residents in hard-hit southern provinces like Khuzestan, Hormozgan, Sistan, and Baluchestan describe strikes not only on military facilities, but also on critical civilian infrastructure, including fishing ports, bridges, telecommunications networks, power plants, hospitals, and transportation corridors.
Dozens of communications towers have been knocked offline in repeated attacks, disrupting internet and telephone services. One attack on a transmission tower near Tappeh Aluakbar in Bandar Abbas killed five people, including a woman who died shielding her son with her body, local residents told Drop Site.
Transportation infrastructure has sustained similar damage. Alireza, a resident of Hormozgan who studies screenwriting and is carefully tracking recent events in the hopes of making a documentary about the war, described strikes on Tappeh Aluakbar overlooking Bandar Abbas, bridges linking Bandar Abbas to Khamir and Rudan, railway infrastructure, and key transportation routes connecting the province. At one destroyed crossing, road crews carved a temporary dirt route through a dry riverbed within hours simply to keep vehicles moving.
The damage extends to the sea as well: Alireza estimates that roughly 300 civilian fishing boats have been destroyed across Bandar Abbas, Bandar Lengeh, Sirik, and Jask, affecting the livelihoods of thousands of people. Two maritime search-and-rescue vessels operating near Bandar Abbas, Qeshm, and Hormuz Island were also put out of service.
Kharg Island, Iran’s principal oil export terminal, has long featured in discussions among U.S. officials and defense analysts as a strategically significant site and was bombed in March during the U.S.-Israeli aerial campaign. According to an Iranian military analyst who spoke to Drop Site on condition of anonymity for security reasons, if the U.S. ever sent ground troops to take over the island, Iran’s ability to reinforce Kharg would depend heavily on the transportation networks running through Hormozgan.
“They’re not simply destroying roads,” the analyst said. “They’re reducing Iran’s ability to move personnel, equipment, and supplies before any future operation ever begins.”
Residents and medical workers in Khuzestan also describe the toll on civilians caused by the bombing campaign, particularly children.
Just after midnight on July 15, explosions shook the area surrounding Shahid Baghaei Hospital in Ahvaz, one of southwestern Iran’s principal treatment centers for children with cancer and blood disorders. While the hospital was not destroyed in the attack, the blast forced the emergency evacuation of 211 pediatric patients, including children undergoing chemotherapy and several dependent on ventilators.
Hassan, a doctor who works at one of the hospitals where patients were transferred to, said the attack revived memories of the war’s opening day in February, when a missile strike on Minab Elementary School killed more than 150 people, most of them children.
“The memory of Minab came back to us immediately,” he said. “When we heard the explosion, everyone feared the hospital had been hit.”
The children were physically unharmed, but emotionally distraught. “We tried to reassure them,” Hassan told Drop Site. “We kept telling them nothing had happened. But children understand more than adults sometimes think. They knew the strike happened next to the hospital, and they were terrified.” Many had already lived through the 12-day war the previous year. That trauma, doctors say, will not disappear when this fighting ends.
“This isn’t something that simply goes away after the war,” Hassan said. “These children will carry it with them.”
Razieh, whose apartment overlooks the neighborhood of the hospital, ran outside after hearing the blast and saw smoke rising into the night sky. Since that night, she said, her three-year-old daughter can barely sleep.
“She wakes up even on nights when there isn’t any bombing,” Razieh said. “She tells me, ‘Mom, we’re being attacked. I hear bombs.’ At some point I couldn’t keep pretending nothing had happened.”
Hadis, another mother in the same neighborhood, described a similar pattern. Too scared to sleep, her children remain awake until the early hours of the morning. Loud sounds trigger panic. Some refuse to sleep unless a parent lies beside them.
Across parts of Hormozgan, repeated strikes on electricity and communications infrastructure have interrupted power, internet, and phone service during the hottest weeks of the year when daytime temperatures frequently approach 50 degrees Celsius (122 Fahrenheit). The prolonged outages also cause water pumps to stop operating and refrigeration to fail.
“The pattern documented across these accounts touches on core protections under international humanitarian law,” said Mohamed Habibi, a human rights lawyer who holds a master’s degree in international law from Imam Sadiq University. “The Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocol I require that attacks distinguish between military and civilian objects, and that any incidental harm to civilians remain proportionate to the concrete military advantage sought. Article 54 of Protocol I explicitly prohibits attacks on objects indispensable to the survival of the civilian population, including water and power infrastructure—a threshold that Hormozgan residents say has already been crossed amid summer temperatures exceeding 50 degrees Celsius.”
A second military analyst, who also spoke on condition of  anonymity, said the repeated strikes on electricity, communications, and transportation infrastructure appear designed to exacerbate  the civilian cost of the conflict.
“In this climate, electricity is part of basic survival,” he told Drop Site. “If you remove power, communications, and water at the same time, you’re putting enormous pressure on civilian society. The calculation seems to be that if enough pressure is placed on everyday life, people eventually become exhausted and begin questioning whether continued resistance is worth the cost.”
Even at military sites, the targets appeared designed to maximize casualties rather than just weaken military capabilities.
Shortly after 12:30 a.m. on July 15, residents near the Iranian Army garrison in Bampur, in the Sistan and Baluchestan Province, were awakened by two powerful explosions. Jalalzehi, who lives near the base, rushed outside to find smoke rising above the compound and the surrounding area dark.
By morning, the Army confirmed at least seven soldiers had been killed, including a conscript with fewer than forty days left in his mandatory service. Iranian media reported that thirteen missiles struck the garrison, hitting a dormitory, a guesthouse, and guard posts.
“Military installations such as the Bampur garrison remain lawful targets,” Habibi said. “However, the decision to repeatedly strike sleeping quarters rather than command posts or weapons depots raises a separate question long debated among legal scholars: whether maximizing casualties, rather than degrading military capability, played a role in the targeting.”
The second military analyst also raised similar questions. “If the objective is simply to reduce a garrison’s operational capability, barracks are not the most decisive target,” he said. “A strike on command facilities, communications, or weapons depots would have a more direct military effect. Concentrating repeated strikes on dormitories suggests that maximizing casualties may also have been part of the calculation.”
Eight days later, on July 23, missiles struck the Shalamcheh border crossing connecting Khuzestan Province with Iraq, as thousands of pilgrims prepared to travel to Karbala for Arbaeen, one of the largest annual religious gatherings in the Shiite calendar. Local residents reported two people killed and eleven wounded, with additional strikes hitting nearby towns.
Hassan, an Iranian pilgrim present during the attack, has crossed the border to make the religious pilgrimage every year for the past decade. Normally, he said, the route is filled with mokabs—volunteer stations providing food, water and medical assistance free of charge to pilgrims making the journey.
“When the missiles hit, people screamed,” he recalled. “But no one ran.” Instead, men moved toward the perimeter while women and other pilgrims formed lines to carry the wounded until ambulances arrived. “It showed something about our society,” Hassan said. “People were frightened, but they chose to help each other before thinking about themselves.”
* All residents asked to be referred to by their first names only for security reasons.
