reads.title: USS Abraham Lincoln sailors try to jump overboard after 250 days at sea; Third person dies after Newark ICE facility detention; Israel sets wildfires in Lebanon
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 13, 2026
reads.body:
- An F/A-18F Super Hornet launches from the flight deck of aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln in support of Operation Epic Fury on February 28, 2026 at Sea. Photo by U.S. Navy via Getty Images.Thursday, August 13, 2026 – Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warns of “even bigger miscalculation” on Hormuz after U.S. President Donald Trump claims U.S. has “total control.” Washington Post: U.S. intelligence viewed Israeli warning of Iranian plot to kill Trump as “low confidence.” Slight bump in Hormuz traffic. Iran reports oil pollution off Qeshm Island, calls for Hormuz environmental fees. Iran kills two accused of intelligence ties to U.S. and Israel. Yemen’s Saudi-backed government claims success against Ansarallah attack. Saudi tankers reroute around Africa as empty fleet heads toward Gulf. X suspends Ansarallah spokesperson account. Israel kills Palestinian child in Gaza City strike. Israeli strikes kill two, including Gaza police chief. Israel detains Palestinians, destroys homes, and re-establishes settlement in occupied West Bank. Hamas says it will participate in Palestinian elections in November. Israeli forces blow up and burn homes in southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework. U.S. official says Israel expected to abide by Lebanon framework after Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz vows not to withdraw. Lebanese presidency denies report that President Joseph Aoun called Hezbollah a “cancer” in meeting with Trump. Multiple USS Abraham Lincoln sailors have tried to jump overboard amid extended deployment. Third detainee dies after detention at Newark ICE facility. DHS spent $464M on planes for deportations that have mostly sat unused. Trump administration awards controversial anti-trafficking group $158M contract for migrant child legal services. Treasury permanently halts shell company ownership reporting requirement. War Secretary Pete Hegseth says “anti-trafficking coalition” will do “bad things to bad people”. Russian military officer assassinated in Crimea. Civilian toll in Ukraine in July at highest level since May 2022. Taiwan throttles internet during anti-blockade drill. Turkey shares details of planned military cooperation under new defense pact. Japan protests Russian official visit to disputed islands. Australian military whistleblower released on parole. Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces appears to retake Kurmuk as drone offensive widens. RSF-appointed Kordofan governor defects, urges fighters to “return to homeland.” Cholera kills 1,721 people in South Sudan, over 110,000 infected in country’s longest-running outbreak on record.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Iran FM warns of “even bigger miscalculation” on Hormuz after Trump claims U.S. has “total control”: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned the United States on Thursday against what he called “an even bigger miscalculation on the Strait of Hormuz,” a day after President Donald Trump claimed Washington had “total control” of the waterway. “The U.S. has long miscalculated due to intelligence failures. Case in point: The war on Iran,” Araghchi wrote on X. “Worse than fake news is fake intelligence. Be careful.” He ended his post: “Allah is Great, Greater than ANY power on Earth. In Allah we trust.”

- Trump wrote on Truth Social on Wednesday that the U.S. had “total control over the Strait of Hormuz,” describing the U.S. naval blockade as a “WALL OF STEEL” and claimed “there is nothing Iran can do about it,” before concluding his post with: “Praise be to Allah!”

- Washington Post: U.S. intelligence viewed Israeli warning of Iranian plot to kill Trump as “low confidence”: U.S. intelligence officials were skeptical of Israeli intelligence alleging an Iranian plot to assassinate President Donald Trump, with one official describing the warning as “Israeli-derived, not U.S.-generated, and viewed as low confidence,” The Washington Post reported. Despite the doubts, the Secret Service took extraordinary precautions as Trump left a NATO summit in Ankara on July 8, secretly moving him from Air Force One in an airport catering truck to another military aircraft that flew him to Britain under F-16 escort.

- “The Secret Service has had three near misses with this president, so they’re not taking any chances,” one official said.

- Some U.S. intelligence officials, however, believed Israel provided the warning partly to influence U.S. policy, with a former official saying it fit a broader pattern of Israeli intelligence reporting “designed as much to shape presidential decision-making as to inform it.”

- Slight bump in Hormuz traffic: Fourteen vessels crossed through the Strait of Hormuz on August 11, up from twelve on both August 9 and 10, according to data cited by Kpler.

- Of the 14 crossings, 12 vessels entered the Persian Gulf and only two exited.

- Iran’s Persian Gulf Waterway Management Organization rejected claims by President Trump and U.S. officials that Hormuz was open on Wednesday, saying that the Strait “remains blocked and will not be reopened until Iran’s conditions are accepted.”

- Hapag-Lloyd, one of the world’s top container shipping companies, reported on Thursday that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz due to conflict in the Middle East cost the group $600 million in its second quarter.

- Iran reports oil pollution off Qeshm Island, calls for Hormuz environmental fees: Oil pollution was documented at three coastal sites on Qeshm Island and in surrounding waters, with preliminary evidence pointing to a foreign bulk carrier as the source, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said in a post on X Thursday.

- Baghaei said the incident underscored the need to include environmental protection fees in any future arrangement governing the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that all parties benefiting from shipping through the waterway have a “legal and moral obligation” to address environmental damage.

- Iran kills two accused of intelligence ties to U.S. and Israel: Iranian forces killed two members “affiliated with American and Israeli intelligence agencies” during a confrontation in southeastern Iran, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported on Thursday. The Iranian intelligence ministry also announced the arrest of four people accused of planning to destabilize the Sistan and Baluchestan province and damage its infrastructure.

## Yemen

- Yemen’s Saudi-backed government claims success against Ansarallah attack: The Yemeni army repelled an Ansarallah attack on positions on the Al‑Mafalis zone in the southeastern province of Taiz in Yemen, according to an official of the Tor al‑Bahah military axis, an affiliate of the Saudi-backed government.

- The official claimed that “the terrorist Houthi militias suffered heavy losses.” The government side also suffered casualties, with at least one soldier killed and another critically wounded in the clashes, Yemeni military officials told AP.

- Saudi tankers reroute around Africa as empty fleet heads toward Gulf: Saudi tanker movements are shifting amid continued shipping risks around the Bab Al-Mandab and Strait of Hormuz, according to researcher Ali (@MerruX). A fleet of Saudi VLCCs is sailing around the Cape of Good Hope, avoiding potential Ansarallah attacks near Bab Al-Mandab, while nearly all Saudi tankers remaining in the Red Sea have reportedly switched off their AIS tracking.

- More than 12 empty Saudi tankers are reportedly heading toward the Gulf of Oman and UAE ports, potentially preparing to cross Hormuz and load crude. Their entry could replenish the shrinking pool of tankers inside the Gulf as outbound oil flows accelerate.

- At Bab Al-Mandab, traffic rose modestly to 40 crossings on August 11, up from 36 on August 9 and 35 on August 10, though normal shipping patterns remain heavily disrupted.

- Ambrey joins major salvage operation for stricken tanker off Oman: Maritime risk firm Ambrey said it is involved in the salvage of the Caroline Bezengi tanker, which was struck near Oman’s Hallaniyat Islands in Dhofar, as part of a major international response involving salvage vessels, aircraft, specialist personnel, and more than 100 tons of equipment. Specialists have boarded the tanker with support from the Royal Air Force of Oman to begin stabilizing the vessel and its cargo. An international oil-spill response company has also been contracted.

- Ambrey said the operation is complicated by extreme weather and sea conditions brought on by the Khareef monsoon. The internationally sanctioned tanker, carrying an estimated 800,000 barrels of Russian oil, ran aground on June 30 near an Omani marine nature reserve that is home to wildlife. The vessel had reported difficulties off Yemen on June 8 following an explosion. No group claimed responsibility for the attack.

- X suspends Ansarallah spokesperson account: The X account of Yahya Saree, the spokesperson for Ansarallah, has been suspended. It is unclear what prompted X to take down the account, which had over 121,000 followers, though a notice on the account says, “X suspends accounts which violate the X Rules.” For those who want to follow in real time, the spokesperson maintains a presence on Telegram.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, one Palestinian was killed and seven injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,389 killed, with 174,266 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,260 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,154, while 808 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- VIDEO: Ryan Grim discusses Israel’s continued violations of the Gaza ceasefire agreement on Breaking Points here.

- Israel kills Palestinian child in Gaza City strike: An Israeli strike in the Beit Lahiya area of Gaza City on Wednesday killed a 10-year-old Palestinian child and wounded several others.

- Israeli strikes kill two, including Gaza police chief: An Israeli airstrike killed the director of police in the Gaza Governorate, Col. Jamal Abu Kamil, 43, after targeting his vehicle on Al-Rashid Street southwest of Gaza City on Thursday, according to Gaza’s Interior Ministry. Separately, a Palestinian was killed and several others wounded on Thursday in an Israeli drone strike on the Al-Amal neighborhood, west of Khan Younis in the southern Gaza Strip, WAFA reported.

- Israel detains Palestinians, destroys homes, and re-establishes settlement in occupied West Bank:

- Bethlehem: Israeli settlers assaulted a child in Artas on Thursday, violently entering a home near the Solomon’s Pools tourist area and brutally beating a 16-year-old. Israeli settlers attacked a farm in Minya, stealing over 100 sheep and uprooting over 100 olive trees, WAFA reported. During the attack, the settlers reportedly attacked two residents of the farm, stole a vehicle and damaged another, and vandalized the house, with Israeli forces detaining three family members.

- Jenin: Israeli settlers re-established the “Ganim” settlement on Thursday, 21 years after settlers left the area as part of a 2005 disengagement plan, tightening controls in the surrounding area and closing several roads. Defense Minister Israel Katz participated in the ceremony for the settlement’s reopening, alongside settler leader Yossi Dagan and members of the Knesset. The move comes days after Israel began demolishing 27 Palestinian buildings in the governorate.

- Nablus: Israeli authorities forcibly evacuated the Palestinian families occupying two homes in Qusra, and seized 16 other homes as temporary military barracks, the village’s mayor told WAFA on Thursday. A Wednesday statement from the Israeli human rights group B’Tselem condemned the escalations in Qusra, noting that outposts are being used to “force the families out and take over their homes,” and said they were “not an isolated incident.”

- Qalqilya: Israeli forces detained seven Palestinians in Qalqilya on Thursday morning, according to WAFA, all of whom were related to Palestinians recently killed by Israel.

- Jericho: Israeli settlers demolished around 20 seasonal shelters used by Palestinian migrant farmers near Jericho on Thursday.

- Hebron: Israeli forces detained 3 young Palestinian men from Beit Ummar on Thursday, according to WAFA.

- East Jerusalem: Dozens of Israelis stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem on Thursday, WAFA reported.

- Hamas says it will participate in Palestinian elections in November: Senior Hamas official Husam Badran told Al-Aqsa Radio that the movement has made a “clear decision” to participate in legislative and Palestinian National Council elections in November, calling for clarity about the schedule for elections to replace President Mahmoud Abbas as well.

- Badran said the group seeks “the largest and broadest possible national coalition” of factions, independents and political blocs.

- He also rejected attempts to sideline the group, saying that “no one has the right to impose a political condition for participation” in the elections.

## Lebanon

- Israeli forces blow up and burn homes in southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework: Israeli forces demolished and set homes on fire in Majdal Zoun and Mansouri and the surrounding valleys on Thursday, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported. Israeli forces also carried out explosions in Majdal Zoun and nearby valleys, while an Israeli infantry force was seen moving in the area between Aita Al-Jabal and Beit Yahoun in the Bint Jbeil district. Separately, Israeli aircraft struck Mansouri in two waves overnight.

- Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam on Thursday reposted a statement on X condemning Israel’s “systematic destruction” of southern Lebanese villages after the original post was deleted, saying someone had gained access to his account and removed it.

- Salam condemned Israeli attacks in Mansouri, Zawtar Al-Sharqieh, and Kfartabnit in the post, rejected Israel’s claim that it was targeting military facilities, and added that Lebanon’s sovereignty and southerners’ right to return and rebuild “are not matters open to compromise.”

- Report: Israeli forces are deliberately setting southern Lebanon ablaze: Israel dropped incendiary materials from drones and fired white phosphorus and flares into woodlands nearly every day since the June 17 ceasefire, Civil defense chief Hussein Fakih told The Guardian. He estimated fires have affected 30% to 40% of land near the frontline. Conservationist Hisham Younes called the campaign “ecocide,” saying the destruction is making the land uninhabitable.

- U.S. official says Israel expected to abide by Lebanon framework after Katz vows not to withdraw: The U.S. expects Israel to act in accordance with the framework agreed with Lebanon, a State Department official told Asharq, responding to Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz’s declaration that Israeli forces would not withdraw from areas they control in Lebanon, Syria, and Gaza.

- The official said a “permanent military presence in southern Lebanon is inconsistent with the commitments made under the framework,” which provides for a conditional, phased Israeli redeployment tied to Hezbollah’s disarmament.

- Katz said Wednesday during a visit to an Israeli military position in southern Lebanon: “We will not move from here and we will not withdraw.”

- Lebanese presidency denies report that Aoun called Hezbollah a “cancer” in meeting with Trump: The Lebanese presidency’s media office denied an Al-Akhbar report, saying the remarks attributed to President Joseph Aoun were “incorrect.”

- The Al-Akhbar report claimed Aoun told Trump that repeated attempts at dialogue with Hezbollah had failed, that the group was now under Iranian leadership, and that Lebanon’s Shiites did not support it to the extent it claimed. It also alleged that Aoun described Hezbollah as “the cancer Lebanon is suffering from” that required “complete eradication” rather than dialogue or partial solutions.

## U.S. News

- Multiple USS Abraham Lincoln sailors have tried to jump overboard amid extended deployment: Concerns are growing about a mental health crisis and the risk of self-harm aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln as 5,000 sailors and marines are in their ninth month at sea—a record for an aircraft carrier—with worsening conditions onboard, according to reports in the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes.

- Both papers reported thwarted suicide attempts by service members, with multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard. The USS Abraham Lincoln was sent to the Gulf amid the Iran war and U.S. blockade.

- Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao on Wednesday demanding to know what action is being taken to improve conditions for sailors onboard. “There have been widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system,” Blumenthal wrote.

- Rep. Mike Levin of California also cited military families describing poor conditions onboard, including “Moldy showers, broken toilets, laundry down for weeks, long stretches with no hot water, a meal that came down to half a cup of rice and two tortillas.”

- Third detainee dies after detention at Newark ICE facility: Jose Chajon-Raxon, a Guatemalan immigrant, died at a hospital as a result of a “medical emergency,” according to a Wednesday Department of Homeland Security statement, making his the third death connected to the Newark facility since it reopened in May 2025.

- A nurse at the facility reported Chajon-Raxon had a seizure the day after he arrived at the facility, after which he was taken to the hospital, according to the DHS statement.

- The New Jersey Attorney General’s office opened a civil rights investigation into the facility last Friday amid mounting scrutiny over its medical care and conditions.

- DHS spent $464M on planes for deportations that have mostly sat unused: The Department of Homeland Security spent $464 million on a no-bid contract last fall to buy ten used airplanes, justified as urgently needed for deportation flights, but has largely left the fleet idle, The New York Times reported on Thursday. Three luxury business jets were loaned or proposed for loan to other agencies, including one leased to the FBI for Director Kash Patel’s travel, and seven Boeing 737s parked for months at an airport in Lake Charles, Louisiana.

- The contract went to Daedalus Aviation Corporation, an Arlington, Virginia firm with no prior federal contracts whose chairman donated to a political committee tied to former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem and separately received a nearly $700 million contract under her leadership.

- Trump administration awards controversial anti-trafficking group $158M contract for migrant child legal services: The Trump administration awarded Utah-based Our Rescue, formerly known as Operation Underground Railroad, a no-bid $158 million contract to provide legal services to unaccompanied migrant children, according to a Friday notice from the Department of Health and Human Services cited by NPR, though it remains unclear whether the group employs immigration lawyers.

- Our Rescue was founded by activist Tim Ballard, subject of the 2023 film “Sound of Freedom,” who was later quietly removed after facing sexual exploitation accusations he has denied, and is now led by CEO Derek Benner, a former ICE official.

- Treasury permanently halts shell company ownership reporting requirement: The Treasury Department announced Tuesday it is permanently halting collection of “beneficial ownership” data about private American companies previously under the 2021 Corporate Transparency Act, a law intended to help law enforcement track shell companies used for money laundering and drug trafficking.

- Beneficial owners are those who own 25% or more of a reporting company, according to the law. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called it a move to eliminate “a burdensome reporting requirement for millions of law-abiding business owners without compromising our national security.”

- Sen. Elizabeth Warren said the move was “a gift to cartels, criminals and U.S. adversaries” that dismisses law enforcement warnings about the risks of underreporting.

- Hegseth says “anti-trafficking coalition” will do “bad things to bad people”: Hegseth called on military leaders from 18 Latin American countries to expand joint operations against drug traffickers at a Panama meeting of the U.S.-led counter-cartel coalition, declaring the group’s motto would be “we do bad things to bad people.”

- Hegseth said Honduras and Colombia had agreed to allow joint operations alongside Ecuador and Guatemala, building on a Pentagon campaign that has conducted 66 boat strikes killing at least 221 people.

- Hegseth claimed at the conference the strikes cut suspected drug vessels by more than half, though a recent Times investigation found cocaine remains as accessible in the U.S. as before the campaign began.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Russian military officer assassinated in Crimea: A Russian military officer was killed in a bombing in the city of Sevastopol in Russian-annexed Crimea. A Russian woman was arrested and accused of carrying out the assassination on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence services.

- Russian Telegram channels identified the officer as Robert Shageyev, a former Ukrainian naval commander who reportedly defected to Russia during its 2014 annexation of Crimea.

- Myrotvorets, an unofficial Ukrainian website ​that provides a database of people alleged to be as war criminals or ‌traitors, ⁠said Shageyev had been “liquidated.”

- Civilian toll in Ukraine in July at highest level since May 2022: The number of civilians killed in Ukraine in July reached its highest level since the first months of the Russian invasion, according to the United Nations. “At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 injured in Ukraine in July 2026, a 30% increase compared to June 2026...and a 70% increase compared to July 2025,” according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission. “The number of child casualties (17 killed; 166 injured) was the highest since April 2022.”

- Taiwan throttles internet during anti-blockade drill: Taiwan deliberately slowed mobile internet service across the island’s north for 30 minutes on Thursday, testing communications disruptions during a simulated Chinese attack during a raid that included air-raid sirens and police clearing the streets of Taipei.

- The exercise was part of the 10-day Han Kuang war games, which include military and civil-defense preparations for a potential invasion.

- Taiwan’s navy and coast guard also held their first joint anti-blockade exercise on Wednesday, escorting a simulated merchant vessel to an east-coast port as a minesweeper cleared a navigation channel.

- Turkey shares details of planned military cooperation under new defense pact: Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia plan to establish high-level political and military bodies, conduct joint exercises, and expand defense production under the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed on August 7, Turkey’s defense ministry said.

- The countries plan exercises involving ground, naval, and air forces, air-defense systems, and drones. They will also pursue joint weapons development and production, focusing on autonomous systems, electronic warfare, and artificial intelligence.

- Turkey says the pact could expand to include other countries, including Egypt, and is also participating in talks in Jeddah over a proposed international coalition to protect Red Sea shipping.

- Japan protests Russian official visit to disputed islands: Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the island of Iturup on Thursday, marking his first trip to the Russian-administered Kuril Islands claimed by Japan. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit “absolutely unacceptable,” while Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned Russia’s ambassador to lodge a formal protest.

- The islands have been disputed since the end of World War II when they were occupied by Russian forces who expelled the existing Japanese population and their status has remained contested between Tokyo and Moscow.

- Australian military whistleblower released on parole: Former Australian military lawyer David McBride was released on parole Thursday after serving 27 months for leaking classified defense documents that helped expose alleged war crimes by Australian special forces in Afghanistan.

- McBride was sentenced in 2024 to five years and eight months in prison after pleading guilty to leaking classified documents and providing them to the Australian Broadcasting Corporation.

- A subsequent government inquiry found credible evidence that Australian soldiers unlawfully killed 39 Afghans and two former Australian special forces soldiers were charged with war crimes.

- McBride, who has been diagnosed with treatable lung cancer, will serve the remainder of his sentence under community supervision.

- RSF appears to retake Kurmuk as drone offensive widens: Sudan’s Rapid Support Forces appear to have retaken Kurmuk, a strategic town on the Ethiopian border, just one month after the army recaptured it, according to Sudanese analysts and local reports. Reports accused Ethiopia of enabling RSF operations in Blue Nile through drone flights and troop movements through its territory and Reuters had previously uncovered an RSF training camp near Assosa.

- The army has not confirmed the loss, and the claim has not been independently verified.

- The apparent capture followed an RSF advance through nearby Geisan, where fighting killed more than 20 civilians Tuesday and displaced roughly 2,500 people, according to UN agencies.

- On Wednesday, the RSF launched drone attacks on Khartoum, Bahri, Omdurman, Atbara, Ed Damer and el-Obeid, marking its first strikes on the capital since May. Around eight drones hit el-Obeid, killing at least two people and wounding others, Reuters and the UN reported.

- Emergency Lawyers separately accused an army vehicle of killing five civilians, including women and children, near Jabra al-Sheikh in North Kordofan. Sudan Tribune reported that the SAF thwarted an RSF assault on the area.

- RSF-appointed Kordofan governor defects, urges fighters to “return to homeland”: Hamad Mohammed Hamid, appointed governor of Sudan’s Kordofan region last year by the Rapid Support Forces-linked Tasis government, announced his defection from the RSF in an interview with Al Arabiya.

- Hamid said the Sudanese people had no choice but to unite against what he called “unruly militias.” He accused the RSF of stoking tribal, communal, and racial tensions across the country, and said the Tasis government serves only as a political front for the paramilitary force.

- Hamid, who was also named to the Tasis presidential council, called for legitimate state institutions to be restored across Kordofan and Darfur.

- Cholera kills 1,721 people in South Sudan, over 110,000 infected in country’s longest-running outbreak on record: South Sudan is battling its worst cholera crisis in recorded history, with more than 110,000 cases and 1,721 deaths reported across 55 counties since late September 2025. National Health Minister Luke Thompson Thoan cited poor sanitation, low immunity, and large displaced populations as key drivers of the outbreak. “That is a big number of deaths, and we are doing all we can to stop the epidemic,” he said,

reads.title: Spot Gamma Heatmap - A Breakdown
reads.subtitle: A Primer on Spot Gamma Heatmaps
reads.body:
Spot Gamma Heatmaps: Reading where dealers are positioned
Market makers are the most predictable traders in the market. It’s not because they’re dumb, but rather because they don’t have a choice. When they sell you an option they have to hedge it, and that hedging leaves a footprint on the tape.
The newly released Spot Gamma Heatmap (available with any platform subscription) is a visual of those footprints: every strike and expiry for any underlying, shaded by how badly dealers have to hedge there and which direction that hedging pushes price.
Before we dive into this breakdown just know that there are other methodologies to analyze GEX, and this one ranks among the top.

-
-

## Interpreting the Colors
Every cell in the grid is a strike (rows) at an expiry (columns), shaded along a red to green gradient.

A cell shaded green suggests that dealers are long gamma at that level. Long-gamma dealers hedge against the move. They sell into strength and buy into weakness. That’s a stabilizing force. Green zones are where you get pinning, chop, and ranges that refuse to break.

Red cells suggest that dealers are short gamma at that level. Short-gamma dealers hedge with the move. They buy higher and sell lower, which pours fuel on whatever direction price is already going. Red zones are where volatility expands: gap-and-go, squeezes, and the air pockets that turn a normal day into a spicy one.

That’s the whole intuition. Green = suppressed. Red = amplified.

## How the values are derived
Now you know what the colors mean. Here’s how the values are derived.
GEX represents the dollars needed to hedge against a 1% move in the underlying stock price.
GEX = gamma * 100 * 0.01 * volume * stock price * stock price
VEX measures how hedging changes as implied volatility moves.
VEX = vanna * 100 * 0.01 * volume * stock price * iv
For directionalized GEX, market makers are on the opposite side of the trade. If a trade is closer to the ask, the customer is assumed buying and the market maker is selling, so the value is multiplied by -1.
100 represents the number of shares in one contract.
For GEX, 0.01 represents a 1% move in the stock price.

## The Gamma Flip
A number of importance is the gamma flip, which is the price level where net dealer gamma crosses from positive to negative.

-
- Using the same screenshot as above… on this $AAPL example it’s marked at 290.84.

Above this level dealers are net long gamma across the board, so the market is in a dampening regime: moves get faded, ranges hold, and mean reversion tends to win.
With spot above 306 $AAPL is comfortably above its flip.
Below the flip dealers turn net short and the market moves into an amplifying regime. This is where downside gets disorderly, because the same hedging that used to calm the tape now accelerates it.
The flip is why the character of a stock can change so violently at a specific price.

##
Call Wall and Put Wall: the ceiling and the floor
Two levels get called out explicitly:

The Call Wall is the strike with the largest positive gamma concentration above spot. Big positive-gamma strikes act like magnets that also resist being pierced: price often drifts toward the wall into expiration and then stalls, because dealers are leaning against every push through it. Think of it as a soft ceiling.

The Put Wall is its downside twin - the largest concentration below spot. It tends to act as support, and it’s often the last stop before the gamma flip. Lose the put wall and you’re frequently trading your way toward that amplifying regime, which is why breaks of the put wall often get people’s attention.

##
Putting it together
Find the flip to know the regime; above it, expect dampening; below it, expect fireworks.
Mark the call wall and put wall as your near-term ceiling and floor. Watch whether cells are green (suppression) or red (amplification) around current price.

Nothing here is investment advice. Options are risky and dealer positioning is one lens among many. Email support@unusualwhales.com with any inquiries.

This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Pakistani Interior Minister arrives in Tehran: Pakistan’s interior minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran on Wednesday for a meeting with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, part of mediation efforts to halt the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, according to Al Jazeera.

- A spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry said after the meeting that Pakistan was “working to bring” the U.S. and Iran “to the negotiating table.”

- Pakistan, alongside Qatar, has been a principal mediator in the five-month conflict, which began with U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.

- Iranian National Security Head pares down Hormuz conditions: Mohsen Rezaei, the newly appointed Secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, laid out Tehran’s conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, saying in a post on X that Iran would not reopen the Strait “until the U.S. ends the war and blockade, releases Iran’s frozen assets, and agrees to a region-wide ceasefire, including in Lebanon and Gaza.”

- “Until all conditions are met, the strait will remain closed,” he reiterated.

- The list is narrower than that presented by his predecessor, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, on August 8, which also included full compensation for war damages and sanctions relief, and which explicitly included Yemen and Iraq in its ceasefire call.

- U.S. claims 9 million barrels of oil pass through Hormuz daily: U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright claimed on Tuesday that military operations and cooperation with Gulf allies had pushed the seven-day average for oil leaving the Strait of Hormuz to nearly 9 million barrels per day.

- In a post on X, he claimed more than 20 million barrels left the region on Sunday alone, exceeding prewar levels, without providing a source for his estimates.

- Kpler estimated exports of 2.3 million barrels per day last week, and even with “dark transits,” experts still say that the true number falls far short of Wright’s Tuesday estimates.

- Separately on Wednesday, the International Energy Agency (IEA) projected that global oil supply would fall by 4.3 million barrels per day (bpd), or about 4%, this year, citing disruptions both in Hormuz and the Bab Al-Mandab Straits. The 4.3 million bpd supply drop is larger than the 3.7 million bpd reduction forecast in the IEA’s July report.

- Clashes reported in Iraqi Kurdistan: Iran fired several missiles and drones at locations in Iraq’s Erbil province on Wednesday, a Kurdish Peshmerga commander told Rudaw, targeting fighters from the Komala Party and the Kurdistan Democratic Party of Iran (KDPI). No casualties were reported.

- Al Jazeera reported that four drones hit Erbil, and cited a separate report from Reuters, which said that the attacks targeted Iranian Kurdish opposition camps in the region.

- IRGC adviser discusses war strategy with U.S. media: In a Tuesday interview with PBS, senior IRGC adviser Mohammad Reza Naqdi said Iran has thwarted Washington’s objectives, learned how to fight the U.S. military, and may prolong the war until the next American presidency to impose sustained costs and establish deterrence.

- Naqdi told PBS that Washington failed to topple Iran’s leadership or break the country apart, leaving it to wage “a war without a strategy” and repeatedly announce new objectives.

- “We have also seen how the American military is weaker than what we perceived,” he said.

- The adviser said Iran has “no need” for a nuclear weapon, citing popular support for the country during the war.

- When asked why Iran’s new supreme leader has not appeared publicly during the war, Naqdi claimed it was for security reasons.

- Iran to join BRICS’s New Development Bank: Iran will soon join the BRICS-backed New Development Bank (NDP), Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said Wednesday ahead of a BRICS finance meeting in India, according to Reuters. (BRICS is Brazil, Russia, India, China, and South Africa.) Hemmati said Tehran sees the bank as one of the most important outcomes of BRICS cooperation and is also seeking greater bilateral and trilateral monetary cooperation with member states, including conducting trade in national currencies.

- Iran joined BRICS in 2024 and has since sought membership and a shareholding in the NDB, which was established in 2015 to finance infrastructure and sustainable development projects.

- Former Mossad chief alleges spies repeatedly visited Fordow nuclear site: Yossi Cohen, who led Mossad from 2015 to 2021, claimed that Israeli spies “toured” Iran’s Fordow nuclear site “many times”  to understand the facility, at a conference on Tuesday.

- Cohen did not specify when the visits occurred or who carried them out, and offered no further evidence.

- He added that the American bombing of Fordow was “the fulfillment of all my dreams,” a reference to U.S. strikes on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan during the 12-day war Washington and Israel launched against Iran in June 2025.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah launches new attack on Al-Makha: Ansarallah launched new ballistic missile attacks on the strategic port of Al-Makha (Mocha) near the Bab Al-Mandab Strait in southwestern Yemen, Saba TV reported on Wednesday.

- The attack comes one day after the Saudi-backed Yemeni government said Ansarallah had launched 10 ballistic missiles and four drones at the city.

- Death toll from Ansarallah attack on vessel rises to six: The death toll from an attack by Ansarallah on a Yemeni commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandab Strait on Tuesday has risen to six people, including three Pakistani nationals. Pakistan’s Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar condemned the attack in a post on X. “Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea,” Dar wrote.

- U.S. strikes in Yemen killed 153 civilians, Pentagon says: The Pentagon admitted to Congress in a report on Wednesday that U.S. airstrikes killed 153 civilians and wounded 243 others in Yemen last year.

- The deaths come from three April 2025 strikes: one that killed five, another that killed 80, and a third that killed 68. Human Rights Watch had said the second of these, a strike on the Ras Isa fuel port, should be investigated as a war crime.

- The Yemen Data Project has recorded at least 238 civilians killed and 467 wounded in the campaign, which ran from March to May 2025 and was codenamed Operation Rough Rider, and the monitor Airwars put the toll around 258.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. One body was also recovered from beneath the rubble.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,388 killed, with 174,259 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,259 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,148, while 808 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel detains Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mohamed Awad: Israeli forces detained Palestinian journalist and Drop Site contributor Mohamed Awad, 38, from his home in Bitunia, west of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, early Wednesday morning. Two other Palestinians were arrested after raiding and searching their homes in the nearby city of Al-Bireh, according to Wafa.

- Soldiers first raided an apartment in a different neighborhood that Awad’s family had moved out of months earlier, breaking down the door only to find it empty, Awda’s wife Eman Awad told Al-Araby.

- They then went on foot to the family’s current home and pounded on the door until Awad opened it. He was blindfolded, handcuffed behind his back, and forced to walk down five flights of stairs before being taken away in a military jeep in a scene captured on video.

- Awad’s reporting for Drop Site has covered escalating violence by Israeli settlers across the West Bank, including the burning of a mosque in Qusra, south of Nablus, and an attack in Masafer Yatta last week that wounded five Palestinians and burned four homes.

- With his detention, the number of Palestinian journalists held in Israeli prisons has risen to 40, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

- Israel has killed more than 260 journalists since it began its genocide in Gaza, two of whom died in Israeli prisons.

- Conditions for prisoners in Ganot deteriorating rapidly: Living and humanitarian conditions for Palestinians imprisoned in Ganot prison in southern Israel are deteriorating rapidly, the Palestinian government’s Commission for Detainees and Ex-Detainees Affairs said in a Wednesday report.

- Ministry officials who visited several prisons reported overcrowding, regular beatings, and insufficient supplies.

- The report also noted a lack of access to basic hygiene routines and supplies. At Ganot, prisoners wear the same clothing for up to two weeks, go without access to washing machines for the same period, and are forced to share razors and nail clippers.

- UN: Thousands in Gaza still await medical evacuation: Thousands of patients in the Gaza Strip are still awaiting medical evacuation despite the ceasefire, a spokesperson for the World Health Organization said on Tuesday.

- The spokesperson noted the difficulties of evacuation in remarks to reporters and said they were conducted three or four times per week, as Israel continues to restrict movement through the Rafah crossing.

- Around 15,000 Palestinians in Gaza require medical treatment abroad, according to the Strip’s Health Ministry.

- Israel continues to ravage the occupied West Bank:

- Nablus: Israeli settlers continued to besiege the Qusra home of the Palestinian-American Abu Rida family for a fourth consecutive day on Wednesday, according to WAFA, circling the property and preventing entry or exit, blocking the road to the property with rocks, and attempting to enter the home. The settlers have attempted to seize the property for months, often with the backing of the Israeli military.

- Hebron: Israeli authorities closed the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron on Wednesday, preventing worshippers from reaching it, while conducting raids in the area. Additionally on Wednesday, Israeli forces bulldozed a home in Hebron without notice or explanation. On Tuesday, settlers demolished a Palestinian house, leaving nine people homeless, and filled in a water well in the Bedouin community of Yatta.

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces demolished a three-story residential building in the village of Ma’sara on Wednesday morning.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli settlers continued to work on a settlement expansion project on pastoral land near the Ma’azi Jaba Bedouin community, north of East Jerusalem, on Wednesday, WAFA reported. Separately on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished a home in Silwan, according to the Jerusalem governorate.

- Tubas: Israeli settlers vandalized the main water supply line of the Ras al-Ahmar community in the Tubas governorate, cutting off water to 30 Palestinian families.

- Security Council holds West Bank meeting, official says area “at breaking point”: At a meeting of the United Nations Security Council, UN Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process Ramiz Alakbarov warned on Tuesday that the occupied West Bank was at a “breaking point,” with settler attacks across Areas A, B, and C increasing at a rapid clip.

- Alakbarov told the Council that, as of August 10, Israel had killed 76 Palestinians in the West Bank, including 18 children. “The pattern is clear,” he said, “Palestinians are being forcibly displaced across the West Bank before settlers seize the vacated land.”

- At the meeting, UNICEF also noted that Israel had killed 174 Palestinian children in the West Bank—or more than one per week—since January 2024. UNICEF also noted that at least 355 Palestinian children from the occupied West Bank are currently being held in Israeli military detention, according to the Israeli Prison Service—the highest number in eight years.

- NCAG meets with UN: The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, the sole Palestinian body operating under Trump’s “Board of Peace,” convened a joint meeting with UN agencies on Tuesday, hoping to align their strategies and to establish mechanisms for coordinating relief, recovery, and reconstruction.

## Lebanon

- Israel continues attacks in Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework:

- Israeli forces bombed a four-story public school in the center of the village of Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah on Wednesday, according to the country’s National News Agency (NNA).

- An Israeli drone struck a religious Ashura procession on the Kafra–al-Asi road in the Tyre (Sour) district, wounding several, the NNA reported.

- Israeli forces conducted additional bombing operations in Haddatha and Beit Yahoun on Wednesday, the NNA reported, calling the second of these a “massive explosion.”

- The Lebanese army said Israeli forces blew up the municipal building in Zawtar Al-Sharqiyah in Nabatieh, along with the town’s public school, health clinic, children’s nursery and several homes. It added that Israel is continuing its “destructive approach” in southern Lebanon, saying the attacks were hindering the army’s deployment and the return of residents.

- Lebanon becomes first Arab country to abolish death penalty: Lebanon’s parliament voted Tuesday to abolish the death penalty, making it the first Arab country to replace the sentence with life imprisonment with “aggravated” hard labor, AP reported. Lebanon had observed an unofficial moratorium on executions since January 2004, although courts continued to issue death sentences that were later suspended or commuted.

- A majority of the 128-member parliament backed the measure, with Justice Minister Adel Nassar calling the vote a “historic step.”

- Lebanon passes first general amnesty law since 1991: Lebanon’s parliament passed a general amnesty law on Wednesday, alongside exceptional reductions to some sentences, in the country’s first such measure since the end of its civil war in 1990, Al Jazeera reported. The law is expected to benefit thousands of prisoners, detainees and wanted individuals and is aimed primarily at easing severe prison overcrowding, including cases of detainees held for years without trial.

- Official figures put Lebanon’s prison population at 6,268 as of March 30, while the National Human Rights Commission reported prison overcrowding at 300% in 2025.

- Critics, including victims’ families and civil society groups, have warned that the law risks granting impunity without addressing deeper failures in the justice system.

## U.S. News

- Tuesday’s primary results:

- Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley narrowly defeated chef and state legislator Francesca Hong in Tuesday’s Wisconsin Democratic gubernatorial primary. Crowley re-entered the race in July, two weeks before the election, and received the backing of the state’s Democratic establishment, most notably outgoing Gov. Tony Evers. Crowley will face Trump-backed Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany in the November general.

- Progressive Peggy Flanagan defeated Rep. Angie Craig in the Minnesota Democratic Senate primary. With endorsements from Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Bernie Sanders, Flanagan overcame Craig’s significant fundraising advantage. Flanagan noted Craig’s long ties to AIPAC and her support for the hardline “Laken Riley Act” ahead of Trump’s deadly crackdown in Minneapolis. She will face sports broadcaster Michele Tafoya, who won Tuesday’s Republican primary, in the general.

- Progressive Matt Little defeated centrist Matthew Klein in the Democratic primacy race to replace Angie Craig in Minnesota’s 2nd Congressional District. Pro-Israel groups spent heavily in their unsuccessful attempt to defeat Little, boosting a third candidate, Kaela Berg (Drop Site’s full story on that effort is available here). Little is expected to win in the heavily blue Minneapolis-area district in November.

- Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman advanced to an August 25 Republican runoff in the special election to replace Graham’s late brother, Lindsey Graham, NBC News projected on Tuesday. The Trump-backed Graham led Norman by 8 points in the first round of voting, which saw 10 candidates competing for a maximum of two slots.

- Poll shows Democrat within striking distance for Kansas Senate: A new poll on the race for U.S. senate in Kansas paid for by the Democratic Senate super PAC has Democratic candidate Adam Hamilton—a megachurch pastor running against the Iran war and Trump’s tariffs—running only one point behind incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, 46% to 45%, with 9% of surveyed respondents undecided.

- The poll also tested each candidate’s favorability ratings. Sen. Marshall found himself 9 points underwater, with 38% of those polled approving of his tenure and 47% disapproving, while Hamilton is running 6 points above water, with favorables of 29%, unfavorable of 23%, and 47% of respondents “unsure.”

- Among Kansas voters polled, 57% said they voted for President Donald Trump in the 2024 election, compared to just 41% who voted for Kamala Harris, demonstrating a sea change in public opinion leading to a Democratic Senate candidate positioned for potential victory just two years later.

- AP: ICE plans to give agents gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks: ICE officers and agents may soon be equipped with gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks intended to “gain compliance from combative individuals,” according to the Associated Press.

- Known as the the G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, the devices are manufactured by the Lexington, Kentucky-based firm Compliant Technologies. ICE plans to spend up to $20 million to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” by March, according to a notice published Monday by Homeland Security.

- “ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the ACLU, told AP. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

- Paramount CEO threatens California exit: Paramount CEO David Ellison told the company’s senior executive team on August 5 that the company will relocate out of California unless California Attorney General Rob Bonta agrees to settle the states’ antitrust lawsuit against the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger, Variety reported.

- Bonta called the threat “an attempt to blackmail the state into letting an illegal deal through” in a post on X, adding that Paramount “has lost the plot as it continues to lose in court.”

- Ellison cited cost pressures from a $7 million-per-day fee owed to WBD shareholders starting Oct. 1 as the reason for the potential move.

- Hegseth’s Pentagon advisory board appointees have financial ties to Trump family-linked venture fund: War Secretary Pete Hegseth appointed venture capitalist Marc Andreessen and Peter Thiel protégé Blake Masters to the Pentagon’s Defense Policy Board. Andreessen’s firm, Andreessen Horowitz, invests in defense contractors including Anduril Industries, Hadrian, and SpaceX alongside 1789 Capital, a fund where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner. Masters serves on three boards related to 1789 Capital, as well. Read more from the Guardian.

- Companies jointly backed by the two firms have drawn billions of dollars in federal contracts and loans since President Donald Trump’s second term began.

- Justice Samuel Alito made up to $2.9 million from fossil fuel holdings since 2005: Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito gained between $390,000 and $2.9 million from oil and gas interests between 2005 and 2024, according to an analysis by judicial watchdog Court Accountability shared exclusively with the Guardian.

- Most of the gains stemmed from a Grady County, Oklahoma property in which Alito’s wife, Martha-Ann, holds a mineral interest, along with an inherited ExxonMobil stock bequest.

- The findings come as the Supreme Court prepares to hear oral arguments on October 5 in a case where Suncor Energy and Exxon are seeking to block subnational governments from suing fossil fuel producers over climate effects.

- NYC Council investigates marketing practices of prediction market platforms: The New York City Council is investigating marketing practices by prediction market platforms Polymarket, Kalshi, Coinbase, and Gemini Titan, the office of Council Speaker Julie Menin said Wednesday.

- Menin’s letters to the four companies cited a Wall Street Journal investigation alleging Polymarket ran misleading campaigns making it appear content creators were winning with their own money—reporting that prompted a Commodity Futures Trading Commission probe.

- New York state is separately litigating against Kalshi, Coinbase, and Gemini over allegations of running illegal gambling operations.

- Mayor Mamdani vs. Amazon: On Monday, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani endorsed a bill to force Amazon to employ its delivery drivers, rather than use an army of subcontractors. Amazon’s lead lobbyist on the bill is Chuck Schumer‘s daughter, The American Prospect reported. She has worked at Amazon since 2020.

- General Dynamics’s $533 million Texas artillery factory never produced a usable shell, investigation finds: General Dynamics’ artillery shell factory in Mesquite, Texas cost American taxpayers $533 million and never produced a single usable 155 mm shell, according to a ProPublica investigation. The manufacturing process has featured blown deadlines, malfunctioning robots that repeatedly caught fire, and equipment failures.

- The Pentagon has continued awarding the General Dynamics billions in new contracts, including $2.5 billion since the company stopped production on the artillery shell.

- Read the full investigation from ProPublica here.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Russia threatens to seize European vessels in retaliation for possible ship seizures: Russian President Vladimir Putin said Moscow would respond “in kind” if European countries carry through their threat to seize Russian merchant ships suspected of circumventing sanctions, denouncing the proposed measures as “piracy and robbery.”

- Putin warned that Russia could retaliate against European vessels wherever it considers necessary rather than limiting its response to the waters where Russian ships are detained.

- 15 killed and dozens missing after ferry capsizes in Zimbabwe: At least 15 people were killed and 27 remained missing after a ferry capsized in strong waves on Lake Kariba on Tuesday, according to Zimbabwe’s Civil Protection Unit.

- At least 77 people were rescued, while police, military divers, speedboats and a helicopter continued searching the lake.

- A survivor said the ferry departed in bad weather and appeared to lose engine power after being struck by a wave, while poor conditions delayed the rescue response.

- Ten Nigerian police officers killed in clash with bandits in Kebbi state: Ten Nigerian police officers were killed and two wounded on Monday in a clash with a gang of suspected bandits in northwestern Kebbi state, police said Tuesday.

- A police spokesperson added that officers killed at least 17 of the attackers, and that reinforcements have since been deployed as security forces pursue fleeing suspects.

- The clash is the latest in Nigeria’s northwest, where armed gangs frequently carry out killings, kidnappings for ransom, and cattle theft.

- Colombia and Venezuela rebuild ties with Israel: Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar designated 2026 a “Year of Latin America,” a push to rebuild Israel’s influence in the region.

- This week, Colombia became only the second country, after the U.S., to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the occupied Golan Heights, which Israel seized from Syria in 1967 and annexed in 1981 in a move the UN Security Council declared void. The reversal came from Colombia’s new right-wing president Abelardo de la Espriella, backed by Trump, who is rapidly undoing the pro-Palestinian policies of leftist predecessor Gustavo Petro: restoring ties, planning a Jerusalem embassy, and quitting South Africa’s ICJ genocide case.

- Venezuela, separately, agreed to a mechanism for consular services and technical cooperation with Israel, its first official link since Caracas cut ties in 2009, but stopped short of restoring full diplomatic relations. An Israeli aid team also staged a heavily photographed visit to Venezuela following the June earthquakes.

- North Korea launches ballistic missile ahead of U.S.–South Korean military drills: North Korea launched a ballistic missile from the Wonsan area toward the Sea of Japan on Wednesday, marking Pyongyang’s second weapons test in less than a week and its 11th suspected ballistic-missile launch of 2026.

reads.title: In West Bank Village, a New Israeli Order Enables Settler Attacks While Claiming to Prevent Them
reads.subtitle: The Israeli military declared the Palestinian village of Taybeh a closed military zone to "maintain order" but residents say settlers are still allowed to raid the area.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- Israeli settlers continue their raids on the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank despite the Israeli army declaring the area a 'closed military zone,' on August 10, 2026. Photo by Issam Rimawi/Anadolu via Getty Images.TAYBEH, Occupied West Bank*—On Sunday, the Israeli military declared the Palestinian village of Taybeh in the occupied West Bank a closed military zone, claiming the order was aimed to prevent escalating attacks by marauding Israeli settlers. It ostensibly bars Israelis and foreigners from entering the area.
But residents of the village and the surrounding area told Drop Site News that the military order is designed to further isolate Taybeh from the outside world, barring solidarity activists from the area while allowing settler attacks to continue. One of the few Christian-majority Palestinian villages in the West Bank, Taybeh has come under growing attacks by Israeli settlers who have expanded colonial outposts encircling it over the past several weeks.
“The order says that Israelis and foreigners are prohibited from entering the area. What about the settler roaming around the area? What is he? Is he Israeli or not? Why is he in the area?,” said Jack Abed, the priest of the Greek Catholic Church in Taybeh. “This order is intended to prevent human rights defenders from being present to defend us against what these settler thugs are doing—attacking us in an extremely brutal manner.”
The observation was echoed by Nayef Kaabneh, head of the Bedouin community in Taybeh that lives in the lands around the village. “They told us the area had been declared a closed military zone to stop the settlers from coming here. But it turned out that was all lies. The settlers still come here, while the activists are prevented from coming to us,” Kaabneh said. “They want to isolate us so they can come after us.”
Kaabneh recounted a recent incident when a settler arrived in the area followed by several international solidarity activists. “We called the police and the army. The army came and said, ‘This is a closed military zone. Leave.’ So the activists left, and the settler left. But the settler just went over there, and once the army left, he came back. And the activists didn’t come back. So the order is really aimed at the activists, not the settlers,” he said.
On Tuesday, the Israeli military issued a similar decree, announcing a military closure on the villages of Kufr Qallil and Jalud, both in the northern Nablus governorate, again claiming it was necessary to protect Palestinian residents from settlers.
Despite occasional statements by Israeli authorities that it does not tolerate attacks by settlers, collaboration by Israeli forces in settler attacks is well established. A UN report by the Commission of Inquiry on the ‌Occupied Palestinian Territory in June concluded that Israeli authorities are directly involved in settler attacks that have killed, injured, and displaced Palestinian communities in the West Bank. “The increasing participation of Israeli security forces in settler attacks amounts to a de facto collapse of the distinction between settlers and soldiers,” the report said.
The commission found that “settler violence in the West Bank functions as a means of implementing Israeli State policy, with the State and violent settler groups and individuals working towards the same strategic objectives, including the maintenance of the unlawful occupation, the entrenchment of illegal Israeli settlements, the annexation of Palestinian territory and the displacement of Palestinians from their land.” It added, “Israeli authorities have enabled such attacks through financial and military support while Israeli judicial and law enforcement authorities have granted impunity for settler violence for decades.”
While attacks by Israeli settlers and soldiers on Palestinians in the West Bank have been a frequent occurrence for years, they have accelerated sharply since October 2023 in parallel with Israel’s genocidal assault on Gaza, with over 1,100 Palestinians killed and tens of thousands forcibly displaced.
Last month, the UN warned that attacks by Israeli settlers and the creation of settlements and outposts have hit “an all-time high.” Over the past two and a half weeks, the attacks escalated even further following a raid by settlers on the village of Tell that ended with four Palestinians and two settlers being killed. Over the past week alone, there have been over 500 reported attacks, according to the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
Palestinians in the village of Taybeh, which is home to some 1,500 people and lies several kilometers northeast of Jerusalem and Ramallah, said that the settler violence has become all but intolerable. Just over a third ⁠of Taybeh—including most of the built up section of the village—is designated as Area B, a classification under the Oslo Accords where the Palestinian Authority is in charge of civil administration while Israel officially retains security control. The rest of Taybeh’s lands are designated as Area C, where Israel officially exercises full civil and security control.
“There were attacks before, but nothing like what we’re seeing these days,” Kaabneh said. “Over the past 15 days, the settlers have been coming two or three times a day, in the morning and in the evening. They’ve really intensified the pressure on us.”
“They want to forcibly displace us,” he added. “God willing, we’ll remain patient, and God will give us the strength not to leave this place and to remain steadfast here.”
Taybeh’s churches date back to the Fifth Century. “Taybeh is a Palestinian village, regardless of whether it’s Christian or Muslim,” Abed, the local priest, said. “The Jewish settler doesn’t distinguish—all he sees is a Palestinian.”
Israeli settlers have also targeted Taybeh’s olive groves, which provide one of the primary sources of income to the village. Multiple residents told Drop Site that settlers bring sheep and other livestock to graze on their lands and use up the water in local wells and also bring camels to chew at the tops of the olive trees and ruin them.
“The camels are destroying the trees because they’re such tall, large animals. The tops of the olive trees have been completely destroyed…. These are Roman era olive trees. It’s truly heartbreaking,” Fouad Maadi, a local resident, said. “Every aspect of life [is affected], everything. Commerce is finished, agriculture is finished, livestock is finished.”
“It’s a campaign of revenge against us aimed at forcing us out of this land. But we’re staying here,” he added. “We’re not going to leave, no matter what.”
* A journalist in the West Bank contributed reporting. Drop Site News Middle East Research Fellow Jawa Ahmad also contributed to this report.

reads.title: Hormuz at Breaking Point and Remembering Journalists Killed in Gaza
reads.subtitle: Financial expert Brett Erickson joins Drop Site's Murtaza Hussain and Ryan Grim followed by Sharif Abdel Kouddous and Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed.
reads.body:
The U.S. war against Iran has transformed into a form of economic siege as U.S. ships blockade Iranian ports and Trump promises a prolonged naval confrontation aimed at forcing Iran to relinquish its control over the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Iran is imposing its own retaliatory siege aimed at the U.S. and its allies by striking ships attempting the pass the strait without its permission—vowing not to relent until the U.S. concedes  a list of demands including economic compensation to Tehran and military withdrawal from the region.
On this week’s episode of the Drop Site News livestream hosts Murtaza Hussain and Ryan Grim discuss the economics of this war of blockades and its impact on the global economy with financial expert Brett Erickson.
In the following segment Murtaza and Ryan are joined by colleagues Sharif Abdel Kouddous and Abubaker Abed to discuss the one year anniversary of the assassination of Palestinian journalist Anas al-Sharif and five of his colleagues on August 10, 2025, and the ongoing targeting of Palestinian journalists covering the genocide in the Gaza Strip.
