reads.title: Israel's Brutal Retaliation Against Imprisoned Palestinian Doctors Seeking Legal Appeals
reads.subtitle: The escalated abuse against Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya following a legal challenge to his detention has sent a chilling message to the families of detained medical workers in Gaza.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- A Palestinian man walks past a portrait of imprisoned Kamal Adwan Hospital Director Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, painted by Palestinian artist Abu Karsheli on the rubble of the Italian Tower, which was destroyed in Israeli attacks in Gaza City, Gaza, Palestine, on June 27, 2026. Photo by Ahmed Jihad Ibrahim Al-Arini/Anadolu via Getty Images.GAZA CITY—Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, the former director of the Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza, suffered multiple injuries, including fractured ribs, after enduring severe beatings by Israeli prison authorities on July 27, according to the Palestinian Prisoners’ Media Office. The group described it as the “most difficult day” of his imprisonment since being detained without charge over a year and a half ago.
In a statement issued on Wednesday, the office said Abu Safiya, who suffers from heart disease and high blood pressure, has been subjected to “brutal torture” since June 24, when he was transferred to Rakevet—an underground detention facility within the Ramla prison complex in central Israel—including spending 21 days in solitary confinement.
Previously, Abu Safiya told his lawyer, Nasser Odeh, during a prison visit on July 2, that following an appeal filed with the Israeli Supreme Court at the end of April, the assaults and abuse against him escalated dramatically. Abu Safiya  told Odeh that after a court hearing in June, where he appeared via a video link looking gaunt, several prison guards entered his cell and beat him with batons and a hammer.
Abu Safiya’s son, Elias, 27, told Drop Site News that Odeh found his father in extremely critical condition during the July 2 visit—unable to breathe normally and speaking with great difficulty, with marks of beatings and torture visible on his face and body.
According to Elias, Abu Safiya told Odeh that this might be the last time he would see him. For the family, it felt like “a farewell message from a human being who feels his life is nearing its end,” said Elias. “Since that moment, we have been living every day in genuine fear of receiving the news of his martyrdom at any moment.”
The apparent repercussions against Abu Safiya in prison following the legal challenge to his detention and similar cases involving detained medical workers have sent a chilling message to the families of Palestinian detainees—particularly doctors—that seeking justice, either through legal means or public campaigns, can have severe consequences.
As director of the Kamal Adwan Hospital, Abu Safiya gained prominence for his refusal to abandon patients as the hospital came under heavy assault by the invading Israeli military. He was detained in December 2024 when Israeli forces raided the facility, arresting him and hundreds of other healthcare workers, many of whom, like Abu Safiya, remain in Israeli prison without charge.
Abu Safiya’s family filed the Supreme Court appeal in a bid to improve his legal circumstances and prison conditions, but the opposite occurred.
“We thought we would see an improvement in his legal and health situation, but unfortunately, we witnessed a massive deterioration in his condition and an escalation in the violations he was subjected to,” said Elias.
On June 16, Israel’s Supreme Court rejected the appeal and said the state could hold him without charges based on “confidential materials” that were not shared with his lawyer. At least 14 other doctors have been held for more than a year without charges.
“Whenever we tried to resort to the law and justice to protect him, our fear increased that he would pay the price inside the prison,” Elias said. “We began to fear that demanding his rights would be a cause for further revenge and torture against him.”
Islam Abdo, spokesperson for the Prisoners and Ex-Prisoners Affairs Commission in Gaza, told Drop Site that Abu Safiya’s case has created widespread fear among families of detained medical workers, who are now are now hesitant to pursue legal or media campaigns because Israeli authorities react to public attention brought on detainees by increasing pressure inside prison.
“The case of Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya has created a state of great anxiety,” he said, particularly among families of other detained doctors and medical staff.
“The fear is that Israel uses this symbolic status to increase the suffering of the prisoners,” he said, adding that many families are even afraid to participate in solidarity protests or public statements out of concern that it will lead to more isolation, beatings, or medical neglect for their detained relatives.
When asked whether resorting to Israeli courts or international organizations poses additional risks rather than protection, Abdo replied: “Absolutely.” He described the Israeli judicial system as “a cover for practicing more repression and abuse against prisoners,” saying it has caused families to lose whatever confidence they had left in Israel’s so-called justice system.
Drop Site News is reader-supported. Consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.
Dr. Hassan Khalil Al-Muqayyad, a senior physician from Kamal Adwan hospital, was detained by Israeli forces in October 2024. Like most Palestinian prisoners, he was subject to physical and psychological abuse and was transferred between several prisons, including Sde Teiman, Ofer, and Negev Prison where he remains imprisoned without charge.
Al-Muqayyad’s wife, Nadia, told Drop Site she was advised by lawyers that filing a legal appeal for her husband’s release or even hiring an attorney for him could lead to repercussions. In April 2025, six months into his detention, she considered retaining a lawyer to try and secure a prison visit every two months instead of every six months but was advised against it. “We are afraid. I wanted to appoint a lawyer for him, but they told me ‘No, this could harm him,’ so I stopped, honestly,” Nadia said. “I became afraid that using [legal procedures] could actually work against him or negatively affect him.”
She continued: “Whenever there is a lawyer visit...there is harassment, torture, and oppression. Moving the prisoner from the prison to the court is suffering in itself. He is restrained, blindfolded, and the torture is present for all the prisoners.”
Another case in point is Dr. Marwan Al-Hams, who was detained by undercover Israeli forces outside a Red Cross field hospital in Rafah in July 2025 and has remained in prison without charge for more than a year. Al-Hams has been subjected to repeated, lengthy and intense interrogations lasting over 1,000 hours, his daughter Tasneem, a 24-year-old nurse, told Drop Site. Al-Hams was often severely tortured during these interrogation sessions, Tasneem said. At one point, he suffered a cardiac arrest and had to be resuscitated with a defibrillator.
Al-Hams has also suffered from psychological isolation and medical neglect inside prison, including never receiving treatment for injuries to his feet, and being denied requests for medication and an electrocardiogram, his daughter said.
Tasneem also stressed that her father is subjected to beatings before every lawyer visit and said she fears any public campaign for his release may trigger Israeli authorities. “There are genuine fears that any legal or human rights move will backfire on my father inside the prison, and many times we hesitated out of fear for his safety,” she told Drop Site.
In October 2025, less than three months after her father’s arrest, Tasneem was detained by Israeli forces on her way to work at a medical point in Al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. She said interrogators informed her that her imprisonment was intended to pressure her father.
“They sat me down with my father in the interrogation room to pressure him, and I realized that what happened to me was part of an attempt to coerce him,” she said. Tasneem was eventually released nearly six weeks later. She added that her father’s case, along with Abu Safiya’s, has deepened her conviction that Israel was engaging in systematic retaliation against families for speaking out.
“After what happened with Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, a bitter reality materialized before us,” she continued. “The occupation respects neither medical immunity nor international law, but rather takes revenge on anyone who raises their voice. This reality has created an extremely cruel equation for us.”
Israeli forces have killed approximately 1,700 health care workers since October 2023 and arrested more than 370 others, 82 of whom remain in custody, including Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, Dr. Marwan Al-Hams, Dr. Nahed Abu Taima, and Dr. Mohammed Obaid, along with several surgeons and specialized doctors, according to the director general of the Ministry of Health in Gaza, Dr. Munir Al-Bursh. Every hospital in Gaza has come under attack by the Israeli military and less than half are partially functioning while the rest have been closed down. The absence of these doctors has led to the suspension of vital medical services that thousands of patients rely on, Al-Bursh told Drop Site.
“In light of the complete collapse of the health sector, the absence of a doctor like my father, who managed hospitals and led the response to emergency cases, does not only mean stripping him of his freedom, but also depriving thousands of patients of his expertise at a time when they need it most,” Tasneem said. “Enough silence in the face of the targeting and arrest of medical staff. We demand that international organizations take urgent action to break the isolation imposed on imprisoned doctors and save them before it is too late.”
Al-Bursh warned that previous cases—like the death of Dr. Adnan Al-Bursh in prison in April 2024 apparently as a result of severe torture—give the health ministry clear reason to fear for the lives of the doctors still being held in detention, particularly high-profile cases like Abu Safiya.
Abu Safiya’s family said despite the risk of retaliation, they refuse to back down.
“We still believe in justice and institutions, and that every voice can make a difference. We are the rightful owners of our cause, and my father is being tortured even though he has not been charged with anything,” his son, Elias, said. “We no longer ask for anything greater than my father’s right to life.”

reads.title: Dozens reported killed in Ansarallah attacks; Saudi Arabia, Turkey, and Pakistan sign defense deal; Trump targets birthright citizenship
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 7, 2026
reads.body:
- Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan (2nd L), Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (C) and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif (R) sign a trilateral joint defense agreement in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, on August 7, 2026. Photo by TUR Presidency/Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Anadolu via Getty Images.Friday, August 7, 2026 – Explosions heard near Qeshm. Iran deal on Hormuz with Oman nears. Iran parliament speaker Mohammed Baghar Ghalibaf slams U.S. President Donald Trump’s “theater diplomacy.” Tehran sent Gulf countries list of power plants that it could strike if U.S. attacked its infrastructure, report says. Trump says Iran war “going very well,” to end “pretty soon.” Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian discusses effects of war, leadership of country. Mossad fires two senior officials over Iran war failure. White House tells Emiratis to silence Iran war critic. Traffic through Hormuz drops sharply. Ansarallah clashes with Saudi-backed government in Marib and Hadramout. Traffic increases through Bab Al-Mandab. UNICEF reports one Palestinian child killed every day in Gaza since “ceasefire.” Israeli forces withdraw from Qalandia as attacks continue across occupied West Bank. Number of Palestinian children held in Israeli prisons without charge sharply rises. Lebanese soldier wounded, water station set ablaze in Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon. U.S. says Hezbollah did not violate ceasefire in Majdal Zoun. Trump issues new executive orders targeting birthright citizenship. U.S. economy shed 23,000 jobs in July. Trump says he’ll keep Todd Blanche as acting attorney general if Senate confirmation fails. ICE will release body camera footage only when in “agency’s best interests.” Democratic National Committee autopsy author says Gaza war hurt Kamala Harris in 2024. University of Minnesota to pay pro-Palestine professor after nixing job offer. Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan sign defense deal. U.S. intelligence claims Russia could test NATO with limited attack. Bombing near Damascus wounds 14. Former Mexican governor arrested for evidence destruction in missing students case. Uganda’s parliament approves potential military deployment to Gaza. Attack on former Bangladesh cricketer Shakib Al Hasan’s home follows his appearance alongside exiled Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announces new sanctions on Cuba. Iraqi resistance leader urges pause to operations against Saudi Arabia. Pro-Palestine protester acquitted in UK court.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Explosions heard near Qeshm: Two explosions were heard on Qeshm Island on Thursday, Iran’s Tasnim News Agency reported, and were reportedly caused by Iranian forces engaging with “hostile enemy targets” near the entry to the Strait of Hormuz.

- Iran deal on Hormuz with Oman nears: Hassan Ghashghavi, a spokesperson for the National Security Commission and an MP, said on Friday that a “framework of understanding” with Oman regarding the Strait had been agreed upon. “The general framework of the understanding with Oman has been determined, and the final text and details will be announced soon,” Ghashghavi told the official IRNA news agency, noting that the “final decision” would be made at “higher levels.”

- A senior Iranian official told Drop Site’s Jeremy Scahill that Iran and Oman have finalized technical talks and agreed on temporary rules for the “security, supervisory, and economic management” of the Strait of Hormuz, following several rounds of negotiations.

- The official said Iran’s implementation of the agreement remains conditional on the “full and tangible return” of the United States to the temporary ceasefire understanding, stressing that merely suspending the naval blockade would not be sufficient.

- Iran parliament speaker slams Trump’s “theater diplomacy”: Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad and lead negotiator Mohamed Bagher Ghalibaf criticized President Donald Trump’s repeated shifts between threatening a major attack on Iran and announcing negotiations, calling it “theater diplomacy on loop.”

- Ghalibaf said, in a post on X, that using “bullying + broken promises + fake news as leverage” was a failed strategy and urged Washington to “acknowledge the facts and fulfill your commitments,” adding: “We don’t need more theater.”

- Tehran sent Gulf countries list of power plants that it could strike if U.S. attacked its infrastructure, report says: Iran sent Gulf mediators a detailed list of power plants and desalination facilities it could strike if the U.S. attacked Iranian energy infrastructure earlier this week, the AFP reported on Thursday, threatening to “black out the Gulf, country by country” in response to Washington’s potential attacks. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE subsequently urged Trump not to launch the planned strikes, according to the agency.

- Trump says Iran war “going very well,” to end “pretty soon”: In a post on Truth Social on Thursday, Trump claimed that the war on Iran was going “very well,” adding that the country was “decimated.” He also said he was “extremely happy” with War Secretary Pete Hegseth, who he reportedly confronted during a Cabinet meeting last week about low munitions supplies. “Everything has been extraordinary.”

- While taking questions in the Oval Office from reporters, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the war on Iran would end “pretty soon,” speculating that the Iranian government could not “go much longer.”

- Trump also asserted that the Strait of Hormuz remained “sort of open” right now, despite acknowledging the previous day that Iran maintained its ability to threaten shipping through the waterway with its naval power.

- Pezeshkian discusses effects of war, leadership of country: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said in an interview with Iran’s IRNA news service that attacks on the country’s power infrastructure caused “a daily shortage of approximately 230 million cubic metres of gas,” and that the U.S. exerted “maximum pressure” on Iran, “expecting the country to collapse.”

- He also discussed his relationship with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, saying that communication with Khamenei, who has not appeared publicly since his appointment in March, is currently “very difficult,” but calling him a “major asset” in allowing Iran to continue its successful defense of the country.

- Mossad fires two senior officials over Iran war failure: Israel’s Mossad chief, Roman Gofman, fired two of the spy agency’s top officials over a failed plan to topple Iran’s government, Israel’s Channel 12 and Haaretz reported on Thursday.

- One of the officials had served as the head of Mossad’s intelligence directorate since September, and the other was the head of the agency’s Iran division.

- The two drafted the written plan to remove Iran’s leadership by mobilizing the country’s minority groups to rebel and whip up mass protests to oust the government.

- White House tells Emiratis to silence Iran war critic: The White House has reportedly told the government of the United Arab Emirates to “shut down” Amjad Taha, a political strategist and journalist with ties to the government and a staunch advocate of Israel and the Abraham Accords, whose criticism of the U.S.’s war in Iran has “irked” Trump and his allies, according to a report from the Washington Times on Thursday.

- Traffic through Hormuz drops sharply: Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz dropped to 33 vessels between Monday and Thursday, down from 50 the previous week, according to data published by the maritime tracking firm Kpler on Friday.

- Citing data from ship-tracking company Kpler, Reuters said that only four vessels transited the strait on Thursday, including the very large crude carrier Nissos Kea, which was carrying about two million barrels of crude oil from Iraq.

- Several Chinese and Indian refiners have unsuccessfully sought vessels this week to enter the Strait and load crude at Iraq’s Basrah Oil Terminal, following steep discounts offered by Iraq’s state oil marketer.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah clashes with Saudi-backed government in Marib and Hadramout: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces reported that Ansarallah missile and drone attacks on the Yemeni provinces of Marib and Hadramout on Thursday killed at least 18 of its soldiers, with other reports putting the death toll as high as 58.

- The health minister of the Saudi-backed government later announced that a second round of attacks on Friday had killed two civilians and wounded 14 others.

- An Ansarallah political bureau member described Thursday’s operations as a “preemptive” response to alleged plans by Saudi forces to attack Sana’a. Ansarallah’s Supreme Political Council claimed Saudi Arabia had been preparing a ground invasion to create internal chaos and prevent an end to the country’s “12-year siege,” according to Tasnim.

- The Saudi-backed government said that its army had shot down multiple Ansarallah drones launched towards Marib on Friday, with several explosions reported.

- In the southwestern Saudi city of Najran, the Saudi-led coalition said projectiles launched by Ansarallah wounded 11 civilians, seven of whom were Saudi nationals and one of whom was a 4-year-old child.

- Traffic increases through Bab Al-Mandab: 26 vessels transited the Bab Al-Mandab Strait on Thursday, up from 19 the previous day, according to Kpler data.

## Palestine

- UNICEF reports one Palestinian child killed every day in Gaza since “ceasefire”: “At least 300 children have been killed in Gaza in the 300 days since a ‘ceasefire’ went into effect on October 10, 2025, UNICEF said in a statement on Thursday. “A ceasefire that leaves an average of one child dead each and every day is failing children,” UNICEF’s Regional Director for the Middle East and North Africa, Edouard Beigbeder, said. “With hundreds more children injured, many severely, children in Gaza are still waiting for the end to the violence they were promised.”

- Israeli forces withdraw from Qalandia as attacks continue across occupied West Bank:

- Qalandia: Israeli forces withdrew from Qalandia refugee camp and Kafr Aqab in Jerusalem late Thursday after a two-day military raid that left 51 Palestinians injured and more than 60 detained or subjected to field interrogation, including women and children, according to the Jerusalem Governorate. Israeli troops also demolished seven shops and a car wash, damaged dozens of homes and businesses, and converted homes into military posts. Families also reported money and gold jewelry stolen during raids.

- Jenin: Israeli forces shot and wounded two Palestinians in Jenin on Thursday, including a 14-year-old, who soldiers shot in the lower back, according to WAFA. The Israeli military closed off a roundabout, detained a group of young Palestinian men, and raided multiple shops. The military also issued a series of new orders targeting land in several towns in Jenin on Thursday, including orders to uproot trees and seize more land in the town of Marka.

- Ramallah: Israeli settlers attacked a Bedouin community near the town of Taybeh on Thursday, injuring three people from a single family, one international activist, and arresting a Palestinian, WAFA reported. In another attack on Thursday evening, Israeli forces beat and fired stun grenades at an 80-year-old Palestinian-American man near Turmus Ayya. He sustained cuts and bruises from the attack.

- Sen. Chris Van Hollen demanded on Thursday that U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee resign, pointing to the attack, following reporting from Zeteo that the man who was attacked is an American citizen.

- Tubas: Israeli forces stormed the city of Tamman, near Tubas, early Friday morning, raiding the town and ransacking a house, according to WAFA. On Thursday, Israeli forces released the body of a 28-year-old Palestinian who had been shot in Tubas in April, and whose body had been withheld from his family since.

- Drop Site’s Mohamed Awad interviewed residents from Tuba in Masafer Yatta, who were attacked by Israeli settlers on Wednesday. “They smashed and burned everything,” one resident said, describing the attack that wounded five Palestinians, including a child whose nose was broken, and burned at least four homes.. “They left nothing untouched.” Watch Mohamed’s video dispatches here and here.

- Hamas urges mediators to prevent Israel from derailing Gaza agreement: Hamas called on mediators and the U.S. administration on Thursday, asking them to intervene to prevent Israel from derailing the Gaza agreement, saying continued Israeli violations threaten implementation of its second phase.

- The movement said Palestinian factions have engaged “positively and responsibly” with efforts to complete the agreement and presented their position on the roadmap “in a national spirit” that clears the way for implementing Phase 2.

- Number of Palestinian children held in Israeli prisons without charge sharply rises: At least 191 Palestinian children are being held in “administrative detention” in Israeli prisons in March 2026, according to data from the organization Parents Against Child Detention, up from 103 in January of 2025, the Times of Israel reported on Friday..

- Palestinians in administrative detention can be held indefinitely and without trial, are not informed of the allegations against them, and evidence presented against them in court is routinely classified and withheld from the accused and their attorneys.

## Lebanon

- Lebanese soldier wounded, water station set ablaze in Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon: Israeli forces carried out a series of attacks across southern Lebanon on Friday, continuing near-daily violations despite the U.S.-backed ceasefire.

- An Israeli drone carried out an airstrike on Al-Mansouri, south of Tyre (Sour) district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

- A Lebanese soldier was wounded when an Israeli attack targeted an army bulldozer in Al-Mansouri while it was clearing roads and removing rubble, according to the Lebanese Army.

- Israeli artillery shelled Meiss Al-Jabal, in Marjayoun district,  while Israeli forces simultaneously fired machine guns toward the town, NNA reported.

- Israeli forces set fire Friday to the Shaqra water station in the Bint Jbeil district.

- U.S. says Hezbollah did not violate ceasefire in Majdal Zoun: Washington informed Israel that Hezbollah did not violate the ceasefire in Thursday’s incident in Majdal Zoun, in which an IED explosion killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded several others, an Israeli security source told Israel’s public broadcaster, as reported by Al Jazeera.

- Israeli assessments also indicate that the explosive device in Majdal Zoun was planted before the ceasefire took effect, according to the broadcaster.

- The comments come as U.S. State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott told Sky News Arabia the Rome talks between Lebanon and Israel were “effective and positive,” saying progress was made on several technical issues.

## U.S. News

- Trump issues more executive orders attempting to rewrite birthright citizenship law: President Donald Trump signed two executive orders Thursday seeking to deny birthright citizenship to children born to certain foreign diplomatic staff, alleged “alien enemies” including those tied to designated terrorist groups, mothers who deceptively enter the U.S. for commercial “birth tourism,” and, contingent on future congressional action, people born in U.S. territories such as Puerto Rico, according to Axios.

- A second order directs the secretaries of state and homeland security to issue rules targeting the “birth tourism” industry both domestically and abroad.

- The move marks Trump’s second attempt to curb birthright citizenship after the Supreme Court struck down his broader executive order on June 30.

- Legal experts expect the new orders to face 14th Amendment challenges.

- U.S. economy shed 23,000 jobs in July: The U.S. economy lost a seasonally adjusted 23,000 jobs in July, according to a Bureau of Labor Statistics report released Friday.

- The figure is well below the Dow Jones consensus forecast, which had anticipated a gain of 83,000.

- The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1%, while the labor force participation fell to 61.4%, its lowest level in more than five years.

- Trump says he’ll keep Blanche as acting AG if confirmation fails: President Donald Trump said he would keep Todd Blanche as acting attorney general if his Senate confirmation fails, telling Punchbowl News, “We’ll try it again,” as Blanche’s path narrowed following Alaska Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s decision to join Maine Sen. Susan Collins in opposing him. Murkowski cited the Justice Department’s handling of Jeffrey Epstein-related files, sweeping immunity promised to Trump and his family, and statements to anti-abortion groups as reasons for her opposition, saying, “I simply do not have confidence” Blanche would check “the worst impulses of this administration.”

- ICE will only release body camera footage when in “agency’s best interests”: Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which plans to equip all field officers with body cameras by the end of September, has adopted a policy that allows release of footage from shootings or serious confrontations only when the agency’s director determines it is “in the best interests of the agency,” according to an Associated Press investigation.

- ICE officers shot two men in Houston and Maine last month, and neither incident was recorded, despite the $20 million Congress previously allocated to ICE for body camera equipment in an April spending bill.

- ICE spent $30.9 million in July purchasing camera equipment from Axon, one day after the killing in Maine.

- DNC autopsy author says Gaza war hurt Harris: Paul Rivera, author of the Democratic National Committee’s 2024 election autopsy, confirmed to Axios that he concluded the Gaza war hurt Kamala Harris politically, particularly costing her votes in Michigan communities with large Arab American populations such as Dearborn.

- Rivera said he privately shared the assessment with a pro-Palestinian group, the IMEU project, but did not include it in the autopsy’s final draft.

- University of Minnesota to pay pro-Palestine professor after nixing job offer: The University of Minnesota will pay Israeli-American Holocaust scholar Raz Segal $250,000 after withdrawing an offer to lead its Center for Holocaust and Genocide Studies following backlash over his description of Israel’s assault on Gaza as “a textbook case of genocide,” the Guardian reported on Thursday.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan sign defense deal: Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan signed a trilateral defense agreement in Saudi Arabia on Friday, aiming to “promote peace, security, and stability in the region and beyond,” according to a statement announcing the deal from Pakistan’s Foreign Ministry.

- The agreement “stipulates that any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all,” according to the FM statement.

- A Turkish official told the NYT that the deal only covered mutual defense, and is “not directed against any other country.”

- U.S. intelligence claims Russia could test NATO with limited attack: New U.S. intelligence assessments reportedly warn that Russian President Vladimir Putin could attempt to fracture NATO by launching a calibrated attack on an allied country between this fall and 2029.

- Possible scenarios in the assessments range from a cyberattack or deployment of unmarked armed groups to a limited incursion along NATO’s eastern flank, with a full land assault the least likely scenario.

- The assessment comes amid increasing incidents in which Russian missiles and drones have struck or flown over NATO countries in what U.S. and European officials have described as probes of NATO’s willingness to respond.

- Bombing near Damascus wounds 14: An explosive device planted on a minibus wounded 14 people Thursday night in Jaramana, a predominantly Druze suburb of Damascus, according to Syrian officials.

- Authorities initially reported two fatalities after finding what appeared to be body parts at the scene, but the Health Ministry later said they belonged to people who had been severely wounded. Some of the victims remain in serious condition, including the minibus driver.

- Authorities have not attributed responsibility for the bombing. Jaramana has experienced clashes between Druze residents and Islamist militants aligned with Syria’s new authorities since the 2024 overthrow of Bashar al-Assad.

- Former Guerrero governor arrested for evidence destruction in missing students case: Angel Aguirre, a former governor of Mexico’s southern Guerrero state, was arrested on charges of obstruction of justice and forced disappearance for allegedly ordering the destruction of evidence that could have shed light on the whereabouts of 43 students who disappeared in 2014, Mexican Attorney General Ernestina Godoy announced Thursday.

- Godoy said new testimony from two witnesses helped establish that Aguirre may have ordered the destruction of security camera footage during a meeting with senior officials the night of the students’ disappearance.

- International probes have determined the students, who were on their way to a protest in Mexico City, were killed by organized crime members working with police.

- Pakistan expands press restrictions to cover Pakistani nationals working for foreign media: Pakistan announced new restrictions on journalists on Sunday, imposing routine movement controls on Pakistani nationals working for foreign media outlets for the first time.

- Journalists now require government permission to travel and report outside Islamabad, Lahore, and Karachi.

- The guidelines, whose motivation officials have not explained, come amid protests over recent multi-round elections in Pakistan-administered Kashmir and widening insurgencies in the country’s western provinces.

- The country also ordered foreign outlets without reporting permits to immediately leave Pakistan-administered Kashmir. on Monday.

- Human Rights Watch called the curbs “an alarming step” in Pakistan’s “narrowing space for press freedom.”

- Uganda’s parliament approves potential military deployment to Gaza: Uganda’s parliament voted Thursday to approve deploying its military to the Gaza Strip if needed as part of a proposed multinational security force under President Donald Trump’s ceasefire plan, Reuters reported.

- Defense Minister Kiryowa Kiwanuka told lawmakers before the vote that Trump had contacted Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni through emissaries in July seeking Kampala’s participation.

- The move marks the first public acknowledgment by Uganda, which has peacekeeping contingents in Somalia, South Sudan, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, that it might join the International Stabilization Force envisioned under Trump’s plan.

- Attack on former Bangladesh cricketer Shakib Al Hasan’s home follows his appearance alongside Hasina: A group attacked and set fire to former Bangladesh cricket captain Shakib Al Hasan’s ancestral home in Magura town Wednesday, hours after he joined ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina’s first public media event since her 2024 removal, Al Jazeera reported.

- During the virtual event, held on the second anniversary of her ouster, Hasina, who has been sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh’s war crimes tribunal, said she would return to the country in December despite the risk of imprisonment or death.

- Shakib, a former Awami League lawmaker who has remained abroad since the uprising that toppled Hasina’s government, faces multiple investigations over allegations of murder and money laundering.

- Rubio announces new sanctions on Cuba: Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced new sanctions on Thursday against five Cuban companies and eight individuals, including Defense Minister Alvaro Lopez Miera and Chief of the General Staff Roberto Legra Sotolongo.

- The sanctions target firms including Tecnoimport, which the State Department says imports Russian and Chinese military equipment for Cuba’s armed forces, and Union de Industria Militar, a weapons manufacturer.

- Iraqi resistance leader urges pause to operations against Saudi Arabia: Hadi al-Amiri, head of the Iraqi Badr Organization, part of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), urged Iraqi resistance groups on Friday to postpone retaliatory operations against Saudi Arabia in a video address carried by Iraqi media.

- He called groups to overlook “American-Saudi” aggression for the “sake of Iraq’s highest interest.”

- The U.S. and Saudi Arabia attacked the PMF headquarters in Iraq on July 29, killing more than 20 people and wounding at least 30 others.

- Pro-Palestine protester acquitted in UK court: Paula Akpan, one of the 10 British pro-Palestine protesters charged with criminal damage for spraying red paint across the entrances of Scotiabank in June 2024, was found not guilty in court on Thursday.

- At the time of the protest, the bank was the largest foreign shareholder in Elbit Systems, holding a $500 million stake in Israel’s leading weapons manufacturer, whose military hardware has been used to kill and injure Palestinian civilians.

- Seven of Akpan’s codefendants have been acquitted.

reads.title: Pro-Israel Pressure Group Honest Reporting Received Grant from Knight Foundation
reads.subtitle: Despite a record of endangering Palestinian journalists, Honest Reporting received a $100,000 “emergency grant” from the Knight Foundation.
reads.body:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers. Please consider making a tax-deductible donation to support our work today.
Subscribe now

-
- Palestinian journalists protest against the assassination of their colleague Hassan Eslaiah, outside Nasser Hospital, in Khan Yunis, Gaza on May 13, 2025. Eslaih was killed in an Israeli attack on Nasser Hospital. Photo by Alaa Y. M. Abumohsen/Anadolu via Getty Images.Honest Reporting, a self-described media watchdog and nonprofit with offices in New York, Jerusalem, and Toronto, claims that its mission is exposing “media bias, challenging false narratives, and ensuring that reporting on Israel is rooted in facts, context, and accountability.” In practice, it operates as a pressure group, monitoring international media coverage of Israel, producing reports attacking coverage it deems unfavorable, running access operations that embed international journalists within curated pro-Israel perspectives, and organizing mass campaigns directing its subscribers to contact newsrooms directly until corrections, retractions, and rewordings are secured.
That work has led to the dismissal of journalists at publications around the world. But since October 7, 2023, Honest Reporting’s operations have moved into considerably darker territory, and its activities have contributed to the assassination of at least one journalist, Hassan Eslaiah—a freelance photographer and director of the Gaza-based Alam24 news agency whose images had appeared in the Associated Press and CNN.
The campaign against Eslaiah was not isolated. Honest Reporting has systematically targeted journalists and news organizations—including Drop Site News—across multiple platforms and countries, employing consistent tactics: publishing posts raising questions about individual journalists’ alleged connections to Hamas or other armed groups, characterizing their coverage as propaganda or as “antisemitic,” and mobilizing its subscriber network to contact news organizations directly. The cumulative effect of this approach has been to characterize numerous Palestinian journalists as combatants.
Despite its record as a pressure group that targets and endangers reporters, in 2023 Honest Reporting’s Israeli organization—registered under the name Divuach Ne’eman R’’A—received an “emergency” grant of $100,000 from the Knight Foundation, a widely respected U.S.-based foundation that prominently touts a commitment to freedom of press and the safety of journalists. The grant, listed in Honest Reporting’s Israeli nonprofit filings for 2024, is not reported in the Knight Foundation’s 990 for 2024 or on its website.
The Knight Foundation says that it primarily funds U.S.-based organizations and that international programs and organizations are among the categories it generally prefers not to fund, making grants outside the United States limited and exceptional by the foundation’s own description. Knight’s website states that “most of our grantmaking is tied to strategies with defined goals and outcomes” and that funding “typically emerges through relationships, research and ongoing work,” with most grants initiated by Knight itself rather than through open applications.
When approached for comment, Atena Sherry, Knight Foundation’s director of communications, initially denied that Knight had provided funding to Honest Reporting: “Knight Foundation did not provide any grant to Honest Reporting, and the foundation has not directed any Knight funds to Honest Reporting” through any third party, Sherry told Drop Site. In a follow-up statement, Sherry said, “We reviewed all documentation. Knight Foundation has never provided any funding to Honest Reporting.”
According to Honest Reporting, however, “the grantor, Jewish Federations of North America and United Israel Appeal, notified Divuach Ne’eman R”A and HonestReporting.com, Inc. that a donation of $100,000 was made ‘on the recommendation of the donor, The Knight Foundation.’ Honest Reporting added that “Staff for Divuach Ne’eman R”A and Honest Reporting.com, Inc. were in direct touch with staff at the Knight Foundation throughout the process on the grant and the programs that would benefit from the grant.”
When Drop Site then asked the Knight Foundation about Honest Reporting’s statement, which directly contradicted its own, the Knight Foundation acknowledged that it had provided funds for Media Central, an Honest Reporting program that arranges tours for international journalists. “Knight Foundation did make a one-time, emergency grant of $100,000 in November 2023 to Media Central to support a very specific project: helping international journalists to gain access they wouldn’t otherwise have had to report on the facts from the ground in the West Bank,” said Alejandro de Onis, vice president for communications, in a statement. “Neither the grant agreement nor the grant file contains any reference to Honest Reporting.”
Unlike Gaza, the West Bank has remained accessible to international journalists, raising the question of what access Media Central was providing that journalists could not obtain independently, and whether the access in question was in fact embedded reporting alongside the Israeli military.
Knight declined to answer additional questions about the specific reporting funded by its grant or how it could have been unaware that Media Central was a program operated by Honest Reporting.
Through its Media Central project, Honest Reporting arranges press tours, briefings, and curated access to Israel for international correspondents, presenting itself as a neutral resource while functioning as an operation designed to shape how journalists understand and cover the country. Honest Reporting’s director of press relations, Laura Cornfield, runs the program.
In Honest Reporting’s 2023 first quarter impact report, Cornfield wrote that: “Journalists met with locals to hear how the Lions’ Den terrorist group was using Nablus as its command center. They were then briefed by the IDF to understand the security risks to Israeli civilians,” boasting that “MediaCentral staff enabled exclusive access to these unheard, nearly impossible-to-reach voices. The tour was so sought after it was repeated with three groups, and an additional three one-on-one tours were arranged.”
In that year’s second quarter impact report, Cornfield wrote that the group’s Media Central program “took foreign media outlets on exclusive tours to hotbeds of terror activity, including Nablus and Jenin, to get an up-close look at what Israeli security forces are facing and how they are addressing the threats.” The reports say that journalists from prominent international outlets including the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, the Economist, the Financial Times, and CNN have participated in its events.
The impact report described a media tour of the Israel-Lebanon border, quoting the Israeli military’s Lt. Gen. Herzi Halevi and Military Intelligence Directorate chief Aharon Haliva on Hezbollah. It also included a section on “crime in the Arab sector” and said that journalists had gone on “a field tour to Umm Al Fahm and Jaffa of Nazareth to address the surging crime rate,” referring to largely Palestinian towns and cities within Israel.
More recently, Media Central press tours have taken international journalists to the Al Aqsa compound and Western Wall Tunnels in occupied East Jerusalem and to northern Israel. Media Central has also hosted exclusive briefings for international journalists with senior Israeli political figures, including a recent lunch in Tel Aviv with former Israeli Ambassador to the United States Michael Oren and an “exclusive dinner” with Brigadier General (Res.) Pinchas (Pini) Yungman. Yungman has held senior command roles in the Israeli Air Force and executive positions at the Israeli defense company Rafael.
None of the briefings or meetings organized by Media Central appear to have been led by Palestinians.

-
- Relatives and colleagues of Palestinian journalist Hassan Eslaiah, who was killed in an Israeli drone strike on Nasser Hospital, mourn during his funeral ceremony held in Khan Yunis, Gaza on May 13, 2025. Photo by Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu via Getty Images.

## “We don’t claim to be a news organization.”
On November 8, 2023, one month into the genocide in Gaza and the same month as the Knight Foundation grant, Honest Reporting published what it classified as an exposé on its website. The article featured photographs of several Palestinian freelance journalists who had been covering the events near the Gaza border on the morning of October 7, among them Hassan Eslaiah. It asked, in language the organization has since described as just “raising questions,” whether these journalists could have had advance knowledge of the Hamas attack. The article was then updated to feature a photograph from 2020 of Eslaiah next to Hamas leader Yayha Sinwar—clearly suggesting guilt by association through proximity in a photograph.
Within hours, Israel’s official X account had amplified the post to its own audience of 1.8 million. The Associated Press reviewed its relationship with Eslaiah and later severed it, while stating publicly it had found no evidence he had foreknowledge of the attack beyond what was known to journalists routinely working in the border area. When the AP asked Gil Hoffman, then Honest Reporting’s executive director, to substantiate the allegations, his response was notable. “They acted as if we were stating facts instead of asking questions,” Hoffman said. “We don’t claim to be a news organization.”
Jonthan Dagher, head of the Middle East desk of Reporters Without Borders (RSF), described the November 2023 Honest Reporting article as being “full of conjecture” and “based on circumstantial evidence,” noting that it “provoked a chain of reactions from Israeli authorities and politicians who started accusing Gazan journalists of belonging to Hamas.”
RSF named Honest Reporting in its 2025 list of Press Freedom Predators that it says “smear media and promote mistrust of journalists.”
Eighteen months later, in April 2025, an Israeli airstrike struck a media tent outside Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, killing two journalists and wounding eight others, Eslaiah was among them. The Israeli military publicly announced it had deliberately targeted Eslaiah, claiming he was a member of the Khan Younis Brigade and had participated in the attacks of October 7th. Eslaiah survived the strike but his skull was fractured, his body was burned, and he lost two of his fingers. He was admitted to Nasser Hospital’s burns unit to recover. On May 13, 2025, while he lay in the burn unit, an Israeli drone bombed the hospital and murdered him. Hours later, the Israeli military admitted to assassinating Eslaiah, calling him “Aslih” and posting a screenshot of Eslaiah on Oct. 7, 2023 from a video also posted by Honest Reporting in its “exposé” and saying: “Don’t let Aslih’s press vest fool you…Journalist? More like terrorist.”

## Targeting Palestinian Journalists
Since the start of the genocide in Gaza, one of Honest Reporting’s central goals has been to challenge the records kept by press freedom organizations documenting Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza. The organization has led a sustained pressure campaign against the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), which maintains the most widely cited casualty list of media workers killed in Gaza. It has also sought to attack and pressure other press freedom bodies such as Reporters Without Borders and the International Federation of Journalists.
On June 25, CPJ announced that it would be “conducting a full review of its database of journalists killed during the Israel-Gaza War.” Honest Reporting was quick to claim victory, stating that the review had happened because Honest Reporting had “helped put them in an untenable position.”
In a statement, CPJ denied that Honest Reporting’s pressure campaign was responsible for its database review.
“The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) is an independent organization. We independently research, source and report information related to attacks on journalists and media workers. When new information becomes available, we update our reporting. Our review of the Israel-Gaza war casualties list was spurred by new information published by Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad that identified as combatants individuals previously listed by CPJ as journalists. Honest Reporting’s campaign had absolutely no bearing on the review process or on the decision to remove names from the list.”
CPJ, which receives major funding from the Knight Foundation, did not respond to questions about the foundation’s grant to Honest Reporting.
“We condemn any misrepresentation of that process to serve political agendas or to try to obscure the fact Israel has killed more journalists than any other country in the world and been the leading killer of journalists for the past three years,” CPJ said in its statement.
In response to questions about the direct conflict of interest entailed by funding both a press freedom organization that maintains a database of journalists killed by Israel and a pressure group that targets Palestinian journalists, the Knight Foundation said, “The funding directed to Media Central was specifically and only earmarked to facilitate journalists’ access to report on the war in hard to reach areas and there is no ongoing relationship. Nothing in Knight Foundation’s grant records reflects any reference to a campaign concerning CPJ, and Knight Foundation has never funded advocacy directed at CPJ.”
On the same day that CPJ announced its Gaza database review, Jacob Weisberg, chair of CPJ’s board of directors, emailed fellow board members to say that he was establishing a “special task force to reexamine the question of ‘Who is a journalist?’”
According to reporting in the Columbia Journal Review, Weisberg’s initiative was separate from the database review and grew out of a board discussion of an article in the right-wing Washington Free Beacon that largely repackaged Honest Reporting’s attacks on CPJ and news organizations that report critically on Israel, including Drop Site.
Nika Soon-Shiong, publisher of Drop Site News and a member of the CPJ board, was alarmed by Weisberg’s email and requested a vote on the proposal by the full board, according to a letter she posted publicly. She was then informed by Weisberg that her term on the board had expired. On July 1, the board held an emergency meeting and voted to affirm its “existing definition of who is a journalist.”

## Broader Influence Network
Honest Reporting’s sustained attempts to establish connections between journalists and armed groups, such as Hamas, is particularly striking given the organization’s direct ties to AIPAC, the Israeli government, and the Israeli military, which continues to carry out a genocide in the Gaza Strip.
Prior to co-founding Honest Reporting, Lenny Ben-David spent 25 years at AIPAC, including 15 years directing its Jerusalem office, before serving three years as deputy chief of mission at the Israeli embassy in Washington. He has recounted with evident pride how an early Honest Reporting campaign crashed CNN’s internet servers. The organization he helped build is now led by Jacki Alexander, who spent approximately 15 years at AIPAC before being hired with a mandate to expand Honest Reporting’s reach in the United States.
National Development Director Rebecca Shimonovitc spent more than eight years as an AIPAC regional director before moving into Honest Reporting’s fundraising operation. Justin Pozmanter worked in AIPAC’s political department for over ten years before relocating to Israel, where he served as a senior foreign policy advisor to Israeli government minister Tzachi Hanegbi, and then joined Honest Reporting. David Barish, treasurer of Honest Reporting’s U.S. organization, has held positions on the boards of AIPAC’s Houston Council, Friends of the IDF, the Jewish Federation, Anti-Defamation League, and the United Israel Appeal. He is also listed as a director of the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, a pro-Israel think tank. Laura Cornfield, the group’s director of press relations, also runs the Media Central program. She attends high-level events within Israeli political circles posing and smiling with U.S ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee and Sara Netanyahu.
The connections to the Israeli military are equally direct. Multiple staff members served in the Israeli military, a fact Honest Reporting says “should not be a surprise” given Israel’s mandatory service requirement. Gil Hoffman, former executive director and current board member, for example, served in an Israeli army artillery unit and later as an Israeli military reserve spokesperson following his emigration to Israel, before his journalism career at the Jerusalem Post. Editorial Director Simon Plosker has also served in the Israeli military’s press office. Rachel Safdie, who now appears as a reporter in Honest Reporting’s social media output, spent more than two years in the Israeli military press office, where she served as head of its Iranian-language social media desk.
In a statement, Honest Reporting denied that it has a formal relationship with the Israeli military. “There is no formal affiliation or partnership between the IDF and Divuach Ne’eman R”A or HonestReporting.com, Inc.”
Honest Reporting was launched in 2000 in association with the Jerusalem Fund of Aish HaTorah, an Orthodox Jewish outreach movement whose stated mission is encouraging secular Jews to embrace religious observance, but which also operates one of the most extensive pro-Israel advocacy networks in the world. The organization’s first executive director was Irwin Katsof, who simultaneously served as president of the Jerusalem Fund. In 2001, the Jerusalem Fund lent the newly established Middle East Media Watch (Honest Reporting’s registered name at the time) $158,724. The following year, Aish HaTorah’s Jerusalem operation provided a further $48,100 grant.
Honest Reporting’s 2006 tax return lists Ephraim Shore, who heads Aish’s operations in Israel, as president. Shore is also one of the founders of the Hasbara Fellowships program—the Israeli Foreign Ministry’s campus advocacy initiative that Aish HaTorah was asked to develop and run. His twin brother, Raphael Shore, produced “Obsession: Radical Islam’s War Against the West,” a controversial 2005 film that Honest Reporting initially promoted as its own project on its website and listed as an affiliate in 2006, before later denying any involvement in its production.
When the Israeli Foreign Ministry sought to counter what it characterized as anti-Israel sentiment on university campuses internationally, it turned to Aish HaTorah to design and run the program, which flies hundreds of student leaders to Israel for intensive advocacy training. Multiple current Honest Reporting staff members worked as Hasbara Fellowship lecturers.
The financial relationship between Aish HaTorah and Honest Reporting has not been confined to the founding period. Canadian tax filings show that Honest Reporting Canada made a donation of $15,000 to Aish HaTorah as recently as 2023, demonstrating that the institutional relationship between the two organizations remains active more than two decades after Honest Reporting’s founding.
The network around Honest Reporting extends to some of the most controversial pro-Israel blacklisting operations on the internet, including Canary Mission, the pro-Israel doxxing site that publishes dossiers on students, academics, and activists it accused of anti-Semitism or support for Palestinian rights. At least one former employee of Honest Reporting, Zahava Raymond has worked at Megamot Shalom, the Israeli nonprofit organization funding Canary Mission.

## A Widening Operation
According to Honest Reporting’s filings with Israel’s Corporations Authority, 96.6% of the total 2024 budget of 6,040,198 NIS [$1,632,044] comes from foreign donations. In addition to the $100,000 grant from the Knight Foundation, 4,903,640 NIS [$1,324,950] came directly from Honest Reporting’s U.S. organization. The Israeli operation is almost entirely dependent on American dollars.
Honest Reporting’s recent communications demonstrate the group’s growing ambitions. An update to supporters describes the launch of “Honest Reporting AI Labs,” a proprietary system trained to identify “anti-Israel bias” and intercept narratives “before they reach mainstream credibility.” The system monitors social media in real time, traces what the organization characterizes as “coordinated narrative pipelines,” and feeds findings to what it calls “strategic communications partners,” among them the Foundation for Defense of Democracies.
In May, for example, Rachel O’Donoghue, an employee of Honest Reporting, was invited to publish a column in the Wall Street Journal challenging Nicolas Kristoff’s article in the New York Times about Israel’s use of sexual violence against Palestinian detainees. The organization’s research has also been cited in articles published by the Washington Free Beacon and National Review.
The reach of Honest Reporting and its affiliates extends into the legislative institutions of its English-speaking donor base. In 2018, Honest Reporting submitted evidence to the UK Parliament’s inquiry into fake news, falsely claiming that “Honest Reporting is not aligned with any government or political party or movement.“ The submission was initially absent from the inquiry’s published record and was only made available following the intervention of UK Lawyers for Israel.
The Canadian operation has demonstrated similar objectives. In July 2023, Honest Reporting Canada’s executive director Mike Fegelman said it wanted to “create a digital army for Israel.” A written briefing to the House of Commons’ Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage referred to Palestinian journalists killed by Israel as “so-called journalists” with “connections to Palestinian terrorist groups” and claimed media coverage of Gaza “directly contributes to a spike in anti-Jewish hate crimes.”
Another significant donor identified in Honest Reporting’s 2024 Israeli filings is a vaguely named organization called Canadian Charity Partners, which contributed 507,176 NIS [$137,000]. In January 2026, the Canada Revenue Agency revoked Canadian Charity Partners’ charitable status, citing multiple areas of non-compliance including conducting non-charitable activities and failing to maintain adequate books and records.
Honest Reporting Canada has run its own pressure campaigns against journalists and outlets it deems biased against Israel, claiming to have contributed to the dismissal of two Palestinian journalists in October 2023, one of whom was on maternity leave at the time. In November 2024, Robert Walker, the group’s assistant director, was arrested and faced 17 criminal charges in connection with a string of anti-Palestinian graffiti in Toronto, including the phrase “Fuck Gaza.” The charges were withdrawn in March 2025 after a payment to charity. Walker remains employed by the organization.

reads.title: AIPAC-Linked Super PACs, Pro-Israel Donors Flood Primary to Succeed Angie Craig With More Than $3 Million
reads.subtitle: Progressive Matt Little is getting hit by a flurry of PACs intervening in a three-way Democratic primary.
reads.body:
-  Rep. Kaela Berg, Sen. Matt Klein, and Matt Little on the stage during a Congressional Candidate Forum at Minnesota Farmfest in Morgan, Minn., on Tuesday, August 4, 2026. Photo by Carlos Gonzalez/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images.Four super PACs with ties to AIPAC and Democratic Majority for Israel have surged into a Minnesota House race in the final months of the campaign, hoping to fend off the latest progressive insurgent.
In the three-way race, one candidate, Matt Klein, is unapologetically supportive of Israel, while two others, Matt Little and Kaela Berg, have been critics to varying degrees. Little, however, has the support of the group A New Policy, which was founded to support pro-Palestinian candidates and lobby Congress against Israeli interests. Another PAC, called American Priorities, which was organized to be a counterweight to AIPAC, has jumped into the race to support Little with a spend of some $60,000.
314 Action, a super PAC ostensibly organized to support scientists and medical professionals, this week reported spending nearly $2.5 million supporting Klein, a staggering amount in a previously sleepy race, given that the PAC has raised just $15 million for the full cycle. (A spokesperson for 314 insists none of the funds have come from AIPAC or its allied organizations.)
Subscribe now
In a strategy that has been deployed in other races, the pro-Israel money is boosting Klein, the pro-Israel candidate, while other PACs with ties to AIPAC are boosting the alternative progressive candidate who is trailing in the polls.
The race was reshaped on May 9, when Little won the endorsement of the Minnesota Democratic Farmers and Labor Party. Little released an internal survey conducted between May 18 and 20, which found him well ahead, taking 41% of the vote, with Berg and Klein far behind in a statistical tie for second, with Berg at 13% and Klein at 11%. A little more than a week later, Klein fielded his own poll, which found Little at 26%, only 7 points over Klein’s 19%. Berg was in third with 16%. The largest group of the 403 likely voters surveyed in the poll, 39%, said they “don’t know” who they’d vote for. While Klein’s internal poll demonstrates that Little was firmly the frontrunner in the race two months before election day, it was conducted before the surge in outside spending began.
The congressional seat is being vacated by Democrat Angie Craig, who is running for Senate. The primary is on Tuesday.
Given the numbers, the path to victory for Klein was clear: He needed Little to be brought down by boosting Berg—splitting the vote between the two progressives—and needed big money to get himself past both of them.
On May 1, AIPAC’s super PAC had transferred $350,000 to EDW Action Fund, followed by $100,000 on May 10 and another $400,000 on May 20. EDW did not respond to requests for clarification on why the money was moved and where it was ultimately spent.
EDW Action spent roughly $395,000 supporting Berg between June 26 and August 3. Of the $395,000 burned, $99,999 came directly from EDW and $295,000 came from its sister organization called Pro-Choice Majority Action, a hybrid PAC recently formed on May 1 as a legal affiliate of EDW Action. EDW transferred $626,000 and $100,000 to Pro-Choice Majority Action on May 21 and May 22 respectively, on the two days after receiving the final batch of AIPAC’s $850,000 dump, and sent another $150,000 a week later on May 29, helping to enable Pro-Choice Majority’s ensuing spending.
Moving money between multiple PACs before spending it doesn’t necessarily make it much harder to trace, but it does make it more confusing for voters and local reporters covering the race. AIPAC, for its part, accuses reporters of antisemitism for following AIPAC money through the FEC files toward its final destination. Candidates like Little risk being called conspiracy theorists when they point to the clear source of the money. Indeed, after Drop Site reached out to Berg’s campaign for comment, Berg posted a video on X accusing Little of lying about her and insisting that she doesn’t take AIPAC money: “I never have, and I never will.”
It is true she has not taken AIPAC money directly, but on May 13, four days after Little won the DFL endorsement, DMFI transferred $500,000 to Women Vote, the independent expenditure arm of EMILY’s List, a pro-choice PAC. Then, less than a month later, Women Vote spent $584,448 in independent expenditures supporting Berg.
“Women Vote works with a variety of partners to elect Democratic pro-choice women and build winning coalitions,” a source familiar with Women Vote’s spending told Drop Site. “The donation referenced was for a program in a different race and has nothing to do with Kaela Berg or this race.”
Sara Nelson, head of the Association of Flight Attendants-CWA, AFL–CIO, told Drop Site that unions raised outside support for Berg, also drawing from gun safety, pro-democracy, and pro-choice donors, using Women Vote as the vehicle. A coalition including EDW, Women Vote, and labor unions announced $500,000 in spending for Berg on May 20.
Little told Drop Site that if Berg believes Israeli is committing a genocide in Gaza, she should reject funding from organizations like Women Vote and EDW Action, who take money from AIPAC and DMFI, even if those groups say that particular money was not used in her particular race. “Let’s say all of that is opaque…and we can’t really tie that to Berg,” he said. “We have called on Representative Berg to say to her PACs publicly, stop taking AIPAC money. I don’t want you to take AIPAC money and if you continue to take AIPAC money, I am going to reject your endorsement and give the money back.”
Though the Women Vote source did not disclose the recipient of the $500,000, Women Vote did spend a total of $653,885 supporting Shannon Bird, a DMFI-endorsee, in her unsuccessful bid to become the Democratic nominee in Colorado’s 8th congressional district. Despite securing DMFI’s endorsement, Bird, who ultimately lost to Manny Rutinel, does not list the PACs support on her website.
Nevertheless, the total dollars spent on Berg’s behalf by PACs that have been used as pro-Israel passthroughs at some point, including Women Vote, amounts to $979,448 since June 11. Now, the fact that PACs linked to AIPAC are spending to boost Berg doesn’t mean Berg herself is aware of the links, and doesn’t mean pro-Israel donors affirmatively want Berg to win. DMFI, when reached for comment, rejected any involvement with Women Vote’s support for Berg’s campaign.
“DMFI PAC endorsed Matt Klein in this race. Kaela Berg’s views are equally as anti-Israel as Matt Little’s,” a DMFI spokesperson told Drop Site.
A Berg spokesperson rejected any relation between these groups’ spending in the race and the pro-Israel lobby’s donations to the spenders.
“Matt Little agrees with Kaela on Israel and AIPAC, that’s why AIPAC is funneling millions in dark money into this race at the 11th hour to support Matt Klein,” the spokesperson told Drop Site. “As the only woman running for Congress, Kaela is proud to have the support of the same organizations that have supported Peggy Flanagan and every woman in the MN Congressional Delegation. The truth is, Benjamin Netanyahu continues to be a danger to the world and if she’s elected to Congress, Kaela will do everything in her power to stop the genocide and Netanyahu’s government.”
Berg has earned support from three state senators, 28 of her colleagues in the Minnesota House of Representatives, and national progressive organizations like Our Revolution and End Citizens United. She’s supported by many unions, too: the Association of Flight Attendants, Communications Workers of America, the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, the Carpenters Union, UNITE HERE, United Auto Workers, the Air Line Pilots Association, the International Association of Sheet Metal, Air, Rail, and Transportation Workers, the Amalgamated Transit Union, local members of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, United Steelworkers, and the International Union of Painters and Allied Trades. She has also received some support from D.C., racking up endorsements from Rep. Chris Deluzio, who many speculate is eyeing a primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman (D-Penn.) in 2028, and Rep. Val Hoyle (D-Ore.).
Aside from securing the coveted Minnesota DFL endorsement, Little has also picked up backing from the state’s Attorney General Keith Ellison, and key figures within the existing progressive infrastructure in Congress. Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, former CPC chair, and Rep. Maxwell Frost, one of CPC’s vice chairs, have all publicly supported his candidacy.
The CPC’s PAC is also supporting Little.
Klein, for his part, has also seen a flood of supportive outside spending. 314 Action Fund is a super PAC which backs candidates who are involved in science or medicine, but has sometimes acted in the past as an AIPAC passthrough. FEC records show that the super PAC spent $1,261,341 in independent expenditures backing Klein in four installments between July 20 and July 30. On August 5, 314 Action dropped another $1.2 million into the race.
The state senator has also received an additional $138,440 from 57 individual donors who have also given to AIPAC, UDP, or DMFI. All of the individual donations were given on the same day, June 28, many divided in various increments amounting to the maximum $3,500 individual contribution each.
Among those individuals is James Sprayregen, who sits on the National Board of AIPAC and serves on the Board of Governors for the American Jewish Committee. Sprayregen contributed $129,500 to the pro-Israel groups and to Klein in three separate same-day installments amounting to $3,499.99, one cent below the legal maximum, possibly to avoid being classified as a max-out donor.
Also listed among the individual donors pooled by AIPAC on Klein’s behalf are Jody Forchheimer, who gave $283,456 to pro-Israel PACs and $3,500 to Klein, and Gadi Maier, who gave $135,000 to pro-Israel PACs and $3,500 to Klein. Forchheimer is a Senior Legal Fellow at the Louis D. Brandeis Center, a pro-Israel legal organization fighting antisemitism cases, and publicly discussed her role in pro-Israel advocacy at the AIPAC policy conference in 2019. Maier is an Israeli-American tech entrepreneur who is founder and CEO of ID Handshake, the first and a current board member at Forter, a fraud prevention platform, and formerly served as CEO of both FraudSciences and FreeMonee.
When asked about 314 Action Fund backing Klein’s campaign and an inquiry about the aforementioned prominent pro-Israel donors, the campaign manager provided a statement in response to the latter.
“Our campaign is powered by thousands of supporters from every background and every faith—because that’s who we are, and that’s who I’ve spent my career serving,” Klein told Drop Site. “As a doctor, I’ve cared for Jewish families, Muslim families, Christian families, and families of no faith at all, and I’ve never once asked who they were before helping them. This campaign is no different. I’m proud of the support we’ve received from neighbors, community leaders, and working families of all denominations.”
Addressing the first question, the spokesperson added, “You should talk with 314 about their funding. I have copied Eden from their team on this email.”
The move was eyebrow-raising, as campaigns and independent expenditure groups are not allowed to coordinate campaign activity. Though it is not considered best practice for campaigns and independent expenditure arms to communicate at all, it is legal to discuss some information as long as it doesn’t amount to coordination.
314 Action also received a $2.5 million donation from pro-Israel billionaire Michael Bloomberg on May 4, just months before its spending blitz in Minnesota. Whether Bloomberg’s money is earmarked to the Klein race is unclear; it would be odd if so, as Berg is endorsed by the organization Everytown for Gun Safety, which Bloomberg founded and primarily finances. That would mean Bloomberg was spending against himself in the same race.
Joshua Morrow, 314 Action Fund’s president, said in a statement that the group is not funneling pro-Israel PAC money into the race. “As we have said multiple times, 314 Action Fund has not taken money from AIPAC or its affiliated entities this cycle and we won’t,” Morrow said. “We have spent over $14.5 million supporting STEM candidates in 2026 and not a cent has come from AIPAC, UDP, DMFI or affiliated entities. Similarly, our investments in Dr. Matt Klein are not from AIPAC or affiliated entities, and any suggestion otherwise is false, sensationalized and reported without sources.”
Still, Klein refuses to recognize the genocide in Gaza, instead broadly calling for a two-state solution. Berg and Little, backed by David Hogg’s Leaders We Deserve, on the other hand, have publicly called it one. Little differentiates himself from Berg, however, in supporting a suspension on any further U.S. military aid to Israel, while the latter has advocated for conditioning it. In a video posted Wednesday, she calls for an end “to all weapons sales to Israel,” going further than she had previously.
Klein has racked up endorsements from 19 colleagues in the Minnesota state senate, but has not received any explicit endorsements from Washington. The two-term state senator has also faced some scandal in the race, having placed a $50 wager on Kalshi, a prediction market service, betting that he’d win the MN-02 primary, which ultimately led to an April 2026 fine and five-year ban from the platform. Klein introduced an ultimately unsuccessful bill in the state legislature in 2024 that would have weakened regulations on sports gambling, a highly profitable path for companies like Kalshi.
Update, Saturday, August 8: This story was updated to reflect additional context around the spending provided by AFA President Sara Nelson.
