reads.title: War Is Dangerous, but Miscalculation Is What Makes It Go Global. Here Is How This War Goes Global.
reads.subtitle: The danger is not that the players are reckless. The danger is that they are all being careful, and careful still ends in catastrophe when everyone is reading a different map.
reads.body:
Let me say the thing about this war that actually keeps me up, because it is not the thing most people fear. The common worry is that someone reckless will do something insane and blow the Middle East region or even Europe apart. That is not what worries me. What worries me is the opposite. Everyone at this table is being careful. Every actor is calculating, hedging, trying to stay inside the lines. And careful, calculating, disciplined actors can still walk a region straight into a global war, because carefulness offers NO protection at all when each side is being careful according to a different map. The catastrophe does not require a madman. It only requires that two rational men are each certain about a line that is not where they think it is.
This Substack is reader-supported. To receive new posts and support my work, consider becoming a free or paid subscriber.

> Why regional wars go global
Here is the mechanism, stated as plainly as I can. A regional war stays regional for exactly as long as every major actor correctly reads three things about every other actor: their red lines, their capacity, and their resolve. Where the line is that must not be crossed. Whether the other side actually has the means it appears to have. And whether it possesses the will to use them.
Get all three right, on every axis, and you can fight a contained, brutal, terrible war that stays inside its box for years. Get any one of them wrong, and the box breaks, and the actors who were never in the regional fight are suddenly dragged into a global one.
That is NOT a theory. It is the entire history of how wars go global, compressed into a single variable. Let me show you the record.
Share
Leave a comment

- 1914 was not chosen by anyone. No European leader in July of that year wanted the four-year industrial slaughter that followed. What they wanted was a short, sharp, contained war won by Christmas, and every one of them miscalculated how the alliance system behind their opponent would move. Each read the others’ resolve wrong. Each assumed the other would back down or stay out. The war did not come from a decision to go big. It came from a cascade of leaders who each decided to go small and each misjudged the response.

-
-
- Korea went global on a single misread of a red line. When UN forces drove north toward the Yalu, the assumption in command was that China would not intervene, would not cross the river, did not have the resolve or would not take the risk. Beijing had signalled otherwise. The signal was not believed. Hundreds of thousands of Chinese troops crossed, and a contained war became a different and far larger one, because one commander was certain about a line that was not where he thought it was.

-
- Look across every catastrophic expansion in modern history and the pattern holds. The war did not widen because someone chose to widen it. It widened because someone miscalculated how the other side would respond to a limited move. The escalation was never the plan. It was the price of an error about someone else’s mind.

> The operational anatomy of a misread
Now let me make this operational, because “miscalculation” is a soft word for a set of hard, specific mechanisms, and naming them is how you learn to watch for them.

- The first is the capacity misread. This is misjudging what the other side actually has, as opposed to what it displays. Every military maintains a gap between its real magazine and its theatrical one, deliberately, because deterrence runs on perceived capability. The danger is that you come to believe your adversary’s bluff is real and freeze, or, far worse, you come to believe his real capability is a bluff and act. Both are capacity misreads, and the second one starts wars.

- The second is the resolve misread, and it is the most common and most lethal. This is misjudging not what the other side can do but whether it will. Resolve is invisible. It lives inside the mind of the decision-maker under stress, and it cannot be measured from outside, only inferred, which means it is guessed. Korea was a resolve misread. Most wars of expansion are. An actor concludes the other side lacks the will to respond to a limited provocation, and is wrong.
Subscribe now
Get 7 day free trial

- The third is the red-line misread. This is being certain about where the other side’s threshold sits, and being wrong about its location. Red lines are frequently ambiguous on purpose, because a state that names its exact threshold hands the adversary a map of precisely how far it can push without triggering a response. So the lines stay blurry, and the blur is where the war widens, because each side privately believes it knows where the line is, and the two private maps do not match.

- The fourth, and the one that ties them together, is the mirror-imaging error. This is the analyst’s cardinal sin: assuming the other side reasons the way you do, values what you value, and will therefore respond as you would in its position. It is the reason a Western planner misreads a civilizational strategic culture that measures time in decades and answers late by design. Mirror-imaging feels like empathy but functions as blindness, because it substitutes your own decision-making for the adversary’s, and the adversary is not you.
Every one of these is a reading of another actor’s mind, under stress, with incomplete information, on a compressed clock. That is not a war held together by wisdom. It is a war held together by four or five simultaneous guesses all staying correct at the same time.

> Where the misreads live right now
So look at this theatre and count them, because they are all live, all at once.
Iran is reading how much of America’s magazine is real versus theatre, how many munitions, how much sustained appetite, how much of the pressure is genuine capacity and how much is performance for a domestic audience.
A capacity misread in either direction is dangerous. If Tehran overestimates American staying power it may concede ground it did not need to. If it underestimates it, it may reach for the chokepoint believing Washington cannot sustain the response, and be wrong.
Israel is reading how far it can strike before its patron is forced to choose. That is a red-line misread waiting to happen, because the American threshold, how much Israeli action Washington will absorb before it has to either fully commit or visibly restrain its ally, is genuinely ambiguous, and Israel is navigating by a private estimate of a line the Americans have deliberately left blurry.
Washington is reading how much pressure Tehran absorbs before it reaches for the strait instead of the table. That is a resolve misread in the making, because it depends entirely on a judgment about Iranian will under siege, and Iranian will is precisely the variable that Western analysis has misjudged repeatedly, because it keeps mirror-imaging a patience it reads as weakness.
And behind Iran sit two great powers, Russia and China, each reading whether its own credibility now requires it to move. This is the most dangerous reading of all, because it is recursive: Moscow and Beijing are not just calculating the regional war, they are calculating what their inaction signals to every other client and adversary watching. A point may arrive where a great power concludes that staying out costs more in credibility than coming in costs in risk. That calculation is where a regional war acquires its third and fourth participants.
Every one of those is a guess about another actor’s mind. The war is being held together, right now, by all of them staying correct simultaneously. The moment one breaks, the box breaks with it.

> Why this is worse than recklessness
Here is the part that inverts the usual fear, and it is the core of the strategic-realism read. We instinctively look for the villain, the reckless actor who wants the wider war, because a villain is legible and can be deterred or removed. But the historical record says the wider war almost never comes from the actor who wants it. It comes from the careful actor who has misjudged the board and does not yet know it.
This is why recklessness is, perversely, less dangerous than confident error. A reckless actor announces himself and can be contained. A careful, rational, disciplined actor operating on a wrong map gives no warning, because from the inside his error feels exactly like sound judgment. He is not gambling. He is certain. And certainty built on a misread is the most dangerous condition in strategy, because it removes the very caution that might otherwise save the situation. The man who thinks he might be wrong hedges. The man who is certain he is right commits. And the second man, when his certainty is misplaced, is the one who breaks the box.

The most dangerous sentence in any war room is not “let us escalate.” Escalation, spoken aloud, is a decision that can be debated, resisted, walked back. The most dangerous sentence is “they would never.” Because “they would never” is not a decision. It is an assumption, usually unexamined, often unspoken, that sits underneath the plan and is never stress-tested until it fails. They would never cross the Yalu. They would never let the alliance drag them in. They would never absorb that strike without folding. Every one of those sentences preceded a catastrophe, and every one felt like realism to the person who thought it.

reads.title: "For Your Eyes Only": Israel’s Mole Inside the United Nations
reads.subtitle: Hacked emails show Yahav Lichner, a UN official, repeatedly supplied Israeli diplomats with confidential UN reports and private briefings. He now directs UNICEF’s Washington office.
reads.body:

Subscribe now

-
- An empty seat for Israel during a ministerial high level meeting during a United Nations conference on a two state solution for Israel and the Palestinians, at UN headquarters on July 28, 2025, in New York City. Photo by TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images.On February 20, 2015, an official of the United Nations Population Fund sent two Israeli diplomats an email containing a confidential report about a trip two weeks earlier to Washington, D.C. by Zeid Ra’ad Al-Hussein, then the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights.
“For your eyes only. Do not forward,” Yahav Lichner wrote to then-Israeli Ambassador to the UN Ron Prosor and diplomat Ronny Leshno-Yaar in a message sent from Lichner’s personal email account, describing the report as a “classified internal summary of Zeid’s meetings in Washington.”
The meetings came at a time when Israel was facing an independent commission inquiry by the UN Human Rights Council over its conduct during the 2014 military offensive against the Gaza Strip.
The document recorded private meetings that Al-Hussein held with White House officials, senators, congressional appropriations staff, AIPAC, J Street, and human rights organizations. It also revealed a concern inside Al-Hussein’s office: that congressional anger over the UN inquiry could threaten American funding for the Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR). Lichner added that Al-Hussein had met with members of Congress including “our friend,” the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, adding that Al-Hussein was “trying to do damage control and distance himself from the report.”
Leshno-Yaar responded that he intended to act on the intelligence that Lichner had provided. “Thank you Yahav. I have no choice and of course without addressing this information I must act with members of Congress to make them understand,” before listing the arguments he planned to make about Al-Hussein and the Gaza commission’s secretariat.
“Absolutely,” Lichner replied. “You are right.”
The exchange was far from a one-off: Over a two-year period between 2014 and 2015, emails show, Lichner repeatedly supplied Israeli officials with internal UN documents, private meeting accounts, pre-release material, and other political intelligence—including documentation marked as “strictly confidential”—which was later used by Israeli officials to help shape their own efforts to both proactively lobby the U.S. government and undercut UN initiatives they viewed as unfavorable to Israel.
The communications showing Lichner leaking confidential information to officials in the Israeli government come from a hacked database of emails from Prosor, Israel’s permanent representative to the UN from 2011 to 2015. The emails were posted online by Distributed Denial of Secrets, a whistleblower and file-sharing website, after being obtained by Handala, a hacking group believed to be tied to Iranian intelligence.
Prosor is currently Israel’s ambassador to Germany, while Lichner has served since January 2025 as director of the Washington, D.C., office of UNICEF, the United Nations children’s agency. Prior to joining the UN Population Fund (UNFPA), Lichner worked at Israel’s mission to the UN from 2011 to early 2014.
The emails showing leaks of classified UN information and other communications with Israeli officials came from a period when Lichner served at the UNFPA and does not indicate whether or not it has continued in his role at UNICEF. Lichner previously served as Prosor’s political advisor at Israel’s embassy in London and later as a senior advisor at Israel’s UN mission.
The emails suggest that Prosor personally promoted Lichner’s UNFPA candidacy, drawing on the assistance of then U.S. Ambassador to the UN Samantha Power to privately lobby for his appointment and later providing a glowing reference letter to the agency.
That placement appeared to pay dividends as Lichner continually fed inside information from the UN to Prosor and other Israeli diplomats, including unissued draft documents authored by then–Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon, private accounts of meetings by UN officials, and internal reports marked as confidential. Lichner also provided insight and guidance on internal UN processes and deliberations related to Israel, including informing them of scrutiny of its conduct in Gaza and the West Bank.
UN officials are subject to rules defining staff as international civil servants whose responsibilities are “not national but exclusively international.” The organization’s internal guidelines also strictly prohibit officials from communicating information to any “government, entity, person or any other source any information known to them by reason of their official position.”
A former senior UN official confirmed that the behavior documented in the emails is expressly prohibited by UN guidelines.
“When you join the UN you are bound to serve the UN rather than the country you came from, and as such you are bound to promote the interests of the organization. You sign a piece of paper acknowledging that you have become a UN official and, as a result, are bound to confidentiality and serving the interests of the organization rather than a member state,” Charles Petrie, a former senior UN diplomat and Assistant Secretary-General, told Drop Site News. “But there are no systems in the UN to impose consequences for leaking information. In the U.S. government, when you leak, you are actually committing a crime because you have accepted the conditions under which you are able to access different levels. That does not exist at the UN.”
He added, “It is a sign of an institution that does not have internal accountability. And the higher you go, the less accountability there is.”
Lichner, Prosor, and Power did not respond to detailed requests for comment. UNICEF did not respond to a request for comment.

## Strictly Confidential
On November 10, 2014, Lichner received an internal daily report from the UN Operations and Crisis Centre (UNOCC) providing security and political updates from various regions of the world. The report was marked, “UN STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL - NOT FOR FURTHER DISSEMINATION,” citing the UN’s information classification rules and with an additional note in the body further emphasizing that the report is “sensitive and the Chef de Cabinet has directed that it not be disseminated further,” a reference to Ban Ki-moon’s chief of staff.
Lichner forwarded the report the next morning to six Israeli diplomats with the comment, “For your eyes only,” pointing to a segment on civilian casualties from U.S. operations in Iraq and opining that, “there are no statements of condemnation from the Secretary-General and no commissions of inquiry into harm to innocent people”—an evident contrast to the focus at the time on Israel’s actions in Gaza by the organization.
The UNOCC report was a roundup of assessments from different conflict hotspots and classified confidential. The archive communications do not indicate whether any of its contents were useful to Israeli diplomats.
But other communications in the archive suggest the information that Lichner provided to the Israeli government was useful in their efforts to resist pressure from the international community over the 2014 war in Gaza and the ongoing occupation of the West Bank, including shaping the communications of senior UN officials to whom Lichner had privileged access.
A few months earlier, on July 4, 2014, writing from his UNFPA account, Lichner had sent five Israeli diplomats what he called “the UN internal/confidential weekly report on Jordan.” The document contained accounts of closed consultations with Jordan’s interior minister, border-security developments, and domestic unrest.
Five days later—one day after Israel launched Operation Protective Edge in Gaza—Lichner supplied Prosor, Deputy Ambassador David Roet, and three other mission officials with two additional documents: a letter Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas had sent Ban Ki-moon and an unpublished draft of the UN chief’s reply.
The letter from Ban was still a work in progress and Lichner indicated to Israeli diplomats that he was helping shape it from the inside to be more favorable to Israel’s concerns. Lichner wrote that he was working with an unnamed female “friend” privy to internal deliberations at the organization—a formulation that comes up frequently in the emails—to improve the draft “as much as possible.”
“For your eyes,” Lichner wrote. “I am working with our friend on improvements to the Secretary-General’s letter, as much as possible.” When Roet said the draft had not arrived, Lichner sent it again. “We are working to insert a reference to the rocket fire,” he wrote, referring to rocket fire by Hamas and other Palestinian resistance groups into Israel.
Lichner also sent Israeli diplomats internal accounts of Ban’s meetings with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Iraq’s prime minister, and Amnesty International chief Salil Shetty. The Sisi report included a candid discussion of Gaza, Libya, the status of detained journalists, and human rights in Egypt. Lichner, sharing the reports from his personal email, requested “complete sensitivity.”
Lichner also forwarded the agenda for a meeting of Ban’s Senior Management Group—a high-level body made up of leaders of various UN departments and chaired by the secretary-general—which was scheduled to discuss a draft Security Council resolution on Palestine. He noted that Babatunde Osotimehin, the executive director of UNFPA, would attend the closed door meeting and promised to provide an update afterwards. “Information needs to be collected after the meeting,” Lichner added. “As always, with sensitivity.”
In another 2015 email, Lichner passed an itemized list of information from what he described as “a source in the Secretary-General’s circle,” detailing internal developments at the UN. The email included information on attempts to promote particular individuals to posts within the organization, speculation about Ban Ki-moon’s political future, and discussion of Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov—now director-general of Trump’s Board of Peace overseeing Gaza—as a possible successor as head of the UN. “He is being mentioned in closed discussions in the Secretary-General’s office as a possible candidate to replace Ban,” Lichner wrote. “Keep an eye on him.”
The information that Lichner provided was deemed highly valuable by his former Israeli colleagues. In response to the note about the private discussions on senior appointments,  Prosor replied: “Yahav, as usual, amazing and first-hand information.”
In a separate episode, Lichner gave the Israeli mission what he described as an internal OHCHR summary of a UN General Assembly discussion concerning the then-special rapporteur for the Occupied Palestinian Territories, Indonesian diplomat Makarim Wibisono.
In a response, Israeli diplomat Nelly Shiloh noticed that the internal account inaccurately paraphrased an Israeli statement on the rapporteur’s work. But she told colleagues they could not seek a correction. “For now we cannot change the situation because this is their internal report, which was not supposed to reach us,” Shiloh wrote.
Information Lichner provided also appeared to be intended to help Israel blunt scrutiny over fatal shootings in the West Bank by providing Israeli diplomats advance warning about internal UN deliberations on human rights abuses, thus helping them prepare public responses.
In May 2014, Lichner used his personal Gmail account to send Prosor and three other Israeli diplomats a Haaretz report titled “UN Calls for Probe Into Shooting of Palestinian Youths.” The article said that video taken at the scene suggested that two teenagers killed by Israeli troops, Mahmoud Odeh Salameh, 16, and Nadim Nuwara, 17, posed no threat to Israeli forces and reported that a senior UN official was demanding an “independent and transparent” investigation.
“For the past two days, I have been in contact with our friend about the issue,” Lichner wrote, again referring to an unidentified female contact. He warned that the UN Department of Political Affairs, Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, and the OHCHR would meet the following day and that the shootings would probably be discussed. The high commissioner for human rights, Navi Pillay, had been urged by her Ramallah staff to write to Israel and issue a statement expressing concern about “excessive use of force,” Lichner reported, adding that similar language might enter an upcoming briefing by the UN under-secretary-general for political affairs.
“At the advice of our friend,” Lichner then supplied Israel with two counterarguments: that the UN was disregarding an existing Israeli military investigation by calling for an independent inquiry, and that it should not express concern about excessive force before that investigation was complete.
“I will update [you] after the meeting tomorrow,” he concluded.

## Gaza Accountability
The communications between Lichner and Israeli diplomats at the UN mission came at a time when Tel Aviv was facing unprecedented scrutiny over the mass killing of civilians during the summer 2014 military campaign against Gaza.
In addition to forwarding details about Zeid Al-Hussein’s meetings in DC related to the Gaza commission report, the archive includes several instances in which Lichner gave Israel advance or internal information about UN human rights proceedings involving Gaza. In February 2015, he forwarded an internal OHCHR planning email that disclosed when the UN commission of inquiry intended to release its report.
As usual, he added a warning emphasizing the secrecy of the information. “The information about the publication date of the report—after the elections—is sensitive and was not intended for distribution,” Lichner wrote. “The information was not supposed to pass to the Office’s staff and entered the summary below by mistake, and there is drama now.”
The following month, Lichner supplied Prosor and Leshno-Yaar with internal correspondence between UN official James Rawley, then-Deputy Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, and Guardian reporter Harriet Sherwood. Sherwood was investigating allegations that she said had been leaked to her from within the UN showing that Israeli pressure had disrupted an internal process that recommended listing the Israel Defense Forces as an entity involved in human rights violations against children.
Rawley’s response said the listing process was strictly confidential, remained ongoing, and was not subject to further comment.
Two days after The Guardian published its report about Israeli pressure, Lichner forwarded Leshno-Yaar the correspondence between UN officials and the reporter, stating that it was for his eyes only and not to be used or quoted, while also attempting to identify Sherwood’s source within the UN.
“The fact that The Guardian reporter approached these two (Rawley and June) indicates that the leak did not come from them. My bet is UNRWA/OCHA,” Lichner wrote on March 19, before adding, “Internal correspondence—please do not use or quote.”

## “Intelligence officer in training”
More than a year earlier, Prosor had mounted a private campaign to help place Lichner at UNFPA. In January 2014, following a telephone conversation with U.S. Ambassador to the UN Samantha Power, Prosor emailed her about Lichner’s application for an external-relations position. He told Power that Lichner had ranked first in the interview process, adding: “Please don’t mention that explicitly as we know it from internal sources.”
Prosor claimed that Lichner’s Israeli nationality was the only obstacle to his appointment and asked Power to speak personally with UNFPA Executive Director Babatunde Osotimehin to convey U.S. support for hiring what Prosor called the “best and most professional candidate.” Osotimehin already knew Lichner and his work, Prosor wrote, but “needs support to reach the right decision.”

-
- Correspondence between Prosor and Samantha Power about the hiring of Lichner at the UNFPA in early 2014.When UNFPA requested a confidential reference the following month, Prosor described Lichner as a former political adviser and senior Israeli diplomat who had his “absolute trust.” He gave Lichner the highest possible scores for reliability and teamwork and told the agency that he conducted himself with “the utmost integrity.” By May 2014, Lichner was corresponding from a UNFPA address under the title External Relations Specialist.
Within weeks, he was again advising his former mission—but this time as an active inside source within the United Nations bureaucracy leaking confidential information in violation of UN regulations.
In June of that year, Lichner distributed a UN public-information department organizational chart and identified a unit responsible for Palestine, decolonization, and human rights. He suggested examining its personnel and cutting posts when the department’s budget reached the General Assembly’s Fifth Committee.
The emails suggest that Prosor remained an influential patron in Lichner’s UN career as he progressed higher within the organization.
In May 2015, Lichner prepared third-person talking points for Prosor to use in promoting him for a prospective position as secretary of the UN Development Program (UNDP) Executive Board. The document instructed Prosor, who had an upcoming meeting with the director of external relations at the agency, that it was important to press a senior UNDP official on the importance of Lichner’s appointment even if ultimately his hiring would be decided elsewhere.
The email itemized a list of talking points for Prosor to use to promote Lichner during the meeting. One of them states, “Yahav has very good political and analytical skills - he knows exactly what member states’ political positions are,” adding that he is an “intelligence officer in training and was as a political officer in the Israel embassy in the UK, working with the MPs in the House of Commons and Lords.”
The available emails make no other reference to Lichner working or being trained as an intelligence officer during this period.

## Joining UNICEF
Lichner remained in the UN system after the correspondence documented in the archive and began working on issues more directly tied to Israeli interests at the organization. In 2016, he served as UNFPA’s interim representative in Britain, and by 2019 public materials identified him as a senior UNICEF adviser. In October 2023, he joined UNICEF’s executive director in a meeting with French Foreign Minister Catherine Colonna concerning civilian protection and humanitarian access in Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
Public career listings identify him as having subsequently served as principal adviser to the UN Senior Humanitarian and Reconstruction Coordinator for Gaza. In June 2024, he wrote that he had visited Washington to discuss humanitarian operations in Gaza and the implementation of Security Council Resolution 2720, which called for increased aid to Gaza, with U.S. officials. In March 2026, George Washington University described him as having been “at the forefront” of negotiations with the U.S. government, engagement on Capitol Hill, and implementation of the resolution.
Lichner is now director of UNICEF’s Washington D.C. office. There is no evidence to establish whether his conduct documented in Prosor’s archive continued after 2015, nor is there evidence that UNICEF knew about the correspondence when it appointed him.
But the emails documenting his past private collaboration with the Israeli government and leaks of confidential information concern many of the same institutions and issues now within his public portfolio, including dealings with Congress and humanitarian diplomacy related to the Gaza Strip.
The archive does not connect Prosor or any other Israeli officials to his later appointment to a senior role at UNICEF.
In April 2015, however, after Lichner thanked Prosor for the “tailwind” surrounding a boost to his standing at UNFPA, Prosor offered a satisfied reply on his efforts to help Lichner ascend within the UN bureaucracy: “Glad we had an influence.”

reads.title: The Gaza “Ceasefire” Farce and the Battle for Michigan
reads.subtitle: Sami Al-Arian joins Jeremy Scahill to discuss the latest on Hamas and the Board of Peace. Then, Jeremy and Ryan Grim discuss today's Michigan primary and potential 2028 candidates.
reads.body:
Last week, Hamas and President Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace announced they had formally agreed to terms addressing the weapons held by the Palestinian resistance. Sources from within Hamas told Drop Site that the issue was contentious and hotly debated internally, but ultimately the group moved forward with a strategy that the ball would now be in the court of Israel, the U.S., and regional mediators to uphold the deal. Almost immediately after the agreement was announced, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he would not withdraw Israeli forces, as required by the deal, and intended to continue striking Gaza. Israel has killed more than 1,200 Palestinians since the October 2025 ceasefire was announced and has extended its occupation in total violation of the terms Israel signed and Trump guaranteed. This is part of a longstanding pattern that plays out after Palestinian negotiators accept terms that the U.S. claims will end the war and occupation.
On the Drop Site News livestream, Jeremy Scahill speaks with Palestinian academic and analyst Sami Al-Arian about why Hamas agreed to the terms, which include a decommissioning of heavy weapons and military infrastructure in Gaza. They also discuss the future of Palestinian resistance and the upcoming elections, in which Europe and the U.S. have worked with Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas to create a framework for banning Hamas and other pro-resistance factions from participating.
Then, Jeremy and Ryan Grim discuss Tuesday’s primary elections in Michigan and Missouri, including the closely watched race between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens. Later, they discuss the 2028 campaign, and the difficulty that could be faced by potential candidate Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who passed on an opportunity to be the leading moral voice of opposition to Israel’s genocide, a decision that continues to be a headwind for her.

reads.title: U.S. crowdsources ideas on Iran; Gaza holds mass funeral for 112 killed in 2023; Board of Peace contradicts itself
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: August 4, 2026
reads.body:
- A mass funeral is held for over 100 members of the Abu Sharia and Al-Hasayna families, whose remains were recently recovered after an Israeli attack earlier in the genocide, on August 4, 2026 in Gaza City, Gaza. Photo by Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images.Tuesday, August 4, 2026 – Fire, explosions reported at U.S. base in Kuwait. Cargo vessel hit near Oman. President Donald Trump maintains Iran wants talks with the U.S. U.S. military crowdsourcing “creative” ways to punish Iran. Reuters: U.S. has used up “virtually all” its long-range precision missiles. Ships continue to move through the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi ships avoid Bab Al-Mandab. Ansarallah claims drone strike on Saudi airport. Israel resumes attacks on Gaza. Israeli forces demolish a school, bulldoze land as settlers attack West Bank communities. More than 100 bodies recovered from 2023 Israeli strike laid to rest in Gaza. Qatar, Egypt, and Turkey issue condemnation of Israeli ceasefire violations. Board of Peace claims Israel is set to withdraw only after Hamas disarms, contradicting its own roadmap. Hamas official discusses arms policy. Israel detained 630 Palestinians in West Bank during July, prisoner group says. Hamas Political Chairman Khalil Al-Hayya talks with Turkish, Iranian leaders. Lebanon and Israel resume talks in Rome. Primaries in Michigan, Missouri, Washington state, Kansas, and Virginia. Immigrant dies at Newark ICE facility. DOJ increasingly uses Civil War-era conspiracy law to charge ICE protesters, NPR finds. Twenty-five states sue Trump administration over new Section 301 tariffs. Federal judge strikes down New York’s ban on masked ICE agents. FCC commissioners receive luxury gifts from Paramount ahead of merger. AIPAC moves into the California special election. DRC Ebola death toll surpasses 1,700 as WHO accelerates vaccine, treatment trials. More than 150 migrants rescued from English Channel after boat fire. Russian, Ukrainian attacks kill at least 27. Sudan’s army vows to defeat the RSF by year’s end. Cross-border shelling kills dozens of refugees near the Sudan-Ethiopia border. China accuses Philippines of “political provocation” over cultural programs.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Fire, explosions reported at U.S. base in Kuwait: A large fire broke out at a U.S. base in Kuwait on Monday evening, where several explosions were heard, Iranian outlets reported, though no casualties or damage were reported.

- Cargo vessel hit near Oman: A cargo vessel was struck by an unidentified projectile near Oman on Monday, the UKMTO reported.

- No details about casualties, damage to the ship, or the identity of the vessel were given in the warning.

- Trump maintains Iran wants talks with U.S.: President Donald Trump accused Iran on Monday of secretly seeking talks despite their public denials of Trump’s statements.

- He also claimed that the U.S. currently controls the Strait of Hormuz through a naval blockade, and said that either a “deal” or “total surrender” would end its naval siege.

- Later on Monday, addressing reporters in the White House, Trump said negotiations were “going on right now,” and claimed that Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and “many others” were involved in the talks. He called the talks “the last chance to sign a good document,” and threatened Iran with “decapitation” if an agreement is not reached.

- After noting that the talks were “not very complex” and would “go quickly,” Trump claimed that Hormuz could be reopened by “tomorrow” and that during a “phase 2” they would discuss “nuclear capacity.” “That will take a little while,” he said. His remarks were echoed by U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said Tuesday a deal to reopen the strait could be reached “today or tomorrow.”

- Qatar said Tuesday that efforts to reach a diplomatic solution between the United States and Iran are continuing, but stressed that no direct talks are currently scheduled. The foreign ministry spokesperson said mediators are working with “all parties” on a “short-term solution” to revive negotiations.

- Trump accused Chevron and Exxon Mobil of price gouging, saying they made “too much money” during the U.S.’s war on Iran and demanding that both companies cut prices and return gains to consumers.

- U.S. military crowdsourcing “creative” ways to punish Iran: U.S. Central Command emailed a broad group of military intelligence analysts seeking “creative and unconventional” ways to pressure and punish Iran as Washington reassesses a strategy that has failed to force Tehran into a deal, CNN reported on Monday.

- The “crowdsourcing” comes from Trump’s limited paths to victory, the outlet reported, with U.S. intelligence agencies believing that airstrikes alone are unlikely to change Iran’s position, and that destroying deeply buried nuclear sites could require Trump to deploy ground troops.

- Reuters: U.S. has used up “virtually all” its long-range precision missiles: The U.S. military has used up most of its stockpiles of highly accurate long-range missiles in its war with Iran, according to Reuters. The missiles are primarily surface-to-surface weapons, known as Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM), which cost over $1 million each. The U.S. has used “virtually all” of these weapons, two sources familiar with the data told Reuters.

- Ships continue to move through Hormuz: Roughly 5 million barrels per day are moving through the Strait of Hormuz via “dark” ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, according to estimates from Bloomberg.

- Brent crude settled Monday at $83.77 a barrel, down sharply from above $100 on July 23, as fears of a wider supply disruption haveappeared to ease. ⁠

- Preliminary data released on Monday indicated that the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve fell by another 2.9 million barrels last week. That is substantially slower than several weekly draws of roughly 7 million to 9 million barrels earlier in the planned 172 million emergency release.

## Yemen

- Saudi ships avoid Bab Al-Mandab: Six Saudi-flagged tankers were detected on Monday evening rerouting around the Cape of Good Hope rather than transiting the Red Sea, as shipping adjusts to Ansarallah’s maritime blockade targeting Saudi-linked vessels.

- The diversion adds an estimated two to four weeks to voyages and increases transport costs.

- Ansarallah claims drone strike on Saudi airport: Ansarallah said it carried out a drone strike on a “sensitive” Saudi target at Najran Airport, claiming the attack achieved a “precise hit.” In a statement Tuesday, the group said the strike was in response to alleged Saudi drone incursions into Yemeni airspace over the governorates of Saada and Hajjah, warning that “any violation of our airspace will not go unanswered or unpunished.”

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded in Gaza: Over the past 24 hours, two Palestinians were killed and 10 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,377 killed, with 174,230 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,252 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 4,120, while 804 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel resumes attacks on Gaza: Israeli strikes resumed in Gaza on Monday evening, after a 30 hour pause.

- An Israeli aircraft struck a vehicle on Gaza City’s coastal Rashid Street, killing at least two Palestinians and wounding several others.

- Eyad Amawi, Gaza’s relief coordinator, told Drop Site the strike came immediately after a “Board of Peace” delegation concluded its visit to Israel.

- Israeli forces demolish a school, bulldoze land as settlers attack West Bank communities:

- Bethlehem: Israeli forces bulldozed Palestinian agricultural land in the village of Beit Iskaria on Tuesday, in what local officials said was an effort to expand the Gush Etzion settlement bloc, WAFA reported. The attack also damaged the village’s drinking water network.

- Hebron: Israeli forces demolished two classrooms and a sanitary unit at Shaab Al-Batm Mixed Basic School in Masafer Yatta.

- Nablus: Israeli settlers attacked communities south of Nablus, setting fire to three vehicles between the villages of Jalud and Talfit and attempting to torch a building before residents intervened.

- Tulkarm: Israeli forces raided the home of Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission head Moayad Shaaban in the Dhnaba suburb, interrogated, and threatened that if he continued to call for the formation of popular protection committees, they would raid his home again.

- East Jerusalem: Israeli authorities demolished properties in the neighborhood of Al-Tur after the owners had previously carried out self-demolitions under Israeli pressure. During the operation, Israeli forces assaulted property owners and other residents, seriously injuring one man in the eye.

- More than 100 bodies recovered from 2023 Israeli strike laid to rest in Gaza: Palestinians held a mass funeral Tuesday for 112 bodies recovered over the weekend from the site of a November 2023 Israeli airstrike in Gaza City’s Sabra neighborhood, one of the deadliest attacks of the war. Gaza’s Civil Defense said the remains included 40 children, while 157 bodies are still believed to be trapped beneath the rubble of the strike, which killed more than 300 people.

- Qatar, Egypt, and Turkey issue condemnation of Israeli ceasefire violations: After 4,059 Israeli ceasefire violations documented by the Palestinian side, the mediators of the Gaza ceasefire—Qatar, Egypt, and Turkey—issued their first joint condemnation of Israel’s continuing attacks on Gaza on Monday.

- The three countries condemned Israel’s targeting of healthcare facilities and medical infrastructure, and the killing of civilians, including women and children, calling the attacks “a flagrant violation of international law and international humanitarian law.”

- A Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson told reporters Tuesday that “it is clear to the international community who is obstructing the implementation of the agreement,” and that the recent intensification of Israeli strikes was an attempt by Israel to “obstruct peaceful solutions” to the conflict.

- BoP claims Israel is set to withdraw only after Hamas disarms, contradicting its own roadmap: The U.S.-led “Board of Peace” put out a statement on Monday after a meeting between its envoy, Nickolay Mladenov, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, saying that Israeli withdrawal from Gaza would come only after Hamas fully disarms.

- The statement said that Israeli forces would withdraw “beyond the Yellow Line…once decommissioning is complete,” and that this applied to “light weapons, heavy weapons, and the tunnels alike.”

- A roadmap previously published by the board, however, said that the disarmament process would begin only after a phased Israeli withdrawal from the Strip, as well as the decommissioning of Israeli-backed militias. The roadmap also limited disarmament to “heavy weapons, military production sites, depots of weapons, and tunnels,” but did not include “light weapons.”

- Separately, documents leaked on Monday showed that the BoP is advancing plans for more than 60 infrastructure, economic, and “security” projects across the Gaza Strip, scheduled to launch between August 2026 and January 2027, according to Israel’s public broadcaster Kan.

- Kan also reported that the board pledged to Israel that it would seek countries to receive students and patients from Gaza, in exchange for Israel dropping its displacement plan. Israel had recently renamed the forced displacement plan a “freedom of movement” plan, in an effort to make it more acceptable to foreign governments.

- Hamas official discusses arms policy: During a Monday evening appearance on Piers Morgan Live, Ghazi Hamad, a senior Hamas official, said that Hamas’ planned decommissioning of weapons was an “exceptional phase” accepted out of necessity, and that the group has not changed its goal of ending Israel’s occupation of the Strip, to which it might employ “different techniques, different tools, different methods.”

- Israel detained 630 Palestinians in West Bank during July, prisoner group says: These detentions across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, brought the total number of arrests since the start of the Gaza war to more than 25,000, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society.

- More than 9,400 Palestinians are currently held in Israeli prisons, including around 370 children, 92 women, and 3,198 administrative detainees, held without charge.

- Al-Hayya talks with Turkish, Iranian leaders: Hamas political chief Khalil Al-Hayya met Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalın on Monday to discuss Gaza ceasefire negotiations, Israel’s ongoing attacks, and developments in the occupied West Bank and Jerusalem, Shehab News reported.

- Hamas said Kalın praised the movement and the Palestinian factions’ position in the negotiations, called for implementation of what was agreed, and said Turkey would continue supporting Palestinians’ right to live with dignity.

- Al-Hayya also held a phone call with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. Pezeshkian told Al-Hayya that Iran “stands with [Hamas] and supports [it] in all the measures you take,” according to a Hamas readout, despite the ongoing U.S. attacks on Iran.

## Lebanon

- Lebanon and Israel resume talks in Rome: Lebanon and Israel began a seventh round of U.S.-brokered direct talks in Rome on Tuesday amid the ongoing Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon and violations of the ceasefire. The three-day talks will focus on advancing the framework agreement reached in June that Hezbollah was not a party to.

- Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem accused Lebanon’s political leadership of having “been a help to Israel instead of a help to Lebanon’s sovereignty,” saying it had offered “free concessions” while Israel “took everything,” Lebanon’s National News Agency reported. He urged Lebanese authorities to “stop the free concessions,” open dialogue with Hezbollah, and work to secure an Israeli withdrawal.

- Prime Minister Nawaf Salam rejected Qassem’s remarks, saying “the greatest help to Israel was provided by those who unilaterally dragged Lebanon into futile ‘support’ wars,” giving Israel “the pretexts” to attack the country. He said there can be “no sovereignty for Lebanon except through one independent decision in a state with one army” and argued that dialogue requires “the courage to acknowledge the facts.”

## U.S. News

- At long last, the Michigan primary: Polls close throughout most of Michigan at 8 p.m. ET today, and results in the closely watched race between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens will be coming in quickly. In Missouri, Cori Bush is locked in a rematch with Rep. Wesley Bell, who knocked her out of Congress with a then-record-setting amount of money from AIPAC.

- At 7:30 pm ET, Ryan Grim is going live with Krystal Ball on both the Drop Site and Breaking Points YouTube pages, and we’ll track the results of critical races in Michigan, Washington, Missouri, and Virginia.

- A key list of races we’re watching in Michigan, where over a dozen anti-establishment candidates are hoping to sweep, is available here.

- Immigrant dies at Newark ICE facility: Edwin Lopez-Cornejo, a 41-year-old Salvadoran immigrant, died Saturday at University Hospital in Newark after a medical emergency at the Delaney Hall detention center, federal officials confirmed Monday, marking the second death at the facility in eight months.

- Lopez-Cornejo’s mother, Maria Cornejo, said her son, who had been prescribed medication for diabetes, told her Friday that he had lost feeling in his face and hand.

- DOJ increasingly uses Civil War-era conspiracy law to charge ICE protesters, NPR finds: The Justice Department has charged more than three dozen people in at least 10 cases since President Donald Trump took office last year under a Civil War-era statute barring conspiracy to impede federal officers, according to an NPR review of court records.

- Those charged under the statute include Minneapolis special education teacher Treasure Thoreson, who was arrested in June over alleged blockades outside ICE’s Whipple Federal Building headquarters, and three Spokane, Washington protesters convicted in May after being accused of blocking a van transporting detainees, a case that led the district’s then-U.S. attorney, Richard Barker, to resign rather than sign the indictment.

- Twenty-five states sue Trump administration over new Section 301 tariffs on 60 economies: A coalition of 25 states led by California filed a lawsuit Monday in the U.S. Court of International Trade, alleging the Trump administration exceeded its authority in imposing tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on 60 economies under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

- The states argue that these tariffs are a thinly concealed effort to replace levies struck down by the Supreme Court in February, and that the investigation by the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative that justified the tariffs was rushed, resulting in overly broad hikes.

- This is the third time California has sued the administration over its tariff policy.

- Federal judge strikes down New York’s ban on masked ICE agents: U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino struck down New York’s law barring federal officers from wearing masks, ruling Monday that the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause bars the state from regulating federal law enforcement activities, while upholding a separate New York law that prohibits local and state police from cooperating with ICE through 287(g) agreements.

- The Trump administration has successfully challenged similar mask bans in California and is contesting related laws in Connecticut, New Jersey, Virginia, and Philadelphia.

- FCC commissioners receive luxury gifts from Paramount ahead of merger: FCC Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty accepted luxury Kennedy Center honors gala tickets from Paramount, with Carr’s accepting gifts from CBS or its parent company worth over $75,000 since he took office in 2017 and watching the 2025 Gala in Ellison’s private skybox, ProPublica reports.

- Two complaints by watchdog groups demand investigations into whether they violated federal gift rules and ask that Carr be disqualified from the commission’s pending decision on the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger.

-  Both Carr and Trusty previously voted to approve Paramount’s merger with Skydance, which Carr claimed “advanced the public interest.”

- AIPAC moves into the California special election: Pro-Israel money is pouring into Eric Swalwell‘s old district, trying to lift Melissa Hernandez over Aisha Wahab, using all these same tired vehicles to cloak the money Through United Democracy Project, AIPAC is now actively spending in California’s 14th district., with a minimum $600k booked. The special election to replace Swalwell is on August 18.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## Other International News

- DRC Ebola death toll surpasses 1,700 as WHO accelerates vaccine, treatment trials: The death toll from the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Ebola outbreak has risen to 1,707 out of 3,802 recorded cases since it was declared May 15, making it the second-largest and fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record.

- The World Health Organization said that trials of experimental treatments and vaccines for the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there are no approved medicines, are advancing faster than in past outbreaks due to years of advance planning.

- The response to the outbreak has been hampered by armed group violence, attacks on health facilities, and a funding shortfall, with more than 100 healthcare workers infected and staff in some areas striking over unpaid wages.

- More than 150 migrants rescued from English Channel after boat fire: More than 150 migrants were rescued Tuesday after their boat caught fire while crossing the English Channel from France, according to Al Jazeera.

- More than 2,000 people have crossed the Channel in small boats since Andy Burnham became UK prime minister two weeks ago. Burnham pledged that he will be “relentless” in stopping the crossings.

- Russian, Ukrainian attacks kill at least 27: At least 16 people were killed in Russia and 11 in Ukraine as the two countries continued exchanging attacks Monday and Tuesday, according to local officials on each side, Al Jazeera reported.

- In Russia’s Krasnodar region, a Ukrainian drone strike killed seven people, including three children, in Arkhipo-Osipovka, and wounded 40 others.

- A Ukrainian drone strike in the border region of Belgorod killed four people, and a separate attack on Moscow killed five.

- Ukrainian strikes in Russian-occupied Crimea killed four people.

- In Ukraine, a Russian attack on a petrol station in the Dnipropetrovsk killed three, including an emergency worker and his eight-year-old son.

- A separate Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia killed eight people, including two children.

- Sudan’s army vows to defeat the RSF by year’s end: Sudanese army chief of staff Yasser al-Atta said the military (SAF) is advancing on all fronts and aims to eliminate the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) before the end of the year, Anadolu reported on Monday.

- “Before the end of this year, there will not be a single Janjaweed fighter” or “foreign fighter,” al-Atta told a gathering of soldiers, al-Atta said, referring to the RSF’s antecedent group and the group responsible for the nearly two-decade long genocide in Darfur.

- Al-Atta claimed that the SAF was “advancing in all directions… as happened during the recapture of Khartoum state.”

- His remarks followed what the army said was a rapid operation to seize Bara and other positions along the road linking Omdurman with El-Obeid in North Kordofan.

- The Kordofan region has seen continued SAF-RSF fighting since October 2025, when the RSF seized the Darfur capital of El-Fasher.

- Cross-border shelling kills dozens of refugees near the Sudan-Ethiopia border: Deadly shelling triggered by renewed fighting between Ethiopian federal troops and Tigray regional forces struck refugee camps along the Sudan-Ethiopia border, according to a statement Monday by Sudan’s Interior Ministry.

- The ministry said the confrontations, which started over the weekend, caused artillery to land directly within refugee settlements, resulting in multiple fatalities and injuries.

- Officials did not release an exact death toll, but a Red Cross official in Sudan, Abel Binyam, told Drop Site’s Godfrey Olukya that he saw “over 50” dead bodies.

- The clashes, near Shererina in western Tigray, were the second major outbreak between the two sides since the 2022 African Union-mediated peace pact signed in South Africa. Both accused the other of starting the fighting, which had largely subsided by Sunday. Hundreds of Tigrayans, including wounded fighters, have fled into Sudan, and Tigray’s leadership has urged its people to prepare “to fight for Tigray’s national survival.”

- China accuses Philippines of “political provocation” over cultural programs: The Chinese government accused the Philippines of an “extremely serious political provocation” after the Philippine Defense Department called for greater oversight of foreign state-backed academic and cultural exchange programs, citing Chinese laws requiring citizens and organizations to cooperate with state intelligence agencies.

- China’s Foreign Ministry called the concerns “lies and malicious attacks,” accusing unnamed “anti-China forces” of using the issue to distract from Philippine naval actions in the South China Sea.
