reads.title: Four Palestinians and two Israelis killed in incendiary settler attack; Israel launches major West Bank military operation in response; Oil leaking into Hormuz
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 24, 2026
reads.body:
- Israeli soldiers detain a man at the Nablus Specialized Hospital after a settler attack in Tal, in the occupied West Bank on July 24, 2026. Photo by Jaafar Ashtiyeh / AFP via Getty Images.Friday, July 24, 2026 – U.S. continues strikes on Iran as renewed assault enters second week. Iran conducts retaliatory strikes. Wounded U.S. soldiers transferred to Germany. President Donald Trump says U.S. will use seized Iranian funds to pay for “damages.” Tanker traffic through Hormuz slows to a trickle. Two tankers reportedly leaking oil into the Strait of Hormuz. Four Palestinians killed as Israel orders sweeping West Bank offensive. Israel's campaign of destruction in Gaza continues unabated. Chickenpox continues to spread in Gaza. Gaza floods with wastewater. Israeli settlers destroy Palestinian vineyard. Health condition of detained Gaza surgeon rapidly deteriorating. Israel approves expanded settlements. Israeli banks cut off Palestinian lenders. Moroccan officers make first field tour of Gaza ahead of force deployment. Israeli drone wounds two paramedics in “double-tap” strike in south Lebanon. New Trump tariffs on 80+ countries take effect. Senate blocks Iran War Powers Act. Department of Justice withdraws subpoenas against NYT journalists. Alaska sends 3,000 citizenship-verification letters to voters. 24+ states sue over Trump election, immigration conditions on disaster funding. Top Haley Stevens communications consultant fired for moonlighting with Palantir. Republican Sen. Bernie Moreno comes out against Section 219 of the NDAA. Strikes in Russia, Ukraine kill 17. Greece approves $4 billion Israeli arms purchase. Sudanese army drone strike kills displaced civilians in Blue Nile. Indian activist Sonam Wangchuk ends 26-day hunger strike amid Cockroach protests. Suicide bombing kills 15 at Pakistani checkpoint near Afghan border.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- U.S. continues strikes on Iran as renewed assault enters second week:

- Four people were killed and five others were wounded in overnight U.S. strikes on areas around the southwestern city of Ahvaz in Khuzestan province, according to Al Jazeera.

- The death toll in Iran from U.S. airstrikes since July 6 has risen to 59 people killed, including three children, and 666 wounded, according to Iran’s Health Ministry.

- U.S. Central Command announced its 13th night of strikes on Iran continued on Iranian military sites, and that its ongoing naval blockade on Iran had redirected 12 commercial vessels and disabled one.

- U.S. strikes hit at least six provinces early Friday, local time, with missiles reported in the cities of Ahvaz and Omidiyeh in Khuzestan, on the southern coast of Qeshm island, in the port city of Bandar Abbas (where at least two were reported injured and power was temporarily cut off), and in Khorramabad in the Lorestan province. Multiple sites in the Yazd and Markazi provinces were reportedly struck as well.

- Iranian authorities reported Thursday that U.S. strikes hit an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps naval command headquarters in the northern province of Gilan. The facility in the Zibakenar area was struck in the morning, damaging some equipment inside the complex, according to Iran’s Islamic Republic News Agency.

- Iran conducts retaliatory strikes:

- The Iranian Army reported attacks against U.S. military installations in Jordan, Bahrain, and Kuwait, including Kuwait’s Camp Behring base, on Thursday evening.

- An Iranian missile reportedly struck Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan, where U.S. forces are stationed, according to initial reports cited by Tasnim.

- Iran’s IRGC reported that it struck Ali Al-Salem Air Base in Kuwait on Thursday with a wave of heavy drone attacks, destroying a large ammunition depot and multiple troop housing structures.

- Missile defenses and air sirens in Kuwait were activated on Thursday evening and Friday morning as a result of Iranian missile strikes, according to the country’s army.

- Multiple explosions were also heard on Friday morning near Erbil airport, in Iraqi Kurdistan, a site of multiple Iranian attacks.

- Wounded U.S. soldiers transferred to Germany: About 10 U.S. service members seriously wounded in recent Iranian attacks have been transferred to a U.S. military hospital in Germany, the New York Times reported on Thursday, citing a U.S. military official. The transfers indicate some injuries were more serious than earlier Pentagon descriptions, which said most involved minor traumatic brain injuries.

- Trump says U.S. will use seized Iranian funds to pay for “damages”: President Trump threatened on Thursday to use the Iranian money it has seized to pay for “any and all damages” to ships and cargo from this point forward. “These damages may be very substantial but, nevertheless, this is the fair and equitable thing to do,” Trump said Thursday, without providing a legal justification for the move or citing the precise source of the funds.

- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned in a response that confiscating another country’s assets to pay for unrelated future claims would set an “incendiary precedent,” adding that “Those who celebrate or profit from such funds should remember: once governments normalize confiscation, no one’s assets are safe.”

- WSJ: Iran rebuilding faster than Israeli intelligence expected: Iran has quickly rebuilt infrastructure damaged during months of U.S. and Israeli bombing, from missile bases deep inside mountains to bridges, ports, and production facilities, the Wall Street Journal reported Thursday.

- Planet Labs and Airbus imagery showed repairs at missile bases near Kangavar, north of Kermanshah, and at Dezful, where crews reopened collapsed tunnel entrances and repaved access roads within weeks.

- One Israeli military official said Iran repaired a bridge hit by three Israeli bombs within days. Officials also said that some strikes only collapsed entrances to deeply buried facilities, leaving the missiles inside intact.

- Tanker traffic through Hormuz slows: Tanker traffic carrying oil and other products eastward through the Strait of Hormuz has slowed to a trickle, according to Kpler data, with just 10 recorded transits from July 17-23, including zero on July 22.

- Those tankers carried a combined 15.7 million barrels over seven days, averaging just 2.24 million barrels per day.

- Two tankers reportedly leaking oil in Strait: Two tankers are leaking oil near Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with slicks drifting toward Larak and the Qeshm coastline, according to maritime intelligence firm Windward.

- Satellite and radar imagery from July 21-23 identified one vessel as the Kavomaleas, which was struck in an earlier attack.

- Windward assessed that spill as fuel rather than cargo because the tanker was traveling in ballast.

- The second vessel is an unidentified “dark tanker” operating without AIS tracking. Windward said imagery places it in the same location since May.

## Palestine

- Four Palestinians killed as Israel orders sweeping West Bank offensive: Armed Israeli settlers, backed by Israeli forces, killed at least four Palestinians and wounded eight others during an attack on the town of Tal, southwest of Nablus on Friday. During the assault, a Palestinian man seized a settler’s weapon and opened fire, killing two armed settlers and wounding two others.

- Tal Mayor Walid Zidan said around 20 settlers attacked the village between 7:30 and 8 a.m. before continuing their assault in the Qabala area. “Residents rushed to defend homeowners in the area,” he said. Zidan said the Israeli military claimed that a Palestinian opened fire after taking a settler’s weapon, “while other accounts indicate that Israeli forces opened fire at everyone present.”

- A graphic video of the subsequent killing shows settlers shooting Palestinians in a field.

- In retaliation for the settlers’ death, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz said they have launched a series of military operations including home demolitions, weapons raids, the revocation of work permits in villages Israel labels “terror hotspots,” additional checkpoints and road segregation measures. “The security forces must be allowed to operate freely and with full force,” the two officials said.

- National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank should be made to resemble Beit Hanoun, the Gaza town Israeli forces have razed to the ground, in retaliation for the attack.

- This follows Thursday’s killings of four Palestinians by Israeli forces and settlers across the occupied West Bank: two were killed and four others wounded in Beit Furik, east of Nablus; a 25-year-old Palestinian from Tubas was shot dead by Israeli forces in Jenin; and another young Palestinian died after being shot and arrested by Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint in Shuafat refugee camp in occupied East Jerusalem.

- Settlers also escalated attacks on several neighboring Palestinian communities, subsequently attacking the village of Far’ata, east of Qalqilya, wounding seven Palestinians, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.

- Israeli forces also raided Nablus Specialized Hospital and stormed the emergency department. Hospital officials said soldiers tied the hands of doctors and nurses and detained two brothers, including one who was being treated for a gunshot wound sustained during the attack on Tal.

- Yesh Din and more than a dozen other Israeli human rights groups urged immediate international intervention to prevent what they warned could become “mass pogroms” across the occupied West Bank.

- Israel’s campaign of destruction in Gaza continues unabated:

- Israeli forces struck near Al-Yemen Al-Saeed—a hospital turned shelter in Jabliya refugee camp—killing two, including a child, and injuring others.

- Israeli warplanes destroyed the Al-Noor Mosque and structures surrounding it on Thursday, southeast of Bureij refugee camp, after residents were ordered to evacuate.

- Israeli forces shelled a tent sheltering displaced families south of Khan Younis, wounding several, including multiple children.

- An Israeli strike on Thursday hit a family home in Gaza City, wounding two people.

- An Israeli airstrike later on Thursday hit a residential apartment in Gaza City, killing a woman and wounding a man.

- Unexploded Israeli ordnance detonated in Khan Younis, wounding two Palestinian brothers, Gaza police reported on Thursday, with one of the boys requiring his hand to be amputated.

- Chickenpox continues to spread in Gaza: More than 53,000 chickenpox cases have been recorded since the start of the year, Gaza’s Health Ministry said, warning that the surge is “record-breaking and alarming” and signals a dangerous loss of epidemic control.

- Severe overcrowding in displacement camps, shortages of clean water, collapsing sanitation, and the breakdown of primary health care due to Israeli attacks on hospitals and restrictions on the entry of medical supplies are accelerating transmission.

- Gaza floods with wastewater: A makeshift sewage pit collapsed inside a displacement camp in Gaza, flooding tents with wastewater, damaging families’ belongings, and creating serious health risks, according to Gaza journalist Tamer Nahed.

- Israeli settlers destroy Palestinian vineyard: Israeli settlers destroyed roughly 4,000 kilograms of grapes in a vineyard belonging to the Al-Janazra family in the Wadi Qaboun area of Halhul, north of Hebron, days before the crop was due to be harvested, according to the Palestinian Information Center.

- The family had cultivated the 2.5-dunum plot for a full year. About 50 family members depend on it for income.

- Part of the land had already been cut in two by a settlement road, and the family maintains a near-constant presence there because of the nearby Israeli outpost and repeated threats.

- Health condition of detained Gaza surgeon rapidly deteriorating: Dr. Murad Al-Qouqa, 47, head of orthopedic and spine surgery at Al-Shifa Medical Complex, has lost roughly 45 kilograms and suffered a serious eye injury affecting his vision since Israeli forces seized him from the hospital, the Palestinian Center for the Defense of Prisoners said Thursday.

- Israeli forces arrested Al-Qouqa on March 19, 2024, during their raid on Al-Shifa while he was treating the wounded. Several other medical staff were taken with him. Since then, the center said, he has been subjected to torture and physical and psychological abuse, was denied blood pressure medication, and has a herniated disc and stomach ulcers. He has been denied visits from his lawyers and the Red Cross.

- Israel approves expanded settlements: Israeli authorities have approved a settlement plan covering nearly 6,000 dunums (600 hectares) of Palestinian land east of Bethlehem, the Applied Research Institute–Jerusalem reported.

- ARIJ said the plan, approved by the Gush Etzion Regional Council, would expand the illegal Tekoa settlement southward between Tuqu’ and Al-Minya.

- Israeli banks cut off Palestinian lenders: Israel Discount Bank will end ties with Palestinian lenders on Sept. 1, and Bank Hapoalim will make a similar termination on Oct. 1, Reuters reported.

- Together, these banks process about $16.6 billion a year in Palestinian transactions. Palestinian banks now appear likely to be cut off from Israel’s financial system, threatening imports, salaries, and government operation.

- Moroccan officers make first field tour of Gaza ahead of force deployment: Around 30 Moroccan military officers entered Gaza on Wednesday for what Israeli broadcaster Kan reported was the army’s first field tour of areas where its troops are expected to operate, part of preparations for a multinational force proposed under Trump’s “Board of Peace,” The New Arab reported.

## Lebanon

- Israeli drone wounds two paramedics in “double-tap” strike in south Lebanon: Two paramedics were wounded and their ambulance damaged after an Israeli drone struck a Civil Defense vehicle at the site of an earlier attack in Nabatieh Al-Fawqa, southern Lebanon, on Thursday, according to the Islamic Health Authority.

- At least 130 paramedics have been killed and 260 emergency responders wounded in direct attacks since Israel’s latest war on Lebanon began on March 2.

- Israeli forces also carried out several demolitions on road crossings linking the southern Lebanese towns of Hadatha, Tayri, and Kounine, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency, despite the U.S.-brokered “ceasefire.” Israeli troops conducted a large-scale demolition in the town of Khiam, the agency reported.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## U.S. News

- New Trump tariffs on 80+ countries take effect: The Trump administration imposed tariffs ranging from 10% to 12.5% on goods from more than 80 countries starting Friday, invoking Section 301 of the Trade Act, which targets countries that engage in “unfair or discriminatory” labor practices.

- The Supreme Court rejected Trump’s tariffs in February. Trump’s latest workaround cites the countries’ failure to pass or enforce laws banning products made by forced labor.

- Senate blocks Iran War Powers Act: The U.S. Senate voted 49-47 to block a war powers resolution that would have required Trump to end unauthorized U.S. military action against Iran.

- Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine joined Democrats in voting to advance the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania sided with Republicans to block it. Four Republican senators did not vote.

- The Republican-led House passed a similar measure 214-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats in directing Trump to halt hostilities unless authorized by Congress.

- DOJ withdraws subpoenas against NYT journalists: The Justice Department withdrew subpoenas seeking phone records and grand jury testimony from New York Times journalists after Judge Arun Subramanian pressed prosecutors for nearly an hour over procedural violations.

- The DOJ had attempted to subpoena journalists investigating the security capabilities of Trump’s new Air Force One, donated to him by Qatar, an act the Times claimed was an attempt to intimidate its reporters. The Justice Department says that the investigation “remains ongoing.”

- Alaska sends 3,000 citizenship-verification letters to voters: Alaska’s Division of Elections sent 3,048 letters asking voters to verify their citizenship ahead of the Aug. 18 primary, far more than the roughly 200 names typically flagged, according to the AP.

- Alaska’s elections director attributed the spike to outdated DMV data, saying recipients moved to an “inactive” list can still vote using a special ballot.

- 24+ states sue over Trump election, immigration conditions on disaster funding: More than two dozen states sued the Trump administration in Rhode Island federal court, challenging FEMA and DHS policies that condition billions in disaster funding on states adopting election changes and assisting immigration enforcement.

- Top Haley Stevens comms consultant fired for moonlighting with Palantir: Caitlin Legacki, the vocal Haley Stevens consultant, was secretly consulting for Palantir, Ryan Grim reported. In the wake of Grim’s request for comment, the campaign terminated Legacki. “Haley was unaware of Ms. Legacki’s work for Palantir. Her contract with the campaign has been terminated. She is no longer consulting for the campaign,” a Stevens spokesperson told Drop Site.

- The spokesperson went on: “Haley believes ICE is out of control, putting Michiganders in danger, and needs an immediate overhaul. That’s why she’s voted against giving them another cent without serious reforms, including  prosecuting any ICE agents who commit crimes and abuse their power, forcing ICE agents to wear proper ID and prohibiting them from wearing masks to conceal their identities, and taking away their $75 billion slush fund.”

- Legacki complained that Drop Site is “more interested in my sources of income than Abdul El-Sayed’s, the actual candidate in this race who hasn’t filed his personal financial disclosure.”

- Migrant Insider reports on Stevens’ voting record on ICE, before her current opposition.

- Moreno comes out against Section 219 of the NDAA: Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) told Drop Site’s Julian Andreone that he opposes Section 219 of the National Defense Authorization Act, the controversial measure that would merge the intelligence-gathering capacities of the U.S. and Israeli militaries, and told Andreone he does not think that the measure will make it into the final bill.

- “There’s nobody here who’s more of an ardent supporter of Israel’s right to exist and ability to defend themselves, but I don’t think we should integrate our military with anybody, not even the Bahamas,” he said.

- Julian spoke with other senators on the Hill about the measure. Their responses are here.

## Other International News

- Strikes in Russia, Ukraine kill 17: A Russian missile attack killed six people and wounded “dozens” in the Kyiv region on Friday, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, while a separate strike on the Donetsk city of Sloviansk killed five and injured nine, according to the region’s governor.

- Ukrainian strikes on Russia’s Kirov region killed six and injured 26 at a factory on Friday, the region’s governor said. Kyiv is continuing to target Wildberries warehouses, continuing a campaign against the Russian e-commerce giant that began last weekend, according to the company’s founder

- Greece approves $4 billion Israeli arms purchase: Greece’s national security body approved a procurement worth up to $4 billion for the Israeli-made air defense system Achilles Shield.

- Greece is set to acquire the SPYDER, David’s Sling, and Barak MX missile defense systems. The technology is manufactured by the Israeli state-owned firms Rafael and Israel Aerospace Industries, and expected to be fully operational by 2029.

- Sudanese army drone strike kills displaced civilians in Blue Nile: A Sudanese army drone killed dozens at a gathering of displaced people in the Badia area of Blue Nile state early Thursday. Most of the victims were women and children, according to Sudan Tribune.

- Women in besieged Sudanese city face drones and sexual violence: Women and girls fetching water in Sudan’s besieged El-Obeid face drone attacks during the day and sexual violence after dark, UN Women said Friday.

- “These women and girls have been harassed. They’ve been raped, and they’ve been subjected to other forms of sexual violence, all while trying to access water, one of life’s most fundamental necessities in human rights,” a regional UN director said.

- The UN estimates 12.7 million women and girls across Sudan need support for the sexual violence this year.

- Milei to endorse Flavio Bolsonaro at Brazilian party convention: Argentine President Javier Milei travels to Brazil Friday to endorse Senator Flavio Bolsonaro’s presidential campaign, after months of scandal have left him trailing President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in polls, Reuters reported.

- Bolsonaro has faced fresh scrutiny over his financial ties to a jailed banker, a public spat with his stepmother, and new U.S. tariffs on Brazilian goods.

- Indian activist Wangchuk ends 26-day hunger strike amid Cockroach protests: Activist Sonam Wangchuk announced on Thursday night he ended his hunger strike demanding Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation, citing “a long negotiation on various conditions and in view of possible violence in the country,” Al Jazeera reported.

- Prime Minister Narendra Modi pledged tougher enforcement surrounding exam paper leaks in a video addressed, as well as fast-tracked court proceedings for those responsible.

- Protests in Delhi led by the Cockroach Janta Party continue at the city’s Jantar Mantar, where rights groups have condemned police for “excessive use of force” and suspending mobile internet.

- Suicide bombing kills 15 at Pakistani checkpoint near Afghan border: A vehicle packed with explosives rammed the outer wall of a security post in Pakistan’s northwestern Tank district overnight, killing 12 soldiers and three others, according to the Pakistani military.

- The post, jointly staffed by the army and police, came under attack after militants failed to breach its defenses; the military said 12 attackers were killed in the ensuing fighting. The Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan claimed responsibility in a statement, saying four suicide bombers took part.

reads.title: Ansarallah strikes two Saudi tankers; Oil surges past $100; Over 4,200 Israeli settlers storm Al-Aqsa
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 23, 2026
reads.body:
- Israeli settlers storm the grounds of the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound during the day of Tisha B'Av in occupied East Jerusalem on July 23, 2026. Photo by ilia Yefimovich / AFP via Getty Images.Thursday, July 23, 2026 – U.S. targets Iran for 12th straight night. Iran launches retaliatory attacks. IRGC reports interceptions of tankers. Damaged tanker towed into Iranian waters. Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf says there will be no oil sales in the Gulf until Iran’s security is assured. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi threatens retaliation for any support for infrastructure attacks. Report: U.S. tells Israel it will intensify strikes on Iran. U.S. probes possible Russian role in Iranian drone strikes on CIA sites. Ansarallah strikes two tankers in the Red Sea. President Donald Trump threatens Iran over future Ansarallah attacks. Clashes in Southern Yemen. Israel continues its assault on Gaza. Two Palestinians killed near Nablus; Israel alleges stabbing attack. Israeli attacks on the occupied West Bank. Over 4,200 settlers storm Al-Aqsa compound. Malaysia rejects U.S. pressure to reverse its ban on Israeli citizens. Israeli military conducts multiple operations in Lebanon amid “ceasefire.” Oil surges past $100. Amish Shah wins Arizona House primary. House narrowly passes $95 billion budget for Iran war. Ex-DOGE staffers launch military AI cyber startup valued at $1.4 billion. House passes National Defense Authorization Act. AIPAC-tinged 314 Action PAC backs Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan. House narrowly passes resolution to halt Iran war. Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm posts 200% returns. Trump says U.S.-Saudi deal subject to normalizing relations with Israel. Trump administration weighs military strikes in Mali. Five Thai soldiers killed in attack on southern checkpoint. At least 20 killed in bandit attacks on Nigerian villages. Russia and Ukraine trade strikes, killing eight. Drone strike from Sudan injures civilians in Chad border town. Mexican journalist found dead in Oaxaca. At least 82 dead in floods across India, Pakistan, Afghanistan. China begins two-day live-fire drills in Taiwan Strait. Europe hits Google with $1 billion fine for abusing its market power. U.S. cannot account for $13 billion of Venezuelan oil money, FT reports. Pakistan rejects Amnesty’s call for investigation into deadly Kabul airstrike.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- U.S. targets Iran for 12th straight night: A new wave of U.S. strikes hit sites across Iran starting on Wednesday night, killing at least two and striking additional civilian and energy infrastructure.

- A U.S. missile destroyed an asphalt storage depot in the western Iranian state of Khuzestan on Wednesday night, and explosions were reported around Ahvaz.

- A U.S. missile also hit the Shalamcheh border crossing, at the Iran-Iraq border, according to Iraqi officials, killing two people in a nearby rest facility. Iranian officials said the border crossing, used frequently by religious pilgrims, remained functional.

- Several explosions were heard in Ziyarat, near the southern coastal city of Sirik, according to Tasnim, with additional explosions heard in Bandar Mahshah.

- Iran’s Health Ministry reported on Wednesday the death toll from U.S. airstrikes since June 6 had risen to 53, with 592 people wounded. Among those killed were six women and three children.

- Iran launches retaliatory attacks:

- The IRGC claimed successful attacks on U.S. military assets in Kuwait, saying it damaged a “large warehouse of military equipment, a Patriot missile defence system, and a hangar of American MQ9 drones” at the country’s Ali Al-Salem airbase on Wednesday evening. The IRGC also reported that it had successfully disabled a telecommunications tower in the country.

- The IRGC also said on Wednesday it had struck a U.S. base in Jordan, targeting radars and interceptors.

- Drones hit the Abdali border crossing between Kuwait and Iraq on Thursday, causing material damage but no casualties, Kuwaiti authorities said. The Defense Ministry spokesman said the attack was carried out by “hostile drones,” without identifying the source of the drones.

- Both Kuwait and Bahrain’s militaries reported Thursday that their air defenses were intercepting Iranian attacks.

- IRGC reports interceptions of tankers: The IRGC said that three oil tankers attempted to transit the mined route south of the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, claiming one exploded and caught fire while the other two turned back following multiple warnings from Iranian officials.

- In a statement, the IRGC reiterated that the Strait remains closed to tankers unless passage is coordinated with Iran, and warned of a forthcoming “punitive operation” in response to the “violation,” which it said was encouraged by the U.S.

- U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio bemoaned the disruptions to shipping on Wednesday, telling reporters at the ASEAN summit in Manila that “commercial ships are going through the Straits, and they’re being blown up.”

- Damaged tanker towed into Iranian waters: The Kavomaleas, a Malta-flagged tanker set ablaze off Oman on Sunday night, appears to have been towed into Iranian waters, according to satellite imagery flagged first by open-source analysts and since confirmed by the Financial Times.

- The $55 million ship can carry 500,000 barrels of crude, FT said. It was struck by two projectiles near the Strait of Hormuz, sparking an engine-room fire that forced its evacuation.

- The Kavomaleas was one of two tankers hit that night belonging to Greek shipping tycoon George Prokopiou, whose firm Dynacom is among the most aggressive operators in the strait, sending at least 10 tankers through since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February. Dynacom told FT any move of the ship was unapproved and that it was “trying to verify” its whereabouts.

- Ghalibaf says there will be no oil sales in the Gulf until Iran’s security is assured: Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that Tehran will not allow other countries in the region to export oil if Iran cannot, and said the Strait of Hormuz will not return to its prewar status.

- “The equation of this war is clear: all or nothing,” Ghalibaf wrote. “If we do not sell oil in this region, no one will sell oil. If our security is not guaranteed, no infrastructure will be safe. The Strait will only be secure in the absence of American forces.”

- Araghchi warns retaliation for any support for infrastructure attacks: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Thursday that any attack on Iran’s infrastructure would trigger retaliation against those involved in supporting the attack.

- “Our defense doctrine is clear: eye for an eye,” Araghchi wrote on X, saying “any aggression” would compel “a powerful and decisive response.”

- Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi issued a similar warning on Thursday, telling European governments in Tehran that allowing their territory or military bases to support U.S. attacks on Iran would make them parties to the aggression.

- Report: U.S. tells Israel it will intensify strikes on Iran: The U.S. reportedly informed Israel of its plans to intensify strikes on Iran in the coming days, Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported on Wednesday, including its intention to use heavy bombers against the deeply buried Pickaxe Mountain site near Qom.

- Washington reportedly gave Israel advance notice so it could prepare for possible Iranian missile retaliation, prompting Israel to raise its military readiness to its highest level.

- U.S. probes possible Russian role in Iranian drone strikes on CIA sites: U.S. intelligence analysts are investigating whether Russia provided targeting information or advanced drone technology for Iranian drone attacks that struck at least two CIA facilities in March, including the CIA station at the U.S. embassy in Riyadh, according to Reuters.

- Officials suspect Iran used Russian-enhanced Shahed drones equipped with a more accurate Russian satellite navigation system, the Kometa-M, though sources cautioned no firm conclusions have been reached and Iran may have simply been targeting the embassy generally rather than the CIA station specifically.

## Yemen

- Ansarallah strikes two tankers in the Red Sea: Ansarallah forces said on Thursday they had struck two Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea with ballistic and cruise missiles and drones, setting both vessels on fire.

- The group identified the tankers as Encelia and Layla, saying they had violated its ban on Saudi-linked shipping. Saudi Arabia later confirmed the attack on the Encelia.

- UKMTO separately confirmed a tanker had been struck by an unknown projectile 70 nautical miles southwest of Al-Shuqaiq, Saudi Arabia, causing an onboard fire. No casualties or environmental damage were reported.

- Ansarallah also claimed roughly 10 ships have already turned back since it imposed a blockade on Saudi ships, vowing to continue enforcing its “siege with siege” policy.

- At least nine vessels have made U-turns to avoid the Bab al-Mandab strait as a result of Ansarallah’s blockade, according to the AFP.

- Reuters reported on Wednesday that five vessels, four of them oil tankers, changed course in the Red Sea on Wednesday.

- Trump threatens Iran over future Ansarallah attacks: U.S. President Donald Trump warned Thursday that Washington would hold Iran responsible for any future Ansarallah attacks on commercial shipping. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said any further attacks from the group would bring “major military punishment” against both Iran and Ansarallah, describing the group as an Iranian “surrogate and/or proxy.” He also said he was “very disappointed” with the Yemeni group, whom he claimed had acted “very professionally and smart” during the recent U.S.-Iran conflict.

- Oman’s called for avoiding escalation and threats that could “endanger freedom of navigation,” in a statement from its Foreign Ministry, adding that it is working with Saudi Arabia, Yemeni parties, and the U.N. envoy to “resume the political process and roadmap” aimed at achieving stability.

- Clashes in Southern Yemen: Heavy clashes erupted overnight in southern Yemen between Ansarallah-aligned forces and fighters affiliated with the UAE-backed Southern Transitional Council (STC), according to regional reports.

- Fighting was concentrated west of Al-Dhale province, particularly around Qa’atabah and the Hajar front, with artillery and other heavy weapons reportedly used.

- STC-affiliated sources claimed they repelled the attack and reported four of its fighters killed and 10 wounded, according to  Iran’s Tasnim news.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded: Over the past 24 hours, five Palestinians were killed—three in new attacks and two due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks—and six were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health. One body was also recovered from under the rubble.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,311 killed, with 173,924 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,185 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,816, while 803 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel continues its assault on Gaza:

- An Israeli strike in northern Gaza on Thursday morning killed two Palestinians and wounded several others, the Palestinian news agency WAFA reported.

- Israeli strikes on Gaza killed at least four Palestinians on Wednesday, with one attack killing a man and wounding several others sheltering in the Jabalia refugee camp.

- Israeli attacks on Wednesday also wounded a 13-year-old girl in al-Tawam, northwest of Gaza City, and wounded at least three others near Rafah and Khan Younis.

- Two Palestinians killed near Nablus; Israel alleges stabbing attack: The Israeli military claimed Thursday that two Palestinians stabbed an Israeli citizen near the Alon Moreh settlement in the occupied West Bank. The military said a “civilian at the scene” killed the two Palestinians, aged 20 and 16, presumably referring to an armed Israeli settler. The Palestinian news agency WAFA reported that “Israeli forces” killed them, withheld their bodies and that two other Palestinians were wounded in the attack.

- Israeli troops encircled the nearby town of Beit Furik, east of Nablus, following the incident and were carrying out searches in the area, according to the Times of Israel.

- Israeli attacks on the occupied West Bank:

- Israeli settlers set fire on Thursday to Palestinian lands in the towns of Salem, Beit Furik, and Beit Dajan, east of Nablus, WAFA reported.

- Armed Israeli settlers also attacked water wells and pipelines in several towns near Hebron, bringing the total number of wells seized by settlers in recent days to four, with settlers reportedly diverting, swimming in, and destroying the wells upon seizure.

- Settlers forcibly displaced a Palestinian from their home in Jalud, south of Nablus, on Wednesday, after a months-long campaign which involved setting up a post near their home, setting it ablaze, cutting off electricity to the house, and blocking anyone attempting to bring them food or water.

- Over 4,200 settlers storm Al-Aqsa compound: More than 4,200 Israeli settlers, alongside members of the Israeli Knesset, stormed the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in occupied East Jerusalem on Thursday to mark Tisha B’Av, one of the largest incursions this year, according to the Jerusalem Governorate.

- National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also entered Al-Aqsa under heavy police protection. Ben-Gvir praised the people who took over the site, saying they “felt like owners.”

- As part of the incursion, Israeli forces restricted Palestinian worshippers’ access to the site, assaulting several.

- Palestinian American athlete held by Israel without charge since June 2: Natalie Abudayyeh, 21, a youth leader in her Lutheran church, American citizen, and a member of the Palestinian women’s national soccer team, will remain in Israeli prison until at least September 23 after a military court hearing Wednesday, a bishop from the Evangelical Lutheran Church said, calling the ruling “incomprehensible.”

- Abudayyeh, who was studying journalism at Birzeit University, was seized at gunpoint from her university apartment on June 2 alongside three other female students.

- Israeli authorities have reportedly denied every request from Abudayyeh for bail and refused to let her family visit or contact her in any way.

- She has been held nearly two months without charge at Damon Prison, where prisoners have reported severe conditions and repeated rights violations.

- Malaysia rejects U.S. pressure to reverse its ban on Israeli citizens: Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said on Wednesday that Malaysia will not reverse its pledge to deport any Israeli citizens in the country, despite a letter from eight U.S. lawmakers urging Secretary of State Marco Rubio to suspend military cooperation over the policy, The New Arab reported. Malaysia conducts 14 bilateral and multilateral military exercises with the U.S. every year, according to experts, and U.S. collaboration has dramatically improved its maritime military capacity.

## Lebanon

- Israeli military conducts multiple operations in Lebanon amid “ceasefire”:

- Israeli forces conducted a “massive explosion operation” in the southern town of Al-Tiri in the Bint Jbeil district on Thursday, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported.

- Israeli forces also subjected residents of the town of Ibl al-Saqi to heavy machine gun fire and a series of detonations, according to the NNA. A man was wounded by Israeli gunfire in the same area.

- Israeli forces, backed by bulldozers and military vehicles, also raided the town of Srebbine in the Bint Jbeil district.
📥 Have a tip on Capitol Hill?  Email DC Correspondent Julian Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com

## U.S. News

- Oil surges past $100: Brent crude jumped more than 6% Thursday to top $100 a barrel, its highest price in about two months, the Wall Street Journal reported. The surge triggered a bond selloff and dragged down U.S. stock futures with worries about inflation dominating the market.

- Amish Shah defeats DCCC-backed rival in Arizona House primary: Emergency physician Amish Shah won Wednesday’s Democratic primary in Arizona’s 1st Congressional District, which represents the northeastern parts of the Phoenix metro area, over Marlene Galán-Woods, who was backed by the DCCC, delivering another setback to the party’s national campaign arm, the AP reported.

- Shah will face Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker endorsed by President Donald Trump, in a district that has shifted toward the center in recent years.

- House narrowly passes $95 billion budget for Iran war: House Republicans narrowly passed their $95 billion budget blueprint 216 to 214 on Wednesday to fund the Iran war and impose new voting restrictions, with two Republicans—Reps. Thomas Massie (Ky.), Warren Davidson (Ohio)—voting against it.

- The measure will provide up to $73 billion in additional military funding for the U.S. campaign against Iran, with $12 billion allocated for farmers and $10 billion for Trump’s voting restrictions.

- Ex-DOGE staffers launch military AI cyber startup valued at $1.4 billion: Former Department of Government Efficiency employees—including Gavin Kliger, until recently the Pentagon’s chief data officer—have launched Cathedral, a startup seeking government contracts for AI-driven military cyber operations against adversaries like China, after closing a $160 million funding round led by Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital, Reuters reported Wednesday.

- House passes NDAA: The U.S. House of Representatives passed the $1.1 trillion National Defense Authorization Act 216–212 on Wednesday, with six Democrats—Henry Cuellar, Don Davis, Jared Golden, Vicente Gonzalez, Adam Gray, and Marie Gluesenkamp Perez—voting yes and seven Republicans voting no. The measure includes Section 219, which more tightly integrates the U.S. military intelligence and the defense industrial base with Israel.

- The bill makes U.S. military support for Israel easier and more institutionalized. It creates a Pentagon office tasked with accelerating U.S.-Israeli military technology cooperation, including joint R&D, testing, co-production, data sharing, and moving jointly developed technology into procurement.

- Separately, it extends through 2029 an existing authority allowing the U.S. to transfer weapons already stored in its War Reserve Stockpile in Israel. That authority can permit transfers without Congress voting on each shipment, with Congress only receiving notification under the underlying law.

- AIPAC-tinged 314 Action PAC backs Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan Senate Race: 314 Action, a PAC launched with the stated purpose of electing science and medical professionals to Congress, in 2024 and 2026 took substantial sums of money from a super PAC linked to AIPAC and other pro-Israel donors, as we previously reported. Both high-profile efforts failed: In 2024, their candidate Maxine Dexter (D-Ore.) won but has since called the support “toxic,” has sworn off AIPAC backing, and denounced Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as a war criminal.

- In 2026, the millions put behind Ala Stanford in a Philadelphia congressional race weren’t enough to lift her over Chris Rabb.

- Since then, 314 Action has worked to buff up its image, and endorsed Adam Hamawy in New Jersey, a doctor who volunteered in Gaza, and now El-Sayed, also a doctor and strident AIPAC critic.

- Rabb told Drop Site he’s pleased to see his old nemesis on his side of a race: “Glad to see [Executive Director] Erik Polyak learned from the ass-whooping his org got in PA-03 in the May primary, and that 314 Action has decided—albeit belatedly—to back another excellent candidate with a STEM background who’s ardently opposed to AlPAC and is unabashedly pro-Medicare for All! First Hamawy for Congress in NJ, then El-Sayed for Senate in MI! As the saying goes, ‘even a broken clock is right twice a day!’”

- 314 Action also spent $300,000 to boost Amish Shah in Arizona on Tuesday. Shah beat another Democrat who was backed by the DCCC and Bold PAC, which has also been a vehicle for AIPAC cash. By playing both with and against AIPAC, it becomes harder to know when 314 is genuinely pursuing its mission of backing doctors and scientists, and when it is acting as a vehicle for AIPAC.

- House narrowly passes resolution to halt Iran war: The House voted 214-208 on Thursday to pass a resolution requiring congressional approval for continued U.S. military action against Iran, with a handful of Republicans joining Democrats, the AP reported.

- Rep. Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.), who led the resolution, said the war has “no clear mission, no strategy, no end goal” in a speech in favor of the resolution on the House floor.

- Trump Jr.’s investment firm posts 200% returns: Donald Trump Jr.’s investment firm 1789 Capital has generated returns of roughly 200% as of June 30, far outpacing the venture capital industry average of around 21%, the Times reported on Wednesday.

- 1789 Capital has grown from a fund managing a few hundred million dollars to one managing more than $3 billion in assets by investing in companies benefiting from Trump administration policies, The New York Times reported.

- The firm’s investments include rare-earths producer Vulcan Elements, which received a $620 million Defense Department loan months after 1789 invested and is now under congressional Democratic scrutiny, and Polymarket, now valued at $15 billion after federal regulators granted it a U.S. operating license.

- Centrist Dem backing data centers takes data center cash: Matt Maasdam, who is running against Will Lawrence in a Michigan House race, returned a contribution from Palantir executive Mehdi Alhassani after the killings of Reneé Good and Alex Pretti, given Palantir’s links to ICE. But Alhassani was also a key player in Palantir’s push for data center expansion, Drop Site’s Ryan Grim reports, while Maasdam and Lawrence have clashed in the campaign over the issue. Lawrence has made data center opposition core to his campaign, while Maasdam has argued that opposition is futile. “If we don’t participate in these in the way that it’s coming, all those opportunities will go to other states,” Maasdam has argued. “They’ll go to Indiana, and they’ll go to Ohio, and we will not have a say in how to guide and lead the AI future revolution. And I want to make sure that Michigan is participating there.”

- While Maasdam returned Alhassani’s money, he has kept large contributions from many other executives connected to data center buildouts, including D.E. Shaw Group executive Cedomir Crnkovic, who is heavily invested in OpenAI and Anthropic and runs his hedge fund’s machine learning arm; Brian Jacobs, co-founder of Emergence Capital, which invests heavily in infrastructure linked to data centers; and Gaurav Kapadia, CEO of XN Investment Group, also heavily invested in data centers. Lawrence’s opponents, meanwhile, have accused the democratic socialist of being in the tank for Big Tech because of an $11,000 401k that includes investments in index funds, which includes Big Tech companies.

## Other International News

- Trump says U.S.-Saudi deal subject to normalizing relations with Israel: President Trump said on Thursday that the U.S.-Saudi nuclear deal is subject to Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel. He added that the deal does not allow the enrichment of uranium. “The Civil Nuclear Deal (There will be no enrichment of material!) being made between the United States Department of Energy and Saudi Arabia, which pertains only to non-military use such as the ones that Iran and UAE (and others) already have, will be approved, but is totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords. The United States is not opposed to Civil (Non-Enriched) Nuclear Facilities,” Trump wrote on social media. In response, the office of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said “Saudi Arabia’s joining of the Abraham Accords would be an historic leap forward for peace in the Middle East.”

- Trump administration weighs military strikes in Mali: The Trump administration is considering military action in Mali against JNIM, an al-Qaeda-affiliated group, which would mark an eighth country where Trump has ordered strikes this term, The Washington Post reported on Wednesday. Senior officials are divided on the move, with National Security Council counterterrorism director Sebastian Gorka one of the most vocal advocates.

- Five Thai soldiers killed in attack on southern checkpoint: Five paramilitary soldiers were killed and six civilians wounded Wednesday evening when about 10 assailants attacked the Buketa Sami checkpoint in Narathiwat province, wielding guns and using pipe bombs, AFP reported. The assault, one of the deadliest against Thai security forces in recent years, came a day after a car bombing outside a police station elsewhere in Narathiwat.

- At least 20 killed in bandit attacks on Nigerian villages: At least 20 people were killed Wednesday when armed gang members attacked villages in Zamfara State in northwest Nigeria, according to the AFP.

- Russia and Ukraine trade strikes, killing eight: Ukrainian strikes on Russia and Crimea killed four people on Thursday, including a three-year-old boy, and Russian strikes on Ukraine’s Dnipropetrovsk and Sumy regions also killed four people while injuring 10, according to Reuters. The attacks follow Ukraine’s Wednesday strikes on Wildberries, a major online retailer in Russia, which destroyed five of the company’s biggest distribution centers.

- Drone strike from Sudan injures civilians in Chadian border town: A drone believed to belong to the Rapid Support Forces attacked positions roughly seven kilometers inside of Chad’s border on Wednesday, injuring two children and destroying vehicles and shops, Sudan Tribune reported.

- Mexican journalist found dead in Oaxaca: Journalist Francisco Leyva, 60, was found dead Wednesday in Oaxaca, marking at least the fourth killing of a journalist in Mexico since June, Reuters reported. Leyva, who reported on government corruption and cartel violence, is at least the fifth journalist killed in Mexico this year, according to press freedom group Article 19.

- Heatwave causes jailed Tunisian opposition leader Ghannouchi to pass out: Jailed opposition leader Rached Ghannouchi, 85, temporarily lost consciousness amid an intense heatwave at Tunisia’s Mornaguia prison, according to the daughter of fellow imprisoned politician Ahmed Nejib Chebbi, who said she witnessed the incident during a Tuesday visit. Ghannouchi, who was imprisoned in 2023, is one of several elderly opposition figures imprisoned by President Kais Saied, whose rule has been described as “increasingly authoritarian.”

- Pardoned ex-Honduran president to seek dismissal of local charges: Former Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernandez, pardoned by President Donald Trump in 2025 after being convicted of cocaine trafficking in 2024, said Wednesday he will seek to have separate fraud and money laundering charges in Honduras dismissed when he returns Sunday, according to Reuters. Trump’s December pardon of Hernandez was announced before the country’s elections, in which Trump supported the right-wing eventual victor Nasry Asfura and threatened to revoke U.S. aid if Asfura did not win. Read a report on the Hernandez pardon by Jose Luis Grenada Ceja, Drop Site’s Latin America editor, here.

reads.title: Asesinan A La Fiscal Que Investigaba Los Ataques Estadounidenses Contra Pescadores Ecuatorianos y Denuncias De Tortura
reads.subtitle: Han surgido nuevas pruebas sobre la actividad de la Guardia Costera Estadounidense tras dos ataques, lo cual corrobora el testimonio de los sobrevivientes.
reads.body:
- Escena del crimen del asesinato de la fiscal Alexandra Bravo y su hermana, Olinda Bravo. Foto proporcionada a Drop Site News por Radio Pichincha.To read this story in English, click here.
QUITO, Ecuador—Alexandra Bravo, la fiscal encargada de investigar los ataques de EE. UU. contra tres embarcaciones ecuatorianas y los relatos de tortura y secuestro de los 36 sobrevivientes, fue asesinada a tiros en la ciudad costera de Manta el mes pasado. Según la policía, el 14 de junio un sicario a bordo de una motocicleta negra disparó contra Bravo cuando ella y su hermana salían de una cafetería alrededor de las 11 de la mañana. La hermana de Bravo, quien se lanzó a protegerla, también murió en el ataque.
Al llegar a la escena del crimen, los agentes dicen que encontraron cinco casquillos de 9 mm y al chofer de Bravo herido, pero ningún rastro de la escolta policial que había sido asignada para protegerla. La Policía Nacional, que opera íntegramente bajo el poder ejecutivo, ha iniciado una investigación para determinar si hubo una falla de seguridad interna.
Bravo es la vigésimo sexta miembro del sistema judicial de Ecuador asesinada desde 2020 y la segunda persona que investigaba delitos de Estado asesinada esa semana. Además de su asignación habitual de casos de homicidio y crimen organizado, Bravo había estado trabajando en los casos Fiorella, Negra Francisca Duarte II y Don Maca —una serie de ataques con drones contra embarcaciones pesqueras civiles que Drop Site dio a conocer en abril. Dos de los tripulantes de las embarcaciones regresaron a casa y denunciaron haber sido secuestrados, vendados y privados de alimentos durante ocho días por hombres armados estadounidenses, vestidos con uniformes militares de EE. UU. a bordo de un barco patrullero con bandera estadounidense, antes de ser abandonados en El Salvador. El Comité de las Naciones Unidas Contra las Desaparición Forzada respaldó los llamados para que se realice una investigación, exigiendo que Estados Unidos proporcione información sobre el paradero de los ocho hombres que aún se encuentran desaparecidos y sobre cualquier implicación en el asunto a más tardar el 27 de abril. Hasta la fecha, Estados Unidos no ha respondido.
Drop Site cuenta con el apoyo de sus lectores. Suscríbete hoy.
Bajo el mandato del presidente de derecha de Ecuador, Daniel Noboa —un multimillonario nacido en Miami a quien a menudo se describe como un “dictador respaldado por Estados Unidos”—el país se ha convertido en un campo de experimentacion importante para la Operación Southern Spear, la campaña de bombardeos extrajudiciales de Washington que supuestamente tiene como objetivo a los “narco-terroristas” y que ha causado la muerte de 221 personas hasta la fecha. No hay evidencia de que muchas de las víctimas, incluidas las de la investigación de Bravo, se hubieran dedicado al tráfico de drogas.
“No puedo sugerir que haya sido un asesinato político, pero evidentemente, cuando matan a un fiscal es por la investigación que está llevando a cabo”, declaró a Drop Site Fernando Bastías, un reconocido abogado de derechos humanos de la CDH de Ecuador y miembro de la Organización Mundial contra la Tortura, con sede en Ginebra, “Eso es algo que hemos aprendido de nuestra experiencia en Ecuador”.
Una fuente dentro del departamento de policía de Manta, que conocía personalmente a Bravo, le dijo a Drop Site News que la fiscal ecuatoriana estaba bajo presión de sus superiores en la Fiscalía General para que tratara los ataques de EE. UU. exclusivamente como “casos de desaparición”. La fuente, que pidió permanecer en el anonimato por temor a represalias, dijo que a Bravo le ordenaron cerrar todas las líneas de investigación después de que se encontraran a 36 de los 44 hombres desaparecidos —a pesar de que llegaron con lesiones graves, entre ellas una pérdida de visión del 70 % y pies desgarrados hasta dejar al descubierto la carne y los huesos, lo cual los expertos médicos consideraron consistente con sus relatos de explosiones y tortura.
La investigadora principal de Human Rights Watch quien entrevistó a Bravo como parte de su investigación sobre las tres embarcaciones, recordó de manera similar que Bravo enfrentó “desafíos internos dentro de la propia institución para avanzar en la investigación”. La investigadora señaló que la fiscal solicitó repetidamente la cooperación de otras entidades a cargo del rescate del barco, incluida la Capitanía del Puerto de Manta, pero “ninguna respondió a sus solicitudes de información”. Durante el bombardeo de La Negra Francisca, Darwin Pico-Flores, un testigo ocular a bordo de una embarcación cercana, le dijo a Drop Site que llamó a la Capitanía del Puerto de Manta para solicitar asistencia de emergencia. Nadie acudió. En abril, como parte de su primera investigación sobre el incidente, Drop Site llamó al puerto en busca de comentarios. Los funcionarios colgaron el teléfono al enterarse de que la llamada era de periodistas.
La investigadora dijo a Drop Site que Bravo, en su última reunión el 8 de mayo, le dijo que “aún se encontraba en las etapas iniciales de la indagación y la investigación”. Bastías dijo que Bravo “estaba investigando a un país [Estados Unidos] que ha sido presentado en los medios como un aliado contra el crimen. Esa investigación no ha avanzado en absoluto, y eso se debe a la intención de evitar meterse en líos o problemas con nadie”. La fuente dentro del Departamento de Policía de Manta dijo que Bravo, debido a la falta de cooperación de otras agencias estatales, había pedido consejo sobre cómo buscar nuevas fuentes de evidencia.
En los días previos a su muerte, Bravo fue reasignada a la Fiscalía General en Montecristi, un municipio vecino. Consecuentemente, ella fue reasignada a otros casos y ya no estaba a cargo de investigar los tres ataques a las embarcaciones. Drop Site se comunicó con varios representantes de la Fiscalía General para solicitar comentarios sobre por qué se había reasignado a Bravo, pero no recibió respuesta. Drop Site intentó comunicarse con el sustituto de Bravo para obtener comentarios, pero se le había ordenado explícitamente que no hablara con la prensa. Tras varias semanas de intentos por obtener una respuesta de la Fiscalía General del Estado, la institución respondió a Drop Site que la investigación se encuentra bajo reserva y que no podía pronunciarse sobre las razones del traslado de Bravo.
Dentro del régimen militar ecuatoriano respaldado por Estados Unidos, la Fiscalía General se ha convertido en una institución cada vez más opaca y politizada. “Ya es un gran obstáculo para que los fiscales investiguen a los agentes estatales locales. Ahora imagínese a los agentes estatales internacionales”, dijo Bastías. “El Poder Ejecutivo ha implementado una serie de marcos legales que dejan en impunidad a estos agentes estatales extranjeros.”, agregó, refiriéndose a la inmunidad diplomática otorgada a todo militar estadounidense y al personal del Departamento de Defensa a través de los 22 decretos de ley marcial del presidente Noboa.
El Pentágono, la Guardia Costera y el Comando Sur de EE.UU. han negado tener conocimiento o responsabilidad alguna sobre los incidentes con las embarcaciones. Después de que Drop Site publicó pruebas fotográficas del bombardeo de La Negra Francisca, los legisladores estadounidenses interrogaron al secretario de Guerra de EE. UU., Pete Hegseth, durante una audiencia en el Congreso. El 13 de junio, el día antes del asesinato de Bravo, los diputados Joaquín Castro (D-Texas) y Bill Keating (D-Mass.) publicaron una carta dirigida a Hegseth, al secretario de Estado Marco Rubio y al jefe de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU., Kevin Lunday, en la que exigían una auditoría completa de la participación del gobierno de EE. UU. en los ataques. A pesar de que el plazo venció el 10 de julio, ninguna de las agencias ha emitido una respuesta pública. La secretaria de prensa de Keating, Lauren McDermott, le dijo a Drop Site que su oficina había recibido una respuesta de la oficina de Rubio, pero ninguna del Departamento de Guerra ni de la Guardia Costera. No reveló el contenido de la respuesta.
Los sobrevivientes que regresaron a casa, tanto como las familias de los que no, aún no han recibido ninguna respuesta. Le dijeron a Drop Site que “las autoridades nos cerraron la puerta en la cara”. María, la esposa de uno de los pescadores, le contó a Drop Site que su suegra murió esperando el regreso de su hijo, y que sufría de una depresión grave y dejó de comer en las semanas previas a su muerte.
A pesar de los esfuerzos de ambos gobiernos por obstaculizar la investigación, siguen surgiendo pruebas que respaldan los testimonios de los pescadores sobre los secuestros, ataques aéreos y tortura. Drop Site obtuvo un video exclusivo de la actividad de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. en las inmediaciones del bombardeo de La Negra Francisca, inteligencia de fuentes abiertas que corrobora los testimonios de La Negra Francisca, y entrevistas policiales con testigos presenciales que confirman la presencia de EE. UU. alegada por los sobrevivientes y documentada por Drop Site. Con la ayuda de Tomi McCluskey, analista de OSINT de Airwars y exmiembro del Cuerpo de Marineros de EE. UU., Drop Site tuvo acceso a imágenes térmicas adicionales de la NASA que corroboran el bombardeo del “Negra Francisca”, así como a datos de rastreo de embarcaciones que sitúan la actividad de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. a lo largo de la ruta por la que, según los pescadores, fueron llevados tras el ataque.
Video obtenido por Drop Site que muestra una presunta actividad de la Guardia Costera cerca de la huelga de Negra Francisca.

## Lawfare político bajo el régimen militar ecuatoriano respaldado por Estados Unidos
Noboa, quien gobierna mediante toques de queda militares y el hambre masiva de los presos políticos, ha hecho todo lo posible por convertirse en el aliado más fuerte de Trump en Sudamérica. Desde que asumió la presidencia, ha hecho caso omiso de la prohibición constitucional de Ecuador sobre la presencia militar estadounidense—ratificada por el 60% de los votantes en noviembre de 2025— que se introdujo originalmente hace casi 20 años precisamente debido a un historial de hundimientos de embarcaciones por parte del ejército estadounidense frente a la costa de Manta. Además, su administración autorizó la primera oficina del FBI en territorio ecuatoriano, apoyó una iniciativa de la embajada de EE. UU. para incriminar falsamente a miembros del gobierno de izquierda de Colombia antes de las elecciones y colaboró con EE. UU. en el bombardeo de trabajadores agrícolas civiles inocentes a lo largo de la frontera entre Colombia y Ecuador—todo ello en nombre de la lucha contra el narcotráfico.
Cabe destacar que se descubrieron embarcaciones de la empresa exportadora de la familia de Noboa traficando con €26 millones de libras esterlinas en cocaína —un detalle que no ha disuadido al Departamento de Estado de nombrarlo socio clave en la Guerra contra las Drogas de Trump—. El mes pasado, The Guardian informó que un denunciante que investigaba los vínculos de Noboa con el narcotráfico fue asesinado.
Aun así, Noboa sigue siendo miembro de pleno derecho del “Escudo de las Américas” de Trump. La Coalición de las Américas contra los Cárteles, como también se conoce al Escudo, funciona como una alianza tanto militar como altamente política, y ha intervenido abiertamente para respaldar los intereses de Estados Unidos en Bolivia mientras el presidente Rodrigo Paz se enfrentaba a un paro nacional contra la austeridad.
Que un fiscal local acuse a las fuerzas estadounidenses de bombardeos extrajudiciales y tortura de civiles ecuatorianos socavaría la alianza y dañaría las relaciones entre Ecuador y Estados Unidos.
Otros funcionarios públicos que han estado investigando la presunta colusión delictiva entre Estados Unidos y Ecuador también han recibido amenazas de muerte. Mónica Palacios, asambleísta para los ecuatorianos radicados en Estados Unidos, quien declaró que llevaría el caso de La Fiorella ante las Naciones Unidas, enfrentó meses de lawfare político tras destapar un escándalo de corrupción presuntamente cometida por una empresa estadounidense y el Estado ecuatoriano. El pasado viernes, Palacios denunció haber recibido amenazas de muerte contra ella y su hijo de un año, junto con imágenes del exterior de su vivienda en Nueva York. La legisladora responsabilizó directamente al presidente Daniel Noboa y sostuvo que las amenazas fueron una represalia por su investigación sobre el peculado.
“Existe una persecución directa contra jueces y fiscales que, en el marco de sus funciones, toman decisiones que no se alinean totalmente con lo que quiere el Poder Ejecutivo y terminan siendo sancionados”, dijo Bastías, el abogado de derechos humanos. “Por otro lado, también existe el riesgo que viene del contexto de criminalidad”. De todos modos, afirmó, la muerte de Bravo “tiene mucho que ver con lo que hace o no hace el Estado, porque hasta ahora no ha habido mecanismos de seguridad efectivos para los funcionarios del sistema judicial. Eso genera una responsabilidad automática del Estado. Eso es indiscutible.”

-
- Alexandra Bravo, fiscal de la Fiscalía General de Ecuador, durante una entrevista con Radio San Mateo. Foto proporcionada a Drop Site News por Radio San Mateo.Diego Vintimilla Jarrín, exdiputado de la Asamblea Nacional de Ecuador y actual portavoz del Partido Comunista de Ecuador, se expresó de manera similar a Drop Site: “El gobierno de Noboa es la agenda más anti soberana que hemos tenido desde el inicio de la democracia. No tengo pruebas de quién asesinó a la fiscal, pero el hecho de que ella estuviera investigando ciertos elementos y que estos luego dejaran de parecer importantes también dice mucho sobre los problemas subyacentes”.

## Surgen nuevas pruebas que implican a EE. UU.

## The Negra Francisca
Estados Unidos sostiene que nunca interactuó con ninguna de las tres embarcaciones. Un portavoz de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. declaró a The Guardian que la única participación de la agencia en los hechos fue el despliegue del USCGC Bertholf en una misión de búsqueda y rescate tras recibir una alerta MAYDAY de que la Negra Francisca estaba en llamas, y que finalmente no encontró nada.
Sin embargo, los datos de rastreo de los movimientos del Bertholf, proporcionados en exclusiva a Drop Site por McCluskey, sitúan al buque cerca de la Negra Francisca en el momento del bombardeo antes de que este apagara su señal —sólo para reaparecer frente a la costa de Costa Rica en las mismas fechas en que la tripulación de la Negra Francisca fue llevada a aguas centroamericanas y transferida al Comando Naval de El Salvador, con extremidades destrozadas y quemaduras graves a causa del ataque. Hernán Flores, capitán de la Negra Francisca, le dijo a Drop Site que los oficiales salvadoreños le informaron específicamente que “personal estadounidense había llamado para coordinar el traspaso”.
La Guardia Costera Estadounidense negó haber coordinado el traspaso. “La Guardia Costera no desempeñó ningún papel en el traslado de los pescadores de La Negra Francisca Duarte II”, afirmó un portavoz.

-
- El USCGC Bertholf operaba en aguas costarricenses en las mismas fechas (horas convertidas desde UTC) en que los tripulantes de la Negra Francisca fueron trasladados a Centroamérica y recibidos por la Armada y la Guardia Costera de El Salvador. Tanto el buque identificado como el no identificado comparten el mismo número de identificación, lo que confirma que se trata del Bertholf en ambos puntos de datos. Foto de Global Fishing Watch, proporcionada por el analista de OSINT Tomi McCluskey.El USCGC Bertholf partió de la base militar de Galápagos a las 4 p. m. del 16 de marzo y dejó de transmitir su ubicación poco después. Un día más tarde, La Negra Francisca fue bombardeada a 170 millas de distancia —una distancia que normalmente se recorre en barco en entre 3 a 10 horas. Drop Site solicitó a la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. que diera cuenta de la actividad del buque patrullero después de que su señal se interrumpiera. La Guardia Costera respondió que “no divulga los movimientos de los buques patrulleros durante las misiones de aplicación de la ley por razones de seguridad operativa”.
A la 1:02 p. m. del 17 de marzo, el sistema FIRMS de la NASA registró una anomalía térmica compatible con un incendio provocado por explosivos, lo cual corrobora la hora y el lugar en que los pescadores de la Negra Francisca le dijeron a Drop Site que su barco fue incendiado por ataques de múltiples drones. La tripulación afirma que luego fueron capturados a punta de arma por hombres de cabello rubio que hablaban inglés y vestían uniformes de faena de color caqui con parches de la bandera estadounidense cosidos en las mangas; sus descripciones coinciden con los uniformes que aparecen en los comunicados de prensa del Comando Sur de EE. UU. A bordo del buque patrullero con bandera estadounidense, los hombres armados presuntamente los mantuvieron como rehenes, hundieron su barco ya bombardeado, les colocaron capuchas en la cabeza, golpearon a algunos de los pescadores y les negaron comida durante ocho días mientras los transportaban a Centroamérica.

-
- OSINT provided to Drop Site by Tomi McCluskey document the USCGC Bertholf’s movements near the Negra Francisca around the time of the bombing (times converted from UTC).
-
- Las fotografías de OSINT proporcionadas a Drop Site por Tomi McCluskey documentan los movimientos del USCGC Bertholf cerca de La Negra Francisca en el momento del bombardeo (horas convertidas desde UTC).La señal del USCGC Bertholf reapareció en aguas costarricenses el 22 de marzo cerca del puerto de Golfito, a aproximadamente 450 millas náuticas de las aguas de El Salvador. Apagó su transpondedor y no lo reactivó hasta el 24 de marzo, 24 horas después de que la Guardia Costera de El Salvador anunciara públicamente que tenía bajo su custodia a los pescadores de La Negra Francisca.
Como parte de nuestra primera investigación, Drop Site se puso en contacto con 11 funcionarios del gobierno de El Salvador. Todos se negaron a hablar oficialmente, alegando una orden de silencio de su gobierno.
Existen precedentes de que el Bertholf ha participado en la transferencias de víctimas de ataques aéreos de EE. UU. a las autoridades centroamericanas alrededor del mismo período; medios costarricenses informaron que el Bertholf entregó los restos de dos fallecidos y un sobreviviente herido en el puerto de Golfito, en Costa Rica. El inspector náutico de Costa Rica, Wilber Urroz Guido, dijo que no tenía información sobre los movimientos del buque, pero que este estaba autorizado a actuar en virtud de un memorándum de entendimiento entre Estados Unidos y Costa Rica —similar a los acuerdos que Estados Unidos mantiene con Ecuador y El Salvador.
Los testimonios de testigos presenciales también ponen en duda la versión de los hechos de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. Un video compartido en exclusiva con Drop Site por Darwin Pico-Flores, testigo presencial del ataque y sobrino del capitán de la Negra Francisca, muestra a una lancha patrullera de la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. patrullando las aguas donde ocurrió el bombardeo.
Video obtenido por Drop Site que muestra una presunta actividad de la Guardia Costera cerca de la huelga de Negra Francisca.
Darwin dijo que el 17 de marzo estaba pescando en las cercanías, a bordo de su barco, el Solavil, cuando vio humo elevándose en la distancia alrededor de las 2 p. m. Mientras intentaba repetidamente comunicarse por radio con la tripulación de La Negra Francisca, vio una aeronave estadounidense sobrevolando la zona en círculos. No fue sino hasta horas más tarde que se enteró por una señal de radio de que La Negra Francisca estaba en llamas y se apresuró a dirigirse al lugar, donde encontró el barco consumido por el fuego y sin rastros de sobrevivientes.
Recuperó dos botes de emergencia carbonizados, tomó fotos como evidencia del incendio y luego llamó al Puerto de Manta para pedir ayuda. Nadie acudió.
Darwin decidió emprender el regreso al puerto para buscar ayuda de emergencia y, justo cuando se alejaba del lugar del incendio, unas luces rojas y verdes se posaron sobre la Negra Francisca. Temiendo por su seguridad, alejó su embarcación del lugar.

-
- The Negra Francisca burning, photographed and shared with Drop Site by Darwin Pico-Flores.A la tarde siguiente, Darwin le contó a Drop Site que su barco fue abordado por la Guardia Costera de EE. UU., la cual detuvo e interrogó a la tripulación durante casi 12 horas a través de un traductor de español con acento puertorriqueño. Dijo que el personal de la Guardia Costera confirmó que las luces rojas y verdes eran de su patrulla y reconoció haber llegado al lugar donde se encontraba la Negra Francisca la noche anterior, pero se negó a dar más detalles sobre lo que habían encontrado. En cambio, interrogaron a los pescadores sobre si habían visto algo y por qué Darwin había rescatado las lanchas.
Después de decirles a los oficiales de la Guardia Costera que la Negra Francisca era el barco de su tío, Darwin dice que de repente dejaron de interrogarlo y comenzaron a comunicarse por radio en inglés con sus colegas a bordo del guardacostas cercano que se ve en el video. “Como éramos los únicos que lo habíamos visto todo, temíamos que nos hicieran algo”, dijo Darwin. Sintió que la Guardia Costera de EE. UU. mostró poco interés en ayudarlo a localizar a su familia y, en cambio, parecía más enfocada en “asegurarse de que no fuéramos testigos de nada”.
McCluskey afirma que la táctica de múltiples drones —descrita por las tres embarcaciones— refleja una doctrina estadounidense. Argumenta que es poco probable que otras potencias regionales, desde países vecinos hasta grupos del crimen organizado, cuenten con el presupuesto o el acceso a dicha tecnología. No se conoce ningún precedente de que los cárteles utilicen drones de vigilancia tipo “ojo en el cielo” en la alta mar, aunque la Guardia Costera también ha negado operar drones armados en aguas ecuatorianas.
Además, la decisión de mantener con vida a los sobrevivientes —a pesar de que esto implicara testimonios de tortura— y los esfuerzos y gastos para transportarlos, refleja mucho más un protocolo del Departamento de Defensa —diseñado para evitar ramificaciones legales internacionales— que lo que cualquier grupo del crimen organizado se molestaría en practicar. “Si hubieran sido los cárteles, nunca los hubieras encontrado”, dijo McCluskey. “No habría sobrevivientes con quienes hablar, no habría historias.”

## The Fiorella
La Fiorella fue atacada frente a la costa de las Galápagos el 20 de enero; los ocho pescadores a bordo siguen desaparecidos. El día antes de que el barco desapareciera, la esposa del capitán recibió una llamada de su esposo a través de una línea de emergencia, en la que le advertía que había aeronaves estadounidenses sobrevolando la zona.
Drop Site obtuvo las transcripciones de las entrevistas policiales a dos testigos presenciales, Christian Flores y Dimas Ignacio Álvarez, quienes confirmaron haber visto La Fiorella envuelta en humo y rodeada por unidades estadounidenses. Los dos hombres formaban parte de la tripulación de La Fiorella, pero llevaban varias horas fuera del barco colocando un palangre en una balsa cercana cuando la embarcación se incendió.
En sus declaraciones a la policía, Flores y Álvarez describieron dos aeronaves estadounidenses sobrevolando La Fiorella el 18 de enero; múltiples drones grises estadounidenses y un barco patrullero con bandera de EE. UU. rodeando la embarcación el 19 y el 20 de enero —el día en que desaparecieron sus compañeros de tripulación—, el gran buque patrullero de bandera estadounidense cerca del humo. Desde la distancia, no pudieron distinguir al personal a bordo del buque, pero sus relatos coinciden con los de la tripulación de la Negra Francisca, quienes afirmaron que fueron tomados como rehenes por estadounidenses armados a bordo de un buque patrullero de bandera estadounidense. Las descripciones de los testigos también coinciden con las aeronaves y el equipo que aparecen en publicaciones del Comando Sur de EE. UU.
Tras avistar el humo, los dos pescadores dijeron que escucharon a sus compañeros de tripulación llamando al capitán por radio en señal de socorro. Nunca más se los volvió a ver.
El abogado que representa a los dos sobrevivientes de la “Fiorella”, Juan Ávila, le dijo a Drop Site que la fiscal asesinada, Alexandra Bravo, era su sobrina.
La Guardia Costera le dijo a Drop Site que “no tiene registro de haber estado involucrada con La Fiorella”.

## En la nación más violenta del Occidente, Bravo no es una excepción
La ausencia de una escolta policial asignada cuando Bravo fue asesinada presenta similitudes con el asesinato del candidato presidencial favorito Fernando Villavicencio en 2023. Una comisión del Congreso determinó que la escolta policial de Villavicencio era insuficiente, que había sido escoltado de manera poco convencional a través de una salida expuesta a nivel de la calle, contrariamente al protocolo estándar, y que el vehículo blindado designado para proteger a Villavicencio durante la campaña electoral había sido dejado por su equipo de seguridad en Guayaquil ese mismo día. Estas fallas lo hicieron particularmente vulnerable cuando los agresores se le acercaron y le dispararon en la acera mientras salía de una reunión con otros funcionarios del gobierno.
La muerte de Villavicencio preparó el camino para que la campaña del ahora presidente Daniel Noboa —que en las encuestas tenía un 3 %— se disparara hacia la victoria. En una entrevista con Señal Colombia, la diputada de la Asamblea Nacional y miembro del partido de Villavicencio, Gisella Molina, quien estaba con él y resultó herida durante el asesinato, sugirió que los funcionarios del gobierno tenían conocimiento previo del complot.
Durante la investigación del asesinato de 2024, Drop Site publicó mensajes privados de la entonces fiscal general Diana Salazar que revelaron un complot para implicar al partido del expresidente socialista democrático Correa en el asesinato de Villavicencio, en el marco de una estrecha colaboración con el embajador de Estados Unidos.
Posteriormente, el Estado concluyó que el cártel de Los Lobos había cometido el asesinato de Villavicencio y alegó que los exmiembros del partido de Correa eran los autores intelectuales. Los fiscales afirman que Los Lobos mataron a Villavicencio por desenmascarar su red criminal. Mientras Villavicencio hacía campaña en pro de erradicar la narco economía, Ecuador bajo el mandato de Noboa —acusado de ofrecer inmunidad a los jefes del crimen organizado a cambio de apoyo electoral— se ha convertido en el principal centro de distribución del 70 % de la cocaína del mundo.
Inmediatamente después de la muerte de Bravo, la Fiscalía General emitió un comunicado público en el que atribuía su asesinato a una represalia contra los fiscales que combaten el crimen organizado. Al ser consultada por Drop Site sobre la decisión de atribuir el asesinato al crimen organizado y sobre los avances en la investigación del equipo policial encargado de la protección de Bravo, la Fiscalía General del Estado respondió que el caso se encuentra bajo reserva y declinó hacer comentarios.
Aunque la Fiscalía General aún no ha presentado pruebas que respalden su afirmación, Bravo se lamentó ante Human Rights Watch de que “el peligro siempre estaba presente” en su trabajo. “Dijo que ser fiscal en un contexto de crimen organizado era complejo y arriesgado, pero no dio más detalles”, explicó la investigadora de Human Rights Watch a Drop Site. Manta se encuentra en el epicentro de la crisis del crimen organizado en Ecuador, a medida que este pequeño país sudamericano se convierte en la nación más violenta del hemisferio occidental.
Bravo también estaba a cargo de investigar la desapari

reads.title: Prosecutor Investigating U.S. Boat Strikes and Claims of Torture Was Murdered in Ecuador
reads.subtitle: New evidence has emerged of U.S. Coast Guard activity in the aftermath of two strikes, further corroborating survivor testimony.
reads.body:
As a reader-funded independent news outlet, we operate free from the influence of governments, advertisers, and corporate backers. This is essential to our mission: to report on what matters most, beholden only to the truth. In that spirit, we made a commitment to ensure that our journalism is free for everyone, not locked behind a paywall. But that means we rely on the voluntary support of our community of readers.
