reads.title: Trump threatens Iran’s bridges and power plants over Hormuz; U.S. and Saudi agree to nuclear deal; RSF drone kills 21 in North Darfur
reads.subtitle: Drop Site Daily: July 22, 2026
reads.body:
- U.S. President Donald Trump speaks to the press before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on July 22, 2026. Photo by Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images.Wednesday, July 22, 2026 – Renewed U.S. campaign against Iran enters its 12th day. Iran launches wave of retaliatory attacks. President Donald Trump threatens to bomb a civilian target for every attack on shipping in Hormuz. Trump says U.S. will strike Pickaxe Mountain “pretty soon” despite no evidence of nuclear enrichment. Kuwaitis are rationing electricity. U.S. Department of Energy claims that its petroleum reserve can run far lower than previously estimated. International Energy Agency warns of tightening fuel markets. Pakistan requests $10 billion fund for role in Iran negotiations. Iran executes man convicted of links to “anti-revolutionary terrorist group.” Israeli forces continue incursions and airstrikes in southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework. Lebanese PM hails Israeli withdrawal as beginning, Parliamentary Speaker says it “barely qualifies.” Trump promises to “help” Lebanon in meeting with Lebanese President Joseph Aoun, offers no concrete policy. Israel continues to bombard Gaza. Gaza sees rise in miscarriages, Health Ministry warns of cancer drug shortages. Israeli arrests, attacks and seizure of land in West Bank, Jerusalem. Israeli government officials march to ethnically cleanse Gaza of Palestinians. Israel confirms it is walling off the half of Gaza it controls. U.S. House of Representatives passes funding bill. U.S. Trade Representative signals new tariff wave. Studies find Presidential Aids Program cuts sharply reduced HIV prevention, treatment. Trump administration freezes over $1B in Medicaid funds to California, Minnesota. Van passengers dispute ICE account of fatal Houston shooting. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani backs down on threat to arrest Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. War Secretary Pete Hegseth estimates cost of Iran war at $37.5 billion during tense congressional testimony. Appeals court overturns release order for Palestinian activist Mohsen Mahdawi. Yemen’s Ansarallah says it forced 6 ships to reroute as part of blockade. Saudi Arabia and U.S. reportedly agree to nuclear deal. Indian opposition leader detained, released during “Cockroach” protests. RSF drone strike kills at least 21 civilians at Sudan water source. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy fires his military chief amid protests. Cuba condemns new U.S. State Department report, warns of military aggression. U.S. sends first humanitarian flight to Cuba under new $100 million aid package. At least 143 dead or missing after migrant boat disaster off Mauritania. Global hunger falls to 645 million in 2025, but Africa remains hardest hit, UN report finds. HRW report accuses U.S.-Ecuador military campaign of torturing, attacking civilians.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free news recap We send it Monday – Friday

## Iran

- Renewed U.S. campaign against Iran enters its 12th day: The U.S. launched strikes on Iran for the 11th consecutive night on Tuesday, with CENTCOM claiming its strikes targeted “military command centers, maritime capabilities, aircraft hangars, drone storage sites, and logistics infrastructure.”

- Explosions were heard overnight in the cities of Omidiyeh, Mahshahr, and Behbahan, all in the southwestern province of Khuzestan, the southern coastal cities Sirik, Bandar Abbas, and Bushehr, the western cities Kabudarahang and Kangavar, and the southeastern cities Chabahar and Konarak.

- Explosions were also reported in Baneh, in Iran’s Kurdistan, for the first time, according to Al Jazeera.

- A U.S. airstrike reportedly hit a military base in Tabriz, a populous northeastern city of historic importance.

- U.S. attacks also struck Iran’s Bushehr province, home to the country’s only nuclear power plant, with officials reporting a missile strike on an electrical substation near the facility that temporarily cut power to a nearby village but caused no reported casualties.

- CENTCOM also claimed it had redirected 8 commercial vessels and disabled 1 as of July 21 as part of its naval blockade on Iran.

- Iran launches wave of retaliatory attacks: The Iranian military reported that it had carried out several attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday in response to the ongoing U.S. bombing campaign.

- Iran’s army said it had launched a large-scale drone attack on U.S. forces at the Al-Doha camp in western Kuwait, aimed at disabling its logistics infrastructure, damaging its U.S. Army command center, and incapacitating its ammunition depots.

- The IRGC also reported attacks Wednesday morning on the King Faisal base in Jordan, claiming to have damaged F-15 warplanes, MQ-9 drones, as well as two helicopters. Iran conducted a separate strike on Wednesday on the Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Afraq, Jordan, according to the Mehr news agency.

- Iranian drones hit Bahrain’s Sheikh Isa Air Base on Wednesday, targeting “large equipment warehouses and sheds” and the “heavy aircraft maintenance and repair sheds,” according to an army statement.

- The IRGC claimed on Tuesday that it had taken tactical radar systems at the Ali Al-Salem and Bubiyan Island bases in Kuwait “out of operation,” as part of its “ongoing efforts to clear the region of radar systems.”

- The IRGC also struck Erbil in northern Iraq, where it said its strikes hit the headquarters of an anti-Iranian Kurdish opposition group. Flights at the city’s airport were suspended, according to the Iraqi News Agency.

- Trump threatens to bomb a civilian target for every attack on shipping in Hormuz: President Donald Trump said the U.S. would bomb one Iranian bridge or power plant for every attack by Iran on a ship in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that the policy would apply to strikes carried out with “missiles, rockets, drones, or any other device or weapon.” In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the targets could include infrastructure “located next to, or in, the capital city of Tehran.”

- Trump says U.S. will strike Pickaxe Mountain “pretty soon” despite no evidence of nuclear enrichment: Addressing reporters at the White House on Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump said that he possessed no evidence that Iran had begun enrichment at a facility underneath Kolang Kouh (commonly referred to as “Pickaxe Mountain”), but added that the U.S. would be “hitting that area probably pretty soon.”

- In response, Iran’s Central Military Command warned that any U.S. attack on Iran’s nuclear or other sensitive sites would mark a major expansion of the war and trigger “powerful attacks” on U.S. interests, allies, and supporters across the region.

- “Washington’s obsessive focus on Kolang Kouh where no nuclear activity is taking place is nothing more than a fabricated pretext for aggression, destruction, and sabotage,” Esmaeil Baghaei, the Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman, said in a post on X Wednesday.

- Trump addresses further aspects of the war: At the same meeting, Trump added several comments about the course and outlook of the U.S. war against Iran.

- Trump told reporters that the U.S. had “no interest” in meeting with its Iranian counterparts unless the talks promised to be “meaningful,” even though he claimed that, “privately,” the Iranians “desperately want to meet” as a consequence of what he characterized as recent American military success.

- Trump indicated that he had no timetable for the conflict’s end, and threatened further escalation, saying that the Iranians “haven’t seen anything yet” and suggesting that America had been “nice” to Iran in its most recent campaign.

- Trump told reporters he thought Iran was “probably” attempting to influence the upcoming midterm elections by closing the Strait, but that this had no “impact” on him, and that he believed Americans were “very impressed” by the current situation in the Gulf.

- Kuwaitis rationing electricity: Kuwaitis are rationing electricity as repeated Iranian strikes hit the country’s power and water infrastructure, Al-Monitor reported on Tuesday.

- Iranian attacks have struck several facilities over four consecutive days, sparking fires and raising fears of outages during the country’s extreme summer heat, when temperatures often exceed 50°C (122F), and air conditioning drives demand for power.

- The country’s desalination plants, which have also sustained damage in strikes, are integrated into the country’s power generation infrastructure, which threatens Kuwaiti access to freshwater as well.

- Authorities have urged residents to cut consumption, and officials say public compliance has already helped keep electricity use below projected levels and stabilize the grid.

- U.S. DOE claims that petroleum reserve can run far lower than previously estimated: A spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Energy told MarketWatch on Tuesday that the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve’s “true operational minimum” is roughly 70 million barrels, well under the 250 to 300 million barrels the oil industry has generally treated as the practical limit.

- The SPR, which has drained to its lowest level in 40 years, has roughly 246 barrels remaining for emergencies, the DOE claimed. It has shed more than 104 million barrels since the beginning of the U.S. war on Iran.

- International Energy Agency warns of tightening fuel markets: Fatih Birol, the Director of the International Energy Agency Director, said Tuesday that emergency releases of oil stock and alternative export routes are still cushioning oil markets, but warned there is “no room for complacency” as threats to the Bab al-Mandeb strait compound the disruption at Hormuz.

- Birol called for a full and unconditional reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, saying it remains “essential” to avoid further deterioration in global energy security.

- Pakistan requests $10 billion fund for role in Iran negotiations: Pakistan has asked the U.S. for a $10 billion “Bilateral Exchange Stabilization Support Facility,” a financial backstop with a maturity of up to five years, according toReuters, as a reward for its role brokering talks between the U.S. and Iran.

- The fund would be aimed at relieving pressure on Pakistan’s currency reserves and reducing its dependency on foreign financing, according to Reuters.

- The request came as Pakistani Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb met Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in Washington on Tuesday.

- Iran executes man convicted of links to “anti-revolutionary terrorist group”: Iran executed a man accused of belonging to an “anti-revolutionary terrorist group” and carrying out “operational acts benefitting the U.S. and Israel,” according to Iran’s Fars news agency. The man, identified as Mehdi Khanki, was arrested in Karaj after security forces said they found an arsenal in his home, including handguns, homemade grenades, shoulder-fired explosive tubes and high-destruction bombs.

## Lebanon

- Israeli forces continue incursions and airstrikes in southern Lebanon despite “ceasefire” framework: Israeli forces continued military operations across southern Lebanon on Wednesday despite the U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed on June 26 and the Lebanese Army’s deployment into an area within the “pilot zones” a day earlier.

- Israeli forces pushed into the Dbayeh area on the outskirts of Shaqra, reaching the historic Dbayeh Castle, where they searched homes, raised an Israeli flag over the archaeological site, and conducted raids, Lebanon’s National News Agency reported.

- Another Israeli force entered the village of Srebbine, opening fire.

- An Israeli drone strike also hit Nabatieh Al-Fawqa.

- In Marjayoun district, Israeli soldiers advanced to the outskirts of Burj Al-Muluk, raided and searched a resident’s home, questioned him, confiscated his passport, and later withdrew.

- Lebanese PM hails Israeli withdrawal as beginning, Speaker says it “barely qualifies”: Following the deployment of the Lebanese army into Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh according to the “pilot zones” operations under the agreement with Israel, Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam visited the area, raising the Lebanese flag in the town square, and calling the Israeli pullback “the beginning of the Israeli withdrawal from our land.”

- Salam said in a post on X that the government remains committed to achieving a complete Israeli withdrawal, adding that the return of displaced residents to the south was “the truest expression of Lebanon’s unity and sovereignty.”

- Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, however, said Tuesday that the real test was “results on the ground.” He said the withdrawal from Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh “barely qualifies as a withdrawal,” arguing the village had not been fully occupied. “The criminal demolitions of homes, civilian neighborhoods and infrastructure continue, as do attacks on residents on the outskirts of occupied villages,” he said, adding that “the measure of success” would be securing a lasting ceasefire and full Israeli withdrawals.

- Trump promises to “help” Lebanon in meeting with Aoun, offers no concrete policy: President Donald Trump met Lebanese President Joseph Aoun at the White House on Tuesday, pledging vague support while claiming Israel is “in the process” of withdrawing from southern Lebanon.

- Trump also renewed his suggestion that Syria intervene militarily to help disarm Hezbollah, and said he would be open to speaking directly with Hezbollah if Aoun wanted him to. Aoun avoided mentioning continued Israeli violations and instead praised the U.S.-brokered framework conditioning Israeli withdrawal on Hezbollah’s disarmament.

- Trump announced Tuesday that U.S. carriers can resume direct flights to Lebanon, ending a suspension in place since 1985 when Washington banned Middle East Airlines following a Hezbollah hijacking of two TWA planes at Beirut’s airport.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded: Over the past 24 hours, 12 Palestinians were killed, one due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks, and 12 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,305 killed, with 173,918 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,180 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,810, while 802 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel continues to bombard Gaza: Israeli attacks on Gaza killed at least 12 people on Monday.

- An Israeli strike on Gaza City Tuesday killed four Palestinians and wounded several others. The strike hit the entrance of the Muslim Young Women’s Association in the city.

- Israeli forces killed two in a Tuesday strike on a civilian vehicle at the entrance to Al-Zahra, north of Nuseirat refugee camp.

- Israeli forces also shot and wounded two Palestinians, including a young girl, in Al-Mawasi, Khan Younis.

- Gaza sees rise in miscarriages, Health Ministry warns of cancer drug shortages: Gaza recorded 3,958 miscarriages among pregnant women in the first half of 2026, according to Bassam Zaqout, director of Medical Relief in the Strip.

- Zaqout attributed the unprecedented rise to pregnant women being forced to travel over rough roads in unsafe transport, these same women facing constant terror from Israeli bombardment, being forced to sleep on the ground, and the lack of hot water and hygiene supplies in the Strip.

- Separately on Tuesday, Gaza’s Health Ministry warned that an unprecedented shortage of cancer drugs has forced the suspension of chemotherapy protocols for breast, colorectal, gastrointestinal, head and neck cancers, sarcomas, and other tumors.

- Some life-saving drugs have been completely depleted, the ministry said, amid continued Israeli restrictions on the entry of aid and medical supplies into Gaza.

- Of Gaza’s 11,000 cancer patients, 4,000 have referrals for treatment abroad but remain waiting for Israeli approval to leave.

- Israeli arrests, attacks and seizure of land in West Bank, Jerusalem:

- Israeli forces arrested at least 25 Palestinians across the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, between Tuesday evening and Wednesday morning, according to the Palestinian Prisoner’s Society. Those detained included five women, as well as 15 workers from Gaza who were arrested in Qalqilya after Israeli forces raided the barracks where they were staying and beat them.

- The Palestinian Ministry of Religious Endowments said on Tuesday that Israeli settlers had carried out 45 attacks on mosques across the occupied West Bank since the start of 2026. Israeli settlers set five of these mosques on fire, and partially demolished or damaged five others.

- Israeli authorities also issued a military order on Tuesday seizing 5,283 dunams (about 1,317 acres) of land belonging to the town of Jaba’, north of occupied Jerusalem, under the pretext of “military purposes,” according to the Palestinian news agency WAFA. The Jerusalem Governorate said the land would be used to build a settler road.

- Israeli government officials march to ethnically cleanse Gaza of Palestinians: Nearly half of Israel’s government joined a settler march on Tuesday to the Gaza fence calling for new Jewish settlements in the Strip, +972 Magazine reported. Police and soldiers reportedly allowed thousands of Israelis to approach the fence, handed out water, and even transported some back in military vehicles.

- “There will be no more Arabs in Gaza, period,” settler leader Daniella Weiss told the crowd.

- Freed Palestinian prisoner dies after release from Israeli prison: Ahmed Samir Odeh, a 23-year-old native of Huwara recently released from Israeli detention, died on Tuesday according to reports from Palestinian prisoner advocacy groups, which held Israel fully responsible for his death.

- Odeh was most recently arrested in February 2026. He was repeatedly beaten in prison, and had spent more than a year and a half in administrative detention without charge or trial prior to his arrest.

- Israel confirms it is walling off the half of Gaza it controls: The Israeli military built more than 23 kilometers (14 miles) of earthen barriers cutting through Gaza, physically dividing the roughly 50% of the territory it occupies from the crowded coastal strip where Palestinians have been forced to live, according to Planet Labs satellite imagery reported by The Associated Press.

- The findings confirm and extend reporting Drop Site News first published in January, when analysis by Forensic Architecture revealed Israel had begun turning the so-called “yellow line” into a physical barrier of raised berms. Drop Site reported in May that the berms had grown into a mostly unbroken wall, often running west of the line and deeper into Palestinian land.

- Presented with the images, Israel’s military confirmed to the AP for the first time that it has built the barrier, and said it established a “security zone” around the line. One southern section splitting the ruins of Rafah from the Mawasi tent camps grew from 500 meters to 2.4 kilometers in the first two weeks of July alone.

- Netherlands to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements starting September 22: The Dutch government gave final approval Tuesday to a decree banning the import, purchase, and sale of goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories, joining Belgium, Spain, and Ireland in restricting trade with settlements, Al Jazeera reported.

- Research from the Global Echo group found the Netherlands accounts for a third of agricultural exports from the settlements and nearly half of those bound for the EU, with the new measure also barring Dutch brokering of such trade and covering products from the occupied Golan Heights.

## U.S. News

- Arizona primary results:

- Rep. Greg Stanton defeated progressive organizer Kai Newkirk in Tuesday’s Democratic primary for Arizona’s 4th Congressional District. Newkirk had criticized Stanton over his support from AIPAC and his vote for a Trump-backed law that increases DHS detention powers. Stanton will face Republican Zuhdi Jasser in November.

- Rep. Andy Biggs won the Republican gubernatorial primary, setting him up to face Democratic Gov. Katie Hobbs, who ran unopposed. Biggs, a former House Freedom Caucus chair endorsed by President Donald Trump, beat out Rep. David Schweikert and two businessmen. Cook Political Report updated the race to “lean Democrat” this month, after it was previously rated a “toss up.”

- House passes funding bill: The House passed a government funding bill Tuesday night, 220-205, that would extend federal operations through Dec. 4, ahead of the Sept. 30 shutdown deadline. The bill was shepherded by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who managed to ensure its passage with a very narrow Republican majority.

- Democrats played no part in drafting the bill, which does not alter or omit ICE or DHS funding, one of their key demands in the months-long funding fight.

- The measure now heads to the Senate, where Majority Leader John Thune has proposed several short-term plans to fund the government in anticipation of the August recess. The chamber’s appropriators are tasked with navigating the “anomalies” that could pause funding to vital government agencies.

- USTR signals new tariff wave: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC’S “Squawk Box” on Tuesday that “we expect to see some action soon” on new tariffs, as the Trump administration works to rebuild its protectionist trade agenda using Section 301 authority after the Supreme Court struck down its broader IEEPA-based tariff regime in February.

- Greer said the Section 301 tariffs his office proposed in June, which could total as much as 12.5%, would cover “about 99% of our trade” across 60 economies including China, the EU and India.

- Trump’s temporary Section 122 tariffs lapse on Friday.

- Studies find PEPFAR cuts sharply reduced HIV prevention, treatment: New survey results set to be presented at an international AIDS conference in Rio de Janeiro found that Trump administration cuts to the President’s Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR) led three-quarters of surveyed organizations to stop serving those at highest HIV risk, The New York Times reported, with the additional result that at least 1,700 service sites were closed and more than 16,000 aid workers had been laid off.

- A separate study found the program supported treatment for about 77,000 fewer children in 2025, a 14% decline.

- Nearly half of all children with AIDS do not have access to treatment, according to UNAIDS.

- Trump administration freezes over $1B in Medicaid funds to California, Minnesota: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) said Tuesday it is deferring about $867.5 million in Medicaid payments to California and $199 million to Minnesota, Axios reported.

- CMS claims that its financial reviews revealed “unsupported claims” for in-home care and other services in the states. Minnesota state officials called the change “unprecedented and punitive,” noting their full collaboration with CMS’ inquiry.

- CMS announced in May that it would defer $1.3 billion in Medicaid funds to California, in what CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz claimed was the agency’s biggest ever deferral.

- Van passengers dispute ICE account of fatal Houston shooting Court statements filed Monday by passengers in the van of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, the Mexican man fatally shot July 7 by an ICE agent in Houston, contradict the agency’s claim that Salgado Araujo tried to run over an officer, saying instead that ICE vehicles rammed the van from behind and the side and that agents fired after it had come to a full stop, the Texas Tribune reported.

- “At no moment were the agents in front of the vehicle,” one passenger said.

- A federal judge in Houston has ordered DHS to not deport one passenger, whose account contradicts that of the agency, to a detention facility outside the region without the court’s permission.

- Mamdani backs down on threat to arrest Netanyahu: New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani released a video statement on Tuesday saying that, even though he believes that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu “is a war criminal,” he had concluded that New York City does not “have the independent legal authority” to enforce the ICC’s outstanding warrant against him.

- In the statement, Mamdani called on the federal government to execute that warrant and said Netanyahu was “not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large.”

- Hegseth estimates cost of Iran war at $37.5 billion during tense congressional testimony: War Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine testified before the Senate Appropriations committee Tuesday in a hearing over an $87.6 billion emergency funding request for the Iran war.

- Hegseth estimated the war had cost Americans at least $37.5 billion since it began on February 28.

- When asked by Sen. Patty Murray (D-Wash.) to defend a funding request to defeat an enemy that Trump has repeatedly said the U.S. has defeated, Hegseth said there was “no doubt” that Iran possessed “capabilities,” but that they were at the “worst place they’ve ever been.”

- Appeals court overturns release order for Palestinian activist Mahdawi: A three-judge panel of the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Tuesday that a lower court should not have ordered Columbia University activist Mohsen Mahdawi’s release from immigration detention, finding the case should have been resolved in immigration court, though the ruling does not order his immediate re-arrest.

- The American Civil Liberties Union, which represents Mahdawi, said there is no legal basis to deport or re-detain him during his appeal.

- Mahdawi, a lawful permanent resident, was arrested at what he believed to be an interview as part of his application for U.S. citizenship

- Blinken endorses Lawrence opponent in Michigan: President Joe Biden’s Secretary of State Antony Blinken, who oversaw unconditional U.S. support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, has endorsed former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine Bridget Brink in the three-way Democratic primary for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District.

- The race notably includes progressive challenger Will Lawrence, who is endorsed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.).

## Other International News

- Yemen’s Ansarallah says it forced 6 ships to reroute: Yemen’s Ansarallah movement says its newly declared naval blockade of Saudi Arabia has already disrupted the country’s shipping industry, forcing six vessels in the Red Sea to reroute on Tuesday, according to the SABA news agency, which is affiliated with the group.

- Three Ansarallah officials separately told The Associated Press that shipping companies were warned Monday to avoid the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the 20-mile-wide gateway to the Red Sea at the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula through which roughly 12% of global trade passes.

- The maritime intelligence firm Kpler reported that it had identified two tankers departing from Saudi Arabia carrying crude oil that had abruptly reversed course in the Red Sea, and Windward said 5 tankers were reversed on Tuesday, 4 from the Bab al-Mandab and one from the Gulf of Aden, including Saudi tankers carrying crude, gasoline, and naphtha.

- Saudi Arabia and U.S. reportedly agree to nuclear deal: The Trump administration plans to formally sign and announce a nuclear cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia on Wednesday that could eventually let the kingdom enrich its own uranium, multiple news outlets reported.

- The administration plans to justify the deal by pointing to its economic benefits to the U.S., The New York Times reported, with Trump officials estimating that billions of dollars might flow into major American

reads.body:
U.S. strikes Iran for tenth straight night. Iranian issues waves of retaliatory attacks. Nearly 100 U.S. service members wounded this month, CBS reports. Iran’s IRGC says it will repel any U.S. incursion into Iran. Multiple attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. Shipowners offering bonuses to crews transiting Hormuz. Iran confirms Turkey helped block Kurdish insurgency plan. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich says Israel has “no interest” in joining Iran war. Israeli attacks continue in Lebanon despite U.S.-backed “ceasefire.” “Pilot zone” operations begin in Lebanon; Lebanese Army reports being fired on by Israel. Israel continues escalated assault on Gaza. Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank. France urges European Union to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas reportedly planning election law change that could block Marwan Barghouti from Palestinian Liberation Organization leadership. Man killed fleeing ICE in Florida was on a valid tourist visa. Department of Homeland Security revives rule tying immigrant benefit use to green card eligibility. Judge temporarily blocks Paramount’s $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal. Department of Justice sought phone records of New York Times journalists, relatives. New Orleans police briefly published policy allowing weaponized drones. State Department releases report accusing Cuba of “infiltrating” American left-wing. Israel shoots two children in southern Syria. U.S. hits Canada with new 50% tariffs. Police clash with ‘Cockroach’ movement protesters in India. Flash floods kill at least 20 in eastern Afghanistan. Floods and landslides kill at least 25 across northern India. Saudi coalition responds to Ansarallah maritime blockade, Saudi-backed government announces resumption of oil exports. Militants kill at least 50 soldiers in Mali. UN: Nearly 400,000 face emergency food insecurity in North Kordofan. President Daniel Ortega says Nicaragua will no longer hold elections. UN official: Haitian children jailed for years without trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro secures U.S. green card. Ed Miliband appointed UK foreign secretary.
This is Drop Site Daily, our free daily news recap. We send it Monday through Friday. Today’s edition is being sent to more than 750,000 subscribers. Help us grow that number by forwarding and recommending this newsletter.

## Iran

- U.S. strikes Iran for tenth straight night: The U.S. continued its bombing campaign in Iran on Monday and Tuesday, hitting several cities in the country’s south and claiming “disruptions” to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as justification.

- U.S. airstrikes on Monday hit Chabahar and Konarak in the southeastern Sistan and Baluchistan province, according to Iranian state media.

- Explosions were heard on Monday evening in the southern cities of Sirik, Bandar Abbas, and Bandar-Lengh as well as on Qeshm Island.

- Two explosions were also heard in the central city of Isfahan.

- Iranian retaliatory attacks: Iran launched attacks on U.S. military bases in the Gulf in response, claiming that it had successfully targeted U.S. missile-defense radar systems, air defense infrastructure and fighter planes, and units used to house U.S, military personnel.

- Iran’s military claimed that a Monday strike on a U.S. base in Jordan destroyed a F-15 fighter jet and a radar system, and that a separate attack struck a complex housing U.S. troops. This attack reportedly killed several American servicemembers, though the IRGC did not provide an estimate.

- Iran claimed three successful attacks on U.S. bases in Kuwait on Monday, including Camp Arifjan, the Al-Adhari military camp, and a barracks at the Ahmed Al-Jaber base. The attack on Camp Arifjan reportedly struck an HIMARS missile systems, according to the Iranian Army. This attack comes one day after U.S. Central Command posted a photo of HIMARS systems deployed in the Middle East.

- Iranian strikes hit and destroyed defense technology at bases near Manama, Bahrain, including a Patriot system, its military reported.

- Iranian missiles also struck what the Iranian military characterized as “the central data infrastructure” used by Amazon in Bahrain, according to a Monday statement.

- On Tuesday, Kuwait’s Energy Ministry said that Iranian strikes had damaged its power and desalination plants, causing fires at several sites.

- Nearly 100 U.S. service members wounded this month, CBS reports: Iranian strikes have wounded nearly 100 U.S. service members on American bases across the Middle East since July 7, U.S. officials told CBS News. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell maintained that most suffered minor concussions and said that about 96% had already returned to duty.

- IRGC says it will repel any U.S. incursion into Iran: The deputy commander of the IRGC’s ground forces said on Monday that his troops would “immediately” repel any U.S. incursion into Iranian territory, describing them as at “the highest level of readiness.”

- Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz: At least two ships were struck in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, with the U.S. blockade of Iran still ongoing and with Iran insisting vessels pass through the Strait through its northern route.

- A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile about eight nautical miles northeast of Oman on Monday evening, forcing the vessel’s crew to abandon ship, according to the UKTMO.

- Another vessel was struck on Tuesday morning by a projectile about 17 miles east of the United Arab Emirates. The projectile, also of uncertain provenance, reportedly damaged the vessel’s steering gear, according to the UKTMO, but resulted in no crew casualties.

- These attacks followed a statement from Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) that “massive fires” have broken out on two oil tankers that attempted to “pass through the unsafe southern route in the Strait of Hormuz.”

- Shipowners offering bonuses to crews transiting Hormuz: Sinokor, the world’s largest supertanker owner, has offered six months’ extra pay for a roughly month-long round trip which would involve a transit through the Strait of Hormuz, Bloomberg reported on Monday.

- For the lowest paid crew members, this could total as much as $9,000, and for captains, it could equal $90,000.

- Shipowners often earn millions of dollars per Hormuz voyage, according to Bloomberg.

- Iran confirms Turkey helped block Kurdish insurgency plan: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi confirmed in a Sunday interview that Turkey played an “effective” role in preventing an alleged U.S.- and Israeli-backed Kurdish insurgency from being launched against Iran from Iraqi Kurdistan earlier in the war.

- Araghchi’s remarks corroborate earlier claims by President Donald Trump that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan persuaded him to abandon the plan.

- Smotrich says Israel has “no interest” in joining Iran war: Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said on Tuesday that Israel has “no interest in joining the campaign” against Iran, speaking at a conference. “The current situation is good for us, and we have no interest in pushing ourselves into it,” he said, adding that Israel is “prepared for any scenario.”

## Lebanon

- Israeli attacks continue in Lebanon despite U.S.-backed “ceasefire”:

- Israeli forces shelled the Ali Al-Taher hills near Nabatieh Al-Fawqa on Tuesday, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.

- The Israeli army carried out two rounds of demolitions in Majdal Zoun, while citizens reported large explosions near the towns of Beit Yahoun and Kounine in Bint Jbeil district, and  the town of Kfar Tebnit in Nabatieh.

- Israeli forces also carried out a “massive demolition operation” in the town of Mays Al-Jabal, the NNA reported.

- On Monday, Israel struck the outskirts of Al-Mansouri, shelled Nabatieh Al-Fawqa and Kfartebnit, and demolished homes and infrastructure in Beit Yahoun, Deir Seryan, Tyri, Kfartebnit, Taybeh, and Zawtars, according to Press TV correspondent Hadi Hodeit.

- Israeli forces also opened fire toward Haddatha, Majdal Zoun, Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh, and Buyout Al-Sayyad on Monday, Hoteit reported.

- “Pilot zone” operations begin in Lebanon: The U.S. State Department said that operations in the southern Lebanese villages of Froun, Srifa, and Zawtar al-Gharbiya were scheduled to begin on Monday, under the U.S.-brokered trilateral framework between Lebanon and Israel.

- The Lebanese Army announced on Tuesday a deployment to the town of Zawtar Al-Gharbiyeh in Nabatieh, after coordinating with the “Military Coordination Group for Lebanon,” established under the framework, advising citizens to avoid returning to the town.

- Israeli forces opened fire near Lebanese troops as they were deploying in the town on Tuesday, according to a statement from the Lebanese Army. The army warned the incident could “hinder the implementation of deployment steps” in the pilot zones.

- The trilateral framework calls for the Lebanese Army to take control in designated “pilot zones,” and for the disarmament and dismantling of Hezbollah and other armed groups’ infrastructure. It also urges Israel to withdraw from southern Lebanon, but holds Israel, which has indicated it has no intention to leave the “security zone,” to no concrete commitments.

## Palestine

- Killed and wounded: Over the past 24 hours, 10 Palestinians were killed, one due to wounds sustained in earlier attacks, and 42 were injured in Israeli attacks across Gaza, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.

- The total recorded death toll since October 7, 2023 has risen to 73,293 killed, with 173,906 injured. Since October 11, the first full day of the so-called ceasefire, Israel has killed at least 1,168 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded 3,798, while 802 bodies have been recovered from under the rubble.

- Israel continues escalated assault on Gaza: Israeli attacks on Gaza on Monday killed at least eight Palestinians and wounded more than 20 others.

- An Israeli drone struck a civilian vehicle near Al-Ghafri Junction in Gaza City, wounding up to 14 people, including children, according to local reports.

- Drop Site correspondent Mohamed Ahmed spoke to eyewitnesses to an attack on a makeshift shelter inside a hospital building, with a man describing its initial stages by noting that “children [were] having fun and playing football, and suddenly they started screaming.” The attack killed four Palestinians and wounded at least 16 others, according to WAFA. Video of that reporting is available here.

- In Khan Younis, a separate Israeli drone strike hit a civilian vehicle near the British Hospital in al-Mawasi, killing three Palestinians and wounding others.

- Israeli forces killed an entire family of six, including three children, in an overnight strike on a home in Gaza City as families slept. The house, which was engulfed in flames, was reportedly struck at least three times, hampering efforts to rescue survivors.

- “From 13 to 20 July alone, our office has recorded that the Israeli military killed at least 57 Palestinians, including six children and eight women,” UN human rights office spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan said Tuesday, addressing Israel’s escalating attacks on Gaza.

- Israeli attacks in the occupied West Bank:

- Israeli settlers set fire to olive trees in the town of Beit Ilyan, northwest of occupied Jerusalem, as part of a series of attacks on Palestinians on Monday.

- Israeli settlers also continued to raid the village of Al-Mughir, northeast of Ramallah, storming homes in the area.

- Three Palestinians were injured after settlers attacked a home in the town of Raba, east of Jenin, assaulting a man and two of his sons.

- France urges EU to ban imports from illegal Israeli settlements: France is calling on the European Union to halt all imports of products from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said Monday.

- A European Commission options paper has floated an import licensing system, higher tariffs, and even an outright ban on products from the West Bank, though the bloc remains split over whether and which measures to enact.

- France, Spain, Sweden, Belgium, and Ireland have been pushing for the EU to restrict settlement trade, while Germany, Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and others oppose EU-wide action. A 2024 International Court of Justice opinion said states must avoid trade that sustains the settlements, which are illegal under international law.

- Abbas reportedly planning election law change that could block Barghouti from PLO leadership: Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas is preparing to amend election law to restore the Palestinian Legislative Council to 132 seats while allocating 68 additional Palestinian National Council seats to be filled by “consensus,” widely understood to mean appointment, The New Arab reported, citing two Palestinian officials.

- Constitutional law expert Rashad Tuam said the change would likely be used to keep imprisoned Fatah leader Marwan Barghouti from becoming PLO chairman even if elected Palestinian Authority president, since only National Council members could seek the PLO’s top post.

## U.S. News
By Julian Andreone, with Ryan Grim. Have a tip on Capitol Hill? Email Andreone at Julian@dropsitenews.com.

- Man killed fleeing ICE in Florida was on valid tourist visa: Juan Jairo Coronilla Duran, the 28-year-old Mexican man killed by a semi-truck while fleeing an ICE traffic stop in St. Augustine, Florida, on July 14, was in the U.S. on a valid tourist visa and had been in the country for just three weeks, his wife Yésica Alamilla López told Spectrum News.

- Coronilla Duran was days away from a planned return flight to Mexico when he died, according to farmworker advocate Isaret Jeffers, who has been assisting Duran’s family in the wake of his killing.

- DHS revives rule tying immigrant benefit use to green card eligibility: The Department of Homeland Security published a new “public charge” policy Monday that restores the ability for immigration officers to weigh immigrants’ use of Medicaid, CHIP, and SNAP when deciding green card eligibility, Axios reported, reversing Biden-era limits that largely restricted such determinations to cash welfare benefits.

- A KFF-New York Times survey found that 11% of adult immigrants said they stopped participating in public benefit programs in 2025 due to immigration-related concerns.

- Public health groups, including the president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, warned the rule could deter immigrant families from seeking health coverage even for citizen children.

- Judge temporarily blocks Paramount’s $111 billion Warner Bros. Discovery deal: A federal judge issued a 14-day temporary restraining order Monday halting Paramount’s $111 billion purchase of Warner Bros. Discovery while she weighs a lawsuit brought by 12 states arguing the merger violates antitrust law, The New York Times reported.

- Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California said the states made “a strong showing” the deal would substantially lessen competition and set an early August hearing on a possible injunction.

- DOJ sought phone records of NYT journalists, relatives in leak probe: The Trump administration issued subpoenas to third-party providers seeking phone and text records of several New York Times journalists and their relatives, including one reporter’s mother, as part of an effort to unmask sources for reporting on security concerns with Trump’s new Air Force One jet, according to a motion unsealed Monday by Judge Arun Subramanian of the U.S. District Court in Manhattan.

- The Times, seeking to quash the subpoenas, argued the Justice Department violated its own guidelines for media subpoenas and sought records dating back to January, well before the disputed articles, calling it a “bad-faith effort to intimidate the journalists.” A hearing is scheduled for Thursday.

- Judge dismisses DOJ challenge to Minnesota immigration laws A federal judge nominated by President Trump sided with Minnesota on Monday, dismissing the Justice Department’s lawsuit challenging state and local laws that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities, according to the New York Times.

- The Trump administration filed the lawsuit before federal agents flooded Minnesota last year. During the crackdown, Trump and his allies repeatedly accused Minnesota of subverting federal authority by insufficiently cooperating with immigration agents.

- New Orleans police briefly published policy allowing weaponized drones: A draft version of the New Orleans Police Department’s drone operations manual, live on its website in June, would have allowed the department to arm quadcopter drones with the police superintendent’s written approval, before being replaced July 1 with language again banning weaponized drones, 404 Media reported.

- NOPD said the weaponization language was an early draft that was never adopted, though the department did not explain how or why it was published.

- Trump-linked ‘Freedom Fuel’ gas chain tied to operators with history of fraud: The “Freedom Fuel Network,” a chain of discounted gas stations launched in Philadelphia and promoted by the White House as delivering a 50-cent-per-gallon discount in Trump’s honor, is run by brothers Syed and Shamikh Kazmi, who have a history of unpaid debts, default judgments and failed business deals, Maureen Tkacik of the The American Prospect reports.

- The company’s incorporation documents name energy trader Yonatan Gontownik, whose family has deep ties to pro-Israel lobbying group NORPAC. Gontownik’s trading firm, Mercuria, has seen its profits skyrocket in the wake of the U.S.-Iran War.

- Read Tkacik’s full piece for TAP here.

- Trump says Netanyahu will not be arrested: In response to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s comments that an arrest of Israeli Prime Minister in New York remains “in active consideration,” President Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday that Netanyahu, would “not be arrested, in any way, shape, or form” while in the United States.

- The ICC issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu on November 21, 2024; he is accused of war crimes, including using starvation as a method of warfare and intentionally directing attacks against civilians.

- State Department releases report accusing Cuba of “infiltrating” American left-wing: The State Department released a 100-page report on Monday purporting to show connections between the government of the island nation and various figures on the American left, including the national Democratic Socialists of America, Reps. Ilhan Omar and Ayanna Pressley (as well as Omar’s daughter), Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, the Black Lives Matter Movement, CODEPINK founder Medea Benjamin, and streamer Hasan Piker.

- The report alleges that Cuba has “infiltrated the highest reaches of the U.S. government” and “cultivated generations of American activists,” citing a visit to March 2026 junket to Cuba, then as now under a crippling fuel blockade, as its primary evidence.

- Benjamin told Drop Site that CODEPINK is now under Treasury Department investigation for bringing medical supplies to Cuban children’s hospitals. “The people delivering medicine are under investigation, not the officials enforcing policies that deprive Cubans of medicine, food, fuel, and electricity,” she said.

- “Why is the State Department naming American citizens in their Cuba report where they seemingly complain about our opinions on US sanctions policy?” Piker wrote. “This is absolutely protected by the 1st Amendment. They are trying to chill speech through intimidation.”

- On Tuesday, Rep. Pramila Jayapal gave an outline of the effects of Washington’s decades-long blockade, calling the policy one of “collective punishment” and noting how it chokes off access to food, medicine, fuel, and other basic necessities.

## Other International News

- Israel shoots two children in southern Syria: Israeli forces shot and injured two Syrian children on Monday during a raid into the southern village of Jamla, Syria’s state news agency SANA reported. Syrian authorities gave no further detail on the children’s condition.

- Jamla is part of the Yarmouk basin, a border region into which Israeli troops have expanded their presence since the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government in 2024. Syria says that these operations violate the 1974 disengagement agreement, which Israel unilaterally declared void upon the fall of Assad’s government.

- U.S. hits Canada with new 50% tariffs: President Trump announced on Monday that the U.S. would impose 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, alleging that these tariffs are a response “discriminatory treatment” of American cars, alcohol, and dairy exports by Canada.

- Trump invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 to justify his newest series of tariffs, a largely untested provision which some Democratic lawmakers attempted to appeal last year, anticipating Trump’s future use of it and its potential economic effects.

- The tariffs take effect August 19 and cover goods ranging from wine and hockey sticks to cement, as well as goods that had previously been protected from import taxes by the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement. Energy products, potash, and critical minerals are among the exemptions.

- Police clash with ‘Cockroach’ movement protesters in India: Police fired tear gas and used batons on more than 10,000 protesters from India’s youth-led “Cockroach” movement as they marched on the New Delhi parliament on Monday, the group’s largest demonstration yet.

- The “Cockroach” movement, which is focused on corruption in the country’s education system, is demanding the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, after his role in exam leaks that forced more than 2 million prospective medical students to retake their exam.

- Activist Sonam Wangchuk, who has been on hunger strike for three weeks in solidarity with the movement, was forcibly hospitalized on Saturday, adding to the anger of the protesters.

- Flash floods kill at least 20 in eastern Afghanistan: Flash floods in eastern Afghanistan’s Nuristan province on Monday killed at least 20 people and left 80 more wounded, Afghan officials said, with more than 100 people still missing.

- The worst-hit area was Parun, the province’s capital, where floodwaters destroyed a municipal center, hotels, and dozens of shops, according to AFP. The missing include the Parun’s mayor and several government employees. The death toll is expected to rise.

- Floods and landslides kill at least 25 across northern India: At least 25 people were killed over the weekend in floods and landslides across Indian-administered Kashmir and in the state of Nagaland following days of torrential monsoon rain, local officials said Monday.

- Kashmir’s Poonch, Rajouri, and Doda districts saw at least 15 deaths and reported several people missing, while nine died in landslides in the northeastern Nagaland. One person also died in Assam.

- The flooding prompted authorities to suspend the Amarnath and Vaishno Devi pilgrimages, the first of which drew over 400,000 people last year. India’s weather office warned active monsoon conditions are expected to persist for weeks.

- Saudi coalition responds to Ansarallah maritime blockade, Saudi-backed government announces resumption of oil exports: The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen, a military alliance assembled by Riyadh in 2015 to fight Ansarallah, said on Monday it was taking steps to shield vessels in the Red Sea and would respond “decisively and forcefully” after Ansarallah’s recent declaration of a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia.

- A spokesperson for the coalition also dismissed claims that Yemeni ports and airports had been closed as “misinformation,” and denied accusations from Ansarallah that Saudi Arabia was “besieging” the Yemeni people.

- Rashid al-Alimi, the head of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, also announced the resumption of oil exports from the country, suspended since late 2022, in a televised address on Monday.

- Al-Alimi said the government would seek to resume exports “by all available means” starting July 20, but did not detail how. Yemen’s exports of oil, which were minor but steady prior to a rapid decrease during the war, were halted after Ansarallah struck oil terminals in southern Yemen.

- On Tuesday, Yemeni Defense Minister Taher al-Uqaili announced that his armed forces were prepared with “the highest level of combat and morale to end the Houthi coup,” calling the conflict a “war for freedom.”

- Militants kill at least 50 soldiers in Mali: Al-Qaeda-linked and Tuareg separatist fighters ambushed a Malian army convoy on Saturday in the northern Gao region, killing at least 50 soldiers and capturing more than 20 others, according to the AFP.

- The al-Qaeda affiliate JNIM and the Tuareg separatist Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) claimed responsibility for the assault, which they characterized as a joint operation, saying they inflicted “great human losses” and destroyed army vehicles. The army said its partners, likely a reference to Russia’s Africa Corps mercenaries, were also hit.

- UN: Nearly 400,000 face emergency food insecurity in North Kordofan: The United Nations warned on Monday that nearly 400,000 displaced people across North Kordofan’s Sheikan, Bara and Gharb Bara districts face emergency levels of acute food insecurity, citing estimates from the World Food Programme.

- UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric noted the body’s particular concern about conditions in El Obeid, where thousands have been displaced as a result of fighting in the region, and where humanitarian conditions have sharply deteriorated.

- Ortega says Nicaragua will no longer hold elections: Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega told supporters on Sunday that Nicaragua will stop holding elections, framing the move as necessary to block a U.S.-backed opposition from seizing power, Reuters reported.

- Ortega, who has held power since 2007, made the announcement at an event commemorating the 1979 Sandinista revolution.

- Ortega’s government has been accused by the UN Human Rights Council of “arbitrary detentions, torture, extrajudicial executions [and the] persecution of civil society and the media”.

- Nicaragua’s last elections were held in 2021, with Ortega being elected co-president alongside his wife, Rosario Murillo.

- UN official: Haitian children jailed for years without trial: UN Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict Vanessa Frazier told the Security Council on Monday that some children in Haiti have been jailed up to eight years without appearing before a judge.

- Frazier said these child detainees are often held in overcrowded cells designed for minors, but mostly housing adults.

- She called the situation “amongst the most alarming anywhere in the world,” and pleaded that these children, who are often arrested for their gang ties, be treated primarily as victims and be released.

- Eduardo Bolsonaro secures U.S. green card: Eduardo Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of Trump, told Reuters on Monday he had received permanent U.S. residency.

- Eduardo, who has lived in the U.S. since early 2025, was sentenced in June to four years and two months in prison in Brazil for soliciting U.S. interference in his father’s trial.

- He claimed that he was approved under the EB-1A category, which permits “individuals with extraordinary ​abilities” to move to the U.S.

reads.title: In Southern Lebanon, a Gloss of Diplomacy Can't Hide the Reality of Occupation
reads.subtitle: Occupied by Israeli forces and depopulated, Majdal Zoun overlooks the nearby village of Al-Mansouri, where the few remaining residents come under Israeli attack on a near daily basis.
reads.body:
Drop Site is a reader-funded, independent news outlet. Without your support, we can’t operate. Please consider becoming a paid subscriber or making a 501(c)(3) tax-deductible donation today.
Subscribe now

-
- Much of Al-Mansouri lies in ruins, with the Israeli-occupied village of Majdal Zoun just across the valley. Despite the destruction and continued Israeli attacks, around 100 residents have chosen to remain. Al Mansouri, Lebanon. July 16, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.AL-MANSOURI, Lebanon—The road into Al-Mansouri winds through a shattered landscape. A barber shop stands without walls, its broken mirror still clinging to the remaining structure. The village cemetery is scarred by craters. The mosque is still standing, though parts of its façade were ripped away by Israeli airstrikes.
Nevertheless, over the past month, signs of life have returned to Al-Mansouri, a village in the Sour (Tyre) district near the coastline in southern Lebanon. On Thursday, a handful of men sat on plastic chairs outside their homes, sipping small cups of coffee. Others swept dust from damaged shops. Men on scooters wove between the ruins.
The same cannot be said for the neighboring village of Majdal Zoun which lies perched on a hill overlooking Al-Mansouri just a few hundred meters away. The two villages are closely intertwined and even share areas of territory that overlap. Last month, Israeli ground troops invaded and occupied Majdal Zoun, where they have been systematically destroying homes and civilian infrastructure. The remaining residents of Al-Mansouri now live in full view of the occupying Israeli forces and under constant threat. Al-Mansouri is attacked on a near daily basis from its sister village with Israeli airstrikes and stun grenades dropped from drones.
Last month, Israeli aircraft dropped leaflets over Al-Mansouri, declaring the area a “threatened zone,” telling residents to “stay away” and warning that anyone who approached Israeli forces would “put themselves in danger.” Despite the threats, around 100 people have chosen to remain in the village, according to Yousef Shehemy, the mayor of neighboring Majdal Zoun, who has been displaced from his home by the occupying Israeli forces.
“People here believe their souls belong to this land,” Shehemy told Drop Site as he drove past a row of destroyed houses in Al-Mansouri. Shehemy was in the village when the leaflets fell from the sky. “They want to control people’s lives from above with leaflets, drones, sound grenades—all of it to frighten civilians.”

-
- On June 29, Israel detonated what it described as a 200-metre Hezbollah tunnel beneath Majdal Zoun, leaving behind a massive crater. The blast site is visible on the left side of the hill. Majdal Zoun, Lebanon. July 16, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.Like dozens of villages and towns in southern Lebanon, Al-Mansouri and Majdal Zoun are either occupied by Israeli forces and being systematically destroyed, or being attacked from the air on a routine basis despite a U.S.-brokered framework agreement signed in Washington by the governments of Lebanon and Israel on June 26. The reality on the ground in Lebanon stands in stark contrast to what is being billed as an ongoing diplomatic effort to bring about a lasting peace deal.
On Tuesday, Lebanese president Joseph Aoun met with U.S. President Donald Trump, wrapping up a four-day visit to Washington. It marked the first meeting between leaders of the two countries for almost 20 years. “I would like to thank President Trump, really, and his team for the historic visit and for the historic achievement that we did together by signing the framework with the ultimate objective of ending the state of hostility between Lebanon and Israel forever,” Aoun said in the White House.
The signed framework agreement requires the Lebanese Armed Forces to disarm Hezbollah before Israel withdraws from parts of Lebanese territory it occupies. Hezbollah has rejected the deal, which has been criticized for extracting few guarantees from Israel and placing nearly all obligations on the Lebanese government. Meanwhile, Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have repeatedly vowed to keep occupying forces long term in a “security zone” in southern Lebanon.
In Al-Mansouri, the threat of Israeli troops invading the village is ever present. On Friday, videos circulating on social media appeared to show an Israeli military vehicle advancing toward the Lebanese Army checkpoint at the entrance to the village before withdrawing.
“Israel is unpredictable,” Shehemy said. “You never know what comes next.”
Shehemy has served as mayor of Majdal Zoun for the past year. He fled the hilltop village with most of its residents when the war between Israel and Hezbollah escalated again on March 2. Before the latest phase of the war, around 1,500 people lived in Majdal Zoun. Today, the village stands empty and largely in ruins. According to Shehemy, 90 percent of Majdal Zoun has been destroyed by the Israeli military.
Across Lebanon, over 1.2 million people were forced from their homes by the Israeli assault, with more than 700,000 people in Lebanon still displaced despite a so-called “ceasefire,” according to the United Nations.
“Everything has been put on standby. The war has prevented us from dreaming,” Shehemy said.
For many families from Majdal Zoun, displacement has brought another painful uncertainty: the fate of missing relatives. Residents call Shehemy daily, inquiring about loved ones who disappeared after the village came under Israeli control in June. Some were civilians. Others fought alongside Hezbollah.
“They need to know the fate of their children,” Shehemy said. “If it turns out they are dead, they would accept it. But without answers, these families will never find peace.” Those answers remained out of reach. With Israeli forces still controlling Majdal Zoun, many residents see little chance of returning home anytime soon.
On Monday, the State Department announced that operations in three Lebanese villages deemed part of the so-called “pilot zones” had begun. The zones are nominally designed to allow the Lebanese army to replace Israeli troops in occupied areas.
Two of the villages, Froun and Srifa, were not under Israeli military control in the first place. On Tuesday, the Lebanese army began deploying to the third village, Zawtar al-Gharbieh, after Israel withdrew. However, Israeli forces opened fire near Lebanese troops as they were deploying, according to a statement from the Lebanese Army which warned the incident would “hinder the implementation of deployment steps” in the pilot zones.
To many residents of southern Lebanon, the agreement is little more than words on paper.
“As long as they are still occupying our land, I don’t see any benefit in the framework agreement,” Shehemy said from a coffee shop in Sour (Tyre) as an Israeli surveillance drone buzzed overhead. “They should make Israel withdraw from the occupied areas, not from zones that aren’t even occupied.”
He argued that the U.S. brokered negotiations have largely ignored the concerns of civilians who remain displaced. “For now, the negotiations are only one-sided, with Lebanon being used as a puppet by Israel.”
Amnesty International has also criticized the framework agreement for appearing to “acquiesce to the prolonged and indefinite forced displacement of tens of thousands of residents of vast swathes of southern Lebanon occupied by Israeli forces.” The deal violates international law, Amnesty said, as it “effectively consents to the prolonged and indefinite displacement of tens of thousands of residents of southern Lebanon by making their return, as well as reconstruction, contingent on conditions subject to ‘confirmation.’”
Many residents in the south remain caught between distrust in the state and continued support for Hezbollah as a source of protection. Ali Ghandour, from Nabatieh in south Lebanon, spent months displaced in Saida after fleeing his home early in the war. At one point, he lived out of his car before eventually returning to his hometown. “What would you do if someone occupied your country and your president did nothing? You would fight back,” he told Drop Site.
Ghandour said he feels abandoned by the Lebanese state, accusing the government of prioritizing U.S. and Israeli interests over its own citizens. “Only God protects us. And Hezbollah. As long as we have Hezbollah, we will be fine. When it comes to our country, we will never give up,” he said.

-
- Rescue workers from the Nabatieh Ambulance Association overlook the Nabatieh district as Israel continues to carry out air and drone strikes and demolitions despite the framework agreement. Nabatieh, Lebanon. July 16, 2026. Photo by Katrine Dige Houmøller.Standing at Al Najda Al Shaabiya Hospital located on a hilltop overlooking Nabatieh, Israeli airstrikes echoed across  the area on Thursday. Explosions shook surrounding villages, and smoke rose above the area of Zawtar on the horizon.
Over the past several weeks, the Israeli military has routinely violated the “ceasefire,” conducting regular airstrikes, shelling, house demolitions, and other military operations. Residents and paramedics in Nabatieh said these actions are an almost daily reality in their district.
At the hospital, Fadel Sheet, a freelance journalist reporting for the Nabatieh Ambulance Association, pointed toward a rising cloud of smoke from an Israeli airstrike on Nabatieh Al Fawqa. “We are used to it. What can we do?” Sheet said. Just weeks earlier, another strike in the same village killed four people. The victims included a school principal, her mother, and two domestic workers who had gone to inspect their house. The Israeli military acknowledged the attack, describing the four as approaching a “security zone” and claiming the strike was carried out to “eliminate the threat” of the four civilians to its forces.
Since March 2, more than 4,300 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to Lebanon’s health ministry, including over 250 children. Over 12,200 have been injured.
Mahmoud Maoussa, a paramedic at the hospital, took a drag from his cigarette and pointed toward the smoke rising in the distance. “They are supposed to withdraw, but does it look like they are?”
